events.title: Yuanmou Man
events.short: Fossils of Homo erectus found at Yuanmou in Yunnan date to about 1.7 million years ago and are the earliest confirmed human remains in China.
events.detail: Yuanmou Man, also called Yuanmou Homo erectus, is known from two upper central incisors of a single adult, found in 1965 by geologists near Shangnabang village in Yuanmou County, Yunnan. The teeth are robust and shovel-shaped on the tongue side, typical features of Homo erectus. Later, a few crude stone tools, charcoal fragments and animal bones bearing traces of human work were found in the same stratum. Some scholars take this to mean Yuanmou Man may have used fire, though the point remains disputed. Paleomagnetic dating places Yuanmou Man at about 1.7 million years ago, although some scholars argue the date may be as recent as 600,000–700,000 years ago, and discussion continues. Standard Chinese history textbooks use the figure of c. 1.7 million years and list Yuanmou Man as the earliest confirmed human ancestor in China. Yuanmou Man lived in the Early Paleolithic, when the Yuanmou Basin was warm, with forest and grassland and animals such as stegodons and Yunnan horses. He could chip simple stone tools and lived by gathering and hunting. China has one of the largest numbers of early human sites in the world, and Yuanmou, together with Peking Man and Upper Cave Man, provides important evidence for the origin and evolution of humans in East Asia. A Yuanmou Man museum in Yuanmou County displays the fossils and artifacts. The discovery pushed the history of human activity in China back more than a million years.

events.title: Peking Man
events.short: Peking Man of Dragon Bone Hill at Zhoukoudian lived c. 700,000–200,000 years ago, walked upright, made chipped stone tools, and learned to use and keep fire.
events.detail: Peking Man, or Peking Homo erectus, is known from a site on Dragon Bone Hill at Zhoukoudian in Fangshan District, southwest of Beijing. Chinese and foreign scholars excavated here from 1921, and the name “Peking Man” was given on the basis of excavated teeth. In December 1929 the young scholar Pei Wenzhong found the first complete Peking Man skullcap, and traces of fire were confirmed the same year, causing a worldwide sensation. Five more fairly complete skullcaps were later unearthed, along with fossils of more than 40 individuals, nearly 100,000 stone artifacts and many animal fossils. Unfortunately, around the outbreak of the Pacific War in 1941, these precious skull fossils went missing in transit and have never been recovered. Peking Man is dated to about 700,000–200,000 years ago. He had a low, flat forehead, heavy brow ridges and a protruding mouth, and an average brain size of about 1,088 ml, smaller than that of modern humans, but he already walked upright. Peking Man made pointed tools, scrapers and other chipped tools from stone and animal bone, lived by gathering and hunting, and lived in groups. Thick ash layers, burnt stones and burnt bones at the site show that they not only used fire but kept it burning for long periods, using it to cook, keep warm, give light and drive off animals. Mastering fire was a milestone in human evolution. The Peking Man site at Zhoukoudian is rich in remains and was added to the World Heritage List in 1987. It provided strong evidence for the Homo erectus stage and is important for the study of human origins, earning Zhoukoudian the title “treasure house of ancient human culture.”

events.title: Upper Cave Man
events.short: Upper Cave Man, c. 30,000 years ago, looked much like modern humans, polished and drilled objects, sewed clothes with bone needles, made fire, and wore ornaments.
events.detail: Upper Cave Man was a late Homo sapiens who lived about 30,000 years ago. The fossils were found in a cave near the top of Dragon Bone Hill at Zhoukoudian, Beijing, hence the name. The site was discovered in 1930 and excavated in 1933–1934 under Pei Wenzhong, yielding three complete skulls and skeletal fossils representing at least eight individuals. Their brain size and skull form are close to those of modern humans. Sadly, these fossils disappeared in 1941 together with the Peking Man fossils, and today research relies on carefully made casts. Upper Cave people still used chipped stone tools but had mastered polishing and drilling. A bone needle about 8 cm long with a tiny eye, found at the site, is the earliest sewing tool found in China and shows they sewed clothes from animal skins. They could make fire and lived by gathering, hunting and fishing. The site also yielded ornaments such as perforated animal teeth, stone beads and clam shells, some dyed red with hematite, which reflects a sense of beauty; the shells came from a distant seashore, suggesting exchange with faraway groups. They also buried their dead, sprinkling hematite powder around the remains. They lived collectively, working and sharing together, with no distinction of rich and poor. Upper Cave Man was dated by the carbon-14 method, which is suitable only for organic remains younger than about 50,000 years. The discovery shows that early humans in China had reached a stage close to modern humans.

events.title: The Neolithic Age Begins
events.short: About 10,000 years ago China entered the Neolithic: people settled down, made pottery and polished stone tools, and farming and animal husbandry gradually arose.
events.detail: In archaeology, the age marked mainly by polished stone tools is called the Neolithic. About 10,000 years ago, as the last Ice Age ended and the climate warmed, China entered the Neolithic. At first people only lightly ground the edges of stone tools; by more than 10,000 years ago, fully polished axes, adzes and spades appeared, and until metal tools became common, polished stone remained the main production tool. Early people discovered that clay becomes hard when fired and so invented pottery, which could be used to cook food and store grain and drinking water, helping people settle and farm. Pottery sherds from Xianrendong in Wannian, Jiangxi, and Yuchanyan in Daoxian, Hunan, are more than 10,000 years old; the Xianrendong pot is among the earliest pottery found anywhere in the world. In the Neolithic, primitive farming, herding and handicrafts gradually emerged. People built houses, formed villages and lived a relatively stable settled life, and primitive religion and art appeared. Neolithic sites are spread across the Yellow River, Yangtze River and Liao River basins, including the Peiligang, Yangshao, Hemudu, Hongshan, Liangzhu and Longshan cultures. Each distinctive yet influencing the others, they form a “starry sky” pattern that laid the foundation for the origins of Chinese civilization. The Neolithic marked humanity's gradual shift from a gathering-and-hunting economy dependent on nature to a producing economy, a profound change that some scholars call the “Neolithic Revolution.”

events.title: Domestication of Rice and Millets
events.short: Around 10,000 years ago, people along the middle and lower Yangtze began growing rice, and northern farmers grew foxtail and broomcorn millet; the world's earliest such crops are from China.
events.detail: China has a long agricultural history. About 20,000 years ago, people began to consciously manage certain wild plants; around 10,000 years ago the earliest cultivated crops appeared. In the middle and lower Yangtze, people began to grow rice, and sites such as Xianrendong–Diaotonghuan in Wannian, Jiangxi, Yuchanyan in Daoxian, Hunan, and Shangshan in Pujiang, Zhejiang, have yielded early rice remains dated to about 12,000–10,000 years ago. In the north, people began growing drought-tolerant foxtail millet and broomcorn millet; sites such as Donghulin in Mentougou, Beijing, and Xinglongwa in Chifeng, Inner Mongolia, have produced cultivated millet remains dated to about 10,000–8,000 years ago. The world's earliest cultivated rice, foxtail millet and broomcorn millet have all been found in China, an important contribution by early Chinese to human civilization. Over the following two thousand years or more, a pattern of “rice in the south, millet in the north” gradually took shape. Farming methods developed from slash-and-burn to tillage with soil-turning tools such as the lei and si, and agriculture came to occupy a growing share of daily life. People also began raising pigs, dogs and chickens. The growth of crop planting, livestock raising, settled villages and polished stone tools marks the rise of primitive agriculture, which laid the material basis for population growth, the division of labor and the formation of ancient civilization. Rice farming later spread to East and Southeast Asia and profoundly influenced world agriculture; rice and millet remain important staple crops in China today.

events.title: Jiahu Site
events.short: The Jiahu site in Wuyang, Henan, over 8,000 years old, yielded charred rice grains, bone flutes and incised symbols; the flutes are among the world's earliest.
events.detail: The Jiahu site lies in Jiahu village, Beiwudu Town, Wuyang County, Henan, in the upper Huai River basin. Dated to about 9,000–7,500 years ago, it is an important settlement of the Peiligang culture of the early Neolithic. Excavated repeatedly since 1983, it has yielded house foundations, storage pits, pottery kilns and several hundred burials. The people of Jiahu could already make fine stone, pottery and bone objects. Charred rice grains and domestic pig bones show that rice farming and animal raising were developing, and the site is important evidence of early rice agriculture in the Huai River basin. Jiahu's most famous finds are bone flutes made from the ulnae of red-crowned cranes. Dozens have been found, mostly with seven holes. Tests show they can produce musical tones including a seven-note scale and can play tunes, making them among the earliest and best-preserved playable instruments known in the world. Some tortoise shells and bone objects placed in graves bear carved symbols, some resembling Shang oracle bone script, which is valuable for studying the origin of Chinese characters. Researchers have also detected residues of a fermented drink made from rice, honey and hawthorn in pottery, considered among the world's earliest traces of alcohol. Jiahu shows the high material and spiritual culture of people in the Huai River basin more than 8,000 years ago. Some of the flutes are kept in the Henan Museum, where they are among its treasures, and Jiahu was named one of the “100 Great Archaeological Discoveries in 20th-Century China.”

events.title: Hemudu Culture
events.short: The Hemudu site in Yuyao, Zhejiang, c. 7,000 years old, shows rice farming, stilt houses and wooden wells, and is a major representative of Yangtze River civilization.
events.detail: The Hemudu culture was a Neolithic culture found on the plain south of Hangzhou Bay and on the Zhoushan Islands, dated to about 7,000–5,000 years ago. It is named after the Hemudu site in Yuyao, Zhejiang, first discovered in 1973. Seven or eight thousand years ago the lower Yangtze was warm and humid, and the Hemudu people grew mainly rice. The site contains large deposits of rice grain, husks, stalks and leaves, up to about 1 meter thick, and the grains are close in form to modern cultivated rice, showing that the middle and lower Yangtze was one of the origins of rice farming in Asia. A typical farm tool was the bone spade made from water buffalo shoulder blades, and domestic animals included pigs, dogs and water buffalo. Hemudu houses were stilt buildings: wooden piles were driven into the ground, a floor laid on top and the house built above, which kept out damp and animals. Mortise-and-tenon joints were widely used and had a deep influence on later Chinese timber architecture. One of the earliest known wooden-lined wells was also found. The Hemudu people made black pottery, jade objects and bone whistles, and carved ivory and bone into art such as the “two birds facing the sun” piece, one of China's earliest ivory carvings; a vermilion-lacquered wooden bowl shows they knew how to use natural lacquer. The Hemudu culture strongly demonstrates that the Yangtze, like the Yellow River, was an important cradle of Chinese civilization. A site museum at Hemudu has reconstructed stilt buildings. Together with the Majiabang culture, Hemudu forms the rich prehistoric culture of the lower Yangtze, on whose land the later Liangzhu civilization developed.

events.title: Banpo Site (Yangshao Culture)
events.short: The Banpo site in Xi'an, c. 6,000 years old, belongs to the Yangshao culture: its people lived in semi-subterranean houses, grew millet, raised animals and made fine painted pottery.
events.detail: The Banpo site lies in Banpo village on the east bank of the Chan River in the eastern suburbs of Xi'an, Shaanxi. Discovered in 1953 and extensively excavated in 1954–1957, it is a representative settlement of the Yangshao culture of the Yellow River basin, about 6,000 years old. The Yangshao culture is named after Yangshao village in Mianchi, Henan, where it was first found in 1921, and is spread across the middle Yellow River. The layout of the Banpo settlement is clear: in the center is the residential area with houses, storage pits and a large house, surrounded by a moat five or six meters deep and wide; north of the moat is the communal cemetery and to the east are the pottery kilns. Houses were mostly round or square semi-subterranean buildings with wooden posts supporting the roof and a hearth pit inside. Banpo people cleared land with polished stone and bone tools, grew mainly millet, raised pigs, dogs and other animals, hunted and fished with bows, harpoons and nets, and gathered wild fruit as a supplement. Their everyday utensils were mostly pottery, the most distinctive being painted pottery, mainly black designs on a red ground, with geometric patterns and animal motifs such as fish and deer; the most famous piece is the painted bowl with human face and fish design. Some pots carry incised signs that some scholars link to the origin of writing. Bone needles, spindle whorls and clay ocarinas show they could spin, weave and sew clothes. A Banpo Museum, the first prehistoric site museum in China, now stands at the site.

events.title: Liangzhu Ancient City
events.short: The Liangzhu city in Yuhang, Hangzhou, c. 5,300–4,300 years ago, with palaces, inner and outer cities and a huge water system, shows an early state on the lower Yangtze.
events.detail: The Liangzhu site is in Yuhang District, Hangzhou, Zhejiang, first discovered by Shi Xingeng in 1936. The Liangzhu culture, centered on the ancient city, dates to about 5,300–4,300 years ago and spread around Lake Tai. In 2007 archaeologists confirmed the city walls. The city consists of a palace area, an inner city and an outer city; the inner city covers about 3 million square meters, and with the outer city about 6.3 million. At its center stands the artificially built Mojiaoshan platform, about 300,000 square meters in total, with a large plaza and several groups of high-status buildings. To the north and west lies an outer water-control system of many dams, stretching over 20 km and affecting an area of about 100 square kilometers, one of the largest hydraulic works in the world at that time. The city and water system together required more than 10 million cubic meters of earthwork, reflecting the rulers' strong powers of organization and mobilization. Elite cemeteries such as Fanshan and Yaoshan contain many fine jade objects, including cong tubes, bi discs and yue axes symbolizing military power, with motifs of a deity-and-beast face commonly carved on them, while ordinary graves hold few goods, showing clear social differentiation. The Liangzhu site proves that an early state had appeared on the lower Yangtze about 5,000 years ago, entering a civilized society, and is an important witness to more than 5,000 years of Chinese civilization. On 6 July 2019 the Archaeological Ruins of Liangzhu City was inscribed on the World Heritage List.

events.title: Dawenkou Culture
events.short: The Dawenkou culture of Shandong, c. 5,000 years ago, had advanced farming and crafts, and sharply unequal grave goods point to growing social inequality.
events.detail: The Dawenkou culture was a Neolithic culture of the lower Yellow River in Shandong and northern Jiangsu, dated to about 6,300–4,500 years ago. It is named after the Dawenkou site in Tai'an, Shandong, first excavated in 1959, and later developed into the Shandong Longshan culture. The Dawenkou people grew mainly millet, with a fairly developed farming economy, and raised pigs, dogs and other animals; pig jawbones were often buried as grave goods, as a symbol of wealth. Their crafts were well developed: they made red, black and hard white pottery, in forms such as the bei hu flask, gui tripod and tall-stemmed cup, as well as jade, ivory and bone objects such as ivory combs and openwork ivory tubes. Late Dawenkou graves differ sharply in size and goods: some large tombs had coffins and outer coffins and more than a hundred fine jade, ivory and pottery items, while some small graves had nothing. This shows that private property and wealth inequality had appeared, and that society was beginning to divide into classes. Some Dawenkou pottery vessels bear pictographic symbols, such as a design of sun, clouds and mountain, which many scholars link to the origin of Chinese characters. The Dawenkou people also practiced distinctive customs such as removing the lateral incisors and artificially deforming the skull. The Dawenkou culture influenced both the Central Plains and the lower Yangtze and is important for studying the origins of Chinese civilization. The many pottery, jade and bone and ivory objects from the site vividly show the production, life and society of people in the Haidai region more than 5,000 years ago, and the site is now a nationally protected cultural site.

images.caption: White pottery gui from the Dawenkou site

events.title: Yan–Huang Alliance and the Battle of Zhuolu
events.short: Legend says the Yellow Emperor beat the Yan Emperor at Banquan, allied with him, then defeated Chiyou at Zhuolu; their tribes formed the Huaxia, hence “descendants of Yan and Huang.”
events.detail: Ancient China preserved many myths and legends of remote times, the best known of which concern the Yan Emperor and the Yellow Emperor. Tradition holds that five or six thousand years ago, large tribes such as those of the Yan Emperor, the Yellow Emperor and Chiyou lived in the Yellow River basin, constantly attacking and merging with one another and eventually forming tribal alliances. The Yan Emperor's tribe was active in the Wei River valley in Shaanxi; he is said to have taught people to clear land and farm, made the lei and si plows, planted the five grains, tasted hundreds of herbs and invented medicine, and made pottery and taught people to trade goods. The Yellow Emperor, named Xuanyuan, is said to have built houses, made clothing, dug wells, made boats and carts and invented the bow and arrow; his wife Leizu raised silkworms and reeled silk, and his historian Cang Jie created writing. According to the Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji), “Basic Annals of the Five Emperors” and other sources, the Yellow Emperor fought the Yan Emperor at Banquan; the Yan Emperor was defeated and submitted, and the two great tribes formed an alliance. The Yan and Yellow tribes then fought Chiyou, leader of the Jiuli tribes in the east, at Zhuolu (in present-day Hebei) and finally defeated him, and the Yellow Emperor was chosen leader of the tribal alliance. This alliance gradually absorbed neighboring tribes and developed into the later Huaxia people; for this reason the Yan and Yellow Emperors are revered as the common ancestors of the Chinese nation, and Chinese at home and abroad often call themselves “descendants of Yan and Huang.”

events.title: Longshan Culture
events.short: The Longshan culture, over 4,000 years ago, is known for black pottery, including “eggshell” ware under 1 mm thick; walled towns multiplied and social divisions deepened.
events.detail: The Longshan culture refers broadly to a series of late Neolithic archaeological cultures in the middle and lower Yellow River region, dating from about 2500 BC to 2000 BC. In 1928 archaeologists first found such remains at the Chengziya site in Longshan Town, Zhangqiu, Shandong, hence the name. Because glossy black pottery is common at the sites, it was once called the “Black Pottery Culture.” The fast potter's wheel was widely used, and the vessels are regular and fine. The “eggshell” black pottery tall-stemmed cups of the Shandong Longshan culture have walls as thin as an eggshell, under 1 mm at the thinnest, the highest level of Neolithic pottery-making in China. Agriculture developed further, animal raising became more common, and a few copper objects appeared. Rammed-earth walled towns appeared in many places, such as Chengziya in Shandong, Wangchenggang in Henan and Taosi in Shanxi; some were large and had defenses. Graves differ sharply in size and goods: large tombs hold sets of pottery, jade and ritual vessels, while small ones have almost nothing, showing deepening social divisions and the concentration of rank and power. The period roughly corresponds to the legendary age of Yao, Shun and Yu. The Longshan culture follows the Yangshao and Dawenkou cultures and precedes the Erlitou culture, a key stage in China's move from tribal alliances to early states. Chengziya is one of the earliest prehistoric sites excavated independently by Chinese archaeologists, and the study of Longshan also offers clues in the search for Xia culture.

events.title: Taosi Capital Site
events.short: The Taosi site in Xiangfen, Shanxi, c. 4,300–4,000 years ago, has a palace city, large tombs and a possible observatory; some scholars think it may be “Yao's capital Pingyang.”
events.detail: The Taosi site lies around Taosi village northeast of Xiangfen County, Shanxi, and dates to about 4,300–4,000 years ago, belonging to the Taosi type of the Longshan culture. Systematically excavated since 1978, a large walled city was confirmed after 1999, covering about 2.8 million square meters, one of the largest contemporary cities in the middle Yellow River region. In the middle of the city is a walled palace enclosure containing several large rammed-earth foundations, with architectural elements such as clay tiles that may have roofed palaces. The city has a cemetery with clear ranks: large tombs contained ritual items such as painted pottery drums, stone chimes, jade yue axes and painted dragon-design plates, showing the high status of the occupants, while many small tombs had almost no goods, indicating clear social stratification. The site also produced small copper objects such as a bell, and a pottery flask with symbols written in cinnabar, which some scholars consider writing. Particularly striking is a semicircular rammed-earth structure southeast of the city, with observation slits formed by rammed-earth pillars, thought possibly to have been an observatory for watching the sunrise position and fixing the solar terms. Based on its location, date and scale, many scholars suggest Taosi may be the “Yao's capital Pingyang” of the texts, indicating that an early state had appeared in the middle Yellow River, which is of great significance for exploring the origins of Chinese civilization. Taosi was named one of the “100 Great Archaeological Discoveries in 20th-Century China” and is a key site of the Project to Trace the Origins of Chinese Civilization.

images.caption: Bronze bell, painted dragon-design pottery plate and pottery pot with cinnabar-written symbols from the Taosi site

events.title: Abdication of Yao, Shun and Yu
events.short: Legend says Yao, Shun and Yu led the tribal alliance in turn, passing leadership to the worthy by abdication, which later Confucians saw as the ideal form of rule.
events.detail: Tradition says that after the Yellow Emperor, many tribes lived in the Yellow River basin. To grow stronger, tribes such as the Taotang, Youyu and Xiahou formed an alliance, and Yao, Shun and Yu served in turn as its leader. A system of abdication was practiced: leadership was passed by selection to a capable and virtuous person rather than to one's own son. Yao is said to have encouraged people to clear farmland and ordered Xihe and others to observe the heavens and draw up a calendar, guiding people to farm on time. When Yao grew old, he consulted tribal leaders, who recommended Shun, known for his filial conduct. Yao tested Shun for years before yielding the leadership to him. Under Shun, penal laws were made, the worthy were chosen, institutions were improved and order kept; he also sent Yu to control the floods. When Shun grew old, he in turn yielded to Yu, who had succeeded in taming the floods. The abdication system reflects the democratic tradition of choosing leaders in tribal alliances at the end of primitive society. Later Confucians regarded it as the ideal of “the world as a shared possession,” and the Book of Rites (Liji), “Liyun,” sums up the age as one when “the Great Way prevailed and the world was shared by all; the worthy and able were chosen.” Some ancient texts, such as the Bamboo Annals, give different accounts of the abdications, showing how legendary this history is. After Yu died, his son Qi took the throne and the “world shared by all” became the “world owned by one family,” the abdication system being replaced by hereditary succession.

images.caption: Abdication system

events.title: Yu the Great Controls the Flood
events.short: Learning from his father Gun's failed damming, Yu controlled the floods by dredging, “passing his door three times without entering,” and ended the disaster after over ten years.
events.detail: Tradition says that in the time of Yao and Shun, floods swamped the Yellow River basin, drowning crops and houses and bringing great suffering. Yao ordered Yu's father Gun to control the floods; Gun tried building dikes to block the water, but after nine years failed and was later executed by Shun at Mount Yu. Shun then ordered Yu to continue the work. Learning from his father's failure, Yu switched to dredging: following the lay of the land, he cut channels and led the floodwater into rivers and finally into the sea. He is said to have devoted himself wholly to the task, traveling for more than ten years and “passing his own door three times without entering,” his hands and feet calloused as he labored alongside the people. After years of effort the floods were finally ended, and the people could again live in peace and farm. Because of his success, Yu was loved by the people and honored as “Yu the Great.” When Shun grew old, he yielded the leadership to Yu. Yu is also said to have divided the realm into Nine Provinces and cast Nine Tripod Cauldrons as symbols of state power. After Yu died, his son Qi succeeded him and founded the Xia dynasty. The story appears in the Book of Documents, Mencius, the Records of the Grand Historian and other works; though legendary, it reflects early people's struggle against natural disasters. Yu's spirit of selflessness, hard work, fearlessness and working with nature is still celebrated. Many sites and place names are associated with Yu, such as the Mausoleum of Yu in Shaoxing, Zhejiang, and the Yu King Terrace in Dengfeng, Henan; he has been honored through the generations, and the “spirit of Yu the Great” is a treasured part of Chinese heritage.

events.title: Founding of the Xia Dynasty
events.short: Yu founded the Xia dynasty c. 2070 BC; after Yu's son Qi took the throne, hereditary succession replaced abdication and the world became “one family's,” making Xia China's first dynasty.
events.detail: The Xia was the first hereditary dynasty recorded in Chinese histories. Founded by Yu c. 2070 BC and destroyed by the Shang c. 1600 BC, it lasted about 470 years. During his reign Yu conquered the Sanmiao in the south, built a city at Yangcheng (around present-day Dengfeng, Henan) and set up various institutions. Archaeologists found a walled site at Wangchenggang in Dengfeng, dated to about the 21st century BC, thought to be Yu's legendary capital Yangcheng. In his later years Yu intended to pass leadership to Boyi, but after Yu's death his son Qi took the throne with his strong following, held a great feast for the lords at Juntai and defeated the opposing Youhu clan at Gan. From then on hereditary succession replaced abdication and the “world shared by all” became the “world of one family”; the Three Character Classic puts it as “Xia passed to the son, the world of one family.” The Xia set up an army, made penal laws and established prisons, forming the machinery of a state, and society was divided into nobles, commoners and slaves. Its core area was mainly central and western Henan and southern Shanxi; the Records of the Grand Historian, “Basic Annals of Xia,” records fourteen generations and seventeen rulers, with the surname Si. The founding of the Xia marks the emergence of an early Chinese state, and its hereditary succession was followed by later dynasties. Because no Xia writing has yet been found, Xia history is studied mainly through later texts and archaeological finds such as Erlitou. Later Chinese often called themselves “Huaxia” and “Zhuxia,” and “Xia” became one of the names for China.

events.title: Erlitou Site
events.short: The Erlitou site in Yanshi, Henan, matches the late Xia capital; its palaces, bronze ritual vessels and turquoise dragon are key to the search for Xia culture.
events.detail: The Erlitou site lies at Erlitou village, Zhai Town, Yanshi District, Luoyang, Henan. Discovered in 1959 by the archaeologist Xu Xusheng while surveying the “Xia ruins,” it covers about 3 million square meters and dates to about 1750–1530 BC, corresponding to the late Xia, so many scholars take it to be a late Xia capital. At its center is a palace enclosure of about 100,000 square meters containing several large rammed-earth palace foundations laid out in an orderly plan, the earliest example of the central axial symmetry of ancient Chinese palace architecture; outside the enclosure is a crisscross network of roads, including the earliest cart ruts known. The site includes aristocratic graves, commoners' residential areas and cemeteries, and workshops for bronze casting, bone working and turquoise working, reflecting clear class divisions. Erlitou yielded sets of bronze wine vessels such as the jue, jia and he, and bronze plaques with turquoise-inlaid animal faces. The bronze ding found here is considered the earliest bronze ritual vessel found in China. In 2002 archaeologists found in an aristocratic tomb a large dragon-shaped object made of more than 2,000 turquoise pieces, hailed as a “super national treasure” and the “Chinese dragon.” Erlitou is a key site for exploring Xia culture and the formation of China's early state, and an Erlitou Xia Capital Site Museum now stands there. The Erlitou culture, centered on western Henan and southern Shanxi, influenced areas as far as the Yangtze and the northwest, reflecting the strong reach of Central Plains dynastic civilization, which leads some scholars to call Erlitou the “earliest China.”

events.title: Tang of Shang Overthrows Xia
events.short: Jie of Xia was cruel and lost the people's support; Tang, leader of the Shang tribe, rallied other tribes, defeated Jie at Mingtiao and founded the Shang dynasty c. 1600 BC.
events.detail: After more than 400 years, the Xia state had weakened by the reign of its last ruler, Jie. Tradition says Jie was extravagant and cruel, taxed the people heavily, built lavish palaces, drank and feasted all day and harmed the people by force, so that they cursed him, even crying out, “When will this sun perish? We will die with you!” Meanwhile the Shang tribe, active in eastern Henan and southern Hebei, was growing stronger. Its leader Tang employed able ministers such as Yi Yin, first eliminated some of Xia's vassal states to build his strength, then rallied neighboring tribes to attack Jie. The two sides fought a decisive battle at Mingtiao (said to be east of Fengqiu, Henan, or near Yuncheng, Shanxi); Jie was routed and fled, and died at Nanchao, ending the Xia. About 1600 BC Tang founded the Shang dynasty with its capital at Bo. This change of dynasty was later called the “Tang Revolution,” and the Book of Changes says that “Tang and Wu's revolutions obeyed Heaven and answered the people.” Learning from the fall of the Xia, Tang employed the talented, treated the people leniently and developed agriculture, crafts and trade, restoring the economy, and the Shang soon grew strong. Archaeologists found the earliest Shang city, the Yanshi Shang City, in Yanshi, Henan, and the larger early Shang capital, the Zhengzhou Shang City, in Zhengzhou. Many experts believe Yanshi Shang City may be the “Western Bo” and Zhengzhou Shang City the Bo of the texts, providing important evidence for early Shang history.

events.title: Pangeng Moves the Capital to Yin
events.short: The early Shang moved its capital many times; King Pangeng relocated it to Yin (present-day Anyang, Henan), where it stayed over 200 years and Shang rule stabilized.
events.detail: After the Shang was founded, because of struggles for the throne within the royal house, Yellow River floods and wars abroad, the capital was moved many times in the early period, known as “eight moves before, five after.” About 1300 BC King Pangeng overcame noble opposition and moved the capital to Yin (northwest of present-day Anyang, Henan), urging his subjects to settle and prosper. After the move to Yin, Shang politics stabilized, and until the dynasty fell, over 250 years, the capital was never moved again; hence the Shang is also called “Yin” or “Yin-Shang.” Under Pangeng's nephew Wuding, who employed able ministers such as Fu Yue and campaigned against the Guifang, Tufang and other tribes, the state reached its height, known as the “Wuding Restoration,” and the area under Shang control kept expanding. To consolidate rule, the Shang set up prisons and harsh punishments and tightened control of commoners and slaves. Slaves had no personal freedom and were forced to labor in fields and workshops; they were often sacrificed to ancestors or buried with their masters, and one large royal tomb at Anyang held several hundred such victims. The Yin capital site is today's Yinxu; scientific excavation began in 1928 and revealed palace and ancestral temple foundations, 13 royal tombs and thousands of commoner graves and craft workshops, with many oracle bones and bronzes, including the tomb of Wuding's wife Fu Hao. Yinxu is the first Shang capital in Chinese history verified both by texts and by archaeological excavation and oracle bone inscriptions, and was added to the World Heritage List in 2006.

events.title: Oracle Bone Script
events.short: Oracle bone script, carved on turtle shells and bones in Shang and Zhou times and found by Wang Yirong in 1899, is China's earliest known systematic writing.
events.detail: Oracle bone script was carved or written on turtle shells and bones of oxen, sheep and other animals in Shang and Zhou times, mainly as records of divination by the late Shang royal house; it is also called “divination inscriptions,” “carved script” and “Yinxu script.” Shang kings divined when matters arose: small holes were bored in the back of a shell or bone and heated with fire, the cracks on the front were read for good or ill fortune, and the date, subject and result were carved on it. The contents concern sacrifices, war, farming, astronomy, illness, hunting and more, a precious source for Shang history. In 1899 Wang Yirong, Imperial Academy chancellor of the Qing, first recognized oracle bone script on “dragon bones” sold as Chinese medicine; afterwards large numbers of bones were found at Yinxu in Anyang, Henan, Zhouyuan in Shaanxi, Shandong and elsewhere. About 150,000 inscribed Shang bones have been found, with more than 4,400 distinct characters, of which about 1,500 have been deciphered. The script already used pictographic, indicative, associative, phonetic-compound and loan methods of forming characters; pictographs make up about 40%, and phonetic compounds had appeared, giving it the basic structure of Chinese characters, and the forms of many characters are still in use. It is the earliest known mature systematic writing of China and East Asia. Scholars such as Luo Zhenyu, Wang Guowei, Guo Moruo and Dong Zuobin contributed greatly to its study, forming the discipline of oracle bone studies. Its discovery confirmed the reliability of the Shang royal lineage in the Records of the Grand Historian and pushed back China's documented history to the Shang. In 2017 oracle bone script was inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register.

events.title: Houmuwu Ding and Shang–Zhou Bronzes
events.short: Shang and Zhou bronzes were varied and highly skilled; the Houmuwu ding, 832.84 kg, is the heaviest known ancient Chinese bronze, and the Four-Ram Zun is exquisitely shaped.
events.detail: Copper objects have been found at several sites dating 5,000–4,000 years ago. In the Xia, Shang and Zhou, bronze casting was highly developed, with more objects in great variety, used mainly for food and drink, sacrifice and war. Ritual vessels such as the ding, jue, jia, gui and zun became symbols of nobles' rank and even of state power. Shang nobles loved wine, and the number of bronze wine vessels marked noble rank; the Western Zhou valued ritual, and the numbers of ding and gui marked rank: nine ding and eight gui for the Son of Heaven, seven and six for feudal lords, five and four for senior officials. Craftsmen had by then accurately mastered the ratios of copper, tin and lead and cast fine objects in clay molds, with decorations mostly of taotie, kui dragons and cloud-and-thunder patterns. The Houmuwu ding is a square bronze ding used in late Shang royal sacrifices, found in 1939 at Wuguan village, Anyang, Henan. It stands 133 cm tall, with a mouth 112 cm long and 79.2 cm wide, and weighs 832.84 kg, the heaviest known ancient Chinese bronze; it is named for the three characters “Houmuwu” cast inside (formerly “Simuwu ding”). It is generally thought to have been cast by a Shang king to honor his mother, “Wu.” The Four-Ram Zun, found in Ningxiang, Hunan, has a curled-horn ram at each corner, an imposing form and the largest of the Shang square zun. Western Zhou pieces such as the Li gui, Mao Gong ding and Da Yu ding bear precious inscriptions. Shang and Zhou bronzes represent the peak of world bronze civilization of their time; the Houmuwu ding and Four-Ram Zun are now in the National Museum of China.

events.title: Sanxingdui Site
events.short: In 1986 sacrificial pits at Sanxingdui in Guanghan, Sichuan yielded a gold scepter, a bronze sacred tree and many bronze figures and masks, showing the distinctive ancient Shu civilization.
events.detail: The Sanxingdui site is in Nanxing Town, Guanghan, Sichuan, on the northern Chengdu Plain, and is named for three artificial mounds at the site. In 1929 a local farmer, Yan Daocheng, found a pit of jade and stone objects while digging a ditch, and archaeologists have surveyed and excavated here many times since. In 1986 two large sacrificial pits were found one after another, yielding thousands of precious gold, bronze, jade, stone and ivory objects and stunning the world. The most important include a gold scepter 1.42 m long, covered in gold foil and engraved with human heads, fish and birds; a bronze sacred tree about 3.96 m high with divine birds perched on it; a bronze standing figure over 2.6 m tall, the tallest bronze figure of its age in the world; a bronze mask 1.38 m wide with protruding eyeballs; and many strangely shaped bronze heads and masks. The main dates of Sanxingdui are about 4,500–3,000 years ago, with the sacrificial pits roughly late Shang. It was the capital of the ancient Shu state, with a city area of about 3.6 square kilometers. Sanxingdui culture has strong local features but also close links to Central Plains Shang culture and middle Yangtze culture, showing that Chinese civilization originated in a pluralistic yet unified way. Since 2019 six new sacrificial pits have been found, producing gold masks, bronze altars and many other important objects. The Jinsha site in Chengdu is regarded as another center of ancient Shu civilization after Sanxingdui.

events.title: King Wu Defeats Zhou (Battle of Muye)
events.short: In 1046 BC King Wu of Zhou and his allies fought the Shang at Muye; the Shang troops turned their weapons, King Zhou burned himself, and the Shang fell and the Western Zhou began.
events.detail: In the late Shang, social conflicts sharpened and the slave-owning aristocracy grew more decadent. The last Shang ruler, Di Xin (King Zhou), campaigned against the Dongyi year after year, draining the state, built luxurious palaces, raised taxes and tortured people with punishments such as the “roasting.” According to the Records of the Grand Historian, “Annals of Yin,” he made “a pool of wine and a forest of hanging meat” and held drinking feasts through the night, the origin of the idiom “pool of wine, forest of meat.” Meanwhile the Zhou tribe, based on the Zhouyuan plain in the Wei River valley in Shaanxi, was an agricultural state that expanded under King Wen until it held “two thirds of the realm.” After Wen's death his son King Wu, aided by Lu Shang (Jiang Taigong), Duke of Zhou and others, joined the Yong, Shu, Qiang and other tribes and the lords in 1046 BC and marched east against Shang with a large allied army. The two sides fought a decisive battle at Muye (around Xinxiang, Henan) outside the Shang capital Chaoge. Though the Shang army was larger, it contained many slaves and prisoners hastily armed who were unwilling to die for King Zhou and turned their weapons on him; the Zhou army swept into Chaoge, King Zhou climbed the Deer Terrace and burned himself to death, and the Shang fell. King Wu founded the Zhou dynasty with its capital at Haojing (southwest of present-day Xi'an), known as the Western Zhou. The Li gui, unearthed in Lintong, Shaanxi, in 1976, records that King Wu attacked Shang on the morning of the jiazi day, confirming the ancient texts. The Xia–Shang–Zhou Chronology Project, using astronomical and archaeological study, sets the year of King Wu's conquest at 1046 BC.

events.title: Western Zhou Enfeoffment System
events.short: The Western Zhou enfeoffed kinsmen and meritorious officials as lords across the land, forming the ranks of king, lord, senior official and scholar-gentleman.
events.detail: After the Western Zhou was founded, to stabilize its rule and secure the newly conquered lands, the king practiced the enfeoffment system: according to closeness of kinship and size of service, he granted kinsmen, meritorious officials and descendants of ancient rulers the authority to govern land and people and found feudal states, “enfeoffing relatives to be a screen for Zhou.” According to records, more than 70 states were enfeoffed in the early Zhou, including: Boqin, eldest son of the Duke of Zhou, in Lu (Qufu, Shandong); Lu Shang in Qi (Zibo, Shandong); a son of the Duke of Shao in Yan (Beijing); Shuyu in Tang (later renamed Jin, around Yicheng, Shanxi); and Weizi Qi, half-brother of King Zhou of Shang, in Song (Shangqiu, Henan), to pacify the Shang remnants. Lords had considerable independence in their states and could appoint officials, raise armies and levy taxes, but had to obey the king's orders, pay tribute regularly, join him in war and defend the royal house. Within their own lands they could in turn enfeoff senior officials, who enfeoffed scholar-gentlemen, forming the hierarchy of king, lord, senior official and scholar-gentleman. Alongside enfeoffment went the clan law centered on succession by the eldest son by the principal wife and a system of ritual and music distinguishing ranks. Enfeoffment extended Western Zhou rule to the Yellow and Yangtze river basins, strengthened control over the regions and promoted economic and cultural exchange and ethnic integration. But as the lords grew stronger, the Zhou royal house gradually declined, and by the Spring and Autumn period the enfeoffment system was breaking down and was replaced by the system of commanderies and counties.

events.title: Uprising of the Capital Dwellers
events.short: In 841 BC King Li of Zhou monopolized the resources of forests and waters and silenced criticism, provoking an uprising of the capital's people; he fled, and the “Gonghe Regency” followed.
events.detail: The Uprising of the Capital Dwellers, also called the “Disturbance at Zhi,” was a large popular uprising in the late Western Zhou. “Capital dwellers” (guoren) was the term in the Western Zhou and Spring and Autumn periods for those living in the capital and its suburbs, mainly commoners and lower nobles. During the reign of King Li of Zhou, Duke Yi of Rong was employed to carry out a policy of “monopoly,” taking the forests, hills, rivers and lakes that the capital dwellers had shared into royal ownership and cutting off their livelihood. The king was also tyrannical, sending shamans from the state of Wei to spy on critics and killing those reported, so that people meeting on the road dared only exchange glances, a situation known as “speaking with the eyes on the road.” The Duke of Shao warned, “To stop the people's mouths is worse than to dam a river,” but the king would not listen. In 841 BC the capital dwellers, unable to bear more, rose up spontaneously and stormed the palace; King Li fled in panic to Zhi (present-day Huozhou, Shanxi) and later died there. After the uprising, the Duke of Shao, the Duke of Zhou and other ministers ran the government together (another account says Lord He of Gong acted as regent), known as the “Gonghe Regency.” That year, 841 BC, was the first year of Gonghe, from which Chinese history has exact continuous dating; the table of the twelve lords in the Records of the Grand Historian starts from it. King Li died at Zhi fourteen years later and Crown Prince Jing took the throne as King Xuan of Zhou.

events.title: Fall of the Western Zhou and King Ping's Move East
events.short: Court corruption under King You let the Marquis of Shen and the Quanrong take Haojing in 771 BC, ending the Western Zhou; King Ping moved the capital to Luoyi in 770 BC.
events.detail: Under King Xuan of Zhou there was a period of “revival,” but under his son King You the court was corrupt and social conflicts sharpened, with repeated earthquakes and droughts leaving the people destitute. According to the Records of the Grand Historian, “Annals of Zhou,” King You doted on Bao Si, deposed Queen Shen and Crown Prince Yijiu, and made Bao Si's son Bofu crown prince. Tradition says that to win a smile from Bao Si the king once lit the beacon fires to fool the lords, the tale of “toying with the lords with the beacon fires,” though many scholars consider this episode unreliable. The Marquis of Shen, father of Queen Shen, was furious; in 771 BC he joined the state of Zeng and the Quanrong of the northwest in attacking Haojing. The lords did not come to the rescue, King You was killed at the foot of Mount Li, Haojing was sacked and the Western Zhou ended. The Marquis of Shen and other lords then installed the former crown prince Yijiu as King Ping of Zhou. Because Haojing was ruined and close to the Rong, in 770 BC King Ping, escorted by Jin, Zheng, Qin and other lords, moved the capital east to Luoyi (present-day Luoyang, Henan), known as the Eastern Zhou. Duke Xiang of Qin was made a lord for his service in the escort, and Qin began to rise. King Ping's move east was the turning point from the Zhou's prime to decline: the area directly controlled by the royal house shrank to the Luoyi region, its economic and military strength was greatly weakened, and though still nominally the common overlord it could no longer control the lords. The Eastern Zhou is divided into the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods, and Chinese history entered an age of great change.

events.title: Duke Huan of Qi and the Struggle for Hegemony
events.short: With the Zhou royal house weak, states vied for supremacy; Duke Huan of Qi, reformed by Guan Zhong and using the slogan “revere the king, expel the barbarians,” became the first hegemon.
events.detail: After King Ping's move east, the Zhou royal house declined; its direct domain was only around Luoyi, it could no longer control the lords, who no longer paid tribute regularly, and the royal finances came to depend on lords' support. Some large states, to expand their power, annexed one another and competed for hegemony, controlling affairs in the realm and in effect taking the place of the Son of Heaven, known as the Spring and Autumn “struggle for hegemony.” The state of Qi, in northern Shandong, grew strong early thanks to fish and salt and developed industry and trade. After taking the throne, Duke Huan of Qi set aside old grudges and made Guan Zhong, who had once shot him, his chancellor, and carried out reforms: reorganizing government, taxing land by quality, developing agriculture, fish and salt and ironmaking, and combining military and administrative organization, greatly strengthening Qi. Duke Huan raised the slogan “revere the king, expel the barbarians,” helped Yan fend off the Shanrong, helped Xing and Wei resist the Di, and led an allied army against Chu, forcing it to sign a treaty. In 651 BC he convened the lords at Kuiqiu, where the Zhou king also sent a representative, and became the first hegemon of the Spring and Autumn period. Afterwards Duke Wen of Jin defeated Chu at Chengpu and became hegemon of the Central Plains; King Zhuang of Chu “asked about the tripods” and held sway for a time; Duke Mu of Qin dominated the western Rong; and late in the period Wu and Yue also moved north to contest hegemony. The wars of hegemony brought disaster to the people but also promoted ethnic integration and regional unification, while the Zhou royal house grew ever weaker and enfeoffment gradually collapsed.

events.date: Western Zhou to Spring and Autumn
events.title: Classic of Poetry (Shijing)
events.short: The Classic of Poetry, China's first poetry anthology, collects 305 poems from the early Western Zhou to the mid-Spring and Autumn in three parts: Feng, Ya and Song.
events.detail: The Classic of Poetry (Shijing) is China's first anthology of poetry, collecting 305 poems from roughly 500 years, from the early Western Zhou to the middle Spring and Autumn period. In the pre-Qin period it was called the Poems or the “Three Hundred Poems,” and only when honored as a Confucian classic in the Western Han was it called the Shijing. By musical type it is divided into three parts, “Feng,” “Ya” and “Song.” “Feng,” the “Airs of the Fifteen States,” has 160 poems and consists of folk songs from different regions, the most realistic of all. “Ya,” divided into Greater and Lesser Ya, has 105 poems, mostly songs for banquets and court assemblies of the nobility. “Song,” including the Songs of Zhou, Lu and Shang, has 40 poems, songs for ancestral temple sacrifices. Its poems variously reflect working life and folk customs, celebrate love and noble sentiment, or expose the exploitation and oppression of rulers: “Big Rat” compares exploiters to a great rat, “Cutting Sandalwood” mocks nobles who gain without working, and “Guan Ju” and “Jian Jia” are beloved love poems. The Classic of Poetry is mainly in four-character lines, often uses repeated stanzas and the techniques of “fu, bi and xing” (narration, comparison and association), and its language is simple, beautiful and musical. Tradition says Confucius edited it and taught it to his disciples, saying, “If you do not study the Poems, you will have nothing to say.” It preserves rich materials on Shang and Zhou society, began the realist tradition of Chinese poetry and, with the romantic Chuci (Songs of Chu) represented by Qu Yuan, makes up “Feng and Sao,” and has deeply influenced poetry for over two thousand years.

events.title: Confucius and Confucianism
events.short: Confucius, founder of Confucianism, taught a philosophy centered on “benevolence,” urged rule by virtue, opened private schools for all, and edited the classics.
events.detail: Confucius (551–479 BC), personal name Qiu and courtesy name Zhongni, was born in Zouyi, Lu (present-day Qufu, Shandong) in the late Spring and Autumn period, of a declined noble family. A keen learner from childhood who studied ritual and music, he served as a minor official managing storehouses and livestock, then opened a private school and became a well-known scholar. In his fifties he briefly held posts in Lu such as magistrate of Zhongdu and Minister of Justice, but soon left and traveled among the states for about 14 years promoting his political ideas, which no state adopted. In old age he returned to Lu to devote himself to education and the editing of ancient texts; tradition says he edited the Poems, Documents, Rites, Changes, Music and Spring and Autumn Annals. His core idea was “benevolence” (ren): “the benevolent love others,” “do not do to others what you would not want done to yourself,” with “ritual” regulating social order. Politically he admired Western Zhou institutions, advocated rule by virtue, opposed harsh government and arbitrary punishment, and urged rulers to spare the people's strength. A great educator, Confucius founded private schools, breaking the nobles' monopoly on education, and held that there should be “teaching without distinctions of class”; he is said to have had three thousand students, seventy-two of them outstanding. He advocated “teaching according to aptitude,” “learning and practicing in due time,” “reviewing the old to know the new,” and the attitude that “to know what you know and know what you do not know is true knowledge.” His words and deeds were compiled by disciples and later disciples as the Analects.

events.title: Sun Wu and The Art of War
events.short: Sun Wu of the late Spring and Autumn period wrote The Art of War in thirteen chapters, with ideas such as “know the enemy and know yourself,” founding ancient Chinese military theory.
events.detail: Sun Wu, courtesy name Changqing, was a native of Qi in the late Spring and Autumn period who later went to Wu; later generations honor him as “Master Sun” and the “Sage of War.” According to the Records of the Grand Historian, Sun Wu presented his thirteen chapters on warfare to King Helu of Wu, who had him drill the palace women; Sun Wu beheaded the two squad leaders (the king's favorite concubines) who disobeyed orders, thereby enforcing discipline, and Helu, seeing his ability, made him a general. With Wu Zixu he assisted the king, and in 506 BC, at the Battle of Boju, 30,000 Wu troops defeated the Chu army, winning five battles in five and entering the Chu capital Ying, making Wu feared in the Central Plains. The Art of War has thirteen chapters of about 6,000 characters, including “Laying Plans,” “Waging War,” “Attack by Stratagem,” “Disposition,” “Energy,” “Weak Points and Strong,” “The Nine Situations” and “The Use of Spies.” It contains famous sayings such as “know the enemy and know yourself, and you need not fear a hundred battles,” “to subdue the enemy without fighting is the acme of skill,” “attack where he is unprepared, appear where you are not expected” and “war is the way of deception,” stressing a full analysis of politics, weather, terrain, commanders and law before war, revealing some universal laws of war and containing plain materialism and dialectics. It is the oldest and most complete surviving Chinese military text, hailed as the “holy book of military science,” laid the foundation of ancient Chinese military theory, and in the Song was placed first among the Seven Military Classics. In the Warring States Sun Wu's descendant Sun Bin carried on and developed his thought and wrote The Art of War of Sun Bin.

events.title: Iron Farm Tools and Ox Plowing Appear
events.short: Iron farm tools and ox plowing appeared in the late Spring and Autumn period, enabling deeper tilling and land clearing and raising farm productivity.
events.detail: The economy developed greatly in the Spring and Autumn period; especially in its later part, iron farm tools and ox plowing began to appear, a key sign of rising farm productivity. Ancient texts record plowing with iron implements, and archaeologists have unearthed iron farm tools such as hoes, spades and sickles from Spring and Autumn tombs in Changsha (Hunan), Henan, Jiangsu and elsewhere. Most iron tools of the time were wooden tools fitted with an iron cutting edge, much sharper and more durable than wooden or stone tools. By the end of the period at the latest, people were using oxen to pull plows; Confucius's disciples Ran Geng, styled Boniu, and Sima Geng, styled Zi Niu, have names and styles linking “ox” and “plowing,” which reflects that oxen and cultivation were already connected. Iron tools and ox plowing promoted deep, careful tillage and made it possible to clear forests and wasteland and expand farmland; much wasteland became private fields, undermining the land system based on the well-field system. Alongside agriculture, crafts expanded, with growth in bronze, ironmaking, textiles, salt boiling and lacquerware; cast iron appeared in China in the Spring and Autumn period, more than a thousand years earlier than in Europe. As output grew, trade became more active, many cities had markets for exchange and metal currency was used more widely. In the Warring States, iron tools and ox plowing spread further and productivity kept rising; the new landlord class gained strength, laying the economic foundation for the reforms of the states and the formation of feudal society.

events.title: Laozi and Daoism
events.short: Laozi of the late Spring and Autumn period founded Daoism, holding that all things follow nature and opposites turn into each other, urged “governing by non-action,” and wrote the Tao Te Ching.
events.detail: Laozi, surname Li, personal name Er, courtesy name Dan, was from Ku County in Chu (around Luyi, Henan) in the late Spring and Autumn period and founded Daoism. He served as keeper of the archives of the Zhou royal house, managing its records, and was learned; tradition says Confucius once made a special journey to ask him about ritual. When the Zhou declined, Laozi resigned and went west; it is said that at the Hangu Pass, at the request of the gatekeeper Yin Xi, he wrote a work of five thousand characters, the Laozi, also called the Tao Te Ching, which became the Daoist classic. Laozi held that the “Dao” is the source of all things, that all things run by natural laws, and that people should follow nature: “Man follows Earth, Earth follows Heaven, Heaven follows the Dao, and the Dao follows what is natural.” He saw that everything has its opposite, such as difficult and easy, long and short, high and low, front and back, misfortune and fortune, and that opposites can turn into each other; “Misfortune is what fortune rests on; fortune is where misfortune hides,” reflecting plain dialectics. Politically he advocated “governing by non-action,” opposed rulers' excessive interference in the people's lives, held that “governing a large state is like cooking a small fish,” and imagined an ideal of “small states with few people,” in which people kept out of quarrels and the world would be at peace. In the Warring States the representative Daoist was Zhuangzi, who developed Laozi's thought, stressing following nature, seeking absolute spiritual freedom and keeping an independent personality, and wrote the Zhuangzi.

events.title: Wu–Yue Rivalry (Goujian Destroys Wu)
events.short: Wu and Yue contended for hegemony on the lower Yangtze; King Goujian of Yue, after defeat, endured hardship, rebuilt his state, and destroyed Wu in 473 BC before moving north to become hegemon.
events.detail: In the late Spring and Autumn period the states of Wu and Yue on the lower Yangtze rose in turn and fought a long, fierce struggle for hegemony. Wu, aided by Wu Zixu and Sun Wu, grew strong and once defeated Chu. In 496 BC King Helu of Wu attacked Yue and was defeated at the Battle of Zuili, dying of his wounds. His son Fuchai, vowing revenge, crushed the Yue army at Fujiao in 494 BC; King Goujian of Yue was besieged on Mount Kuaiji and had to submit and sue for peace, personally serving Fuchai in Wu. On returning home, Goujian bore the shame of his defeat in mind; it is said that he slept on brushwood and hung a gall bladder by his seat, tasting it before sitting, lying down or eating to spur himself not to forget revenge, the origin of the idiom “sleeping on brushwood and tasting gall.” Goujian employed able ministers such as Fan Li and Wen Zhong, encouraged births, developed production, lightened taxes and trained the army, and after “ten years of building up and ten years of training,” Yue grew strong. Meanwhile King Fuchai of Wu grew arrogant, listened to slander, drove the loyal Wu Zixu to death and campaigned north year after year against Qi and Jin. In 482 BC Fuchai led his elite troops to a meeting of the lords at Huangchi, and Goujian took advantage of the empty capital to attack Wu. Yue kept pressing, and in 473 BC it broke Wu; Fuchai killed himself and Wu was destroyed. Goujian then marched north and met Qi, Jin and other lords at Xuzhou, where the Zhou king sent sacrificial meat to him, recognizing him as hegemon. The rivalry was the last hegemony war of the Spring and Autumn period, and Goujian is counted among the “Five Hegemons.”

events.title: Partition of Jin and the Seven Warring States
events.short: Jin was divided among Han, Zhao and Wei, and Qi passed to the Tian clan; in 403 BC the Zhou king recognized the three as lords, forming the Seven Warring States.
events.detail: In the late Spring and Autumn period, powerful senior officials in some states grew stronger and gradually took over the government. In Jin, power long lay with six families of senior officials, Han, Zhao, Wei, Zhi, Fan and Zhonghang, who annexed one another until four were left: Han, Zhao, Wei and Zhi. In 453 BC Zhi Bo joined Han and Wei to besiege the Zhao at Jinyang; Zhao Xiangzi secretly persuaded Han and Wei to switch sides, and the three together destroyed the Zhi and divided most of Jin's land. In 403 BC King Weilie of Zhou formally recognized Han, Zhao and Wei as lords, known as the “Partition of Jin,” the three states together being called the “Three Jins.” Sima Guang's Zizhi Tongjian of the Northern Song begins its narrative with this year. In Qi, the Tian clan won the people's hearts by methods such as “lending with large measures and collecting with small ones” and gradually took power; in 386 BC Tian He was made Marquis of Qi by the Zhou king, known as “the Tian clan replacing Qi.” The stronger states of the Warring States period were thus Qi, Chu, Yan, Han, Zhao, Wei and Qin, the “Seven Warring States.” The Warring States period generally runs from 475 BC to 221 BC and takes its name from the Intrigues of the Warring States compiled by Liu Xiang of the Western Han. In this period the strong lords no longer used the slogan “revere the king, expel the barbarians”; the Zhou house survived in name only, and the states reformed to grow strong and expand their armies. Wars of annexation grew ever larger, with more troops, wider theaters and longer duration, and famous battles such as Guiling, Maling and Changping took place.

events.title: Shang Yang's Reforms
events.short: In 356 BC Duke Xiao of Qin had Shang Yang reform the state: abolishing the well-field system, rewarding military merit and favoring agriculture, making Qin the strongest state.
events.detail: In the Warring States, iron farm tools and ox plowing spread further and the new landlord class grew stronger, and states carried out reforms in order to be rich and militarily strong, of which Shang Yang's reforms in Qin were the most effective. Shang Yang, originally Wei Yang from the state of Wei, was later enfeoffed at Shang for his service, hence the name Shang Yang. After Duke Xiao of Qin took the throne and issued an order seeking talent, Shang Yang came to Qin with Li Kui's Canon of Laws and was put to use. To win the people's trust he set a three-zhang pole at the south gate of the capital and announced ten gold pieces for anyone who moved it to the north gate, later raised to fifty; when someone did, the reward was paid at once, the story of “moving the pole to establish trust.” In 356 BC and 350 BC Shang Yang led two rounds of reform. Politically: the nobles' hereditary privileges were abolished and a county system was set up, with officials sent directly by the ruler; the household registration system was reformed with “mutual responsibility in groups of five and ten”; laws were enforced strictly and private fighting banned. Economically: the well-field system was abolished and the “boundaries opened,” recognizing private land ownership and allowing land sales; agriculture was favored over commerce, and those producing much grain and cloth were exempt from labor service; weights and measures were unified. Militarily: military merit was rewarded, with ranks, land and houses granted according to merit, and privileges of nobles without merit abolished. The capital was also moved to Xianyang.

events.title: Hundred Schools of Thought
events.short: In the Warring States, Confucian, Mohist, Daoist, Legalist and other schools wrote and debated freely, forming the “Hundred Schools of Thought” that shaped Chinese culture.
events.detail: The Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods saw rapid social change; the states competed to attract talent in order to become rich and strong, private schools rose and the class of “shi” (scholars) was active, producing an unprecedented flowering of thought. Different schools formed, each writing and debating with the others, known as the “Hundred Schools of Thought” and the “contention of a hundred schools.” “Zi” originally meant a senior official and later became an honorific for scholars and teachers. The most influential schools were Confucianism, Mohism, Daoism and Legalism. Mozi, founder of Mohism, advocated “impartial love” and “opposing offensive war,” called on people to love and benefit one another, opposed wars of conquest, favored choosing the worthy to govern and urged frugality. The Confucian representatives in the Warring States were Mencius and Xunzi: Mencius advocated “benevolent government” and said “the people are most important, the state next, the ruler least”; Xunzi advocated using both ritual and law, saying “the ruler is the boat and the common people the water; water can carry the boat or overturn it,” and “control the Mandate of Heaven and use it.” The Daoist Zhuangzi carried on Laozi's thought and pursued spiritual freedom. The Legalist Han Feizi brought Legalism to its fullest development, advocating rule by law and a centralized autocratic state, which suited the historical trend toward unification and was adopted by Qin. There were also Sun Bin of the military school, Zou Yan of the yin-yang school, Gongsun Long of the School of Names, Su Qin and Zhang Yi of the diplomatic school and Xu Xing of the agriculturalists.

events.title: Qu Yuan and the Chuci
events.short: Qu Yuan, a poet of Chu in the late Warring States, drew on folk songs and Chu dialect to create the new verse form of the Chuci; his Li Sao began the romantic tradition in poetry.
events.detail: Qu Yuan (c. 340–c. 278 BC), personal name Ping and courtesy name Yuan, was from a noble family of Chu in the late Warring States and is regarded as the first great patriotic poet in Chinese history. Early on he was trusted by King Huai of Chu and held posts such as Zuotu and Sanlü Dafu, advocating clear laws and the promotion of the able at home and an alliance with Qi against Qin abroad. But his proposals met opposition and slander from old nobles, and King Huai listened to slander and kept him at a distance. King Huai was later tricked into going to Qin, was held there and died in Qin; after King Qingxiang took the throne Qu Yuan was again pushed aside and exiled to the Yuan and Xiang river region in the south. In 278 BC the Qin general Bai Qi took the Chu capital Ying, and Qu Yuan, in grief and despair, is said to have drowned himself in the Miluo River on the fifth day of the fifth lunar month. The custom of eating zongzi and racing dragon boats at the Dragon Boat Festival is said to commemorate Qu Yuan. Qu Yuan drew on the best of Chu folk songs and used Chu dialect and strongly local forms to create a new verse form with flexible lines and frequent use of the word “xi,” later called the “Chuci” or “Sao style.” His masterpiece Li Sao is among the longest lyric poems of ancient China, over 2,400 characters, weaving natural phenomena, historical figures and myth together and using fragrant plants and beautiful women as metaphors for lofty character, expressing his love for his country and people; the line “The road is long and far; I will search high and low” has become a timeless saying. He also wrote Nine Songs, Heavenly Questions, Nine Declarations and other works. Liu Xiang of the Western Han compiled works by Qu Yuan, Song Yu and others into the Chuci.

events.title: Battle of Changping
events.short: In the Qin–Zhao Battle of Changping (262–260 BC), Zhao replaced Lian Po with the armchair strategist Zhao Kuo; over 400,000 Zhao troops were destroyed, and Qin's unification became assured.
events.detail: The Battle of Changping was a decisive battle between Qin and Zhao in the late Warring States, fought at Changping (northwest of present-day Gaoping, Shanxi) from 262 to 260 BC and one of the largest and bloodiest battles of ancient China. In 262 BC Qin attacked Han's Shangdang commandery; its governor Feng Ting, unwilling to surrender to Qin, offered Shangdang to Zhao instead, and war broke out between Qin and Zhao. Zhao at first sent the veteran general Lian Po, who, judging that Qin's army had come a long way and wanted a quick fight, built fortifications and held his ground to wear them down, and the two sides were locked in a long standoff. Qin therefore used a ruse, spreading the rumor that “Qin fears only Zhao Kuo as a general.” King Xiaocheng of Zhao fell for it, removed Lian Po and appointed Zhao Kuo, son of the famous general Zhao She. Zhao Kuo had read military books since childhood and talked of strategy fluently but lacked real combat experience. Meanwhile Qin secretly replaced its commander with the famous general Bai Qi. On arriving, Zhao Kuo changed Lian Po's dispositions and attacked; Bai Qi feigned retreat to lure the enemy in, then sent surprise troops to cut off the Zhao army's retreat and supply line and encircled its main force. The Zhao army went without food for over forty days; Zhao Kuo led a breakout himself and was killed by Qin arrows. More than 400,000 Zhao troops surrendered and nearly all were buried alive by Bai Qi, only 240 young boys being sent home. The battle crippled Zhao, the strongest of the six eastern states, after which no single state could resist Qin, and the trend toward Qin's unification of the realm took shape. The idiom “armchair strategy” comes from the story of Zhao Kuo.

events.title: Building the Dujiangyan
events.short: Around 256 BC Li Bing, governor of Shu, led construction of the Dujiangyan, with its Fish Mouth, Flying Sand Weir and Bottle-Neck Channel, which has served for over 2,000 years.
events.detail: In the late Warring States, while reforming its government and developing its economy, Qin paid close attention to building water works. The Min River on the Chengdu Plain ran swift and often flooded, while the east of the plain was often dry. About 256 BC Li Bing, governor of Shu for Qin, building on earlier flood-control work, directed construction of the Dujiangyan (in present-day Dujiangyan City, Sichuan). After careful planning, Li Bing and others chose the point where the Min River leaves the mountains and meets the plain, and made use of the terrain and river course to build this large water project. The headworks have three parts. The Fish Mouth is a dividing embankment built in mid-river like a great fish lying in the water; it splits the Min into an inner river for irrigation and an outer river for flood discharge, and adjusts the flow automatically by season, the “four-six division of water.” The Flying Sand Weir is an overflow and silt-removal structure that sends surplus water and silt into the outer river in flood. The Bottle-Neck Channel is an intake cut through Mount Yulei, shaped like the neck of a bottle, which controls the water entering the inner river and sends it into a dense network of irrigation canals. Tradition says workers cut the Bottle-Neck Channel by heating rock with fire and then dousing it with cold water to crack it. The Dujiangyan combines flood control, irrigation and navigation without needing a dam, a model of harmony between people and nature, and made the Chengdu Plain the “Land of Abundance,” where “flood and drought are at the people's command, and famine is unknown.”

events.title: Qin Unifies the Six States
events.short: From 230 BC King Zheng of Qin destroyed Han, Zhao, Wei, Chu, Yan and Qi in turn and in 221 BC founded the Qin dynasty, China's first unified multiethnic state.
events.detail: In the late Warring States, constant war badly damaged the economy and social stability, and people in every state longed for an end to turmoil and for unification. Through Shang Yang's reforms Qin's economy and military far surpassed those of the six eastern states, and it was ready for unification. King Zheng of Qin (259–210 BC) took the throne at thirteen and after taking personal charge removed Lao Ai and Lü Buwei and held all power himself. He recruited talent regardless of birthplace or background, employing Li Si, a minor official of Chu, and Wei Liao, a commoner of Wei; he adopted Li Si's advice to “destroy the lords and achieve imperial rule,” adopting the strategy of allying with distant states and attacking near ones, defeating them one by one, and bribed powerful ministers of other states with gold to sow discord among the six. In 230 BC Qin launched a strong offensive, first destroying Han, then Zhao (228 BC), Wei (225 BC), Chu (223 BC) and Yan (222 BC), and finally Qi in 221 BC, completing unification and founding the Qin dynasty with its capital at Xianyang. During this time Crown Prince Dan of Yan sent Jing Ke to assassinate the King of Qin, without success. After destroying the six states, Qin struck the Xiongnu in the north and conquered the Baiyue in the south, built the Great Wall and dug the Lingqu Canal, and its domain extended east to the sea, west to Longxi, north to the Great Wall and south to the South China Sea. Qin's unification ended the long division and warfare since the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods and created the first unified, multiethnic, centralized feudal state in Chinese history, in line with the trend of history and the wishes of the people, with deep consequences.

events.title: Qin Establishes Centralized Rule
events.short: After unification Qin created the imperial system, with three top ministers at the center and commanderies and counties in the regions, shaping the next two thousand years.
events.detail: After Qin unified China, it created a full system of centralized rule to strengthen control over the country. First came the emperor system: Ying Zheng, regarding his achievements as surpassing the legendary Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors, took “Emperor” (Huangdi) as the supreme ruler's title and called himself the “First Emperor,” hoping his descendants would rule for ten thousand generations. The emperor held supreme authority and all military and political power; his orders were called “zhi” and “zhao,” he called himself “zhen,” and he used a jade seal. Second, at the center were set up the chancellor, grand commandant and imperial secretary, the “Three Excellencies,” in charge of administration, military affairs and supervision respectively, checking one another with the final decision resting with the emperor; below them were the Nine Ministers handling specific affairs. In the regions, Qin abolished the Western Zhou enfeoffment system: when Chancellor Wang Wan and others proposed enfeoffing imperial sons, the Commandant of Justice Li Si strongly urged the commandery-county system, which Qin Shi Huang supported. The country was first divided into 36 commanderies, later over 40; each commandery had a governor, a military commandant and a supervising censor, with counties below headed by a magistrate, all appointed and dismissed directly by the court and not hereditary. Below the county were township, village and pavilion units. Qin also made unified laws and applied political, legal, military, land and tax systems throughout the country, so that the emperor and court firmly controlled power everywhere.

events.title: Standardizing Script, Currency and Measures
events.short: Qin Shi Huang standardized writing on the small seal script, currency on the round, square-holed banliang coin, and weights, measures and axle widths, promoting trade, cultural exchange and unity.
events.detail: In the Warring States the divided states each had different writing, currency, weights and measures and even cart axle widths, which made governing the unified state and travel between regions very inconvenient. To consolidate unification, Qin Shi Huang adopted a series of measures. For writing, he had Chancellor Li Si and others standardize the script, taking Qin writing as the base and promulgating the regular small seal script as the standard across the country, along with model texts for learning to write; meanwhile a simpler clerical script became popular in popular and official documents. Unified writing let government orders pass smoothly through the country and people everywhere communicate, which was of great significance for transmitting and developing Chinese culture. For currency, Qin Shi Huang abolished the knife money, spade money, ant-nose money and other coins of the six states and made gold the upper currency and the round, square-holed Qin “banliang” copper coin the lower currency, circulated throughout the country. The round, square-holed coin was easy to carry and count and remained in use until the end of the Qing, influencing more than two thousand years. For weights and measures, the Qin system became the standard for the whole country, with the state making standard instruments; many measures and weights are inscribed with an edict of Qin Shi Huang on standardization. Qin also unified cart axle widths, setting the width at six chi, “the same axle width for all carts,” and built imperial roads and straight roads from Xianyang to all parts of the country to aid transport and troop movement.
