events.title: Digging the Lingqu Canal and Taking Lingnan
events.short: Qin Shi Huang sent troops south against the Baiyue, set up Guilin, Nanhai and Xiang commanderies, and dug the Lingqu Canal to link the Xiang and Li rivers, joining the Yangtze and Pearl River systems.
events.detail: The Yue were an old people of southern China, living along the southeastern coast and in the Pearl River basin; because they had many tribes they were called the “Hundred Yue” (Baiyue). After unifying the six states, Qin Shi Huang sent Tu Sui with several hundred thousand troops by separate routes to attack the Baiyue. Because Lingnan was mountainous and distant, transporting supplies was very difficult, the Qin advance was blocked and the commander Tu Sui was killed by the Yue. To solve the supply problem, Qin Shi Huang ordered the Supervising Censor Lu (called “Shi Lu” in the histories) to dig a canal in present-day Xing'an County, Guangxi: the Lingqu. The Lingqu made clever use of the terrain: a diversion head split the upper Xiang River into the South Canal and North Canal, the large and small “Tianping” weirs regulated the water level, and “doumen” (a kind of lock) overcame differences in water level, letting boats cross the Yuecheng Range and linking the Xiang and Li rivers, thus connecting the Yangtze and Pearl River systems. The Lingqu was opened around 214 BC; over 30 km long, it is among the oldest surviving canals in the world and, with the Dujiangyan and Zhengguo Canal, is called one of the three great water works of the Qin. Once it was open, supplies reached the front without interruption, and in 214 BC Qin unified Lingnan and set up Guilin, Nanhai and Xiang commanderies there, moving several hundred thousand people from the Central Plains to garrison the area and live among the Yue, promoting the development of Lingnan and ethnic integration. At the end of the Qin, Zhao Tuo, commandant of Nanhai, held Lingnan and founded the Nanyue kingdom, which was not brought back under a unified dynasty until Emperor Wu of Han.

events.title: Meng Tian Strikes the Xiongnu; the Great Wall
events.short: Qin Shi Huang sent Meng Tian to strike the Xiongnu and retake the Ordos, and joined and repaired the old Qin, Zhao and Yan walls into a Great Wall from Lintao in the west to Liaodong in the east.
events.detail: The Xiongnu were an old nomadic people of northern China who grew powerful in the Warring States and often raided to the south. After Qin unified China, the northern frontier still faced the Xiongnu threat. In 215 BC Qin Shi Huang sent the general Meng Tian with 300,000 troops to strike them, recovering the land south of the Ordos bend (the “Land South of the River”), setting up commanderies such as Jiuyuan and moving people from the interior there to farm and garrison. To strengthen northern defense, Qin Shi Huang ordered Meng Tian to join, repair and extend the old walls of Qin, Zhao and Yan into a Great Wall running from Lintao (present-day Min County, Gansu) in the west to Liaodong in the east, over ten thousand li long: the world-famous “Ten-Thousand-Li Great Wall.” The Qin wall mostly followed the terrain and was equipped with passes, beacon towers and forts, forming a complete defensive system. Building the wall was an enormous task that conscripted several hundred thousand laborers and brought heavy burdens on the people, and the folk tale of “Meng Jiangnü weeping at the Great Wall” reflects their suffering. Qin Shi Huang also had Meng Tian build the “Straight Road” from Yunyang near Xianyang directly to Jiuyuan, over 700 km long, for rapid troop movement. Meng Tian guarded the north for over ten years, and the Xiongnu dared not come south to graze their horses. After Qin Shi Huang died, Zhao Gao and Li Si forged an edict and forced Prince Fusu and Meng Tian to kill themselves. Later the Han, Northern Wei, Northern Qi, Ming and other dynasties all built walls, and the surviving Great Wall is mainly the Ming wall.

events.title: Burning of Books and Burying of Scholars
events.short: To control thought, Qin Shi Huang burned private copies of the Poems, Documents and philosophers on Li Si's advice, and the next year buried over 460 scholars alive.
events.detail: After Qin unified China, some Confucian scholars and men of letters still used the past to criticize the present, urged a return to enfeoffment and criticized Qin policy. In 213 BC Qin Shi Huang gave a banquet at the Xianyang palace, where the erudite Chunyu Yue proposed following the ancients in enfeoffing sons and meritorious officials. Chancellor Li Si firmly opposed this, arguing that scholars “using the past to criticize the present” would disturb people's minds and threaten unification, and proposed that, except for Qin's own histories and practical books on medicine, divination and tree planting, the Poems, Documents and works of the hundred schools held by private persons be delivered to officials and burned within a time limit; anyone daring to discuss the Poems and Documents would be executed, anyone using the past to criticize the present would have his clan wiped out, and those wishing to study the law should take officials as their teachers. Qin Shi Huang adopted the proposal, and many pre-Qin texts were lost as a result: this is the “burning of books.” The next year, 212 BC, the alchemists Hou Sheng and Lu Sheng, who had been seeking elixirs for Qin Shi Huang, slandered him and fled; the furious emperor ordered an investigation of the scholars in Xianyang, who informed against one another, and he buried alive more than 460 implicated people at Xianyang: this is the “burying of scholars.” Those buried included both alchemists and Confucians, so some scholars hold that the term “burying of Confucians” is not entirely accurate. His eldest son Fusu remonstrated and was sent north as army supervisor.

events.title: Terracotta Army of Qin Shi Huang's Mausoleum
events.short: In 1974 farmers digging a well near Lintong, Shaanxi, found the Terracotta Army pits of Qin Shi Huang's tomb; three pits hold about 8,000 clay figures, called the “eighth wonder of the world.”
events.detail: The Mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang lies on the northern foot of Mount Li in Lintong District, Xi'an, Shaanxi, the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor in Chinese history. Construction began soon after he took the throne, and after unification hundreds of thousands of convicts and laborers were mobilized, with work lasting nearly forty years. According to the Records of the Grand Historian, a magnificent underground palace was built within, with “mercury for the hundred rivers, the Yangtze, Yellow River and seas,” and it holds countless rare treasures. The tomb park covers about 56 square kilometers. In March 1974 farmers at Xiyang village, Lintong, digging a well about 1.5 km east of the tomb, unexpectedly found fragments of clay figures; archaeologists then excavated and found Pit 1, Pit 2 and Pit 3. The three pits cover over 20,000 square meters and hold about 8,000 clay warriors and horses close to life size, plus tens of thousands of bronze weapons and over 100 wooden chariots. Pit 1, the largest, is a rectangular formation of infantry mixed with chariots; Pit 2 is an L-shaped formation of crossbowmen, cavalry and charioteers; Pit 3 is thought to be the command post for the three armies. The figures are mostly about 1.8 m tall, each lifelike and different in expression, and were originally painted in bright colors. In 1980 two large painted bronze chariots and horses were found west of the tomb, made with great delicacy. The discovery of the Terracotta Army is one of the most important Chinese archaeological achievements of the 20th century, hailed as the “eighth wonder of the world.” In 1987 the Mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang and the Terracotta Army pits were inscribed on the World Heritage List.

events.title: Chen Sheng and Wu Guang Uprising
events.short: In 209 BC Chen Sheng and Wu Guang rose at Daze Township, crying “Are kings and nobles born to their rank?”, set up the Zhang Chu regime and began the uprisings against Qin.
events.detail: After the Qin dynasty was founded, its rulers were impatient and tyrannical. Qin Shi Huang levied heavy taxes and conscripted labor and soldiers on a large scale: more than 700,000 for building the Mount Li tomb and Epang Palace, 500,000 for the campaign against the Baiyue and 400,000 for the Great Wall, when the country's population was about 20 million. Qin laws were harsh and punishments cruel, and one person's crime implicated relatives and neighbors. After Qin Shi Huang's death his son Hu Hai, the Second Emperor, took the throne and ruled still more brutally, and social conflict reached an unprecedented pitch. In 209 BC the court conscripted 900 poor peasants to garrison Yuyang (southwest of present-day Miyun, Beijing). When the column reached Daze Township in Qi County (southeast of present-day Suzhou, Anhui), days of heavy rain blocked the road and they could not arrive on time. Under Qin law, soldiers who missed the deadline were to be beheaded. Chen Sheng and Wu Guang killed the officers escorting them and called for revolt. Chen Sheng shouted the slogan “Are kings, nobles, generals and ministers born to their rank?” They “cut wood for weapons and raised bamboo poles for banners,” flew the banner of “Great Chu,” and rallied support with devices such as the “cinnabar writing in the fish's belly” and the “fox cry by the campfire.” The rebels quickly took Chen County (present-day Huaiyang, Henan), where Chen Sheng declared himself king with the state name “Zhang Chu.” People everywhere rose in response, killing Qin officials, and the anti-Qin struggle spread across the country. Later the rebels' westward advance was checked, Chen Sheng was killed by a traitor and Wu Guang by his own officers, and the uprising failed after about half a year.

events.title: Battle of Julu and Fall of Qin
events.short: In 207 BC Xiang Yu destroyed the main Qin army at Julu by burning his boats and smashing his cauldrons; Liu Bang entered Guanzhong, Ziying surrendered, and the Qin dynasty fell.
events.detail: After the Chen Sheng and Wu Guang uprising failed, anti-Qin struggles continued everywhere, and the forces led by Xiang Yu and Liu Bang grew into the main anti-Qin forces. In 208 BC the Qin general Zhang Han, having defeated Xiang Liang, crossed the Yellow River northward to attack Zhao and sent Wang Li to besiege King Xie of Zhao at Julu (southwest of present-day Pingxiang, Hebei), with a Qin force said to number 400,000. King Huai of Chu sent Song Yi as commander and Xiang Yu as deputy to relieve Zhao, and sent Liu Bang west to Guanzhong, agreeing that “whoever enters Guanzhong first shall be king there.” Song Yi lingered at Anyang for over forty days without advancing; Xiang Yu killed him and took command. In 207 BC, after crossing the Zhang River, Xiang Yu ordered the cooking pots smashed, the ferry boats sunk and the tents burned, each man carrying only three days' food, to show a fight to the death, the origin of the idiom “smash the cauldrons and sink the boats.” The Chu troops, each fighting like ten, won nine battles in nine, broke the Qin army and captured Wang Li, and the lords' troops who had watched from the walls did not dare look up at Xiang Yu. Soon Zhang Han surrendered with 200,000 Qin troops. The Battle of Julu, a victory of the few over the many, destroyed Qin's main force and laid the basis for its overthrow. Meanwhile Liu Bang avoided the main Qin army, entered Wu Pass in the west and pressed on Xianyang. Inside Qin, Zhao Gao killed the Second Emperor and made Ziying king of Qin, and Ziying then killed Zhao Gao by a ruse. In 207 BC Ziying surrendered to Liu Bang outside Xianyang, and Qin fell.

events.title: Chu–Han Contention and Founding of the Western Han
events.short: After Qin fell, Xiang Yu and Liu Bang fought the four-year Chu–Han contention; Liu Bang, good at using talent and winning hearts, defeated Xiang Yu at Gaixia and founded the Western Han in 202 BC.
events.detail: After Qin's fall, Xiang Yu, with a large army, entered the pass, killed King Ziying of Qin, burned the Xianyang palaces, declared himself Hegemon-King of Western Chu with his capital at Pengcheng, and enfeoffed eighteen kings, making Liu Bang King of Han over Ba, Shu and Hanzhong. Soon discontent arose everywhere over Xiang Yu's unfair enfeoffments, and Liu Bang took advantage, adopting Han Xin's plan to “openly repair the plank road while secretly crossing at Chencang,” retook Guanzhong and began the war for the realm with Xiang Yu, known as the “Chu–Han contention.” The war lasted about four years. Xiang Yu was brave and strong but willful and reliant on force, repeatedly massacring cities and unable to use talent; even his one adviser, Fan Zeng, left out of suspicion. Liu Bang, by contrast, won the people's hearts and knew how to use men: Xiao He held Guanzhong and supplied the rear, Zhang Liang made plans and Han Xin led the troops, and his side gradually grew from weak to strong. The two sides faced each other for a long time around Xingyang and Chenggao, then agreed to divide the realm at Honggou, the origin of the “Chu River and Han border” of chess. In 202 BC Liu Bang, joined by Han Xin, Peng Yue, Ying Bu and others, besieged Xiang Yu at Gaixia (southeast of present-day Lingbi, Anhui). At night Han troops sang Chu songs on all sides; Xiang Yu, thinking Chu had fallen entirely to Han, sang a sad farewell to his consort Yu and broke out with some 800 horsemen, finally killing himself at the Wu River. That year Liu Bang proclaimed himself emperor and founded the Han dynasty, later with its capital at Chang'an, known as the Western Han; Liu Bang was Emperor Gaozu of Han.

events.title: Rest and Recovery and the Rule of Wen and Jing
events.short: Early Western Han policy gave the people rest: Emperors Wen and Jing lowered taxes and labor, abolished mutilating punishments and promoted thrift, restoring the economy in the “Rule of Wen and Jing.”
events.detail: After the wars of the late Qin, the economy was badly damaged and the early Western Han landscape was ruined and desolate; population had fallen sharply, the emperor could not find four horses of the same color for his carriage, and some generals and ministers had to ride in ox carts. Emperor Gaozu of Han, Liu Bang, learning from the Qin's quick fall through tyranny, adopted a policy of rest and recovery: soldiers were demobilized to return home and farm, those who had become slaves through war and famine were freed as commoners, and refugees were encouraged to return home; taxes and labor were lightened, with the land tax set at “one fifteenth.” After Gaozu's death, Emperor Hui and Empress Dowager Lü continued the policy, governing by the Daoist Huang-Lao idea of “governing by non-action.” Under Emperors Wen and Jing, rulers paid more attention to agriculture, took farming as the foundation, repeatedly issued edicts urging farming and sericulture, and cut the land tax to “one thirtieth”; under Wen it was even waived for over ten years. They also reduced labor service so that adult men served once every three years. Stressing “transforming the people by virtue,” they abolished the crimes of slander and the law of collective punishment and mutilating punishments. Emperor Wen advocated thrift in governing; during his twenty-odd years on the throne, palaces, gardens, carriages and clothing were not added to, and when he wanted to build a terrace but heard it would cost the wealth of ten middle-class families, he gave it up.

events.title: Rebellion of the Seven States
events.short: Emperor Jing cut the lords' lands on Chao Cuo's advice; in 154 BC Wu, Chu and five other states rebelled to “purge the court,” but were crushed in three months.
events.detail: In the early Western Han, Emperor Gaozu Liu Bang, while using commanderies and counties, also enfeoffed a number of kings of his own surname, hoping they would guard the center. As the economy recovered and grew, the kings' power swelled: they held large lands and populations, appointed officials and levied taxes themselves, even minted coins and boiled salt and smelted iron, gradually becoming a regional power threatening the center. Liu Bi, King of Wu, grew rich from minting coins at the copper mountains in his state and boiling seawater for salt and did not come to court for over twenty years. Under Emperor Wen, Jia Yi proposed to “enfeoff many lords and reduce their strength.” After Emperor Jing took the throne he adopted the Plan for Reducing the Domains of Imperial Secretary Chao Cuo and began cutting the kings' lands. In 154 BC Liu Bi, King of Wu, joined the kings of Chu, Zhao, Jiaoxi, Jiaodong, Zichuan and Jinan in a revolt under the slogan “execute Chao Cuo and purge the court,” known as the “Rebellion of the Seven States.” Emperor Jing took Yuan Ang's advice and executed Chao Cuo, but the rebels did not withdraw. He then sent Grand Commandant Zhou Yafu to put down the revolt. Zhou Yafu avoided the rebels' main force, held Changyi and sent light cavalry to cut the Wu–Chu supply line; the rebels, out of food, collapsed, Liu Bi fled to Eastern Yue and was killed, the other kings killed themselves or were executed, and the revolt was put down in about three months. Afterwards Emperor Jing took the opportunity to recover the kings' powers to appoint officials and levy taxes, forbidding the kings to govern their states and leaving them only to live off taxes, reducing the status of the kingdoms to that of commanderies.

events.title: Zhang Qian Opens the Western Regions
events.short: In 138 BC and 119 BC Zhang Qian made two hazardous missions to the Western Regions, opening a route west from the Central Plains, a feat later praised as “boring through the void.”
events.detail: Under the Han, the lands west of Yangguan and Yumen passes (in today's Gansu) were called the Western Regions: in the narrow sense the area of modern Xinjiang, in the broad sense also Central and West Asia and beyond. In the early Western Han the region was divided among many small states, mostly under Xiongnu control, and the Xiongnu used it as a base for raids on the Central Plains. Emperor Wu learned that the Yuezhi had been driven west by the Xiongnu and resented them, so he called for envoys to seek an alliance against the Xiongnu. The court attendant Zhang Qian volunteered. In 138 BC he left Chang'an with over a hundred men. He was held by the Xiongnu for ten years and even married and had a son there, but never gave up his Han envoy's credentials. He eventually escaped and reached the Yuezhi by way of Dayuan and Kangju, only to find them settled in new lands and unwilling to fight the Xiongnu again. On the way back he was detained by the Xiongnu for over a year more, and reached Chang'an in 126 BC with only two of his original party. In 119 BC, after the Han defeated the Xiongnu, Zhang Qian went west a second time, reached the Wusun, and sent deputies to Dayuan, Kangju, the Yuezhi, Parthia, Shendu (India) and other states. Envoys from the Western Regions then visited Chang'an in turn, and contacts grew steadily. Zhang Qian was ennobled as Marquis of Bowang. His missions opened the way to the Western Regions and Central Asia, which Sima Qian called “boring through the void.” They laid the groundwork for the Silk Road, promoted economic and cultural exchange, and prepared the way for the Han to set up the Protector General of the Western Regions.

events.date: Reign of Emperor Wu of Han
events.title: Honoring Confucianism, Dismissing Other Schools
events.short: Emperor Wu took Dong Zhongshu's advice, made Confucianism the orthodox ideology, appointed Erudites of the Five Classics and founded the Imperial Academy, so Confucianism became dominant.
events.detail: In the early Western Han, rulers followed the Huang-Lao doctrine of “governing by non-action,” and the Hundred Schools all circulated freely. As the state grew stronger, non-action no longer suited the need for centralized power and unity. After taking the throne, Emperor Wu sought advice on governing. In about 134 BC the Confucian master Dong Zhongshu, in his reply, put forward the doctrines of the “interaction between Heaven and humanity” and “great unity,” urging that whatever lay outside the Six Arts and the teachings of Confucius be cut off and not allowed to advance, so that Confucianism alone be honored and thought unified. Dong kept Confucianism at the core while drawing on Yin-Yang thought and Legalism, and advanced ideas such as the “divine right of kings” and the “Three Bonds and Five Constants,” stressing loyalty to the ruler and observance of ritual. This suited the needs of a consolidated empire and won Emperor Wu's strong approval. The emperor adopted the proposal, made Confucianism the orthodox ideology, and created Erudites of the Five Classics to teach the Confucian canon. In 124 BC he founded the Imperial Academy at Chang'an, using the Poetry, Documents, Rites, Changes and Spring and Autumn Annals as textbooks; graduates who passed examinations could hold office, and commanderies and kingdoms also set up schools. Confucianism was thus joined to the selection of officials, and Confucian scholars entered government at every level. It became the orthodox thought of ancient China, revered by successive dynasties, with a profound influence on politics, education and culture. The Han did not wholly suppress other schools, however; its way of ruling mixed the methods of the hegemon and the true king.

events.date: Reign of Emperor Wu of Han
events.title: The Recommendation System Takes Shape
events.short: Emperor Wu made local recommendation of talent a formal system: each commandery and kingdom nominated men of good character and ability every year, who were examined and then given office.
events.detail: Before the Qin, offices were mostly hereditary among the nobility; the Qin chose officials mainly through military merit. In the early Han the government began trying local recommendation of talent, and Emperor Wen once ordered regions to nominate men who were “worthy, upright and able to speak frankly and remonstrate,” but no fixed system existed. To meet the need for talent in a unified state, Emperor Wu decreed in 134 BC that every commandery and kingdom should nominate one filial son and one honest official each year, known as “recommending the filial and incorrupt” (xiaolian). The recommendation system (chaju) was thus established. Local heads regularly assessed local talent and recommended people on the basis of character and ability, and the court examined them before appointing them. The categories were regular and special: regular ones were held on schedule, mainly xiaolian and xiucai (renamed maocai in the Eastern Han to avoid the name of Emperor Guangwu, Liu Xiu); special ones were decreed as needed, such as the worthy and upright, literary scholars, and those versed in the classics or in law. The system brought in many able men, such as Gongsun Hong, Dong Zhongshu and Zhufu Yan, and broke the aristocratic monopoly on office. But because it depended on local officials' recommendations without objective standards, it was gradually manipulated by great families in the late Eastern Han, giving rise to the saying: “The recommended xiucai cannot read; the recommended filial and incorrupt live apart from their fathers.” In the Wei and Jin it was gradually replaced by the Nine-Rank system, which later developed into the Sui and Tang imperial examinations.

events.date: Reign of Emperor Wu of Han
events.title: The Edict of Extending Favors
events.short: On Zhufu Yan's advice Emperor Wu issued the “Edict of Extending Favors,” letting feudal kings divide their lands among their sons as marquisates, so kingdoms shrank and central power grew.
events.detail: In the early Western Han the feudal kings were powerful: some openly defied officials sent by the court, and some rebelled. Although the Rebellion of the Seven States weakened the kings, certain kingdoms still stretched a thousand li and held dozens of cities, a latent threat to the center, while local magnates also annexed land and defied the authorities. After Emperor Wu took the throne, the minister Zhufu Yan memorialized that forcibly stripping land would provoke resistance and rebellion, as Chao Cuo's attempt to reduce the kingdoms had done; better to let the kings extend their favor to all their sons and divide the kingdom among them as fiefs. In 127 BC Emperor Wu adopted this, decreeing that apart from the eldest legitimate son, who inherited the kingship, a king might divide his land among his other sons as marquisates, with titles set by the emperor. These marquisates belonged to the commanderies and were governed directly by the center. This was the “Edict of Extending Favors.” It seemed a kindness to the kings but in practice made kingdoms ever smaller; they were “weakened without being cut down,” and it provoked little resistance. Emperor Wu later stripped over a hundred marquises of their rank on grounds such as substandard gold offered in sacrifice. To tighten oversight of localities he also divided the realm into 13 inspectorates, each with an inspector who monitored local officials and magnates for the court. After these measures the feudal kings never recovered, the problem of the kingdoms was largely settled, central control grew greatly, and the unity of the Western Han was consolidated.

events.date: Reign of Emperor Wu of Han
events.title: State Salt and Iron Monopolies and the Wuzhu Coin
events.short: Emperor Wu centralized coinage under the court with the standard wuzhu coin and introduced state salt and iron monopolies and price equalization, improving finances and tightening economic control.
events.detail: In the early Western Han, private minting was not fully banned; coins cast by commanderies and individuals varied in weight and the currency was chaotic. The salt and iron trades were mostly in the hands of powerful merchants, who controlled the economic lifeline of the state. During the Rebellion of the Seven States, some profit-minded merchants refused to lend the court money for fear it would lose. Under Emperor Wu, years of war against the Xiongnu and large construction projects strained the treasury. To strengthen control of the economy, he employed Sang Hongyang, from a merchant family, and others to carry out a series of reforms. On currency, casting of wuzhu coins began in 118 BC, and in 113 BC minting was taken over by the central government, with commanderies and kingdoms forbidden to cast coins; an office in the Shanglin Park minted them. The wuzhu coin was of moderate weight and fine make, hard to counterfeit, and remained in use from Emperor Wu's time until the early Tang, over 700 years, one of the longest-circulating coinages in Chinese history. On salt and iron, the court set up salt and iron officials across the country and took over boiling salt, smelting iron and selling them as state monopolies, forbidding private trade. It also introduced the transport-and-equalization and price-stabilization laws, by which the state moved goods between regions and steadied prices, striking at merchants' hoarding. These measures greatly improved state finances and underpinned Emperor Wu's campaigns against the Xiongnu, expansion and water works, though state-run salt and iron suffered from high prices and poor quality. Under Emperor Zhao, a Salt and Iron Conference debated these policies; Huan Kuan later compiled the record as Discourses on Salt and Iron.

events.title: Campaigns Against the Xiongnu (Battle of Mobei)
events.short: Emperor Wu sent Wei Qing and Huo Qubing on repeated campaigns; the Battle of Mobei in 119 BC crushed the Xiongnu main force, leaving “no royal court south of the desert” and securing the frontier.
events.detail: At the end of the Qin and start of the Han, the Xiongnu under Modu Chanyu united the Mongolian steppe and grew powerful, raiding southward constantly. After Emperor Gaozu was besieged at Baideng, the Han adopted “marriage alliances,” sending imperial women and gifts to the chanyu. After the prosperous reigns of Emperors Wen and Jing, the Western Han was strong, and Emperor Wu decided to end this passive stance, building a powerful cavalry to strike back. In 127 BC Wei Qing recovered the Henan region and set up Shuofang Commandery. In 121 BC the young general Huo Qubing twice attacked the Hexi region and defeated the Xiongnu; the Hunye king surrendered with his followers, and the Han set up Wuwei, Jiuquan and other commanderies (later adding Zhangye and Dunhuang), opening the Hexi Corridor to the Western Regions. In 119 BC Emperor Wu sent General-in-Chief Wei Qing and General Huo Qubing, each with 50,000 cavalry, in eastern and western columns deep into the north of the desert, in the largest campaign of the war, the Battle of Mobei. Wei Qing crossed the great desert and met the chanyu's main force; after a day of fierce fighting a gale rose at dusk, and Wei Qing sent troops to envelop both flanks, so that the chanyu was routed and fled. Huo Qubing advanced over 2,000 li north, defeated the Xiongnu Wise King of the Left, killed over 70,000, and pursued them to Mount Lang Juxu (in present-day Mongolia), where he held a sacrifice to Heaven, the “enfeoffment at Lang Juxu,” later the highest honor for a general. After Mobei the Xiongnu main force was crippled and forced to withdraw far away, and the threat to the northern frontier was largely lifted. Huo Qubing's saying, “While the Xiongnu are not destroyed, how can I think of a home?” has been remembered ever since.

events.title: The Silk Road and the Maritime Silk Road
events.short: After Zhang Qian opened the Western Regions, the overland Silk Road linked Eurasia; Emperor Wu also opened sea routes, forming the Maritime Silk Road and fostering East–West exchange.
events.detail: After Zhang Qian's mission, envoys passed frequently between the Han and the Western Regions, and economic and cultural exchange between East and West grew closer. Merchants carried Han silk and other goods from Chang'an through the Hexi Corridor and out of Yangguan and Yumen passes, then along northern and southern routes across the Western Regions and through Central and West Asia to the Mediterranean coast and Europe, bringing back local products to the Central Plains. Because silk was the most representative trade good, the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen named this trans-Eurasian route the “Silk Road” in the 19th century. Along it, Han silk, lacquerware, ironware and techniques such as canal building, well digging and ironworking spread west; walnuts, grapes, pomegranates, alfalfa, fine horses, spices, glass, gems, instruments such as the pipa, and song and dance came into the Central Plains, and Buddhism later entered China the same way. The Romans called China “Seres,” the “land of silk.” The Silk Road was the great artery of ancient East–West contact and did much to promote trade and cultural exchange between China and other countries and regions. Emperor Wu also opened sea routes. From ports such as Xuwen in Guangdong and Hepu in Guangxi, fleets sailed past today's Vietnam, Thailand and the Malay Peninsula as far as Huangzhi (southern India) and Yichengbu (Sri Lanka), forming the prototype of the Maritime Silk Road; routes from the Shandong coast also led to the Korean Peninsula and the Japanese archipelago. In 2014, “Silk Roads: the Routes Network of Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor,” jointly nominated by China, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, was inscribed on the World Heritage List.

events.title: The Taichu Calendar and the 24 Solar Terms
events.short: In 104 BC Emperor Wu issued the Taichu Calendar, which began the year in the first month and was the first to formally include the 24 solar terms, an influence lasting to this day.
events.detail: The early Han used the Qin Zhuanxu Calendar, which began the year in the tenth month. After a century it had drifted from the real heavens. In 104 BC Emperor Wu ordered a revision; Deng Ping, Luoxia Hong, Tang Du, Sima Qian and others compiled a new calendar and issued it that year. Since the era name was changed to Taichu that year, it was called the Taichu Calendar. It began the year in the first month, and for over two thousand years, with few exceptions, China has kept the first month as the start of the year, down to the present lunar calendar. The Taichu Calendar was lunisolar: months followed the moon's phases, with the new moon as the first day of each month and months of 30 or 29 days; years followed the tropical year of a little over 365 days; and a month without a major solar term was made a leap month. Most important, it was the first calendar to formally include the 24 solar terms. Ancient people divided the year into 24 segments of about 15 days each according to the sun's position on the ecliptic: Beginning of Spring, Rain Water, Awakening of Insects, Spring Equinox, Clear and Bright, Grain Rain, Beginning of Summer, Grain Buds, Grain in Ear, Summer Solstice, Minor Heat, Major Heat, Beginning of Autumn, End of Heat, White Dew, Autumn Equinox, Cold Dew, Frost's Descent, Beginning of Winter, Minor Snow, Major Snow, Winter Solstice, Minor Cold and Major Cold. They reflect changes in season, climate and natural phenomena and were vital to farming. The Taichu Calendar was later edited by Liu Xin into the Santong Calendar, China's earliest surviving complete calendar. In 2016 the “Twenty-Four Solar Terms” were inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

events.title: Sima Qian Writes Records of the Grand Historian
events.short: Sima Qian endured disgrace to write Records of the Grand Historian, covering some 3,000 years from the Yellow Emperor to Emperor Wu, China's first universal history in biographical form.
events.detail: Sima Qian (c. 145–c. 86 BC), courtesy name Zichang, a native of Xiayang (present-day Hancheng, Shaanxi), was a great historian and writer of ancient China. His father Sima Tan served under Emperor Wu as Grand Historian, in charge of astronomy, the calendar and the state's records. He read ancient texts at ten and from twenty traveled to famous mountains and rivers gathering material. On his deathbed his father charged him with completing a history; after succeeding as Grand Historian, Sima Qian could read the court's vast collection of records. In 99 BC he angered Emperor Wu by defending Li Ling, who had surrendered to the Xiongnu, and was imprisoned and castrated, suffering terribly in body and spirit. Yet, holding to the thought that “death comes to all, but may be weightier than Mount Tai or lighter than a feather,” he endured the shame and wrote on, completing around 91 BC the great work Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji). It covers about 3,000 years from the legendary Yellow Emperor to the Taichu era of Emperor Wu, in 130 chapters of roughly 520,000 characters: 12 basic annals, 10 tables, 8 treatises, 30 hereditary houses and 70 biographies. It created the biographical form centered on people, later followed by the dynastic “standard histories,” and is China's first universal history in that form and the first of the Twenty-Four Histories. Sima Qian wrote without flattery or concealment; he wrote not only of emperors and ministers but also of knights-errant, merchants and assassins, and placed Chen Sheng among the hereditary houses and Xiang Yu among the basic annals. Vividly written, with sharply drawn figures, it is also a fine work of literature; Lu Xun called it “the historians' unrivaled song, a Lisao without rhyme.”

events.title: Protector General of the Western Regions Set Up
events.short: In 60 BC the Western Han created the Protector General of the Western Regions, seated at Wulei, to oversee the states there, marking the formal incorporation of today's Xinjiang under central rule.
events.detail: After Zhang Qian's mission, the Western Han stepped up its management of the Western Regions. Under Emperor Wu, Han troops campaigned against Dayuan and won its “blood-sweating” horses, and opened military farms at Luntai, Quli and elsewhere under envoy-colonels, securing supplies for envoys and caravans. Under Emperor Xuan the Xiongnu split; the Rizhu king came over to the Han with his followers, and Xiongnu power in the Western Regions collapsed. In 60 BC the Western Han court formally established the Protector General of the Western Regions as the highest military and civil officer for the area. The first holder was Zheng Ji, and the office was based at Wulei (northeast of present-day Luntai, Xinjiang). The Protector General issued Han orders on behalf of the central government, dispatched troops, levied supplies, monitored states such as the Wusun and Kangju, and protected the routes to the west, exercising effective control; at first he oversaw 36 states, later over fifty. His jurisdiction covered today's Xinjiang and the broad areas east and south of Lake Balkhash. Kings and officials of the Western Regions received seals and ribbons from the Han, paid tribute, and sent princes to serve at Chang'an. The creation of the office marked the formal incorporation of the Xinjiang region under central authority, strengthened ties with the Central Plains, promoted the region's economy and kept the Silk Road open. At the end of the Western Han the Xiongnu regained control and contact was briefly cut; in the Eastern Han, Ban Chao spent over thirty years in the region and restored Han authority, and the Eastern Han also established a Protector General and a Chief Clerk of the Western Regions.

events.title: Wang Mang Founds the Xin Dynasty
events.short: Wang Mang, a consort-clan official of the late Western Han, deposed the Han in AD 9 and founded Xin; his idealizing reforms caused unrest and he fell in peasant uprisings.
events.detail: In the late Western Han, land annexation was severe, many peasants lost their land and became vagrants or slaves, and the court grew corrupt, with emperors either weak or very young and consort clans and eunuchs taking power in turn. Wang Mang came from the Wang consort clan; his aunt Wang Zhengjun was Emperor Yuan's empress. In youth he lived frugally and courted scholars, winning a fine name. After Emperor Ai died, Wang Mang became Commander-in-Chief and took charge of government, enthroning Emperor Ping and then the child Ruzi Ying. Using Confucian texts and omens to shape opinion, he deposed the Han in AD 9 and renamed the state “Xin.” As emperor he carried out a series of reforms under the banner of restoring Zhou institutions, known as “Wang Mang's reforms.” All land was renamed “royal land,” banned from sale and redistributed by population; slaves were renamed “private retainers” and could not be traded; under the “five equalizations and six monopolies” the state controlled salt, iron, liquor, coinage and market prices; the currency was changed repeatedly; official and place names were altered often, and the titles of neighboring peoples' chiefs were lowered, causing border conflicts. These measures were impractical and constantly revised; they failed to solve the land and slavery problems and left society more chaotic, and with years of flood and drought the people suffered greatly. From about AD 17, uprisings such as the Lülin and Red Eyebrows broke out. In AD 23 the Lülin army defeated Wang Mang's main force in the Battle of Kunyang against the odds, then entered Chang'an; Wang Mang was killed in the fighting and the Xin ended after only fifteen years. It is regarded as a failed reform, though some modern scholars assess its ideas differently.

events.title: Eastern Han Founded: the “Guangwu Restoration”
events.short: Liu Xiu proclaimed himself emperor in AD 25 and made Luoyang his capital, founding the Eastern Han; freeing slaves, cutting taxes and trimming offices, he brought stability, the “Guangwu Restoration.”
events.detail: After peasant uprisings overthrew Wang Mang, separatist forces rose everywhere. Liu Xiu, a ninth-generation descendant of Liu Bang (Emperor Gaozu) and of Emperor Jing's line, rose with his elder brother Liu Yan at Nanyang at the end of Xin and joined the Lülin army. In AD 23 at the Battle of Kunyang he broke the siege with a small force and, striking with the garrison inside the city, defeated Wang Mang's army of several hundred thousand, winning great fame. He was then sent to manage Hebei, where he gradually built up his strength. In AD 25 Liu Xiu proclaimed himself emperor at Hao (north of present-day Baixiang, Hebei), keeping the Han name, and soon made Luoyang his capital. Because Luoyang lay east of the Western Han capital Chang'an, the dynasty is called the Eastern Han, and Liu Xiu was Emperor Guangwu. Over the next dozen or so years he destroyed the Red Eyebrows and warlords such as Wei Xiao and Gongsun Shu, reuniting the country. To consolidate rule, he repeatedly freed slaves and banned their mistreatment; cut the land tax back to the early Western Han rate of one-thirtieth; eased punishments; merged commanderies and counties, cut officials, tightened supervision and punished corrupt officials; weakened the Three Excellencies and concentrated real power in the Imperial Secretariat; “retired meritorious generals and promoted civil officials,” promoted Confucianism and education; and allowed northern peoples to move inward, easing ethnic tensions. After thirty-odd years of governance, society was fairly stable by the end of his reign, the economy recovered, and the population grew; this is known as the “Guangwu Restoration.” His successors Emperors Ming and Zhang continued similar policies, and the state grew stronger still, in the “Rule of Ming and Zhang.”

events.date: Reign of Emperor Ming of Eastern Han
events.title: Buddhism Arrives and the White Horse Temple
events.short: Buddhism reached China along the Silk Road around the turn of the Western and Eastern Han; under Emperor Ming the White Horse Temple was built at Luoyang, regarded as the first state-built temple.
events.detail: Buddhism, one of the world's three major religions, was founded in the 6th–5th century BC by Siddhartha Gautama (Shakyamuni), a prince of ancient India. It holds that life is full of suffering and that liberation comes only by cutting off desire and affliction; it teaches the equality of all beings, which appealed to poor people yearning for peace, and so spread widely. After Zhang Qian's mission, Buddhism gradually entered China through Central Asia along the Silk Road, and records say sutras were already being transmitted orally in the late Western Han. Tradition says Emperor Ming of the Eastern Han dreamed of a golden man and sent envoys to the Western Regions to seek the teaching; among the Yuezhi they met the Indian monks Kashyapa Matanga and Dharmaratna, and returned to Luoyang in the tenth year of Yongping (AD 67) with sutras and images on a white horse. In AD 68 the emperor ordered a monastery built outside the Yong Gate on the west of Luoyang, and named it the White Horse Temple in memory of the horse that carried the scriptures. It is regarded as the first temple built by the government after Buddhism entered China, honored as the “ancestral court” and “source of Buddhism” in China; thereafter Chinese monasteries were generally called si. Here Kashyapa Matanga and Dharmaratna translated the Sutra in Forty-Two Sections, thought to be the earliest surviving Chinese Buddhist translation. It became widespread only in the Wei, Jin and Northern and Southern Dynasties. It enriched Chinese culture, deeply influencing thought, literature, architecture, sculpture, painting and music, and many Chinese expressions, such as “cause and effect” and “repentance,” come from Buddhist texts.

events.title: Ban Chao Manages the Western Regions
events.short: Under Emperor Ming of the Eastern Han, Ban Chao went to the Western Regions, “threw away the brush for the sword,” and over thirty years restored Han authority there.
events.detail: At the end of the Western Han the Xiongnu regained control of the Western Regions and contact with the Central Plains was cut. In the early Eastern Han the states there, oppressed by the Xiongnu, asked to submit to the Han. Ban Chao was the younger brother of Ban Gu, author of the Book of Han; he earned his living as a copyist in youth and then resolved to emulate Zhang Qian and win merit abroad, “throwing away the brush to join the army.” In AD 73 Emperor Ming sent Dou Gu against the Xiongnu; Ban Chao fought with the army and won merit, then was ordered to lead 36 men as envoys to the Western Regions. In the state of Shanshan, Xiongnu envoys had also arrived and the king was cool toward the Han. Ban Chao said, “Without entering the tiger's den, how can you get the tiger's cub?” and led his men in a night attack on the Xiongnu camp, wiping out the mission, after which the king of Shanshan submitted to the Han. Ban Chao then put down pro-Xiongnu forces in Khotan, Shule and elsewhere, united the states of the Western Regions, and resisted attacks by the Xiongnu and the Kushan Empire. In AD 91 he was appointed Protector General of the Western Regions, stationed at Qiuci, and the next year the Eastern Han restored its authority there, with over fifty states submitting. In AD 97 Ban Chao sent his subordinate Gan Ying to Daqin (the Roman Empire); Gan Ying reached the sea shore at Tiaozhi in western Parthia but turned back because the Parthians exaggerated the dangers of the voyage. It was the farthest west any Chinese envoy had traveled then. After over thirty years in the region, the aged Ban Chao asked to return, writing, “I dare not hope to reach Jiuquan, only to enter Yumen Pass alive.” He came back to Luoyang in AD 102 and died soon after at 71.

events.title: Cai Lun Improves Papermaking
events.short: The Eastern Han eunuch Cai Lun improved papermaking, using bark, hemp waste, rags and old fishing nets, and presented his paper to Emperor He in AD 105; paper gradually replaced bamboo and silk.
events.detail: Before paper, people carved writing on bones and shells, cast it on bronzes, or wrote on bamboo and wooden slips and silk. In the Qin and Han, official documents, letters and books were mostly written on slips and silk; slips were bulky and silk expensive, which greatly limited their use. Later Chinese measure words for books, such as ce, bian and juan, come from the way slips were bound together. In the Western Han people already knew the basics of papermaking, and hemp paper of that period has been found at Fangmatan in Tianshui, Gansu, and at Xuanquanzhi near Dunhuang, but it was coarse and hard to write on. In the Eastern Han the eunuch Cai Lun (d. AD 121), serving as director of the imperial workshops, which made court articles, drew on earlier experience and improved the process, using plant fibers such as bark, hemp waste, rags and old fishing nets, which were chopped, soaked, pounded, formed into sheets and dried, greatly improving paper quality. In AD 105 Cai Lun presented the improved paper to Emperor He, who praised it, and it came into use everywhere as “Marquis Cai's paper.” Cai Lun was later made Marquis of Longting. The raw materials were easy to find, the paper cheap and easy to spread, and its use grew until by the Wei and Jin it had largely replaced bamboo and silk as the main writing material, greatly helping the spread of culture and preservation of texts. Chinese papermaking passed to Korea and Japan, reached the Arab world in the 8th century and then Europe through the Arabs; most papermaking worldwide traces back to China. Papermaking is one of the Four Great Inventions of ancient China and a great contribution to world civilization.

events.title: Zhang Heng Invents the Seismoscope
events.short: Zhang Heng built his wind-and-earthquake instrument in AD 132; it indicated quake direction, registered a Longxi earthquake, and is regarded as the world's earliest seismoscope.
events.detail: Zhang Heng (AD 78–139), courtesy name Pingzi, from Xi'e in Nanyang (present-day Nanyang, Henan), was an outstanding scientist, writer and inventor of the Eastern Han. He twice served as Grand Astrologer, in charge of astronomy and the calendar. In astronomy he put forward the “celestial sphere theory,” likening the heavens to an eggshell and the earth to the yolk, and built a water-driven armillary sphere that vividly demonstrated the motion of the heavens. He also recorded about 2,500 stars and correctly explained the cause of lunar eclipses. Earthquakes were frequent in the Eastern Han, and to track them Zhang Heng built the “wind-and-earthquake instrument” in AD 132. According to the Book of the Later Han, “Biography of Zhang Heng,” it was cast of fine bronze, shaped like a wine vessel, with eight dragons outside facing the eight directions, each holding a bronze ball in its mouth, with an open-mouthed toad beneath each. Inside were a central pillar and mechanisms: when an earthquake struck in some direction, the dragon facing that way released its ball into the toad's mouth, showing the direction of the quake. It is recorded that once the western dragon released its ball while Luoyang felt no tremor, and people doubted it; a few days later a messenger from Longxi reported that an earthquake had indeed occurred, and all were convinced. The instrument is the world's earliest seismoscope, but the original was lost long ago, and those displayed in museums today are reconstructions based on texts. Zhang Heng was also a gifted writer of rhapsodies, author of the Rhapsody on the Two Capitals. In his honor, a crater on the far side of the Moon and an asteroid are named after him.

events.title: Consort Clans and Eunuchs Take Power in Turn
events.short: From the mid-Eastern Han, child emperors let consort clans and eunuchs alternately seize government, appointing cronies and killing rivals, which led the dynasty to decline.
events.detail: From the middle of the Eastern Han, most emperors came to the throne very young, one, Emperor Shang, when only a little over a hundred days old, and could not rule themselves, so power fell to the empress dowager. The empress dowager often relied on her father, brothers and other relatives, so the consort clans swelled in power and took control of government. When the emperor grew up he resented being managed by them and wished to exercise power himself, but could only rely on the eunuchs who attended him daily, and plotted with them to remove the consort clan; the eunuchs thereby won trust and power. A new emperor would often repeat the cycle, producing the alternation of consort clans and eunuchs in the middle and late Eastern Han. For example, Emperor He relied on the eunuch Zheng Zhong to remove Dou Xian of the Dou clan; Liang Ji of the Liang clan successively enthroned Emperors Chong, Zhi and Huan and monopolized power for over twenty years, and when Emperor Zhi called him an “arrogant general,” he poisoned the boy emperor; later Emperor Huan joined five eunuchs including Shan Chao to kill Liang Ji, and all five were made marquises on the same day. With consort clans and eunuchs taking turns holding power, appointing cronies, selling offices and killing opponents, government grew thoroughly rotten, upright officials were shut out and framed, taxes and corvée mounted, and the people suffered. Officials and Imperial Academy students who attacked the eunuchs were slandered as a “partisan faction,” and two “Partisan Prohibitions” under Emperors Huan and Ling saw many scholars killed, exiled or barred from office. This vicious cycle badly shook the Eastern Han's foundations and sent it into decline, until it fell apart in the Yellow Turban Rebellion and warlord wars.

events.title: The Rise of Daoism
events.short: In the late Eastern Han, Zhang Jue founded the Way of Great Peace and Zhang Ling the Way of the Five Pecks of Rice, both venerating Laozi and healing with talisman water, forming early Daoism.
events.detail: Daoism is a religion native to China. It takes the “Dao” as its highest belief, draws on immortality arts and Huang-Lao thought, and seeks to attain the Dao and become immortal. After the middle of the Eastern Han, politics were dark, society unstable, and natural disasters and plagues frequent; the people's extreme suffering and need for spiritual refuge provided fertile ground for Daoism's rise. The Scripture of Great Peace (Taiping Jing) became an important early Daoist text. In the late Eastern Han, Zhang Jue of Julu founded the Way of Great Peace based on that scripture, venerating the Yellow Emperor and Laozi and absorbing popular immortality arts. Calling himself the “Great Worthy Teacher,” he healed the sick with talisman water and spread his teaching, finding favor among the poor. In over ten years he gained several hundred thousand followers across eight provinces, whom he organized into 36 divisions, and on that basis he later launched the Yellow Turban Rebellion. Meanwhile Zhang Ling (later called Zhang Daoling) founded the Way of the Five Pecks of Rice at Heming Mountain in Shu (in present-day Dayi, Sichuan), so named because entrants paid five pecks of rice; it honored Laozi as its patriarch and took the Laozi in Five Thousand Characters as its scripture. The two were the main early Daoist branches, followed mainly by lower-class people. The Five Pecks of Rice later developed into the Way of the Celestial Masters, and Zhang Ling was revered as the “Celestial Master Zhang.” After the Wei and Jin, Ge Hong, Kou Qianzhi, Tao Hongjing and others systematized Daoist theory. Daoism influenced ancient Chinese philosophy, medicine, chemistry, literature, art and folk customs.

images.caption: Mount Qingcheng, Chengdu, Sichuan

events.title: The Yellow Turban Rebellion
events.short: In AD 184 Zhang Jue led followers of the Way of Great Peace in the Yellow Turban Rebellion, crying “The blue heaven is dead”; though suppressed, it dealt the Eastern Han a heavy blow.
events.detail: In the late Eastern Han, consort clans and eunuchs held power and government was deeply corrupt, land annexation was severe and taxes and corvée heavy; floods, droughts, locusts and plagues struck often, driving the poor from their homes, even to “people eating one another”. Zhang Jue of Julu founded the Way of Great Peace, healing with talisman water and preaching, and after over ten years among the lowest classes had several hundred thousand followers in eight provinces. He organized them into 36 divisions and raised the slogan “The blue heaven is dead, the yellow heaven shall rise; in the year jiazi, all under heaven will be blessed,” setting an uprising for the fifth day of the third month of the jiazi year (AD 184). After a betrayal, Zhang Jue was forced to rise early, in the second month. The rebels wore yellow cloth on their heads as a mark and were called the Yellow Turbans; Zhang Jue styled himself “General of Heaven,” and his brothers Zhang Bao and Zhang Liang “General of Earth” and “General of Man.” The capital was shaken. The court sent Huangfu Song, Zhu Jun, Lu Zhi and others to suppress them, lifted the Partisan Prohibitions, and allowed magnates to raise armed forces to join in. Zhang Jue died of illness during the revolt, Zhang Liang and Zhang Bao fell in battle, and the main uprising was put down after about nine months, though Yellow Turban remnants kept fighting for over twenty years. It was the first organized, prepared large-scale peasant uprising in Chinese history. In suppressing it, local magnates and governors built up armies of their own and became regional warlords; the Eastern Han survived in name only, and China entered an age of warlord wars and the Three Kingdoms.

images.caption: Liu Bei, Guan Yu and Zhang Fei take part in putting down the Yellow Turban Rebellion

events.title: Zhang Zhongjing and the Treatise on Cold Damage
events.short: The physician Zhang Zhongjing wrote the Treatise on Cold Damage and Miscellaneous Diseases, establishing pattern-based treatment; he is honored as the “Sage of Medicine.”
events.detail: Traditional Chinese medicine has a long history and by the Han had reached a high level. Bian Que of the Warring States summed up the four diagnostic methods still used today; the Yellow Emperor's Inner Canon laid the theoretical foundation of Chinese medicine; and the Divine Husbandman's Classic of Materia Medica is China's earliest surviving pharmacological work. Zhang Zhongjing, personal name Ji, from Nieyang in Nanyang Commandery (around present-day Dengzhou, Henan), was a famous physician of the late Eastern Han. Tradition says that as governor of Changsha he treated patients in his official hall, the origin of the term “sitting in the hall” (zuotang) for a doctor seeing patients. In the late Eastern Han, with frequent wars and epidemics, his clan of over two hundred lost two-thirds in under ten years, seven-tenths of them to cold damage (typhoid-type illness). Grieved, he resolved to study medicine, sought out famous doctors, collected folk prescriptions, and, drawing on earlier work and his own practice, wrote the Treatise on Cold Damage and Miscellaneous Diseases in sixteen volumes. It systematically describes the causes, symptoms, diagnosis and treatment of many externally contracted and internal diseases, proposes the principle of “treatment by pattern differentiation,” matching drugs to a patient's symptoms and constitution, and records many effective formulas, earning it the name “ancestor of formula books.” The original was lost in wartime; edited by Wang Shuhe of the Jin and others, it survives as two classics, the Treatise on Cold Damage and the Essential Prescriptions of the Golden Cabinet. Zhang Zhongjing is honored as the “Sage of Medicine,” also influential in Japan and Korea.

images.caption: Portrait of Zhang Zhongjing
Medical Sage Shrine, Nanyang, Henan

events.title: Hua Tuo and the “Mafeisan” Anesthetic
events.short: The late Eastern Han physician Hua Tuo excelled at surgery, invented the general anesthetic “mafeisan,” and devised the “Five Animals' Frolic,” an exercise routine imitating five animals.
events.detail: Hua Tuo, courtesy name Yuanhua, from Qiao county in the state of Pei (present-day Bozhou, Anhui), was an outstanding physician of the late Eastern Han, ranked with Dong Feng and Zhang Zhongjing as one of the “three divine doctors of the Jian'an era.” He was skilled in internal medicine, surgery, gynecology, pediatrics and acupuncture, especially surgery, and is honored as the “founder of surgery.” Hua Tuo invented “mafeisan”: the patient took it with wine and, once unconscious, underwent surgery such as opening the abdomen; afterward the wound was sewn and dressed with ointment, and healed in about a month. This is an early record of general anesthesia, over a thousand years before Western surgery used anesthetics. Unfortunately the formula is lost. Hua Tuo also valued disease prevention. He held that the body needs proper exercise, as a door hinge that turns often does not rot: “With movement the grain energy is dispersed, the blood flows, and illness cannot arise.” Imitating the movements of the tiger, deer, bear, ape and bird, he devised the exercises known as the “Five Animals' Frolic” to strengthen the body. According to the Book of the Later Han, “Biography of Hua Tuo,” his disciple Wu Pu practiced them for years and in his nineties still had sharp hearing and sight and firm, intact teeth. He practiced across today's Jiangsu, Shandong, Henan and Anhui, leaving many legendary tales. He cared nothing for office; when Cao Cao, suffering from headaches, summoned him as attending physician, Hua Tuo went home claiming his wife was ill and would not return, and Cao Cao had him jailed and executed. His medical writings were thereby lost. “Hua Tuo reborn” is still used to praise a skilled doctor, and the Five Animals' Frolic survives as a traditional form of exercise.

events.title: Battle of Guandu
events.short: In AD 200 Cao Cao defeated a far larger force at Guandu, raiding Wuchao to burn Yuan Shao's grain and crushing his main army, which laid the basis for unifying the north.
events.detail: At the end of the Eastern Han, warlords fought for control after the Yellow Turban Rebellion. Cao Cao, who held Yan and Yu provinces, sought the political initiative and in AD 196 brought Emperor Xian from Luoyang to Xu (east of present-day Xuchang, Henan), commanding the realm in the emperor's name, “holding the emperor to command the lords.” He recruited talent widely, promoting by ability regardless of origin, and ran military farms in which soldiers and refugees tilled land, which both settled many refugees and secured ample army grain, steadily growing his strength. Yuan Shao, who held the four provinces of Ji, Qing, You and Bing, was of a famous family with many troops and plentiful grain, and was the strongest warlord in the north. Both wanted to absorb the other and dominate the north. In AD 200 Yuan Shao led 100,000 men south against Cao Cao's base at Xu. Cao Cao, with fewer troops and less grain, led his main force to build fortifications at Guandu (northeast of present-day Zhongmou, Henan) and held the line for months. Yuan Shao's adviser Xu You, whose advice was rejected, defected to Cao Cao and told him that Yuan's grain was stored at Wuchao with lax defense. Cao Cao decided at once, led 5,000 elite troops under Yuan's banners in a night raid on Wuchao, and burned all the grain. When news came, Yuan's army fell into panic, generals such as Zhang He surrendered to Cao Cao, the main army collapsed, and Yuan Shao fled back to Hebei with only some 800 horsemen. Guandu is a famous case of victory against the odds in Chinese history. Yuan Shao died soon after in despair, and over the next few years Cao Cao destroyed the remaining Yuan forces and defeated the Wuhuan, largely unifying the north and laying the base for Cao Wei's strength in the Three Kingdoms.

images.caption: Cao Cao defeating Yuan Shao, illustration from Zhou Yuexiao's edition of Romance of the Three Kingdoms
images.author: Zhou Yuejiao (before 1640)

events.title: Battle of Red Cliffs
events.short: In AD 208 the allied forces of Sun Quan and Liu Bei used fire attack at Red Cliffs to defeat Cao Cao's army of over 200,000; Cao Cao withdrew north, setting the stage for the Three Kingdoms.
events.detail: After unifying the north, Cao Cao marched south in AD 208 intending to destroy the southern powers and unify the country. Earlier, Liu Bei had won over Zhuge Liang, who set out the strategy of allying with Sun against Cao. When Cao Cao came south, Liu Biao, governor of Jing Province, died and his son Liu Cong surrendered; Cao's army took Jing Province, and Liu Bei withdrew from Fancheng to Xiakou. Liu Bei sent Zhuge Liang to Chaisang to contact Sun Quan. Heeding Zhou Yu, Lu Su and Zhuge Liang, Sun Quan resolved to ally with Liu Bei against Cao and appointed Zhou Yu as commander. Cao's army was claimed to be 800,000 but was actually over 200,000, while the Sun–Liu force was only about 50,000; the two sides faced each other at Red Cliffs (generally thought to be on the south bank of the Yangtze northwest of present-day Chibi, Hubei). Cao's troops had marched far and were weary; many were northerners unused to naval war and the climate, and disease spread in the camp. They lost the first clash and withdrew to Wulin on the north bank, where Cao Cao chained his warships bow to stern. Zhou Yu's subordinate Huang Gai, noting this, proposed a fire attack and a feigned surrender to Cao Cao. Huang Gai led ships loaded with oil-soaked brush before the southeast wind toward Cao's camp and set them alight as they closed; the burning ships drove into the fleet, the fire spread quickly to the camps ashore, and Cao's army suffered heavy losses. The allies pursued, and Cao Cao retreated north with his remnants by the Huarong Road. Red Cliffs is a famous battle in which the weaker side won. Afterward Cao Cao was unable to move south for a time, Sun Quan consolidated his rule in Jiangdong, and Liu Bei took parts of Jing Province and expanded west, laying the basis for the Three Kingdoms.

events.title: The Three Kingdoms Take Shape
events.short: Cao Pi became emperor and founded Wei in AD 220, Liu Bei founded Shu Han in 221, and Sun Quan founded Wu in 229, creating the three-way division of Wei, Shu and Wu.
events.detail: After Red Cliffs, Cao Cao turned to Guanzhong, put down its separatist forces and completed the unification of the north; Liu Bei first took part of Jing Province, then seized Yi Province and Hanzhong, controlling today's Sichuan, Chongqing, Yunnan, Guizhou and part of Hubei; Sun Quan consolidated Jiangdong and extended his rule to today's Fujian and Guangdong. In AD 220 Cao Cao died, and his son Cao Pi deposed Emperor Xian of Han and took the throne at Luoyang under the name Wei, ending the Eastern Han. In 221 Liu Bei proclaimed himself emperor at Chengdu under the name Han, known as Shu Han or Shu. In 222 Sun Quan was made King of Wu by Wei and that year defeated Liu Bei at the Battle of Yiling; in 229 Sun Quan formally became emperor under the name Wu and soon made Jianye (present-day Nanjing, Jiangsu) his capital. The three-way division of Wei, Shu and Wu was complete. In the Three Kingdoms period each state worked to restore and develop its economy: Cao Wei ran military farms and built water works and was the strongest; Shu Han under Zhuge Liang developed agriculture and Shu brocade and pacified the peoples of the southwest; Eastern Wu developed Jiangdong and had a thriving shipbuilding industry, once sending Wei Wen with a fleet to Yizhou (present-day Taiwan). The division ended the long warfare of the late Eastern Han, promoted the development of Jiangnan and the southwest, and prepared for later reunification. Wei destroyed Shu in 263, Sima Yan replaced Wei with the Western Jin in 266, and the Western Jin destroyed Wu in 280, ending the Three Kingdoms. Chen Shou's Records of the Three Kingdoms, and the novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms written from it by Luo Guanzhong in the late Yuan and early Ming, spread the history widely among the people.

events.title: Wei Wen's Fleet Reaches Yizhou (Taiwan)
events.short: In AD 230 Sun Quan, King of Wu, sent the generals Wei Wen and Zhuge Zhi with a fleet of 10,000 men to Yizhou (today's Taiwan), an early clear record of contact between the mainland and Taiwan.
events.detail: In the Three Kingdoms period, the state of Eastern Wu, based in Jiangdong, paid great attention to naval strength. Wu's shipbuilding was well developed and could make ships of large capacity. It actively developed sea travel, sending people to Liaodong and Hainan Island, and sending Zhu Ying and Kang Tai as envoys to Funan (around today's Cambodia) and other Southeast Asian states. In AD 230 Sun Quan, King of Wu, sent the generals Wei Wen and Zhuge Zhi with 10,000 armored men by sea to Yizhou and Danzhou. After nearly a year's voyage the fleet reached Yizhou but never found Danzhou. Many soldiers fell sick and died from the unfamiliar climate, and the fleet later returned to the mainland with several thousand Yizhou inhabitants. Wei Wen and Zhuge Zhi were jailed and executed for “disobeying the edict and achieving nothing.” The Wu author Shen Ying's Gazetteer of the Lands and Waters of Linhai recorded Yizhou's climate, products and the customs of its people, matching Taiwan's character, and is one of the earliest written records of Taiwan in the world. Scholars generally agree Yizhou is today's Taiwan. Wei Wen's voyage is an early clear record of a mainland regime sending a large fleet to Taiwan; it strengthened ties between the mainland and Taiwan and shows that close contact between the two has existed since early times. Later, the Sui sent people to Liuqiu three times, the Yuan set up an Inspectorate at Penghu, Zheng Chenggong recovered Taiwan at the end of the Ming, and the Qing established a prefecture there, so that ties between Taiwan and the mainland grew ever closer.

events.title: Western Jin Founded; Wu Conquered
events.short: Sima Yan replaced Wei in AD 266, founding the Western Jin with its capital at Luoyang; the Jin destroyed Wu in 280, ending the near-century of division since the late Eastern Han.
events.detail: In the late Three Kingdoms, Wei grew steadily stronger while Wu and Shu declined. Within Wei, the minister Sima Yi repeatedly led armies against Zhuge Liang's northern expeditions for Shu Han, and his power rose. In AD 249, while Emperor Cao Fang and General-in-Chief Cao Shuang were away at a tomb visit, Sima Yi staged the Gaopingling Incident, killing Cao Shuang and taking control of Wei's military and government. After his death his sons Sima Shi and Sima Zhao held power in turn, and Wei's emperors were puppets. In 263 Sima Zhao sent Zhong Hui, Deng Ai and others against Shu; Deng Ai crossed by the Yinping mountain path to Chengdu, the last Shu emperor Liu Shan surrendered, and Shu Han fell. In 266 Sima Zhao's son Sima Yan forced Emperor Yuan of Wei, Cao Huan, to abdicate and took the throne, renaming the state Jin and keeping Luoyang as capital, called the Western Jin; Sima Yan was Emperor Wu of Jin. The last Wu emperor, Sun Hao, ruled cruelly and corruptly. In 279 Emperor Wu sent Du Yu, Wang Jun and others in six columns against Wu; Wang Jun's tower ships, built in Yizhou, sailed down the Yangtze, broke the iron chains Wu had laid, and advanced on Jianye. In 280 Sun Hao surrendered and Wu fell; the Western Jin reunified the country, ending the near-century of division since the late Eastern Han. Early on, land-occupation and household-tax systems brought the “Taikang Era Prosperity.” But the Jin house and many ministers came from great aristocratic and landlord families, the court gave generous privileges to the gentry clans, and the ruling class lived in corrupt luxury. Emperor Wu also enfeoffed many imperial kin as kings and let them command troops, sowing the seeds of civil strife, and the Western Jin's unity lasted only a few decades.

events.date: Reign of Emperor Hui of Western Jin (over a dozen years)
events.title: War of the Eight Princes
events.short: Under Emperor Hui of the Western Jin, eight imperial princes with large armies fought for over a decade for control of the court, the “War of the Eight Princes,” which left the Western Jin in decline.
events.detail: In the early Western Jin, Emperor Wu, Sima Yan, believed that Cao Wei had been usurped by the Sima because it had weakened its imperial princes, leaving the throne isolated. He therefore enfeoffed many kin as kings and sent them to garrison important regions such as Xuchang, Ye and Chang'an. These princes commanded troops and also ran local civil government, and their power grew. Emperor Wu died in AD 290, and the crown prince Sima Zhong took the throne as Emperor Hui, who was feeble-minded and incompetent. Empress Jia Nanfeng seized power and struggled for control with the consort-clan figure Yang Jun. In 291 the empress joined Sima Wei, Prince of Chu, to kill Yang Jun, then killed Sima Liang, Prince of Runan, and the Prince of Chu, setting off years of war among the princes. The main contenders were the eight princes: Sima Liang of Runan, Sima Wei of Chu, Sima Lun of Zhao, Sima Jiong of Qi, Sima Ai of Changsha, Sima Ying of Chengdu, Sima Yong of Hejian and Sima Yue of Donghai, known as the “War of the Eight Princes.” Sima Lun of Zhao once deposed Emperor Hui and took the throne, and the princes called in troops of the Xiongnu, Xianbei and other peoples who had moved inward. The fighting centered on Luoyang and ended only in 306 when Sima Yue took control, lasting sixteen years. The disaster was immense: the price of rice soared to 10,000 cash per shi, the population of the Central Plains died in great numbers, and survivors fled, hundreds of thousands to the south. The war drained the Western Jin's strength and sent it into rapid decline; the chiefs of the peoples who had moved inward took the chance to rise, the Western Jin soon fell, and the north entered a long division.

events.title: Northern Peoples Move Inward; the Sixteen Kingdoms
events.short: Nomadic peoples of the north moved inward through the Han, Wei and Jin; at the end of the Western Jin, Xiongnu, Xianbei, Jie, Di and Qiang leaders founded states, the “Sixteen Kingdoms.”
events.detail: On the broad northern steppes of China lived nomadic peoples such as the Xiongnu, Xianbei, Jie, Di and Qiang, who followed water and grass. In the Eastern Han, Wei and Jin, Central Plains dynasties admitted northern peoples in succession to add labor and soldiers. The Di and Qiang of the northwest moved into Guanzhong in Shaanxi; the Xiongnu and Jie of the Mongolian steppe moved south to Shanxi; some Xianbei moved to Liaoning and some to Shaanxi and the Ordos region. By the Western Jin, the inward-moving peoples made up about half the population of Guanzhong. They lived mixed with the Han and gradually took up farming, promoting ethnic fusion. But Western Jin rule was corrupt: it taxed them heavily, drafted them for soldiering and labor, and even seized and sold them as slaves, provoking fierce resistance. After the War of the Eight Princes their chiefs took the chance to rise. In 304 the Xiongnu noble Liu Yuan rose and founded a state called Han (later renamed Zhao, known as the Former Zhao), which later took Luoyang and Chang'an and destroyed the Western Jin. From 304 until the Northern Wei reunified the north in 439, over twenty regimes appeared in the north, sixteen of them major, hence the “Sixteen Kingdoms.” The north saw frequent war and constant turnover of regimes, and the economy was badly damaged. Among them, Fu Jian of the Former Qin, employing the Han official Wang Meng for reforms, briefly unified the north but fell apart after defeat at the Battle of Fei River. In the Sixteen Kingdoms period, the regimes of the various peoples mostly adopted sinicizing measures and employed Han scholars, promoting ethnic fusion in the north and preparing the way for the Northern Wei's unification and the later Sui and Tang.

events.title: Zu Ti's Northern Expedition
events.short: Known for “rising at cockcrow to practice sword,” Zu Ti crossed the Yangtze in AD 313, vowed while striking his oar mid-river, and recovered much land south of the Yellow River.
events.detail: At the end of the Western Jin, many northerners moved south hoping the Jin could retake the Central Plains; a leading figure among them was Zu Ti. Zu Ti, courtesy name Shizhi, from Qiu county in Fanyang (present-day Laishui, Hebei), had great ambition in youth; with his friend Liu Kun he rose at midnight at the crowing of the cock to practice with the sword, determined to serve the country, the origin of the idiom “rising at cockcrow to practice sword.” Before the Western Jin fell, Zu Ti led several hundred households south to the Huai and Yangtze region. He repeatedly asked Sima Rui, Prince of Langye, who held Jiankang, to send troops north to recover the Central Plains. Sima Rui, wanting only to hold Jiangnan, made him Governor of Yu Province but gave only provisions for a thousand men and three thousand bolts of cloth, telling him to recruit his own army. In 313 Zu Ti led over a hundred households of his followers across the river northward. Midway, standing in the bow and striking his oar, he swore passionately: “If I, Zu Ti, cannot clear the Central Plains and cross this river again, may I be like this great river that flows away and never returns!” Those with him were moved, the origin of the allusion “striking the oar in mid-stream.” After crossing, he smelted iron and cast weapons around Huaiyin and raised a force of over two thousand. After years of hard fighting he defeated Shi Le of the Later Zhao, recovered most of the land south of the Yellow River, and stopped Later Zhao raids south. But the court distrusted him and sent Dai Yuan to check him, and amid the conflict between Wang Dun and Sima Rui, Zu Ti fell ill from frustration and died at Yongqiu in 321. After his death the lands were gradually lost.

events.title: Western Jin Falls; Eastern Jin Founded
events.short: In AD 316 the Xiongnu state of Former Zhao took Chang'an and the Western Jin fell; in 317 Sima Rui restored the Jin at Jiankang as the Eastern Jin, with “Wang and Sima sharing the realm.”
events.detail: After the War of the Eight Princes, Western Jin strength was badly weakened and the chiefs of the inward-moving peoples rose in turn. The Xiongnu noble Liu Yuan founded the state of Han in AD 304; after his son Liu Cong took the throne, he sent troops in 311 to take Luoyang and capture Emperor Huai of Jin, known as the “Disaster of Yongjia.” In 316 Liu Cong's general Liu Yao took Chang'an and Emperor Min of Jin surrendered, ending the Western Jin. Northern gentry and commoners then moved south in great numbers, the “crossing of the gentry to the south.” At that time Sima Rui, Prince of Langye, a Western Jin royal who held the lower Yangtze, was building his base around Jiankang (present-day Nanjing, Jiangsu); in 317 he took the title King of Jin and in 318 formally became emperor, restoring the Jin with Jiankang as capital, called the Eastern Jin, and Sima Rui was Emperor Yuan of Jin. With no roots in Jiangnan, Sima Rui owed his throne to northern and southern great clans led by Wang Dao, whom he relied on in government, with Wang Dao's cousin Wang Dun in military affairs. People of the time called this “Wang and Sima share the realm.” The Eastern Jin was the age of greatest power for the aristocratic clans; the Wang of Langye and Xie of Chen Commandery held power in turn and imperial power was weak. Northern expeditions by Zu Ti, Huan Wen and others briefly recovered some land south of the Yellow River, but the court distrusted and obstructed the commanders, and the Central Plains were never regained. The Eastern Jin held on in Jiangnan for over a hundred years, successfully resisted the Former Qin at the Battle of Fei River, and kept the south stable, creating favorable conditions for developing Jiangnan. In 420 it was replaced by the Song founded by Liu Yu.
