events.title: Wang Xizhi's Orchid Pavilion Preface
events.short: The Eastern Jin calligrapher Wang Xizhi, honored as the “Sage of Calligraphy,” wrote his Preface to the Orchid Pavilion Collection in AD 353, called the “finest running script under heaven.”
events.detail: After the Eastern Han, as papermaking improved, calligraphy gradually became an art appreciated for its own sake. Zhong Yao of Cao Wei excelled at regular script and is revered as its founder. The man who took calligraphy to a new stage was Wang Xizhi of the Eastern Jin. Wang Xizhi (303–361, by another account 321–379), courtesy name Yishao, of the Wang clan of Langye, rose to General of the Right Army and was called “Wang of the Right Army.” He studied under Lady Wei and later drew on Zhong Yao, Zhang Zhi and other masters. His regular, running and cursive scripts were all superb; he changed the plain style of the Han and Wei and created a new, graceful, flowing manner, his writing “drifting like floating clouds, leaping like startled dragons,” and later generations revered him as the “Sage of Calligraphy.” On the third day of the third month of AD 353, Wang Xizhi gathered forty-one noted scholars including Xie An and Sun Chuo at the Orchid Pavilion in Shanyin, Kuaiji (present-day Shaoxing, Zhejiang) for a purification gathering, with wine and poetry; the poems were compiled as the Orchid Pavilion Collection, and in high spirits Wang wrote the preface. Its 324 characters record the beauty of the scenery and the joy of the gathering and express feelings about life; its calligraphy is vigorous and graceful, and the twenty or so characters zhi are each written differently, so it is called the “finest running script under heaven.” Tradition says Emperor Taizong of Tang so loved the original that he had it buried with him at Zhaoling; surviving versions are Tang copies, the best known being Feng Chengsu's “Shenlong” copy. Wang's son Wang Xianzhi was also an outstanding calligrapher, and the two are called the “Two Wangs,” with profound influence on later calligraphy.

events.title: The Mogao Caves at Dunhuang
events.short: The Mogao Caves at Dunhuang, Gansu, were first carved in AD 366 and added to over a thousand years across ten dynasties, preserving over 45,000 square meters of murals and some 2,400 painted statues.
events.detail: The Mogao Caves at Dunhuang, popularly called the Caves of the Thousand Buddhas, lie in a cliff face at the eastern foot of Mingsha Mountain about 25 km southeast of Dunhuang, Gansu, and stretch over 1,600 m from north to south. Dunhuang was an important Silk Road town where Eastern and Western cultures met. Records say that in AD 366 the monk Le Zun, passing by, suddenly saw golden light on the hill like a thousand Buddhas and carved the first cave in the cliff. From then, through the Sixteen Kingdoms, Northern Dynasties, Sui, Tang, Five Dynasties, Song, Western Xia and Yuan, ten dynasties and over a thousand years of continuous carving created a vast cave complex. Today 735 caves survive, over 490 of them with murals and painted statues, preserving over 45,000 square meters of murals and some 2,400 painted statues. They are mostly on Buddhist themes but also vividly reflect social life, trade and exchange between China and other lands, and the flying apsaras are especially beautiful. The Sui and Tang were the high point of the caves. In 1900 the Daoist Wang Yuanlu discovered the Library Cave (now Cave 17) while clearing caves, sealed with over 50,000 manuscripts, silk paintings and other items from the 4th to 11th centuries. Aurel Stein of Britain, Paul Pelliot of France and others later bought large numbers of them cheaply and carried them abroad, a major loss to Chinese cultural history. Study of these documents gave rise to the international field of “Dunhuang studies.” The Mogao Caves, with the Yungang Grottoes of Datong, Shanxi, and the Longmen Grottoes of Luoyang, Henan, are called China's three great grottoes and were inscribed on the World Heritage List in 1987. Generations of scholars, including Chang Shuhong and Fan Jinshi, have worked to protect the caves.

events.title: Gu Kaizhi and Wei–Jin Painting
events.short: The Eastern Jin painter Gu Kaizhi excelled at figure painting and held that “form should convey spirit”; copies of Admonitions of the Court Instructress and Nymph of the Luo River survive.
events.detail: In the Wei, Jin and Northern and Southern Dynasties, painting developed greatly. With Buddhism flourishing, religious painting held an important place, figure painting matured, and landscape painting began to take shape. Gu Kaizhi (c. 345–406), courtesy name Changkang and childhood name Hutou, from Wuxi in Jinling (present-day Wuxi, Jiangsu), was the most famous painter of the Eastern Jin. He excelled at figures, Buddhist images and landscapes, especially figure painting. His lines were fine and continuous like “silk spun by a spring silkworm,” and his figures were lifelike and individual. In theory he proposed ideas such as “form conveys spirit” and “transferring thought to grasp the subtle,” stressing that a painting should express a person's inner spirit and not merely the outward form. It is said he left a portrait's eyes unpainted for years, explaining, “The conveying of spirit lies precisely in the eyes.” No original by Gu survives; the Admonitions of the Court Instructress, Nymph of the Luo River and Wise and Benevolent Women that come down are copies by later hands. Admonitions of the Court Instructress, based on Zhang Hua of the Western Jin's essay of that name, promotes the moral norms women should follow; its Tang copy is in the British Museum in London. Nymph of the Luo River, based on Cao Zhi's famous Rhapsody on the Nymph of the Luo, shows Cao Zhi's meeting and parting with the goddess of the Luo River. His On Painting is among China's earliest painting treatises. In this period, with more landscape poetry and scholars finding solace in nature, landscape painting began to form an independent genre, and the “Six Principles of Painting” put forward by Xie He of the Southern Dynasties became an important theory of Chinese painting.

events.title: Battle of Fei River
events.short: In AD 383 Fu Jian of the Former Qin marched south with a huge army, but the Eastern Jin defeated it at the Fei River with some 80,000 elite troops, “mistaking wind and cranes for pursuers.”
events.detail: In the Sixteen Kingdoms period, the Di-led Former Qin under Fu Jian employed the Han scholar Wang Meng as chancellor, reformed administration and developed production, grew stronger, unified the north, and stood against the Eastern Jin. In AD 383 Fu Jian, over his ministers' objections, conscripted people of all nationalities, gathering more than 600,000 infantry and 270,000 cavalry, claimed as a million, and marched south in force, hoping to destroy the Eastern Jin and unify the country at one stroke. Fu Jian boasted that “if my host threw their whips into the river, they could stop its flow.” The Eastern Jin chancellor Xie An stayed calm and sent Xie Shi and Xie Xuan with some 80,000 elite “Beifu troops,” mostly northern refugees, to meet them. The Jin first defeated the Qin vanguard at Luojian, then faced the Qin on the two banks of the Fei River (southeast of present-day Shou county, Anhui). Xie Xuan asked the Qin to pull back a little so the Jin could cross; Fu Jian, planning to strike them half across, ordered a retreat, but once the Qin fell back their lines fell into disorder, and the captured Jin officer Zhu Xu shouted behind the lines, “The Qin are beaten!” and the Qin army broke. The Jin crossed and attacked fiercely; fleeing Qin soldiers took the sound of wind and the cry of cranes for Jin pursuers and the grass and trees of Mount Bagong for Jin troops, giving the idioms “mistaking wind and cranes for pursuers” and “seeing every bush as a soldier.” It is a famous case of a smaller force beating a larger one. Afterward the leaders of the peoples under Former Qin became independent one after another, the Former Qin collapsed quickly, and the north was divided again. The Eastern Jin kept its rule in Jiangnan and the north–south standoff continued.

events.title: End of the Eastern Jin and the Southern Dynasties
events.short: Liu Yu replaced the Jin with the Song in AD 420; the south then saw four dynasties, Song, Qi, Liang and Chen, all based at Jiankang, the “Southern Dynasties,” until the Sui destroyed the Chen in 589.
events.detail: Liu Yu, a Beifu general, rose by suppressing the uprisings of Sun En and Lu Xun and other rebellions, then led two northern expeditions that destroyed Southern Yan and Later Qin and briefly recovered Luoyang and Chang'an. In AD 420 Liu Yu deposed Emperor Gong of Jin and took the throne under the state name Song, known as Liu Song, and the Eastern Jin fell. From 420 to 589, regimes in southern China changed often, with four dynasties in turn, Song, Qi, Liang and Chen, all with their capitals at Jiankang (present-day Nanjing, Jiangsu), together the “Southern Dynasties,” facing the Northern Dynasties in the “Northern and Southern Dynasties.” The Song was the largest Southern dynasty; during the more than thirty years of Emperor Wu, Liu Yu, and Emperor Wen, Liu Yilong, light taxes and corvée and administrative reform brought relative peace and prosperity to Jiangnan, called the “Yuanjia Era Rule.” In 479 Xiao Daocheng replaced the Song with the Qi, and in 502 Xiao Yan replaced the Qi with the Liang, as Emperor Wu of Liang. In nearly fifty years on the throne, Emperor Wu of Liang devoutly believed in Buddhism and built many temples, four times giving himself to Tongtai Temple, for which the court paid huge sums to redeem him. In 548 Hou Jing, a defecting general of Eastern Wei, rebelled and took Jiankang, Emperor Wu was besieged and starved to death, and Jiangnan's richest regions were plundered, known as the “Rebellion of Hou Jing.” In 557 Chen Baxian founded the Chen dynasty, but its territory was much smaller and the south was clearly at a disadvantage. In 589 Sui troops crossed the river and took Jiankang, the last Chen emperor was captured, the Chen fell, and China was reunified. The economy and culture of Jiangnan greatly developed during the Southern Dynasties.

events.title: Northern Wei Unifies the North
events.short: The Northern Wei, founded by the Tuoba of the Xianbei, grew strong; in AD 439 Emperor Taiwu destroyed Northern Liang and unified the north, ending the division there since the Sixteen Kingdoms.
events.detail: The Xianbei are an ancient people of northern China; their Tuoba branch originally nomadized in the northern Greater Khingan Range and gradually moved south to the Yin Mountains. In the Sixteen Kingdoms period the Tuoba chief Shiyijian founded the state of Dai, which was destroyed by the Former Qin. After the Former Qin collapsed following the Battle of Fei River, Shiyijian's grandson Tuoba Gui restored the state in 386 and soon renamed it Wei, known as the Northern Wei. In 398 Tuoba Gui moved the capital to Pingcheng (present-day Datong, Shanxi) and formally became emperor, as Emperor Daowu. After its founding the Northern Wei learned from Central Plains institutions, employed Han scholars, and developed agriculture, and its strength grew rapidly. In 423 Emperor Taiwu, Tuoba Tao, took the throne. A ruler of great talent and vision, he relied on Han scholars such as Cui Hao, destroyed Daxia and Northern Yan, and defeated the Rouran in the north. In 439 the Northern Wei destroyed Northern Liang and unified the north, ending the division and warfare of more than a century since the end of the Western Jin, and stood in a north–south standoff with the Liu Song in the south; Chinese history entered the Northern and Southern Dynasties. After the unification, order in the north gradually settled; the peoples there had long lived mixed together, and those who had moved inward no longer differed clearly from the Han in production, life and customs. But the Xianbei Tuoba, having moved inward later, kept many old Xianbei customs, and there were also tensions between Xianbei nobles and Han scholars within the ruling class. Governing the vast north was difficult, setting the stage for Emperor Xiaowen's reforms.

events.title: Development of the Jiangnan Region
events.short: Northerners moving south brought labor and techniques; Jiangnan's farming and crafts grew rapidly, laying the basis for the economic center's later shift south.
events.detail: In the Qin and Han, economic development was uneven between north and south China. The Yellow River valley was developed early and prosperous and was the country's economic center, while Jiangnan was thinly populated and backward in production. From the end of the Western Jin, with long warfare in the north, many northerners fled south, known as the “crossing of the gentry to the south.” By the late Eastern Jin the lower and middle Yangtze was filled with refugees, most in present-day Jiangsu, and some continued farther south to Zhejiang, Fujian and Guangdong. Their move brought Jiangnan a great deal of labor and also advanced tools and techniques from the Central Plains. Meanwhile Jiangnan was relatively peaceful, with favorable natural conditions: a warm, moist climate and abundant rain. Northerners and southerners worked together, building water works and clearing wasteland, and Jiangnan was developed on a large scale. In farming, rice-growing techniques improved, ox plowing spread, in places two crops a year were possible, and the Lake Tai basin became a key grain region, so that “if one year's harvest is good, several commanderies forget hunger.” In crafts, textiles, papermaking, ceramics and metalworking all advanced greatly. Commerce also flourished: Jiankang became a populous, bustling metropolis and Guangzhou an important port for foreign trade. The development of Jiangnan changed the old picture of a backward south, narrowed the economic gap between north and south, and laid the basis for the shift of China's economic center southward after the Sui and Tang. Meanwhile the northern gentry and Han culture that moved south blended with local culture, and Jiangnan gradually became a culturally advanced region.

events.title: Carving of the Yungang Grottoes
events.short: Under Emperor Wencheng the monk Tanyao led the carving of the Yungang Grottoes near Pingcheng (Datong); the “Tanyao Five Caves” Buddhas make it one of China's three great grottoes.
events.detail: The Yungang Grottoes lie at the southern foot of Wuzhou Mountain on the western outskirts of Datong, Shanxi. Carved into the hillside, they extend about 1 km east to west and are one of China's largest ancient cave complexes; with the Mogao Caves of Dunhuang and the Longmen Grottoes of Luoyang, they are called the three great grottoes of China. After the Northern Wei made Pingcheng its capital, the rulers strongly promoted Buddhism. Emperor Taiwu once ordered a suppression of Buddhism, which Emperor Wencheng restored after taking the throne. Around AD 460 Emperor Wencheng had the eminent monk Tanyao lead the carving of caves at Wuzhou Mountain; the first five large caves (now Caves 16 to 20) are called the “Tanyao Five Caves,” and their great Buddhas are said to be carved in the likeness of the five emperors from Emperor Daowu to Emperor Wencheng. The open-air Buddha in Cave 20, about 13.7 m high with a full face and broad shoulders, is majestic and is the symbol of Yungang. Carving continued for decades, stopping gradually after the capital moved to Luoyang. Yungang now has 45 main caves and over 59,000 statues of every size, the largest 17 m high and the smallest only a few centimeters. The sculptures inherit the fine tradition of Chinese sculpture from the Qin and Han, absorb features of Gandharan and Gupta art of ancient India and blend Xianbei aesthetics; early statues have an obvious foreign flavor, while later ones show Han-style dress with “loose robes and wide belts,” reflecting the sinicization of Buddhist art and ethnic fusion after Emperor Xiaowen's reforms. The caves also have many flying apsaras, musicians and Buddhist story carvings. In 2001 the Yungang Grottoes were inscribed on the World Heritage List.

images.caption: The main Buddha in Cave 20 at the Yungang Grottoes

events.title: Zu Chongzhi Calculates Pi
events.short: The Southern Dynasties scientist Zu Chongzhi fixed pi between 3.1415926 and 3.1415927, leading the world by nearly a thousand years, and also compiled the Daming Calendar.
events.detail: Zu Chongzhi (429–500), courtesy name Wenyuan, from Qiu county in Fanyang (present-day Laishui, Hebei), lived under the Southern Song and Qi and was an outstanding scientist who made major achievements in mathematics, astronomy and the calendar, and machine building. He was rigorous in study and never followed the ancients blindly. Pi is the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, an important problem in mathematics. Ancient China first used “circumference three, diameter one,” that is, pi as 3. Liu Hui of Wei in the Three Kingdoms devised the “circle-cutting method,” using regular polygons inscribed in a circle to approach its area step by step, a method containing the idea of limits, and obtained pi of about 3.1416. Building on Liu Hui, Zu Chongzhi, through repeated painstaking calculation, fixed pi to the seventh decimal place, between 3.1415926 and 3.1415927, a result that led the world for nearly a thousand years until the Arab mathematician al-Kashi surpassed it in the 15th century. Zu Chongzhi also proposed 355/113 (the “close ratio”) and 22/7 (the “approximate ratio”) as approximations of pi, and later generations call 355/113 “Zu's ratio.” His mathematical classic Zhui Shu, written with his son Zu Geng, was made a main textbook for mathematics at the Tang Imperial Academy and was lost after the Song. In astronomy and the calendar, Zu Chongzhi compiled the Daming Calendar, the first to introduce precession into a calendar, making it more precise; it was issued ten years after his death. In his honor, Purple Mountain Observatory named an asteroid it discovered “Zu Chongzhi,” and a crater on the far side of the Moon also bears his name.

events.date: After the Northern Wei moved its capital to Luoyang
events.title: Carving of the Longmen Grottoes
events.short: Around Emperor Xiaowen's move of the Northern Wei capital to Luoyang, carving began on the Yi River banks; it lasted over four hundred years and left more than 2,300 niches and 100,000 statues.
events.detail: The Longmen Grottoes lie on Longmen Mountain and Xiangshan on both banks of the Yi River south of Luoyang, Henan; the two hills face each other with the Yi water between, like a gateway from afar, anciently called “Yique.” Around Emperor Xiaowen's move of the capital to Luoyang in AD 494, carving began here and continued through the Eastern Wei, Western Wei, Northern Qi, Sui and Tang to the Northern Song, for more than four hundred years, with the greatest number of statues from the Northern Wei and Tang. Longmen now has over 2,300 caves and niches, over 100,000 statues and 2,800 inscriptions. The Northern Wei Guyang Cave, Central Binyang Cave and Lotus Cave are the most representative; their statues have delicate faces and slender bodies with layered drapery, in the “graceful bones and slender forms” and “loose robes and wide belts” style, more sinicized than those at Yungang and reflecting the Chinese character of Buddhist art after Emperor Xiaowen's reforms. The relief Emperor and Empress as Donors, originally in the Central Binyang Cave, showed Emperor Xiaowen and his empress leading attendants in worship and was a masterpiece of ancient Chinese relief carving; sadly it was stolen in the 1930s and taken to the United States, where it is now in museums. The Tang was the high point of Longmen sculpture: the great Vairocana Buddha at Fengxian Temple stands over 17 m high with a full, rounded face and a kindly expression, and is said to have been carved in the likeness of Wu Zetian, who also donated 20,000 strings of cash for cosmetics. The “Twenty Pieces of Longmen” represent Wei stele calligraphy. The Longmen Grottoes, with the Mogao and Yungang caves, are called China's three great grottoes and were inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2000.

events.title: Emperor Xiaowen's Reforms
events.short: Building on Empress Dowager Feng's reforms, Emperor Xiaowen of the Northern Wei moved the capital to Luoyang in AD 494 and enforced sinicizing measures such as speaking Chinese and wearing Han dress.
events.detail: Emperor Xiaowen of the Northern Wei, Tuoba Hong, took the throne at five, with his grandmother Empress Dowager Feng governing from behind the throne. She carried out a series of reforms: she reformed administration, introduced official salaries and punished corruption; in 485 she issued the equal-field order, distributing state-held wasteland to peasants by population; she set up the Three Elders system to strengthen control at the grassroots; and she introduced a new tax system that eased the peasants' burden. These reforms advanced the feudalization of the Xianbei and economic development, and deeply influenced Emperor Xiaowen. After the empress dowager died in 490, he took personal rule and deepened the reforms. In 493, under the pretext of campaigning against the Southern Qi, he led a great army south, and in 494 formally moved the capital to Luoyang, relocating over a million Xianbei and other northern people to the Central Plains. After the move he enforced sinicizing measures: officials had to use Chinese at court and Xianbei was banned; Han dress replaced Xianbei dress; Xianbei compound surnames were changed to Han ones, the imperial Tuoba clan becoming Yuan and the emperor renamed Yuan Hong; Xianbei nobles were encouraged to marry into Han gentry clans, and he set the example himself; Han official systems, rituals and laws were adopted, Confucius was honored, and Confucian classics were studied. The reforms met opposition from some Xianbei nobles. They accelerated the feudalization and sinicization of the Xianbei, promoted fusion among northern peoples, strengthened the Northern Wei, and laid a basis for the later unity and prosperity of the Sui and Tang, giving them great significance in the history of the Chinese nation.

events.title: The Great Fusion of Northern Peoples
events.short: In the late Northern Dynasties, peoples who had moved inward lived and intermarried with the Han and learned from each other in economy, culture and customs, producing a great fusion in the north.
events.detail: From the Wei and Jin on, the Xiongnu, Xianbei, Jie, Di, Qiang and other peoples who had moved inward lived interspersed with the local Han and gradually settled. They learned farming from the Han and shifted from herding to agriculture, while the Han learned herding from the northern peoples and took up their food, clothing and implements; the hu bed, hu cake and hu dress entered the Central Plains. Rulers of the Sixteen Kingdoms and Northern Dynasties mostly cooperated with Han scholars and kept the existing ways of governing the Central Plains. Ethnic relations at times flared into conflict and even war, but the overall trend was that barriers gradually dissolved and relations eased. After Emperor Xiaowen's reforms of the Northern Wei, fusion quickened. By the late Northern Dynasties northern China saw a great fusion of peoples: they were in close contact economically and influenced one another in culture, customs and language; intermarriage grew common, and many who had moved inward merged into the Han, while the Han took in the blood and culture of other peoples and became more vigorous. Northern Dynasties folk songs such as the Ballad of Mulan and the Song of the Chile are products of this blending; the lines “The Chile plain, beneath the Yin Mountains, the sky like a dome covers the four fields” vividly depict the northern steppe, originally in Xianbei and later translated into Chinese. The imperial houses of the Sui and Tang, the Yang and Li, had close blood ties with Xianbei nobles. The great fusion of northern peoples laid the basis for unity and prosperity in the Sui and Tang and promoted the pattern of diversity in unity of the Chinese nation.

events.title: Fan Zhen Writes On the Extinction of the Soul
events.short: Fan Zhen's On the Extinction of the Soul argued that “when the body remains, the spirit remains; when the body perishes, the spirit perishes,” a systematic atheism that attacked Buddhist karma.
events.detail: In the turbulent Wei, Jin and Northern and Southern Dynasties, people turned to Buddhism to escape hardship, and rulers also supported it, so that Buddhism flourished and many temples were built everywhere. Thus there were always some who opposed it, the most famous being Fan Zhen, a thinker of the Southern Qi and Liang. Fan Zhen (c. 450–c. 515), courtesy name Zizhen, was from Wuyin in Nanxiang (present-day Biyang, Henan). Under the Southern Qi, Xiao Ziliang, Prince of Jingling, was a devout Buddhist and gathered guests in his residence to preach the teaching. He asked Fan Zhen: “You don't believe in karma, so why are people rich or poor, noble or humble?” Fan Zhen replied that life is like flowers on a tree, falling with the wind; some land on fine mats and some in a cesspit, and wealth and poverty are chance fortunes unrelated to karma. Fan Zhen later wrote On the Extinction of the Soul, a systematic statement of atheism. He held that “the body is the substance of the spirit and the spirit is the function of the body”: spirit and body are an inseparable whole, so there is spirit only where there is body, and when the body dies the spirit vanishes, that is, “when the body remains, the spirit remains; when the body perishes, the spirit perishes.” He also used the analogy of a blade and its sharpness: sharpness cannot exist apart from the blade; likewise without the body there is no spirit. The essay shook the court and the public. Under Emperor Wu of Liang, when Buddhism was honored as the state religion, the emperor organized over sixty people to write refutations, and Fan Zhen declared he would never “sell his argument for office.” It is an important work of materialist thought in ancient China.

events.title: Li Daoyuan's Commentary on the Water Classic
events.short: The Northern Wei geographer Li Daoyuan, after fieldwork across the land, annotated the Water Classic in the 40-chapter Commentary on the Water Classic, recording 1,252 rivers.
events.detail: Li Daoyuan (c. 470–527), courtesy name Shanchang, from Zhuo county in Fanyang (present-day Zhuozhou, Hebei), was an outstanding geographer and writer of the Northern Wei. Born into an official family, he loved travel from youth, and later, serving in the court and in the provinces, he used his postings to survey the land, traveling across the Yellow River and Huai River basins. Wherever he went he studied the local rivers and waterways, terrain and landforms, and ancient sites, and asked local people about history and customs. In the Three Kingdoms someone wrote a Water Classic, briefly recording 137 rivers across the country, but it was too sketchy and contained many errors. Drawing on a great many earlier geographical works and his own fieldwork, Li Daoyuan took the Water Classic as his framework and annotated it, producing the Commentary on the Water Classic. In 40 chapters of over 300,000 characters, it records the sources, courses, tributaries and outlets or confluences of 1,252 rivers and describes the hydrology, terrain, climate, soil, products, towns, historic sites and customs along them, citing over 400 earlier works. It is a comprehensive geographical work of ancient China, more than twenty times as rich as the Water Classic. It is also a collection of fine landscape prose, vividly written, with scenes like poems or paintings; the passage on the Three Gorges of the Yangtze, “Through seven hundred li of the Three Gorges, mountains line both banks with hardly a break,” is especially well loved and strongly influenced later travel writing.

events.title: Jia Sixie's Qimin Yaoshu (Essential Techniques)
events.short: Jia Sixie of the Northern Wei summarized farming, forestry, herding and fishing techniques in Essential Techniques for the Common People, China's earliest complete surviving farming treatise.
events.detail: Jia Sixie was an outstanding agronomist of the Northern Wei, from Yidu in Qingzhou (around present-day Shouguang, Shandong), who served as governor of Gaoyang Commandery (around present-day Linzi, Shandong) and paid close attention to farming. He traveled widely to study agriculture and humbly consulted old farmers. He gathered agricultural knowledge from ancient books, citing over 150 earlier works, collected popular farm proverbs and songs, drew on the farmers' experience, and tested it in practice. Around the end of the Northern Wei to the Eastern Wei (the 530s to 540s) he wrote Essential Techniques for the Common People (Qimin Yaoshu). “Qimin” means ordinary people and “yaoshu” essential methods of making a living. In 10 volumes and 92 chapters of about 110,000 characters, it systematically summarizes production techniques in northern China in farming, forestry, herding, sidelines and fishing, covering cultivation, seed selection and breeding, crop growing, planting and grafting of fruit trees and timber, raising livestock and poultry, veterinary care, brewing and food processing, and more. Jia Sixie stressed that farming must follow natural laws, suited to local conditions and never missing the season, that is, “follow the seasons and measure the land's advantages, and little effort brings great success.” He also valued better techniques and tools, put forward advanced experience such as crop rotation, seed selection and green manure, and advocated diversified economy and commodity production. It is the earliest and most complete surviving agricultural treatise in China and one of the earliest specialized works in world agronomy, with profound influence on later farming.

events.title: Founding and Unification of the Sui
events.short: Yang Jian founded the Sui in AD 581 with its capital at Chang'an and destroyed the Chen in 589 to unify the country, ending nearly three centuries of division since the Wei and Jin.
events.detail: The last dynasty of the Northern Dynasties was the Northern Zhou, which destroyed the Northern Qi in AD 577 and unified the north. At the end of the Northern Zhou the emperor was a child, and Yang Jian, of the consort clan, held power as chancellor. In 581 Yang Jian forced Emperor Jing of Northern Zhou to abdicate and took the throne, founding the Sui with its capital at Chang'an; Yang Jian was Emperor Wen of Sui. In the south the Chen dynasty was corrupt; its last emperor, Chen Shubao, ignored government and indulged in poetry, wine and building projects. Emperor Wen prepared actively for unification, and in 588 made his second son Yang Guang commander, mustering over 500,000 troops in eight columns against the Chen. In 589 Sui troops crossed the Yangtze, entered Jiankang and captured the last Chen emperor; the Chen fell and the Sui unified the country. The unification ended nearly three centuries of division and followed the trend toward a unified, multiethnic state. After unification the Sui took a series of steps to consolidate rule: it reformed central government and set up the system of Three Departments and Six Ministries; it changed the three levels of local administration (province, commandery, county) to two, province and county; it issued the Kaihuang Code and abolished some cruel punishments; it developed the economy, continued the equal-field system, and entered hidden households on the rolls, which raised state revenue; and it unified currency and weights and measures across north and south. These measures speeded economic recovery, population and cultivated land grew sharply, and state storehouses held ample grain and cloth; the Sui became a vast and strong dynasty, known as the “Rule of Kaihuang.”

events.title: Li Chun Builds the Zhaozhou Bridge
events.short: The Zhaozhou Bridge, designed and built by the Sui craftsman Li Chun, is the world's oldest surviving open-spandrel single-arch stone bridge, still intact after over 1,400 years.
events.detail: The Zhaozhou Bridge, also called the Anji Bridge, stands over the Xiao River south of Zhao county, Hebei; it takes its name from Zhao county's old name, Zhaozhou, and is known locally as the “Great Stone Bridge.” It was designed and built under the direction of the outstanding Sui craftsman Li Chun, around the end of the Kaihuang era to the start of the Daye era (about AD 595–605), over 1,400 years ago, and is the oldest and best-preserved open-spandrel single-arch stone bridge in the world. The bridge is about 64 m long, its main arch spans about 37 m, and the deck is about 9 m wide, built of 28 independent arch rings set side by side. It has several innovations. First, a single large segmental arc, a flat arch that eases the passage of carts and people and saves stone. Second, two small arches on each shoulder of the main arch, forming an “open spandrel,” which lightens the bridge and saves stone, increases flood discharge in high water and reduces the force of floods on the structure, while making the bridge lighter and more beautiful. Third, the arch rings are joined and reinforced with iron clamps and tie rods, making the bridge strong and durable. Over the centuries the bridge has withstood many floods and earthquakes and still stands and can be crossed, a full demonstration of the wisdom and skill of ancient Chinese builders. Similar open-spandrel arch bridges appeared in Europe only in the 14th century, over 700 years later. The balustrade panels carry fine reliefs of dragons and beasts. In 1991 the American Society of Civil Engineers named the Zhaozhou Bridge an International Historic Civil Engineering Landmark.

events.title: Opening of the Grand Canal
events.short: From AD 605 Emperor Yang of Sui had the Grand Canal dug, centered on Luoyang, reaching Zhuojun in the north and Yuhang in the south, over 2,700 km long, a great artery linking north and south.
events.detail: After unification the Sui's political center was in the north while Jiangnan's economy was growing; to improve north–south transport, consolidate rule and ship Jiangnan's grain and goods north, the Sui dug the Grand Canal on the basis of existing natural rivers and ancient canals. After taking the throne, Emperor Yang drew on the state's economic strength and conscripted millions of laborers to dig it in stages from AD 605: in 605 the Tongji Canal was opened, joining the Yellow River and the Huai River, and the Han Canal (Shanyang Canal) was dredged to link the Huai and Yangtze; in 608 the Yongji Canal was dug, drawing the Qin River south to the Yellow River and running north to Zhuojun (around present-day Beijing); in 610 the Jiangnan Canal was dug from Jingkou (present-day Zhenjiang, Jiangsu) to Yuhang (present-day Hangzhou, Zhejiang). Centered on Luoyang, the canal reached Zhuojun in the north and Yuhang in the south, linking the five river systems of the Hai, Yellow, Huai, Yangtze and Qiantang rivers, over 2,700 km long and the longest canal in the ancient world. Emperor Yang overworked the people in digging it, many laborers died of exhaustion, and social tensions rose, one cause of the Sui's fall. But the canal greatly eased north–south travel and exchange and was of great importance for national unity. The Tang poet Pi Rixiu judged: “All say the Sui fell because of this river; yet to this day it carries thousands of li of waves for us.” In the Tang and Song it was the great artery carrying southern grain north. After the Yuan made Dadu its capital, the Huitong and Tonghui canals were dug in straighter courses, forming the Beijing–Hangzhou Grand Canal. In 2014 China's Grand Canal was inscribed on the World Heritage List.

events.date: Reigns of Emperors Wen and Yang of Sui
events.title: Creation of the Imperial Examination System
events.short: Emperor Wen of Sui began selecting officials by examinations, and Emperor Yang created the jinshi degree, marking the formal establishment of the imperial examinations, used for over 1,300 years.
events.detail: In the Wei, Jin and Northern and Southern Dynasties the Nine-Rank system was used, and the selection of officials was monopolized by great clans; family background counted for more than ability, producing the situation in which “no commoners among the upper ranks, no gentry among the lower,” and many talented men of humble origin were overlooked. After taking the throne, Emperor Wen of Sui abolished the Nine-Rank system, paid attention to examining candidates' learning, and began selecting officials by examinations by subject. Under Emperor Yang the jinshi degree was created, choosing talent by examination on policy questions, generally taken to mark the formal establishment of the imperial examinations. The Tang improved the system further: Emperor Taizong expanded the state schools and enrolled more candidates; Wu Zetian created the palace examination and the military examination; and under Emperor Xuanzong poetry and rhapsodies became the main content of the jinshi examination. Regular Tang subjects included the mingjing and jinshi, of which the jinshi was the hardest, as in the saying “a mingjing at thirty is old, a jinshi at fifty is young.” The Song added name-sealing and copying of papers, and the Ming and Qing used the “eight-legged essay.” The creation of the examinations was a major change in China's official selection: it ended the great clans' monopoly on careers, widened the sources of officials, let talented men of humble origin join government, and promoted social mobility; and it promoted education and culture. The examinations became the main way successive dynasties chose officials, lasting until the Qing government abolished them in 1905, over 1,300 years in all, and were also imitated by Korea, Vietnam and other countries.

events.title: Emperor Yang of Sui Sends Three Missions to Liuqiu
events.short: Emperor Yang of Sui sent three missions to Liuqiu (today's Taiwan); in AD 610 Chen Leng and others crossed the sea from Yi'an with over 10,000 men, and the Book of Sui has a dedicated account.
events.detail: The Sui called today's Taiwan “Liuqiu.” After the Sui unified the country, seafaring advanced greatly and knowledge of the overseas lands to the southeast deepened. Soon after taking the throne, Emperor Yang sent people to Liuqiu, three times in all. In AD 607 he sent the cavalry commandant Zhu Kuan and the sea master He Man to sail in search of strange customs; they reached Liuqiu but, unable to communicate, brought back one man. In 608 he sent Zhu Kuan again to pacify Liuqiu, but the people did not accept, and Zhu Kuan returned with a local cloth armor. In 610 Emperor Yang sent Chen Leng, a Wuben general, and Zhang Zhenzhou, a grand master of remonstrance, with over 10,000 men from Yi'an (present-day Chaozhou, Guangdong) across the sea to Liuqiu, where they fought the local inhabitants and finally brought back several thousand people. The three Sui missions strengthened ties between the mainland and Taiwan, and the Sui's knowledge of the Taiwan region advanced greatly beyond earlier dynasties. The Book of Sui, compiled in the early Tang, has a dedicated “Account of the Kingdom of Liuqiu” describing in detail its location, products, social organization, food and dress, marriage and funeral customs and religious beliefs. Scholars generally hold that Liuqiu in the Book of Sui mainly refers to today's Taiwan; after Wei Wen's arrival at Yizhou in the Three Kingdoms, this is another important historical record of contact between mainland dynasties and Taiwan. After the Song and Yuan, ties grew closer; the Yuan set up an Inspectorate at Penghu, and Taiwan gradually came under central government rule. These facts show that Taiwan has had close ties with the mainland since ancient times.

events.title: Fall of the Sui and Founding of the Tang
events.short: Emperor Yang of Sui's extravagance and overuse of labor sparked peasant uprisings; in AD 618 he was killed and Li Yuan took the throne at Chang'an, founding the Tang.
events.detail: Emperor Wen of Sui lived frugally and once warned the crown prince that no emperor since ancient times had loved luxury and lasted long. But his son Emperor Yang, Yang Guang, after taking the throne, loved grand schemes, spared no thought for the people's strength, and indulged in boundless extravagance. During his reign, building the eastern capital Luoyang used two million laborers a month, and digging the Grand Canal, repairing the Great Wall and building imperial roads conscripted millions more; he made many grand tours by dragon boat and launched three wars against Goguryeo, each drawing over a million soldiers and laborers. Heavy service killed many, fields lay waste, and social tensions sharpened. In AD 611 Wang Bo first rose at Mount Changbai (around present-day Zhangqiu, Shandong). Peasant uprisings then broke out everywhere, the most influential being the Wagang army in Henan, Dou Jiande's army in Hebei and Du Fuwei's army in the Jiang–Huai region. Under Li Mi and Zhai Rang, the Wagang army took the Luokou granary and distributed its grain, growing quickly. Emperor Yang, trapped at Jiangdu (present-day Yangzhou, Jiangsu), was strangled in 618 by Yuwen Huaji and other imperial guard officers, and the Sui fell after only thirty-odd years. In the chaos at the end of the Sui, the noble Li Yuan, who garrisoned Taiyuan, rose in 617, took Chang'an, and enthroned Emperor Yang's grandson Yang You. In 618 Li Yuan deposed Yang You and took the throne, founding the Tang with Chang'an as capital; Li Yuan was Emperor Gaozu of Tang. Under Li Shimin and others the Tang spent about ten years destroying rival regimes and largely unified the country. The Sui's fall after two reigns became a lesson for the early Tang rulers.

events.title: Xuanwu Gate Incident
events.short: In 626 Li Shimin, Prince of Qin, staged a coup at Xuanwu Gate in Chang'an, killing the crown prince and the Prince of Qi. He soon took the throne as Emperor Taizong of Tang.
events.detail: After the Tang dynasty was founded, Emperor Gaozu, Li Yuan, made his eldest son Li Jiancheng crown prince, his second son Li Shimin Prince of Qin, and his fourth son Li Yuanji Prince of Qi. In the wars to unify the country, Li Shimin defeated rival warlords including Xue Ju, Liu Wuzhou, Wang Shichong and Dou Jiande. His great merit earned him the title “Celestial Strategist General”, placing him above the other princes, and his household gathered many talents. Crown Prince Li Jiancheng also had achievements, such as putting down Liu Heita, but lacked Li Shimin’s prestige. He allied with Li Yuanji to push the Prince of Qin aside, and the rivalry grew sharper. In 626 the Turks invaded, and Li Jiancheng proposed that Li Yuanji lead the army, hoping to draw off the elite troops and officers of Li Shimin’s household. Li Shimin struck first. On 2 July 626, at dawn, he set an ambush at Xuanwu Gate, the north gate of the Taiji Palace in Chang'an, with Zhangsun Wuji, Yuchi Jingde and others. As Li Jiancheng and Li Yuanji came to court, Li Shimin shot Li Jiancheng himself and Yuchi Jingde killed Li Yuanji; their sons were killed as well. Li Yuan was then forced to name Li Shimin crown prince and hand state and military affairs to him. In the eighth lunar month Li Yuan abdicated as retired emperor and Li Shimin took the throne, adopting the era name Zhenguan the following year. He is Emperor Taizong of Tang. The incident was a brutal palace coup over the succession, but after taking power Li Shimin ruled diligently, accepted criticism and employed capable ministers, inaugurating the “Rule of Zhenguan”. Most accounts of the incident in the histories come from records made during Taizong’s reign, and later generations have differed over its details.

events.title: Rule of Zhenguan
events.short: Emperor Taizong of Tang learned from the fall of the Sui, took advice, chose able officials, lightened burdens and perfected institutions. His reign brought clean government and recovery.
events.detail: In 626 Li Shimin, Prince of Qin, took the throne after the Xuanwu Gate Incident, and the next year adopted the era name “Zhenguan”. He is Emperor Taizong of Tang. During his twenty-three-year reign he created an age of good government. Having lived through the collapse of the Sui, he took its fall as a warning, recognized that “water can carry a boat, and water can overturn it”, and valued the support of the people. He was diligent and readily accepted criticism. The minister Wei Zheng spoke frankly, remonstrating more than two hundred times; he put forward the maxim “listen to both sides and you will be enlightened; heed only one side and you will be misled”, urging the emperor to guard against danger in times of peace and to be thrifty. After Wei Zheng died, Taizong said mournfully: “With bronze as a mirror, one can straighten one’s dress and cap; with history as a mirror, one can understand rise and fall; with people as a mirror, one can see one’s gains and losses.” He lamented that he had lost one of his mirrors. Taizong welcomed talent regardless of origin or ethnicity: Fang Xuanling was skilled at planning and Du Ruhui at decision-making, a pair known as “Fang plans, Du decides”. He perfected the system of Three Departments and Six Ministries: the Secretariat drafted edicts, the Chancellery reviewed them and the Department of State Affairs carried them out, each checking the others. He trimmed the bureaucracy and paid attention to selecting local officials. In the economy he applied the equal-field system and the grain, labor and cloth tax system, lightened taxes and corvée, and encouraged agriculture. Abroad, Tang defeated the Eastern Turks and strengthened its rule over the northwest, and neighboring peoples’ leaders honored Taizong as “Heavenly Khan”.

events.title: Xuanzang's Journey to the West
events.short: The early Tang monk Xuanzang traveled to India for Buddhist scriptures and studied at Nalanda. In 645 he returned to Chang'an with 657 texts and dictated the Great Tang Records on the Western Regions.
events.detail: Xuanzang (602–664), born Chen Yi in Goushi, Luozhou (present-day Yanshi, Henan), was a Tang Buddhist monk, translator and traveler, honored as “Master of the Tripitaka”. He became a monk at thirteen, sought out leading teachers, and resolved to go to India, the birthplace of Buddhism, to obtain true scriptures. In 627 (some say 629) he set out from Chang'an in defiance of a court ban. He passed Liangzhou, left through Yumen Pass and crossed the vast desert, nearly dying of thirst, then climbed snow mountains and went through Gaochang, Kucha and the states of Central Asia. After four years of hard travel he reached India. He visited famous monasteries and studied for five years under Master Silabhadra at Nalanda, then the highest seat of Buddhist learning, before touring the subcontinent and becoming a renowned Buddhist scholar. In 645 Xuanzang returned to Chang'an with 657 Buddhist texts and was received warmly by Emperor Taizong. He then directed translation at Hongfu Temple, Daci'en Temple and elsewhere; in nineteen years he and his disciples translated 75 works in 1,335 fascicles, making him one of the most prolific translators of scriptures in Chinese history, and he founded the Faxiang (Yogacara) school. To store the scriptures and images brought from India, he oversaw construction of the Big Wild Goose Pagoda. His dictated account, written down by his disciple Bianji as the Great Tang Records on the Western Regions (Da Tang Xiyu Ji), describes the landscapes, products, customs, religions and history of 138 states and regions, and is a precious source for the history and geography of ancient Central and South Asia and for exchanges between China and other lands. The Ming novel Journey to the West is based on the story of Xuanzang’s pilgrimage.

events.title: Taizong Defeats the Turks, Named “Heavenly Khan”
events.short: Emperor Taizong sent Li Jing and others to defeat the Eastern Turks and capture Illig Khan. Northern and northwestern leaders honored him as “Heavenly Khan”, reflecting Tang's open ethnic policy.
events.detail: The Turks were a nomadic people of northern China who arose around the Altai Mountains in the mid-6th century and later split into eastern and western branches. In early Tang the Eastern Turks were strong, controlled the area north of the Gobi, and often raided southward. In 626, just after Taizong took the throne, Illig Khan of the Eastern Turks led over 100,000 cavalry to the Bianqiao Bridge on the Wei River near Chang'an. Taizong came to the river and spoke with the khan across the water; they made a covenant and the Turks withdrew, an event called the “Covenant of the Wei River”. Taizong saw it as a humiliation and stepped up training. In 629 the Eastern Turks were weakened by internal strife and snowstorms, and Taizong sent the generals Li Jing, Li Ji and others to attack along several routes. In 630 Li Jing led 3,000 elite cavalry in a night raid on Dingxiang and routed the Turks, then defeated them again at the Yin Mountains and captured Illig Khan, ending the Eastern Turkic Khaganate. Taizong took an open policy toward the surrendered Turks: he settled them in what is now Inner Mongolia, kept their tribal organization, appointed their leaders as military governors and prefects, and many Turkic nobles came to serve at court. In the same year, leaders of northern and northwestern peoples gathered in Chang'an and asked Taizong to be their “Heavenly Khan”, the common ruler of all peoples. Tang later defeated the Tuyuhun, Gaochang and the Western Turks, and set up the Anxi and Beiting Protectorates to strengthen its control of the Western Regions. Han and minority peoples lived together and intermarried, ethnic integration advanced, and many minority generals served in Tang, making this an important period in the development of a unified multi-ethnic state.

events.title: Japan Sends Embassies to Tang
events.short: Japan sent a dozen or so embassies to Tang China to study its institutions and culture. Abe no Nakamaro, Kibi no Makibi and others contributed greatly to Sino-Japanese exchange.
events.detail: Tang China was powerful and culturally flourishing, and attracted neighboring countries. Japan had already sent “envoys to Sui” in the Sui dynasty. In 630 it sent its first embassy to Tang, and over the next two centuries sent a dozen or so more, the largest with over 500 people, accompanied by students, student monks and technicians. They studied Tang political institutions, law, writing, astronomy and calendrical science, books, calligraphy, architecture, music and Buddhism, and brought many books and objects back to Japan, with a profound effect on its development. In 645 Japan carried out the Taika Reform, applying a land allotment system modeled on Tang's equal-field and tax systems and building a centralized government on the Tang pattern; its capitals Heijo-kyo (present-day Nara) and Heian-kyo (present-day Kyoto) were also laid out after Chang'an. Tang clothing, the game of go and customs such as the Dragon Boat Festival also spread to Japan. Among the envoys, Abe no Nakamaro was outstanding. He came to Chang'an with an embassy in 717, took the Chinese name Chao Heng, passed the jinshi examination, and served in Tang office for more than fifty years, forming deep friendships with Li Bai and Wang Wei. In 753, on his voyage home, a storm struck and he was falsely reported dead; Li Bai wrote “Lament for Chao Qingheng” in mourning. He in fact made his way back to Chang'an and died in China. Memorials to him stand today in Xi'an and in Nara. The envoy exchanges are celebrated in the history of Sino-Japanese friendship; Japan stopped sending them in 894.

events.title: Princess Wencheng Enters Tibet
events.short: In 641 Emperor Taizong married Princess Wencheng to the Tubo king Songtsen Gampo. She took seeds, books and craftsmen, aiding Tubo's economy and culture and Han–Tibetan friendship.
events.detail: The Tubo were ancestors of the Tibetans and lived on the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau. In the early 7th century their outstanding btsanpo (supreme ruler) Songtsen Gampo unified the plateau's tribes, founded the Tubo kingdom and made Logzhi (present-day Lhasa) its capital. He had the Tibetan script created, made laws, set up official and military systems and developed production, and Tubo grew steadily stronger. Admiring Central Plains culture, he repeatedly sent envoys to Tang to seek a marriage alliance. In 640 the Tubo chief minister Gar Tongtsen came to Chang'an with much gold and treasure, and Taizong agreed to marry the imperial clanswoman Princess Wencheng to Songtsen Gampo. In 641 Taizong sent Li Daozong, Prince of Jiangxia, to escort her to Tibet, and Songtsen Gampo met her in person at Bohai (near present-day Madoi, Qinghai). Princess Wencheng brought vegetable seeds, tea, silk and fine handicrafts, as well as books on Buddhist scripture, medicine, the calendar and technology, and was accompanied by craftsmen who introduced Central Plains farming, weaving, building, papermaking and wine-making to Tubo. Tradition holds that the life-size statue of Sakyamuni in the Jokhang Temple in Lhasa was brought by her. To learn more of Central Plains culture, Songtsen Gampo sent sons of nobles to study at the Imperial Academy in Chang'an, and asked Tang for silkworm eggs and for craftsmen in wine-making, milling, papermaking and ink-making. After Emperor Gaozong took the throne, he made Songtsen Gampo a son-in-law-commandant and Prince of Xihai. Princess Wencheng lived in Tubo for about forty years, died in 680, and is still remembered by the Tibetan people.

events.title: Friendly Exchanges Between Tang and the Arabs
events.short: During Tang, the Arab Caliphate (Dashi) sent envoys over forty times, its merchants traded in China by land and sea, and Chinese papermaking spread west through the Arab world.
events.detail: In the early 7th century Muhammad founded Islam on the Arabian Peninsula and a unified Arab state, which kept expanding into an Arab empire spanning Asia, Africa and Europe, called “Dashi” in Chinese histories. In 651 Dashi sent its first envoy to Chang'an, establishing formal contact with Tang. Until the end of Tang, Dashi sent more than forty missions. Trade between the two was very active. Arab merchants came by the overland Silk Road or by sea, traded at Guangzhou, Yangzhou, Quanzhou, Chang'an and elsewhere, sold pearls, spices, ivory, rhinoceros horn and medicines, and shipped Chinese silk, porcelain and tea west. Many settled in China for the long term; Guangzhou had a “foreign quarter” (fanfang) for foreign traders, and some served at the Tang court or even passed the jinshi examination. Islam came with them, and the Huaisheng Mosque in Guangzhou is traditionally said to date from Tang, one of China's earliest mosques. In 751 Tang and Dashi fought at Talas in Central Asia and the Tang army was defeated; it is generally held that papermaking passed from China to the Arab world through Samarkand and later to Europe. Friendly relations nonetheless continued, and during the An Lushan Rebellion Dashi even sent troops to help Tang. Du Huan, captured in the battle, lived in the Arab world for over ten years, and after returning wrote Record of Travels (Jingxing Ji), which describes the customs of Dashi and other places and is one of the earliest Chinese eyewitness accounts of the Arab world. Friendly contacts between Tang and Dashi promoted economic and cultural exchange between East and West.

events.title: Sun Simiao and Prescriptions Worth a Thousand Gold
events.short: The Tang physician Sun Simiao wrote Essential Prescriptions Worth a Thousand Gold and its supplement, with many prescriptions and teachings on medical ethics. He is honored as the “King of Medicine”.
events.detail: Medicine reached new heights in the Sui and Tang. The Tang government opened medical schools and compiled the Newly Revised Materia Medica (also called the Tang Materia Medica), the world's earliest pharmacopoeia issued by a state. Sun Simiao (c. 581–682), an eminent Tang physician from Huayuan, Jingzhao (present-day Yaozhou District, Tongchuan, Shaanxi), was frail and sickly as a child and spent his family's wealth on treatment, so he resolved to study medicine. He read widely and mastered both medicine and Daoist thought. Emperors of the Sui and Tang repeatedly invited him to serve but he declined, spending his life practicing medicine and gathering herbs among the people. Sun held that “human life is of utmost importance, worth more than a thousand gold, and one prescription that saves it is a greater virtue still”, and so titled his work Essential Prescriptions Worth a Thousand Gold (Beiji Qianjin Yaofang), in 30 volumes; late in life he wrote a 30-volume sequel, Supplement to the Prescriptions Worth a Thousand Gold. Together they are called the Qianjin Fang. They contain several thousand prescriptions and sum up medical achievements before Tang, covering internal medicine, surgery, gynecology, pediatrics, ear, nose and throat, acupuncture and moxibustion, dietary therapy and health preservation. He was the first to give gynecological and pediatric diseases separate volumes, and recorded effective methods such as treating night blindness with animal liver. The chapter “On the Absolute Sincerity of Great Physicians” sets out the virtues a doctor should have, asking that the physician treat patients without asking “whether they are noble or lowly, rich or poor, old or young, beautiful or plain... all alike”.

events.title: Tang and Silla Exchanges
events.short: After Silla unified most of the Korean Peninsula it kept close ties with Tang, sent many students, and modeled its institutions on Tang's. Choe Chiwon and others became envoys of Sino-Korean culture.
events.detail: In the Sui and Tang period the Korean Peninsula held three states, Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla, which had frequent contact with China. In the mid-7th century Silla joined Tang to destroy Baekje and Goguryeo, and by about 675 had largely unified the peninsula south of the Taedong River. After it grew strong, Silla was very close to Tang, sending envoys almost every year and many students to the Imperial Academy in Chang'an to study Chinese culture, at most over a hundred at a time. Silla modeled its central and local government on Tang's, selected officials by examinations on the Confucian classics, and adopted Chinese medicine, astronomy, calendrical science, architecture and Buddhism; Tang poetry and books flowed in large numbers to the peninsula. Many Silla merchants came to China, forming communities such as the “Silla quarters” on the Shandong Peninsula and in the Yangtze–Huai region. Silla goods such as bezoar, ginseng, seal skins and gold and silver ware were imported in large amounts, ranking first among Tang imports, while Tang silk, tea, porcelain and books were sent to Silla. Korean music also entered China: “Goryeo music” was performed at the Tang court and popular among the people. Choe Chiwon was an outstanding figure of the exchange. He went to Tang to study at twelve, passed the jinshi examination at eighteen, served as a Tang official, and won fame by drafting for Gao Pian a proclamation against Huang Chao, before returning to Silla. His collected writings, Plowing the Cinnamon Grove with a Writing Brush (Guiyuan Bigeng Ji), survive and are important sources on Tang history and Sino-Korean relations; he is honored as the founder of Korean literature in classical Chinese.

events.title: Wu Zetian Proclaims Herself Emperor
events.short: In 690 Wu Zetian renamed the dynasty Zhou and became emperor, the only woman to rule China as emperor. She promoted the examination system and agriculture, bridging the Zhenguan and Kaiyuan eras.
events.detail: Wu Zetian (624–705), personal name Zhao, was from Wenshui, Bingzhou (present-day Wenshui, Shanxi). She began as a concubine of Emperor Taizong and was later brought back to the palace by Emperor Gaozong. In 655 Gaozong deposed Empress Wang and made Wu Zetian empress. Gaozong was frail and often ill, and Wu Zetian, shrewd and decisive, took part in government; the two were called the “Two Sages”. After Gaozong died in 683, she ruled as empress dowager, deposed Emperor Zhongzong in turn and controlled Emperor Ruizong. In 690 she changed the dynastic name to Zhou, made Luoyang the capital (the “Divine Capital”) and styled herself “Sage and Divine Emperor”, becoming the only formally recognized woman emperor in Chinese history; the period is known as the “Wu Zhou”. During her rule she employed ruthless officials, encouraged informing and harshly suppressed hostile officials and nobles, producing many wrongful cases. But she also valued finding talent, greatly developed the imperial examination, created the palace examination and interviewed candidates herself, began the military examination, and allowed officials and commoners to recommend themselves. Capable ministers such as Di Renjie, Yao Chong and Song Jing were promoted. She continued the agricultural policies of the Zhenguan era and the economy kept growing; households rose from over three million in early Tang to over six million. On the frontier she sent troops to recover the Four Garrisons of Anxi and set up the Beiting Protectorate. In 705 the chancellor Zhang Jianzhi and others launched the Shenlong Coup, forcing Wu Zetian to yield to Zhongzong and restoring the Tang name. She died that year and was buried with Gaozong in the Qianling Mausoleum, in front of which stands the “Wordless Stele”.

events.title: Princess Jincheng and the Tang–Tubo Treaties
events.short: In 710 Princess Jincheng married the Tubo king Tride Tsugtsen, and Tang and Tubo called each other “uncle and nephew”. In 821–823 they swore a treaty, with a stele erected before the Jokhang.
events.detail: After Princess Wencheng entered Tibet, Tang and Tubo kept close ties, though they also fought over the Western Regions and Qinghai. In 710, at Tubo's request, they made another marriage alliance: Emperor Zhongzong married his adopted daughter Princess Jincheng to the Tubo king Tride Tsugtsen (also rendered Chidai Zhudan). She brought large quantities of silk and brocade, craftsmen, and a Kucha band. Tradition holds that she moved the Sakyamuni statue brought by Princess Wencheng to the Jokhang and promoted Buddhist practice in Tubo. Tang and Tubo then agreed to trade and set their border at Chiling (present-day Riyue Mountain, Qinghai). Tride Tsugtsen wrote to Emperor Xuanzong that Tang and Tubo were “united as one family”, calling himself “nephew” and the Tang emperor “uncle”, and from then on the two often addressed each other as “uncle and nephew”. After the An Lushan Rebellion, Tubo took advantage of Tang's weakness to seize Hexi, Longyou and other regions, and war was frequent, but they also swore treaties several times. In 821–822, Tang and Tubo held covenant ceremonies in Chang'an and Logzhi (present-day Lhasa), known as the “Changqing Treaty”. In 823 Tubo erected a stele before the Jokhang in Lhasa, inscribed in Chinese and Tibetan with the treaty: the Tang–Tubo Treaty Stele, also called the Uncle–Nephew Treaty Stele. Its text says that the two states were “as one realm” and would “forever honor the friendship of uncle and nephew”. The stele still stands before the Jokhang, a witness to friendly exchanges between Han and Tibetans.

events.title: Kaiyuan Golden Age
events.short: In his early reign Emperor Xuanzong used able chancellors like Yao Chong and Song Jing, reformed officialdom and developed the economy. Tang reached its height, the “Kaiyuan Golden Age”.
events.detail: Emperor Xuanzong of Tang, Li Longji (685–762), was a grandson of Wu Zetian and a son of Emperor Ruizong. In 710 he staged a coup that killed Empress Wei's faction, took the throne in 712, and in 713 adopted the era name “Kaiyuan”. In his early reign he governed diligently and used capable men, appointing Yao Chong, Song Jing, Zhang Yue, Zhang Jiuling and others as chancellors, and carried out a series of reforms. He tidied official administration and cut redundant posts, paid attention to selecting local officials, personally tested county magistrates and dismissed at once those who failed. He developed the economy by registering households that had fled, raising state tax revenue, building irrigation works and promoting military farming colonies. He valued culture and set up the Academy of Worthies to collate and compile books. After over twenty years of rule, Tang had vast territory and Chang'an became a cosmopolitan city thronged with envoys, merchants and students. Government was stable, the economy flourished, the treasury was full, households grew to over eight million, society was calm and grain prices were low. Tang power reached its peak, known as the “Kaiyuan Golden Age”. The poet Du Fu described it in “Recalling the Past”: “I recall the full glory of Kaiyuan, when even a small town held ten thousand households. Rice was glossy and millet white, and granaries public and private were full.” But in the later Kaiyuan years Xuanzong grew complacent and idle and indulged in pleasure, appointing Li Linfu and then Yang Guozhong as chancellors. Government became increasingly corrupt, the military governors grew powerful, and tensions accumulated, until the An Lushan Rebellion broke out in 755 and Tang went from prosperity into decline.

images.caption: Emperor Xuanzong of Tang

events.title: Bohai Kingdom, the “Flourishing State of the East”
events.short: In the late 7th century the Sumo Mohe leader Dae Joyoung founded a regime, made Prince of Bohai by Tang in 713. Modeled on Tang, Bohai prospered and was called the “Flourishing State of the East”.
events.detail: The Mohe were an ancient people of the Songhua and Heilong River basins in northeast China, ancestors of the later Jurchen and Manchu, who in Tang times were divided into the Sumo, Heishui and other groups. In 698 the Sumo Mohe leader Dae Joyoung united the Mohe groups and founded a regime at Mount Dongmou (near present-day Dunhua, Jilin), calling himself “King of Zhen”. In 713 Emperor Xuanzong sent Cui Xin to invest him as “Prince of Bohai” and set up Hulhan Prefecture in his territory, naming him its governor; the regime then took “Bohai” as its name and became a local ethnic regime under Tang. On his way back Cui Xin dug a well at present-day Lushun and left a stone inscription, the “Honglu Well Inscription”, which the Japanese carried off in 1908. Bohai had close ties with Tang, regularly sending envoys and students to Chang'an, and Tang poetry, books, Buddhism and institutions flowed in. Bohai set up a Three Departments and Six Ministries system on the Tang pattern, with five capitals, fifteen prefectures and sixty-two districts, used Chinese characters, and laid out its capital, Shangjing Longquanfu (present-day Bohai Town, Ning'an, Heilongjiang), after Chang'an. Trade with the interior was frequent, agriculture, crafts and commerce grew greatly, and its economy and culture flourished, earning the name “Flourishing State of the East”. At its height its territory included eastern Northeast China, northeastern Korea and part of the Russian Far East. In 926 Bohai was destroyed by the Khitan after more than two hundred years. Its history shows that ethnic groups in the northeast had close ties with Central Plains dynasties from early on, an important part of the pluralistic unity of the Chinese nation.

events.title: Prosperity of High Tang and the City of Chang'an
events.short: In early Tang the curved-shaft plow and noria spread, farming and crafts thrived, and commerce flourished. Chang'an, vast in scale, was one of the world's largest cosmopolitan cities.
events.detail: Over the first century or so of Tang the economy grew quickly and society prospered. Cultivated land kept expanding and techniques improved; important tools such as the curved-shaft plow and the noria were invented and spread. The curved-shaft plow was light and easy to turn, suiting intensive farming; the noria raised water for irrigation by water power, working day and night. Tang built many irrigation works, and grain output rose sharply. Silk weaving, porcelain, papermaking, printing and gold and silver work were all advanced. Porcelain was described as “green in the south, white in the north”: celadon from the Yue kilns in the south and white ware from the Xing kilns in the north. The brilliantly colored Tang sancai is a famed pottery art. Cities such as Chang'an, Luoyang, Yangzhou, Chengdu and Guangzhou thrived, and it was said “Yangzhou first, Yizhou second”. The capital Chang'an was vast and orderly, covering about 84 square kilometers with a population of about a million, among the largest cities of its time. It consisted of the Palace City, Imperial City and outer city, laid out symmetrically along Zhuque Avenue, and was divided into over a hundred walled wards, with residential wards and commercial markets strictly separated. The East and West Markets were two great commercial districts full of goods; the West Market in particular gathered many foreign merchants from the Western Regions, Persia and the Arab world and was called the “Golden Market”. Many foreign envoys, students and monks also lived in Chang'an, a bustling international metropolis. The prosperity of High Tang laid a firm basis for its flourishing culture and foreign exchange.

events.title: Open Social Customs of Tang
events.short: Tang society was open and inclusive: women rode horses, played polo and wore “Hu” dress, foreign food and music were popular, and people had an energetic, upbeat spirit.
events.detail: Tang was strong and its rulers followed open policies. Contact among peoples and with foreign lands was frequent, and social customs were relatively open and full of vigor, with people generally showing an energetic, upbeat spirit. Society was inclusive, and clothing, food, housing, travel and entertainment were much influenced by northwestern minorities and foreign cultures. In dress, “Hu” (foreign) clothes and hats were fashionable in Chang'an and elsewhere, and women wearing men's clothing or Hu dress was common. In food, Hu flatbread, sesame and grape wine were popular. In music and dance, Kucha music and the Hu whirl and Hu leap dances from the Western Regions were all the rage; the poet Wang Jian wrote, “On the city wall the pheasants cry, and every household in Luoyang learns Hu music.” Women had a relatively high status and faced fewer restrictions, could go out fairly freely, and many were educated in literature and music and enjoyed riding, polo, tug-of-war, archery, swinging and board games. Tang pottery figures and murals often show women riding out or playing polo, as in Zhang Xuan's Lady Guoguo's Spring Outing. Tang also had a vigorous martial spirit; many literati aspired to military service on the frontier, so frontier poetry flourished, and the line “better to be a captain of a hundred than a mere scholar” reflects this. Polo, tug-of-war, cuju and go were popular at every level of society. Tang's open customs were closely tied to the nation's strength, ethnic integration and cultural exchange, and reflect the confidence and inclusiveness of the Great Tang.

events.title: Golden Age of Tang Poetry (Li Bai, Du Fu, Bai Juyi)
events.short: Tang was the golden age of poetry: the Complete Tang Poems holds nearly 50,000 poems, and Li Bai, Du Fu and Bai Juyi are its greatest figures.
events.detail: The Tang was the peak of classical Chinese poetry. Scholars used verse exchanges as an important way of socializing and expressing feeling, and the civil service examinations also valued poetry and rhapsodies, so composition thrived. The Complete Tang Poems, compiled in the Qing, contains nearly 50,000 poems by over 2,200 Tang poets, with rich themes, varied styles and many masters. Wang Wei and Meng Haoran wrote landscape and pastoral poems, Gao Shi and Cen Shen frontier poems, and Li Shangyin and Du Mu also had their own distinct voices. The most famous are Li Bai, Du Fu and Bai Juyi. Li Bai (701–762), courtesy name Taibai, praised the grandeur of the land, expressed an upward-striving spirit, and showed contempt for the powerful and a love of freedom. His style is free and bold, full of imagination and strongly romantic, and he is called the “Immortal of Poetry”; his works include “The Road to Shu is Hard”, “Bring in the Wine” and “Viewing the Waterfall at Mount Lu”. Du Fu (712–770), courtesy name Zimei, lived as Tang turned from prosperity to decline and had a hard life. His poems deeply reflect society and the people's suffering around the An Lushan Rebellion and express concern for the country and its people. His style is somber and measured, his work is called the “poetic history”, and he is honored as the “Sage of Poetry”; the “Three Officials”, the “Three Partings” and lines like “Behind vermilion gates wine and meat rot, on the road lie the bones of the frozen” are widely recited. Bai Juyi (772–846), courtesy name Letian, advocated the New Yuefu Movement and wrote plain, easy poems, including “The Charcoal Seller”, “Song of Everlasting Sorrow” and “Song of the Pipa”. Tang poetry is a jewel of Chinese culture and spread to Japan, Korea and elsewhere.

events.title: Jianzhen's Voyage to Japan
events.short: Jianzhen, a senior monk of Yangzhou, accepted an invitation to Japan. After six attempts over twelve years, and blindness, he reached Japan in 754 and spread Buddhism and Chinese culture.
events.detail: Jianzhen (688–763), born Chunyu, from Jiangyang County, Yangzhou, was a senior monk of Daming Temple in Yangzhou, expert in monastic discipline and also versed in medicine and architecture. In 742 the Japanese student monks Eiei and Fusho came to Yangzhou and begged Jianzhen to go to Japan to teach Buddhist precepts. Ignoring his disciples' warning that “the sea is vast and out of a hundred attempts, hardly one arrives”, he resolutely agreed. Over the next ten or so years he made five attempts, all of which failed through official obstruction, storms at sea or ships striking rocks. On the fifth, his ship drifted for fourteen days and was blown to Hainan Island; on the return journey Eiei died, and Jianzhen lost his sight from long travel, exhaustion and heat. Yet he did not waver. In 753 he sailed on a Japanese embassy ship for the sixth time and finally reached Japan in early 754, aged sixty-six. The journey had taken twelve years, and more than thirty of his companions died along the way. In Japan he was warmly welcomed by the emperor and the court, and at Todai-ji in Nara he set up an ordination platform to give precepts to the emperor, the empress and many monks. He later oversaw the building of Toshodai-ji, a temple in Tang style that is now a Japanese national treasure. Jianzhen lived in Japan for ten years; besides teaching monastic discipline he introduced Chinese medicine, literature, calligraphy, architecture, sculpture and painting, deeply influencing Japanese culture, and is honored as the founder of Japan's Ritsu school and the “father of medicine”. He died at Toshodai-ji in 763. In 1980 his seated statue came back to Daming Temple on a “home visit”, a celebrated moment in Sino-Japanese friendship.

events.title: An Lushan Rebellion
events.short: In 755 the military governors An Lushan and Shi Siming rebelled and took Luoyang and Chang'an. It took over seven years to suppress, and Tang went from prosperity into decline.
events.detail: In the later Kaiyuan years, Emperor Xuanzong grew complacent and idle, pursued pleasure, doted on Consort Yang, and appointed Li Linfu and Yang Guozhong as chancellors, and government grew more corrupt. To strengthen frontier defense Tang set up ten military governors on the borders, who gradually held military, administrative and financial power together and kept growing, producing a situation of “strong outside, weak within”. An Lushan, a general of Hu origin and a skilled flatterer, enjoyed Xuanzong's trust, serving as military governor of Pinglu, Fanyang (southwest of present-day Beijing) and Hedong at once, with over 100,000 troops. In 755, on the pretext of punishing the treacherous Yang Guozhong, he rose in revolt at Fanyang with his subordinate Shi Siming, the “An–Shi Rebellion”. The rebels marched south from Hebei and quickly took the Eastern Capital Luoyang, where An Lushan declared himself emperor of Yan. In 756 they broke Tong Pass and Xuanzong fled in haste toward Sichuan; at Mawei Station the escorting troops mutinied, killed Yang Guozhong and forced Xuanzong to order Consort Yang's death. Crown Prince Li Heng took the throne at Lingwu as Emperor Suzong. The rebels soon entered Chang'an. During the suppression, Zhang Xun and Xu Yuan held Suiyang and blocked the rebels' southward advance, while Guo Ziyi, Li Guangbi and others fought bloody battles and recovered Chang'an and Luoyang. The rebels also weakened themselves with killings among father and sons. In 763 Shi Chaoyi was defeated and killed himself, and the rebellion was finally put down. It severely damaged the northern economy and greatly reduced the population, and Tang declined from then on.

events.title: Tang Calligraphy and Painting
events.short: Tang calligraphy produced many masters, including Yan Zhenqing, Liu Gongquan and Ouyang Xun; in painting Yan Liben and Wu Daozi stood out, and Wu Daozi was honored as the “Sage of Painting”.
events.detail: Tang was strong and culturally flourishing, and calligraphy, painting, music, dance and sculpture all reached brilliant heights. Calligraphy produced many masters. In early Tang, Ouyang Xun's regular script, steep and strict in structure, is called the “Ou style”. Zhang Xu of High Tang and Huaisu of mid-Tang excelled in wild cursive, unrestrained and free. Yan Zhenqing was one of Tang's most influential calligraphers. A loyal official who held Pingyuan and resisted the rebels during the An Lushan Rebellion, he was later strangled while trying to persuade the rebel general Li Xilie, and later generations admired both his character and his writing. His upright, strong and sturdy script is called the “Yan style”, with works such as the Duobao Pagoda Stele and the Stele of Yan Qinli; his Draft Eulogy for My Nephew, written in mourning for a nephew killed in the rebellion, is called the “second-best running script under heaven”. Liu Gongquan of late Tang wrote in angular, bold, powerful strokes, the “Liu style”, and later people used “Yan's sinew, Liu's bone” to describe their calligraphy. Tang painting covered figures, landscapes, birds and flowers and religious subjects. Yan Liben of early Tang excelled in figure painting, capturing both form and spirit, and his Emperor Taizong Receiving the Tibetan Envoy depicts Taizong receiving the Tubo envoy Gar Tongtsen. Wu Daozi of High Tang was Tang's most famous painter, skilled in Buddhist and Daoist figures and landscapes, with vigorous strokes, dynamic lines and fluttering robes, praised as “Wu's sashes flutter in the wind”, and later honored as the “Sage of Painting”. Landscapes by Li Sixun and Wang Wei, ladies by Zhang Xuan and Zhou Fang, and horses by Han Gan were also famous.
