events.title: Huang Chao Uprising
events.short: In late Tang heavy burdens and repeated famine led to the Wang Xianzhi and Huang Chao uprising of 875. In 880 Huang Chao took Chang'an and founded the Great Qi, dealing Tang a fatal blow.
events.detail: In late Tang, rule grew more rotten, eunuchs held power, and regional warlordism worsened until the center could no longer control the military governors. Exploitation of the people increased, taxes and corvée were heavy, and with years of flood, drought and locusts many peasants could not live, so social tension was at a peak. In 874 the salt smuggler Wang Xianzhi rose at Changyuan; in 875 Huang Chao, also a salt smuggler, gathered followers at Yuanju (southwest of present-day Heze, Shandong) in response. The rebels fought across Shandong, Henan, Hubei and elsewhere, and after Wang Xianzhi died in battle Huang Chao became the leader. He avoided the main Tang armies, crossed the Yangtze, campaigned in Jiangxi, Zhejiang and Fujian, took Guangzhou, then turned north, attacking officials and landlords, and his force grew to several hundred thousand. In 880 the rebels took Luoyang, broke Tong Pass and entered Chang'an. In early 881 Huang Chao proclaimed himself emperor with the dynastic name “Great Qi”. But the rebels did not pursue the remaining Tang forces and built no secure base, and became isolated in Chang'an; Tang gathered the military governors' armies for a counterattack, the rebel general Zhu Wen defected to Tang, and the Shatuo leader Li Keyong also led troops against them. In 883 Huang Chao was forced out of Chang'an, and in 884 he was defeated and took his own life at Langhu Valley on Mount Tai. The uprising lasted ten years and ranged across much of China, dealing heavy blows to Tang rule and to the decaying aristocratic clans. After its defeat, Tang existed in name only, regional warlords grew stronger, and some twenty years later Zhu Wen destroyed Tang.

events.title: Fall of Tang; Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms
events.short: In 907 Zhu Wen founded the Later Liang and Tang fell. Five successive dynasties then ruled the north and ten separate regimes arose in the south, the “Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms”.
events.detail: After the Huang Chao uprising failed, Tang existed in name only and military governors everywhere annexed one another. Zhu Wen, formerly a Huang Chao general, surrendered to Tang and became military governor of Xuanwu, based at Bianzhou (present-day Kaifeng, Henan); he gradually absorbed northern warlords large and small and took control of the Tang court. In 904 he forced Emperor Zhaozong to move the capital to Luoyang and soon had him killed. In 907 Zhu Wen deposed Emperor Ai of Tang and made himself emperor under the dynastic name Liang, known as the Later Liang, with its capital at Kaifeng, and Tang fell. From 907 to 960, five dynasties arose in turn in the Yellow River basin in the north, the Later Liang, Later Tang, Later Jin, Later Han and Later Zhou, called the “Five Dynasties”, mostly centered around Kaifeng and Luoyang, and they changed frequently. Meanwhile ten regimes appeared in the south and in Shanxi: Wu, Southern Tang, Wuyue, Min, Chu, Southern Han, Former Shu, Later Shu, Nanping (Jingnan) and the Northern Han, which held Taiyuan in the north; these are the “Ten Kingdoms”. The period continued the late-Tang warlord situation: founding rulers were mostly generals holding military power, regimes changed often, mutinies were common, the north was especially wracked by war, and the economy suffered greatly. By comparison the southern states saw less war and more stability, the Jiangnan economy kept growing, and the south gradually outstripped the north. In this period the Khitan in the north grew stronger, and Shi Jingtang of the Later Jin ceded the Sixteen Prefectures of Yan and Yun to them, leaving a lasting danger for later Central Plains dynasties.

events.title: Yelü Abaoji Founds the Khitan State (Liao)
events.short: In the early 10th century the Khitan leader Yelü Abaoji united the tribes, declared himself emperor in 916 and founded a state with its capital at Shangjing Linhuangfu. It was later renamed Liao.
events.detail: The Khitan were an ancient people of northern China who long roamed the Xar Moron and Lao Ha River basins in eastern Inner Mongolia. In Sui and Tang times their ties with the Central Plains grew closer, and Tang set up the Songmo Governorate in Khitan lands and appointed Khitan leaders as governors. In late Tang, constant war in the Central Plains drove many northern Han people north beyond the Great Wall, bringing advanced production techniques and ways of life. By the late 9th century the Khitan had farming, ironworking and weaving and began building houses and towns. In the early 10th century Yelü Abaoji, leader of the Dila tribe, united the Khitan tribes through repeated campaigns. In 916 he formally took the title of emperor and founded the Khitan state, known as Emperor Taizu of Liao, with the capital at Shangjing Linhuangfu (south of present-day Balinzuo Banner, Inner Mongolia). Abaoji employed Han scholars such as Han Yanhui and Han Zhigu, built state institutions on Central Plains models, developed agriculture and settled Han people to farm, and had the Khitan large script created on the model of Chinese characters, and his state grew steadily stronger. In 926 Abaoji led his army to destroy the Bohai Kingdom and soon died. His son Emperor Taizong, Yelü Deguang, helped Shi Jingtang found the Later Jin, obtained the Sixteen Prefectures of Yan and Yun, and in 947 renamed the state “Liao”. Liao followed a policy of “governing according to custom”, with a Northern administration and a Southern administration, “ruling the Khitan by Khitan institutions and the Han by Han institutions”. The dynastic name later changed several times between “Khitan” and “Liao”; the state lasted over two hundred years until the Jin destroyed it in 1125.

events.title: Shi Jingtang Cedes the Sixteen Prefectures
events.short: In 936 Shi Jingtang, a Later Tang governor, ceded the Sixteen Prefectures and called himself the Khitan emperor’s “son” for troops to destroy Later Tang, founding Later Jin.
events.detail: The Sixteen Prefectures of Yan and Yun, also called the Sixteen Prefectures of Youyun or Youji, were sixteen prefectures centered on Youzhou (present-day Beijing) and Yunzhou (present-day Datong, Shanxi), roughly covering present-day Beijing, northern Tianjin and northern Hebei and Shanxi. The area is strategically rugged, with many passes of the Great Wall, and was an important northern barrier for Central Plains dynasties. At the end of the Later Tang, Shi Jingtang, military governor of Hedong, held Taiyuan, and he and Emperor Li Congke of Later Tang suspected each other. In 936 Li Congke ordered Shi Jingtang transferred; Shi rebelled and was besieged at Taiyuan by Later Tang troops. To win Khitan help, Shi Jingtang declared himself a subject of Emperor Yelü Deguang, even called Yelü Deguang, ten years younger than himself, his father, and promised to cede the Sixteen Prefectures to the Khitan and pay an annual tribute of 300,000 bolts of silk. The Khitan sent troops that defeated the Later Tang, and in the same year installed Shi Jingtang as emperor under the dynastic name Jin, known as the Later Jin. In 937 Shi Jingtang destroyed the Later Tang and made Bianzhou (present-day Kaifeng, Henan) his capital, keeping his promise; in 938 the Sixteen Prefectures were formally handed to the Khitan. Shi Jingtang was later called the “son emperor” and reviled. The cession opened the northern gateway of Central Plains dynasties and deprived them of the natural barrier of the Great Wall, so that Khitan cavalry could ride south as far as the Yellow River. Later, Emperor Shizong of Later Zhou recovered Ying, Mo and other prefectures, and Emperor Taizong of Northern Song tried twice to recover the rest, both failing.

events.title: Emperor Shizong of Later Zhou's Reforms
events.short: Chai Rong, Emperor Shizong of Later Zhou, reformed officialdom, evened out land taxes, reorganized the imperial army and curbed Buddhism, laying the ground for Song unification. He died at 39.
events.detail: Chai Rong (921–959), from Yaoshan, Xingzhou (present-day Longyao, Hebei), adopted son of Guo Wei, Emperor Taizu of Later Zhou, took the throne in 954. It was the late Five Dynasties: long unrest, political chaos and a ruined economy, with the Northern Han and the Khitan threatening in the north and Southern Tang, Later Shu and other regimes in the south. Chai Rong had great ambitions and worked to reverse the disorder with a series of reforms. Politically, he strengthened central control, tidied officialdom, punished corrupt officials severely, selected talent and revised the laws. Economically, he stressed production, drew back displaced people, encouraged land clearing, built irrigation works, controlled the Yellow River, and sent officials to survey fields everywhere and even out the land tax, easing the peasants' burden. In religion, he curbed Buddhism, abolishing over thirty thousand temples without imperial approval and forcing many monks and nuns back to lay life, which added labor and state revenue. Militarily, he reorganized and expanded the central imperial army and weakened regional military power. In 954 he personally led the army to defeat the combined Northern Han and Khitan forces at the Battle of Gaoping. He then campaigned against Southern Tang and took fourteen prefectures between the Yangtze and Huai, attacked Later Shu in the west and took four prefectures including Qin and Feng, and in 959 marched north against the Khitan, recovering Ying and Mo prefectures and the three passes of Waqiao, Yijin and Yukou. Just as he prepared to retake Youzhou, he fell suddenly ill and died not long after returning to the capital, at only 39. His reforms strengthened Later Zhou, ended the chaos of the Five Dynasties and laid the ground for Northern Song unification.

events.title: Chenqiao Mutiny and Founding of Northern Song
events.short: In 960 Zhao Kuangyin, commander of the Later Zhou imperial guard, was acclaimed emperor at Chenqiao Station in the “Yellow Robe” mutiny. He returned to Kaifeng and founded the Northern Song.
events.detail: Emperor Shizong of Zhou died in 959 and the seven-year-old Emperor Gong took the throne, a child ruler and an uneasy state. Zhao Kuangyin was commander of the Later Zhou imperial guard, holding the post of Palace Command Inspector, and controlled the capital's troops. In early 960 the court learned that the Liao and Northern Han had joined forces to invade, and sent Zhao Kuangyin north to resist them. When the army reached Chenqiao Station, forty li northeast of Kaifeng (present-day Chenqiao Town, southeast of Fengqiu, Henan), Zhao Guangyi, Zhao Pu and others stirred up the soldiers, draped a yellow robe prepared in advance over Zhao Kuangyin, kowtowed and hailed him “Long live the emperor”, acclaiming him emperor: the origin of the “Chenqiao Mutiny” and of “the yellow robe being put on him”. Zhao Kuangyin then led the army back to Kaifeng, and Emperor Gong was forced to yield the throne. As he had once been military governor of Guide at Songzhou (present-day Shangqiu, Henan), he chose Song as the dynastic name and made Kaifeng, as the Eastern Capital, his capital; this is the Northern Song, and Zhao Kuangyin is Emperor Taizu of Song. On taking the throne he forbade his soldiers from plundering the city. To end division he and Zhao Pu settled on a strategy of “south first, then north”, and he destroyed the southern regimes of Jingnan, Hunan, Later Shu, Southern Han and Southern Tang in turn. After his death his brother Zhao Guangyi took the throne as Emperor Taizong; in 978 Wuyue and Chen Hongjin of Zhangquan yielded their lands, and in 979 the Northern Han was destroyed, largely ending the division of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms.

events.date: Reign of Emperor Taizu of Song
events.title: Releasing Military Power Over Wine; Centralization
events.short: Emperor Taizu removed his generals' commands through the “wine cup” banquet, split the chancellor's powers, sent civil officials to govern prefectures and took finances for the center.
events.detail: Emperor Taizu of Song, Zhao Kuangyin, had taken power through a mutiny and knew well the ills since late Tang and the Five Dynasties: generals dominating government, regional warlordism and frequent regime change. After taking the throne he discussed with his adviser Zhao Pu how to keep the state stable. Zhao Pu advised him to “take away their power a little, control their money and grain, and gather their elite troops”. In 961 Taizu held a banquet for senior imperial guard commanders such as Shi Shouxin, and at the table said he feared that one day their subordinates might put the yellow robe on them too, urging them to give up their commands. The next day the generals all claimed illness and asked to be relieved, and Taizu granted each, with generous rewards: the “releasing of military power over a cup of wine”. Militarily, he concentrated the country's best troops in the imperial guard and separated the authority to command from the authority to deploy: the Bureau of Military Affairs could deploy but not command, and the Three Offices could command but not deploy. A rotation system regularly changed garrisons so that “soldiers did not know their generals and generals did not control their soldiers”. At the center, to stop the chancellor from growing too powerful, he divided his functions among the Participant in Governance, the Military Affairs Commissioner and the Finance Commissioner. Locally, he sent civil officials as prefects, with supervising Vice-Prefects; most local revenue went to the center under transport commissioners, and the best local troops were sent to the capital as imperial guards. These measures ended the warlordism of late Tang and greatly strengthened central authority, keeping Northern Song stable for a long time.

events.title: Civil Over Military Rule and the Examinations
events.short: Song relied on civil officials and curbed generals, so civil officials commanded armies. It greatly expanded examination admissions and perfected the palace examination, name-sealing and copying.
events.detail: To prevent the return of the overbearing generals with private armies seen since late Tang, Emperor Taizu deliberately gave civil officials control of military and government affairs. Emperor Taizong continued policies that held down generals and raised civil officials, and a pattern of civil officials commanding troops gradually formed. Civil officials held key posts at the center and in the localities, even ran military affairs, and had higher status and pay than generals. Generals were checked in many ways; commanders had to deploy according to “battle diagrams” issued by the court, which tightly bound their command and hurt the Song army's fighting strength. Song emphasized culture and education and greatly reformed the examination system. In early Song the number admitted was greatly increased; under Emperor Taizong several hundred jinshi and other degrees were granted in a single sitting, far more than Tang's twenty or thirty at a time. Song further perfected the palace examination, with the emperor presiding over the final round, and, to prevent cheating, adopted name-sealing and copying (a clerk copied each paper before it went to the examiners), making the examinations fairer. It raised the standing of jinshi, who received better posts and rose quickly. Admission did not depend on family background, and many scholars from humble families, such as Fan Zhongyan and Ouyang Xiu, entered office through the examinations, giving Song society a strong culture of study in which “those who excel in study become officials”.

sources.title: Wikipedia (Chinese) - Favoring Civil Over Military Rule

events.date: From the Jingde era of Northern Song
events.title: Song Porcelain and Jingdezhen
events.short: Song was a brilliant age for porcelain, with the five famous kilns, Ru, Guan, Ge, Jun and Ding, known worldwide. Jingdezhen, which rose in the Jingde era, later became the “Porcelain Capital”.
events.detail: The Song was a brilliant era in the history of Chinese porcelain: techniques reached a high level, kilns spread across the country, and wares were varied and distinctive. Later generations call Song's most famous kilns the “five famous kilns”: Ru, Guan, Ge, Jun and Ding. Ru ware, made for the court, is celadon with a sky-blue glaze; Ge ware has a glaze covered in natural crackles called “crackle”; Jun ware, from present-day Yuzhou, Henan, is famed for its transmutation glazes, with endlessly varied colors, said to be “one color into the kiln, ten thousand colors out”; Ding ware, from present-day Quyang, Hebei, is known for white porcelain. Longquan kilns in Zhejiang were famous for celadon. Jingdezhen in Jiangxi, originally Changnan Town, had a long history of porcelain, and in the Jingde era of Northern Song (1004–1007) the court ordered it to make porcelain for the palace, marked on the base “made in the Jingde era”, so the town was renamed Jingdezhen. Its qingbai (bluish-white, or “shadow-blue”) porcelain was fine in body and jade-like in color. Jiang Qi's Record of Ceramics in the Southern Song was China's first monograph on ceramics, and records over three hundred kilns at Jingdezhen then, whose wares were “pure white and flawless” and known everywhere as “Rao jade”. In the Southern Song the Jiangnan region became China's center of porcelain making. In the Yuan, Jingdezhen produced blue-and-white and underglaze red, and in the Ming and Qing it grew into the national center of porcelain, called the “Porcelain Capital”. Song porcelain was exported in large quantities by the maritime Silk Road to Southeast Asia, South Asia, West Asia and East Africa. The English word “china” also means porcelain.

events.title: Treaty of Chanyuan
events.short: In 1004 Liao troops marched south to Chanzhou, and Emperor Zhenzong, urged by Kou Zhun, campaigned in person. In 1005 Song and Liao made peace, Song paying annual tribute, bringing a century of peace.
events.detail: After obtaining the Sixteen Prefectures of Yan and Yun, Liao came into sharper conflict with Central Plains dynasties. After the founding of Northern Song, Emperor Taizong twice campaigned north to recover the Sixteen Prefectures and failed, and Song then adopted a defensive policy toward Liao. In autumn 1004, Emperor Shengzong of Liao and his mother, Empress Dowager Xiao, led 200,000 troops south, taking cities as far as Chanzhou (present-day Puyang, Henan) on the north bank of the Yellow River, threatening the capital Kaifeng and throwing the Song court into panic. Some ministers urged moving the capital to Jinling or Chengdu, but the chancellor Kou Zhun firmly opposed this and urged Emperor Zhenzong to campaign in person. Zhenzong reluctantly came to Chanzhou and climbed the city tower; Song soldiers, seeing the emperor's yellow dragon banner, cheered and their morale soared. Earlier, Song troops had killed the Liao vanguard commander Xiao Talin with a bed-crossbow outside Chanzhou, dulling the Liao edge, and as the Liao army had pushed far in and feared its retreat being cut, it asked for peace. Zhenzong was also eager to end the war, and after negotiations the two sides made a treaty in early 1005: Song and Liao became brother states; Song paid Liao 100,000 taels of silver and 200,000 bolts of silk each year as “annual tribute”; the border was set along the Baigou River, with each side keeping to its frontier and building no new fortifications; and border markets were opened for trade. Because Chanzhou was also called Chanyuan Commandery, it is called the “Treaty of Chanyuan”.

events.title: Champa Rice and the Growth of Song Agriculture
events.short: Early-ripening, drought-tolerant Champa rice, introduced from Vietnam, spread across the Yangtze–Huai region. Southern farming grew fast: “When Suzhou and Huzhou have a harvest, the world has enough”.
events.detail: From the late Eastern Han, Jiangnan's society and economy had been developing. From mid-to-late Tang through the Song, large numbers of northerners moved south bringing advanced production techniques, and southern agriculture accelerated and gradually overtook the north. In the Song, population grew, cultivated land expanded and farming methods improved, bringing unprecedented agricultural growth. The area under southern rice grew quickly. Champa rice, originally from Champa (central and southern Vietnam today), ripens early, tolerates drought and adapts well. In 1012 (the fifth year of Dazhong Xiangfu under Emperor Zhenzong), drought struck the Yangtze–Huai and Liangzhe regions; Zhenzong had 30,000 hu of Champa seed fetched from Fujian, distributed it for planting there, and had farmers taught how to grow it. Champa rice then spread across the south and, bred with existing varieties, produced many early-ripening strains, raising yields greatly and allowing two crops a year in some places. Southern farmers also built polder fields in the Lake Tai region, terraced hills and mountains, and reclaimed fields along lakeshores. Northern wheat was also adopted in the south, and a rice–wheat rotation appeared in Jiangnan. The Lake Tai basin became the country's most important granary, giving rise to the saying “When Suzhou and Huzhou have a harvest, the world has enough”. Cotton spread from Guangdong, Guangxi and Fujian to the Yangtze valley, and tea cultivation expanded. Agricultural growth promoted crafts and commerce and laid a firm foundation for the shift of the economic center southward. In the Southern Song, Lou Shou's Pictures of Tilling and Weaving vividly depicts Jiangnan farmers plowing and weaving.

events.title: Jiaozi, the World's Earliest Paper Money
events.short: Jiaozi appeared in Sichuan in early Northern Song, and in 1023 the court set up an office to issue official jiaozi, the world’s earliest paper money, later used alongside copper coins.
events.detail: Song commerce flourished, trade was frequent and the volume of monetary transactions grew greatly, but the main currency in circulation was still metal. Sichuan used iron coins, low in value and heavy, and inconvenient to carry and trade with. In early Northern Song, merchants around Chengdu issued paper exchange certificates called “jiaozi” to ease trading, which holders could redeem for iron coins. Later sixteen rich merchants jointly ran jiaozi shops and issued them in a unified way, but disputes arose when some failed to redeem them through poor management. In 1023 (the first year of Tiansheng under Emperor Renzong), the Northern Song court set up a “Jiaozi Office” in Yizhou (present-day Chengdu, Sichuan) to issue jiaozi through the government, and the next year began issuing “official jiaozi”, with a fixed issue limit, circulation period and reserve funds. Their issue marks the formal birth of the world's earliest paper money. Jiaozi were a great step forward in Chinese monetary history, easing exchange of goods and promoting commercial growth. In late Northern Song jiaozi were renamed “qianyin”. In the Southern Song paper money circulated alongside copper coins, the most widely used being the “huizi”. But in late Southern Song, because of financial difficulty, the court issued paper money excessively, causing it to depreciate sharply, prices to soar and hardship for the people. In the Yuan, paper money became the main currency, used across the country, and Marco Polo expressed amazement at China's use of it in his travels. The appearance of jiaozi reflects the high development of Song commerce and is of great significance in the world history of money.

events.title: Yuanhao Founds Western Xia
events.short: In 1038 the Tangut leader Yuanhao took the imperial title and named the state Great Xia, with its capital at Xingqing (present-day Yinchuan), known as Western Xia. He modeled it on Tang and Song.
events.detail: The Tangut people originally belonged to a branch of the Qiang and first lived in what is now southeastern Qinghai. In Tang times, pressed by Tubo, they moved gradually inland to eastern Gansu and northern Shaanxi, where contact with Central Plains culture grew and production developed. In late Tang, the Tangut leader Tuoba Sigong was granted the surname Li, made Duke of Xia and appointed military governor of Dingnan for helping Tang suppress the Huang Chao uprising, and from then the Tangut held Xiazhou (north of present-day Jingbian, Shaanxi) as a warlord domain. In early Northern Song, the Tangut leader Li Jiqian and his son Li Deming alternately submitted to Northern Song and to Liao, expanding their influence and seizing Lingzhou and the Hexi Corridor. In 1038, Li Deming's son Yuanhao formally took the imperial title, named the state Great Xia and made Xingqing (present-day Yinchuan, Ningxia) his capital; because it lay to Song's northwest it is called “Western Xia”. He copied Tang and Song institutions in setting up official and military systems and laws, encouraged land clearing and developed a farming and herding economy, and had officials such as Yeli Renrong create the Western Xia script, with over six thousand characters built on the structure of Chinese characters. Western Xia's territory included present-day Ningxia, most of Gansu, and parts of Shaanxi, Inner Mongolia and Qinghai, standing as a third power with Northern Song and Liao (later Jin). It valued Confucianism and Buddhism, founded schools and held examinations. The Western Xia imperial tombs at the foot of the Helan Mountains in the western suburbs of Yinchuan are called the “Pyramids of the East”. Western Xia lasted about 190 years and was destroyed by the Mongols in 1227.

events.title: Bi Sheng Invents Movable-Type Printing
events.short: In the Qingli era the commoner Bi Sheng invented clay movable-type printing, one character per piece, reusable and far more efficient. It is one of China’s Four Great Inventions.
events.detail: China invented woodblock printing in the Sui and Tang. The world's earliest surviving dated woodblock-printed work is the Diamond Sutra, printed in Tang in 868. Book printing flourished under Liao, Song, Western Xia and Jin. But carving blocks was laborious and slow, each block could print only one book, and a single wrong character could ruin a block. After years of exploration, Song printing saw a new breakthrough. According to Shen Kuo's Dream Pool Essays, during the Qingli era of Emperor Renzong (1041–1048), the commoner Bi Sheng invented movable-type printing. He carved characters one by one in reverse in clay, hardened each by firing to make type. To make a page, he spread a mixture of pine resin, wax and paper ash over an iron plate with an iron frame, set the type inside the frame according to the text, filling a frame to make one forme, then heated it; when the mixture began to melt he pressed the surface flat with a board, and when it cooled the type was fixed on the plate and could be inked and printed. After printing, it was heated again so the mixture melted and the type could be removed for reuse. The method, he noted, “is not simple if you print only two or three copies, but for tens, hundreds or thousands it is extremely fast”. Compared with woodblock printing, movable type was both cheaper and quicker. It later spread to Korea, Japan, Southeast Asia and Europe, some four hundred years before Gutenberg's metal movable type in Germany. Printing is one of China's Four Great Inventions and made a great contribution to the spread and growth of human civilization.

events.title: Fan Zhongyan and the Qingli Reforms
events.short: In 1043 Fan Zhongyan, backed by Emperor Renzong, launched the Qingli Reforms for cleaner officialdom and stronger defense. They lasted barely a year but began Northern Song’s reform tradition.
events.detail: Fan Zhongyan (989–1052), courtesy name Xiwen, from Wuxian, Suzhou, was a noted Northern Song statesman, writer and thinker. His family was poor in his youth, and he studied hard, living on cold porridge. After passing the jinshi examination he served as an upright official who spoke frankly and was demoted several times for criticizing government. During the Song–Xia war he held the northwest, strengthened its defenses and kept Western Xia from attacking lightly. By mid-Northern Song the bureaucracy was bloated, with too many officials and a large army of low fighting strength, finances were strained and social tensions grew, known as “poverty and weakness”. In 1043 Emperor Renzong appointed Fan Zhongyan Participant in Governance, and he led reforms with Fu Bi, Han Qi and others. Fan submitted “Ten Proposals in Reply to the Imperial Edict”, calling for clear promotion and demotion, curbs on favoritism, stricter examinations, careful choice of local heads, equal public land, support for agriculture and sericulture, military readiness and lighter corvée. The core was cleaner officialdom: strict evaluation of officials, limits on sons of officials gaining posts by hereditary privilege, examination reform and schools. The reforms touched the interests of senior officials and nobles and met fierce opposition, and opponents slandered Fan and others as a “faction”. In 1045 Fan and others were pushed out of court, and the reforms failed after only just over a year. Though they failed, the Qingli Reforms began the reform tradition of Northern Song and prefigured Wang Anshi's later reforms. In “Yueyang Tower Record” Fan wrote the famous line “To worry before the world worries, to rejoice after the world has rejoiced”, a model of the scholar-official spirit.

events.title: Song–Xia Peace Treaty
events.short: After Western Xia's founding, Song and Xia fought repeatedly; Song armies often lost and Xia was badly drained. In 1044 they made peace, Yuanhao submitting to Song and border trade resuming.
events.detail: After Yuanhao founded Western Xia in 1038, he demanded recognition from Northern Song, which refused and cut off border trade, and war broke out. From 1040 to 1042 Yuanhao repeatedly led armies against Northern Song, inflicting crushing defeats on Song forces in the three great battles of Sanchuankou, Haoshuichuan and Dingchuanzhai. Northern Song, on the defensive, had to station large forces in the northwest and put Fan Zhongyan, Han Qi and others in charge of its defense. Fan Zhongyan built forts, strengthened defenses and won over Qiang tribes, and the frontier gradually stabilized; a ballad of the time said that Western Xia raiders were frightened to the heart at the name of Fan. Though Western Xia often won militarily, it had been founded recently, had a small population and limited resources, and years of war cost it dearly; with Song border trade cut off, it lacked grain, tea and cloth, prices soared, the people suffered and complaints were everywhere. In these conditions both sides wished for peace. In 1044 Northern Song and Western Xia reached an agreement, called the “Qingli Peace”: Yuanhao gave up the imperial title and submitted to Song, which invested him as Lord of Xia; Song “bestowed” on Western Xia each year 70,000 taels of silver, 150,000 bolts of silk and 30,000 jin of tea; and the two sides resumed border trade with markets on the frontier. After the peace, border trade thrived, with Western Xia's livestock and blue salt exchanged for Song grain, tea and silk. War still broke out from time to time, but overall peace held for a long time. Song, Liao and Western Xia stood as three powers checking one another.

events.title: Wang Anshi's Reforms
events.short: In 1069 Emperor Shenzong appointed Wang Anshi to carry out reforms, including the Green Sprouts Law, Service Exemption Law and Baojia Law. They raised revenue but met fierce conservative opposition.
events.detail: In mid-Northern Song the political climate was conservative and administration inefficient. With the bureaucracy and army swelling, official salaries and military costs were huge and revenue fell short; land annexation was severe, peasants were heavily burdened and uprisings came one after another, leaving Northern Song in “poverty and weakness”. Wang Anshi (1021–1086), courtesy name Jiefu, from Linchuan, Fuzhou (present-day Fuzhou, Jiangxi), was a noted Northern Song statesman, thinker and writer, one of the “Eight Great Prose Masters of Tang and Song”. In 1069 the young Emperor Shenzong appointed Wang Anshi Participant in Governance, and the next year chancellor, to lead reform, known as the “Xining Reforms”. The main measures were these. Economic: the Green Sprouts Law, under which the government lent money or grain to peasants in the lean season, to be repaid with interest after harvest; and the Service Exemption Law, under which the government collected exemption fees from households liable for service and hired people to do it. Military: the Baojia Law, which organized households into groups that drilled in the off-season, improvements in weapon making, and the discharge of old and weak soldiers. Education: examination reform, abolishing poetry and rhapsodies in favor of classics and policy essays. The reforms to some extent raised state revenue, strengthened military power and curbed powerful annexers. But they hurt the interests of senior officials and big landowners and met fierce opposition from the conservatives led by Sima Guang, and problems in implementation such as poor choice of personnel and forced enforcement added to some people's burdens.

events.title: Song Ci Poetry (Su Shi, Li Qingzhao, Xin Qiji)
events.short: Ci, a new poetic form with lines of varying length suited to singing, became the main literary form of Song, with Su Shi, Li Qingzhao and Xin Qiji as outstanding masters.
events.detail: Ci is a new form of verse written to be sung to music, with lines of varying length, so it is also called “long and short lines”. It already existed in Tang, grew greatly through the Five Dynasties and the Song, and became the most representative literary form of Song, ranked with Tang poetry and Yuan drama. Each ci is composed to a set tune with a fixed pattern called a “tune title”, such as “Charm of Niannu”, “The River All Red”, “Butterflies Love Flowers” and “Prelude to Water Melody”. Ci at first mostly described parting and longing between lovers and scenes of flowers and moonlight, in a graceful, delicate style. The Northern Song writer Su Shi (1037–1101) contributed greatly to its growth: he widened its subjects, using ci to express personal feeling, describe landscapes, convey philosophy of life and patriotic feeling, and began the bold and unrestrained style; “The great river flows east, its waves wash away the heroes of a thousand ages” is his famous line. Li Qingzhao (1084–c. 1155), who took the name Yi'an Jushi, was the finest woman ci poet of Song and a representative of the graceful school. Her early ci mostly describe life in the women's quarters and longing for her husband Zhao Mingcheng, fresh and bright; her later ci are full of grief for her country and her own fate, and lines such as “Seeking, seeking, cold, cold, lonely, lonely, sad, sad, sorrowful” are deeply moving. Xin Qiji (1140–1207) of Southern Song, who took the name Jiaxuan, joined an anti-Jin volunteer army in the north in his youth, and after moving south urged a northern campaign but was repeatedly sidelined.

events.title: Sima Guang Completes the Zizhi Tongjian
events.short: Compiled under Sima Guang over 19 years, the Zizhi Tongjian records 1,362 years from the Warring States to the Five Dynasties and is China's first great general history in chronicle form.
events.detail: Sima Guang (1019–1086), courtesy name Junshi, from Xiaxian, Shanzhou (present-day Xiaxian, Shanxi), was a noted Northern Song historian and statesman. Fond of history from youth, he judged that the histories of the successive dynasties were so voluminous that rulers could hardly read them all, and resolved to write a concise general history to give rulers lessons. After Emperor Shenzong took the throne, he considered that the book “takes lessons from past events and aids the way of governing”, gave it the name Zizhi Tongjian (Comprehensive Mirror to Aid Governance) and wrote its preface himself. Because he opposed Wang Anshi's reforms, Sima Guang lived in retirement at Luoyang for fifteen years, devoting himself to the book. With assistants such as Liu Ban, Liu Shu and Fan Zuyu he divided the work: first collecting material into a “general index”, then arranging it into a “long draft”, and finally he himself edited and finalized the book, scrupulously. In 1084 the Zizhi Tongjian was complete, after nineteen years. In 294 chapters and over three million characters, it records 1,362 years of history from the early Warring States (the partition of Jin among three families in 403 BC) to the end of the Five Dynasties (959), spanning sixteen dynasties, and is China's first great general history in chronicle form. It records events in order of year and month, concentrating on politics, warfare and ethnic relations, drawing on wide sources and careful verification, using over three hundred kinds of historical materials, and adding comments after important events marked “Your servant Guang says”. It deeply influenced later historiography, and later writers composed works on its model, such as the Continuation of the Zizhi Tongjian.

events.title: Shen Kuo and the Dream Pool Essays
events.short: The Northern Song scientist Shen Kuo wrote the Dream Pool Essays late in life, recording movable-type printing, magnetic declination and petroleum, a “milestone in the history of Chinese science”.
events.detail: Shen Kuo (1031–1095), courtesy name Cunzhong, from Qiantang (present-day Hangzhou, Zhejiang), was an outstanding Northern Song scientist and statesman. Learned and versatile, he was deeply accomplished in astronomy, the calendar, mathematics, geography, geology, physics, chemistry, medicine and water management. He took an active part in Wang Anshi's reforms. As head of the Astronomical Bureau he improved observation instruments and revised the calendar, proposing a “twelve-qi calendar” that set months by solar terms, taking the start of spring as New Year's Day with 31-day long months and 30-day short months, which would help schedule farming. In his later years Shen Kuo settled at Dream Brook Garden in Runzhou (present-day Zhenjiang, Jiangsu) and wrote his lifetime's observations and findings into the Dream Pool Essays (Mengxi Bitan). The book has 26 chapters, plus supplementary and continued essays, over 600 entries in all, covering astronomy, geography, mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology, medicine, engineering, history, literature and art. It records Bi Sheng's invention of movable-type printing, the most important source for that invention; describes four ways of mounting a magnetic needle and was the first to note that the needle “usually inclines slightly east, not due south”, discovering magnetic declination some four hundred years before Europe; it gave the name “shiyou” (petroleum) to the oil of northern Shaanxi and predicted that “this thing will later be widely used in the world”, a name still used today; and, from conch and clam fossils in the rocks of the Taihang Mountains, it inferred that the area was once seashore.

events.title: Entertainment Quarters and Urban Culture
events.short: Song cities developed entertainment districts called “wazi”, with “goulan” stages for variety plays, storytelling and acrobatics, and an urban culture of unprecedented richness.
events.detail: Song urban economies were highly developed: great cities such as Kaifeng and Lin'an held up to a million people, commerce flourished, and a growing urban population formed a large citizen class. As the boundaries between residential wards and markets broke down, demand for entertainment grew, and cities saw venues devoted to it, called “wazi”, “washe” or “waxi”. The performance spaces inside, fenced with railings or ropes, were called “goulan”. The large wazi of Kaifeng had over fifty goulan, the largest holding thousands. In the wazi, performers staged variety plays, storytelling (“shuohua”), puppet shows, shadow plays, acrobatics, wrestling, dance, singing and more, every day regardless of heat, cold or rain, with audiences streaming in. Storytelling meant telling tales of history, heroes and legends and folk life; the storytellers' scripts, called “huaben”, later became the basis of the long chapter novels of Ming and Qing, and Romance of the Three Kingdoms and Water Margin grew from huaben. Song variety plays laid the ground for the rise of Yuan drama. Song cities also had night markets, some open until dawn, and at the Lantern Festival were bright with lanterns and bustling. Books such as Meng Yuanlao's Dreams of Splendor of the Eastern Capital and Wu Zimu's Dream of the Millet records vividly record urban life and entertainment in Kaifeng and Lin'an. The rise of the wazi and goulan reflected the prosperity of Song urban economies and the rise of urban culture, enriched people's spiritual life, and advanced popular literature and drama in China.

events.title: Aguda Founds the Jin Dynasty
events.short: The Jurchen Wanyan tribe leader Aguda unified the Jurchen tribes, rose against Liao in 1114 and founded the Jin dynasty in 1115 with its capital at Huining, as Emperor Taizu of Jin.
events.detail: The Jurchen were an ancient people of Northeast China living in the Heilong River basin and around the Changbai Mountains, living by fishing, hunting, herding and farming. Under Liao rule they were controlled and oppressed: each year Liao demanded large amounts of ginseng, sable pelts, northern pearls and the hunting falcon “haidongqing”, and the Jurchen deeply resented its rule. They were then divided into many tribes, among which the Wanyan tribe of the Anchuhu River (the Ashi River in Heilongjiang today) grew strong and absorbed many others. In the late 11th century Aguda, leader of the Wanyan, completed the unification of the Jurchen tribes. In 1112 Emperor Tianzuo of Liao toured Chunzhou and at a banquet ordered the Jurchen chiefs to dance in turn; Aguda refused, and Tianzuo wanted to kill him but was dissuaded by ministers. In 1114 Aguda rose against Liao and defeated Liao armies in succession at Ningjiangzhou and Chuhedian, winning against greater numbers; Jurchen morale soared, and it was said that “if the Jurchen reach ten thousand men they cannot be beaten”. In 1115 Aguda took the imperial title and founded a regime named Great Jin, with its capital at Huiningfu (in present-day Acheng District, Harbin, Heilongjiang), as Emperor Taizu of Jin. Taizu copied Central Plains institutions, turned the Jurchen military organization of meng'an and mouke into a combined military-civil local system, developed production, and had Wanyan Xiyin create the Jurchen script on the model of Chinese and Khitan characters, and the state quickly grew stronger. Jin forces kept attacking Liao and took its Eastern and Supreme Capitals and other places. In 1125 Jin destroyed Liao and in 1127 destroyed Northern Song, becoming a powerful northern regime facing Southern Song.

events.title: The Compass Used in Navigation
events.short: Song made compasses with artificially magnetized needles, used in navigation by late Northern Song, giving reliable guidance on ocean voyages and later reaching Europe through the Arabs.
events.detail: Ancient China recognized early that lodestone attracts iron and points south. In the Warring States people made a lodestone direction-finder, the “sinan”, shaped like a spoon and set on a square bronze plate marked with directions; the spoon turned on the smooth plate and when it stopped its handle pointed south. But natural lodestone is weakly magnetic and awkward to use. Song people invented artificial magnetization, rubbing steel needles with lodestone to make compass needles. In Dream Pool Essays Shen Kuo recorded four ways of mounting a compass needle: placing it on a fingernail, on the rim of a bowl, hanging it by silk thread, or threading it through a rush stem to float on water. Shen Kuo also noted that the needle “usually inclines slightly east, not due south”, pointing out magnetic declination. People later set the needle inside a disc marked with directions, making the compass. In late Northern Song the compass began to be used in navigation. Zhu Yu's Pingzhou Table Talk records that on Guangzhou sea-going ships “the pilots know the geography; at night they watch the stars, by day the sun, and in overcast weather the south-pointing needle”, the world's earliest record of the compass used for navigation. In Southern Song the compass came into general use at sea. It gave ocean voyages reliable direction, promoted the flourishing of overseas trade in Song and Yuan, and provided an important technical guarantee for Zheng He's voyages in the Ming. The compass later passed to Europe through the Arabs and was an important condition for European ocean voyages and the opening of new sea routes. It is one of the Four Great Inventions of ancient China.

events.title: Qingming Scroll and Song Commerce
events.short: Zhang Zeduan's Along the River During the Qingming Festival depicts the bustle along the Bian River in the capital Dongjing and reflects Song urban commerce, free of the old ward-and-market limits.
events.detail: Song commerce flourished more than in any earlier age. In Tang, cities had a ward-and-market system with residential and commercial areas strictly separated and commercial activity limited by time. Song broke these limits: shops could open anywhere in the city, trading hours were unrestricted, and morning and night markets appeared. Many commercial cities arose along the Yellow River, Yangtze and canals, and Northern Song's Dongjing (Kaifeng) and Southern Song's Lin'an (Hangzhou) each held up to a million people. Beyond the cities appeared periodic “grass markets” and new market towns, spreading commodity trade into the countryside. Along the River During the Qingming Festival is a work of the late Northern Song painter Zhang Zeduan. A silk handscroll in color, about 528 cm long and 25 cm wide, it uses scattered-point perspective to depict, in scroll form, the bustle of the outskirts of Dongjing and the banks of the Bian River at Qingming. It begins in quiet countryside, passes the busy Bian River docks and reaches the lively streets inside the city. It has over 550 figures, fifty or sixty animals, over twenty boats, over twenty carts and sedan chairs, and rainbow bridges, city towers, teahouses, taverns, butcher shops, drugstores, temples and stalls, each with its own manner. At its center is the wooden Rainbow Bridge over the Bian River, thronged with people, while below a large boat lowers its mast to pass under. The painting vividly recreates the look of the Northern Song capital and the lives of all levels of society, is of high artistic value, and is a precious source for the study of Northern Song's economy, urban planning, transport and customs. It is regarded as one of China's Ten Famous Paintings.

events.title: Jin Destroys Liao
events.short: Northern Song and Jin allied against Liao in the “Alliance Concluded at Sea”. Song armies lost repeatedly while Jin took Liao's five capitals, and in 1125 Emperor Tianzuo was captured and Liao fell.
events.detail: After the Jurchen founded Jin, they rose swiftly and kept attacking Liao. Liao and Northern Song were both in deep crisis: Emperor Tianzuo of Liao was devoted to hunting, government was corrupt, internal conflicts were sharp and uprisings were constant; Emperor Huizong of Northern Song believed in Daoism, employed treacherous ministers like Cai Jing and Tong Guan, built lavishly, and ruled decadently. After Jin forces took parts of Liao, the Northern Song court hoped to use Jin to recover the Sixteen Prefectures of Yan and Yun held by Liao, and sent envoys across the sea from Shandong to contact Jin. In 1120 the two sides made a pact to attack Liao jointly: Jin would take Liao's Central Capital and Song its Yanjing; after Liao's fall the Yan and Yun lands would go to Song, which would transfer to Jin the annual tribute it had paid to Liao. Because the envoys traveled by sea, it is called the “Alliance Concluded at Sea”. Jin forces then swept through, taking Liao's Supreme, Eastern, Central and Western Capitals one after another. But when Northern Song attacked Yanjing it was heavily defeated twice by Liao, and in the end Jin took Yanjing. Northern Song's corruption and weakness were fully exposed. Afterward Jin handed only Yanjing and six nearby prefectures to Northern Song, carrying off their people and goods, and Song had to pay Jin an extra “substitute tax” of one million strings of cash a year. In 1125 Emperor Tianzuo was captured by Jin at Yingzhou and Liao fell, after over two hundred years. In destroying Liao, Jin's rulers saw Northern Song's political corruption and military weakness and in that same year launched war against Song, which fell two years later.

events.title: Jin Destroys Northern Song; Southern Song Founded
events.short: In 1127 Jin forces took Kaifeng and carried off emperors Huizong and Qinzong in the “Jingkang Incident”. That year Zhao Gou took the throne at Yingtian and later settled at Lin'an: Southern Song.
events.detail: In joining Northern Song to attack Liao, Jin saw Northern Song's political corruption and military weakness. After destroying Liao in 1125, Jin forces at once marched south against Song in two columns. Emperor Huizong of Song panicked and passed the throne to his son Emperor Qinzong. In early 1126 the Jin eastern army besieged Kaifeng; the pro-war minister Li Gang organized soldiers and civilians to hold on, and the Jin could not take it and withdrew after Song agreed to cede the three prefectures of Taiyuan, Zhongshan and Hejian and pay large amounts of gold and silver. Qinzong and Huizong had no heart to resist and thought only of compromise, and after the Jin withdrew they dismissed Li Gang and relaxed their guard. That autumn the Jin came south again, and a Jin commander remarked: “The southern court has no men. With even one or two thousand guarding the river, how could we have crossed!” In the intercalary eleventh month of 1126 Jin forces broke Kaifeng. In 1127 Jin demoted Huizong and Qinzong to commoners and carried the two emperors, with consorts, the imperial clan and officials, over three thousand people in all, to the north, ending Northern Song. As this occurred in Qinzong's Jingkang era, it is called the “Jingkang Incident” or “Humiliation of Jingkang”. In the fifth month of that year Huizong's ninth son, Zhao Gou, Prince of Kang, took the throne at Yingtian Prefecture (present-day Shangqiu, Henan) and refounded Song as Emperor Gaozong. As the Jin kept pressing south, Gaozong retreated step by step and eventually made Lin'an (present-day Hangzhou, Zhejiang) his capital: Southern Song.

events.title: Yue Fei and the Song–Jin Treaty
events.short: Yue Fei's army routed the Jin at Yancheng and was poised to recover the Central Plains when Emperor Gaozong and Qin Hui sought peace and had Yue Fei killed. The Shaoxing Treaty followed in 1141.
events.detail: Yue Fei (1103–1142), courtesy name Pengju, from Tangyin, Xiangzhou (present-day Tangyin, Henan), was an outstanding Southern Song general against Jin and a national hero. Tradition says his mother tattooed four characters on his back, “serve the country with utmost loyalty”, to encourage him. In early Southern Song, when Jin forces made several large southward drives, Yue Fei fought in many places, repeatedly distinguished himself and recovered Jiankang, Xiangyang and other places. He ran his army with strict discipline, and the “Yue Family Army” was disciplined and fierce; among the Jin it was said, “It is easier to shake a mountain than the Yue Family Army.” In 1140 the Jin broke the treaty and invaded in force; Yue Fei led a northern campaign and defeated the main Jin force at Yancheng and Yingchang, shattering the Jin elite cavalry, the “linked horses” and “iron pagodas”, then pursued to Zhuxian Town, only forty-five li from Kaifeng. Volunteer armies everywhere responded and recovering the Central Plains seemed near. But Emperor Gaozong and Qin Hui sought peace and ordered Yue Fei to withdraw, and he lamented that all had been “ruined in a single day”. Back in Lin'an, Yue Fei was relieved of command and Qin Hui and others had him falsely accused of treason and jailed. In early 1142 Yue Fei, his son Yue Yun and his subordinate Zhang Xian were killed; Yue Fei was only 39. In 1141 Song and Jin made the “Shaoxing Treaty”: Southern Song became a subject of Jin and paid it 250,000 taels of silver and 250,000 bolts of silk a year, with the border along the Huai River to Dasanguan, and the confrontation between Song and Jin took shape. Under Emperor Xiaozong, Yue Fei was exonerated and posthumously given the title “Wumu”, later also made Prince of E.

events.title: Southward Shift of the Economic Center
events.short: The economic center, shifting south since mid-Tang, settled there by the Southern Song, when southern farming, crafts and trade outpaced the north and most revenue came from the southeast.
events.detail: In Qin and Han times the Yellow River basin was the economic center of China, while Jiangnan was thinly populated and backward. In the Wei, Jin and Northern and Southern Dynasties, frequent war in the north drove many northerners south, bringing labor and advanced production techniques, and Jiangnan was first developed. After the An Lushan Rebellion in mid-Tang, the north again fell into war, large numbers moved south, southern economy grew further, and in late Tang the court relied mainly on Jiangnan for revenue. In Song, especially after the Jingkang Incident at the end of Northern Song, northerners again moved south in large numbers and the southern economy quickly overtook the north. By Southern Song the southward shift of the economic center in ancient China was complete, and the central government's revenue came mainly from the south, especially the southeast. The shift showed itself in many ways. In agriculture, the area of southern rice grew, Champa rice spread, the Lake Tai region became the most important granary (“When Suzhou and Huzhou have a harvest, the world has enough”), and tea and cotton growing spread. In crafts, southern silk weaving had already surpassed the north in Northern Song, with silk production flourishing in Sichuan and Jiangsu and Zhejiang; cotton weaving rose in late Southern Song, and Hainan Island had fairly advanced cotton-weaving tools; porcelain making shifted to Jiangnan, with Jingdezhen a famous porcelain capital; shipbuilding at Guangzhou, Quanzhou and Mingzhou was famous and led the world at the time. In commerce, Lin'an was the country's largest commercial city, overseas trade was very active, and Quanzhou and Guangzhou became world-renowned ports.

events.title: Song Overseas Trade and the Maritime Trade Offices
events.short: Song encouraged overseas trade, with Maritime Trade Offices at Guangzhou, Quanzhou and Mingzhou; its ships reached Arabia and East Africa, and trade income became an important source of revenue.
events.detail: Song had advanced shipbuilding and navigation, the compass was coming into use at sea, and the northern overland Silk Road was blocked by Western Xia, Liao and others, so overseas trade flourished as never before, surpassing earlier ages, and Song became one of the world's major trading countries. Song rulers encouraged overseas trade; Emperor Gaozong said: “The profit of maritime trade is greatest; if well managed, it can yield millions.” The court set up Maritime Trade Offices at main ports such as Guangzhou, Quanzhou, Mingzhou (present-day Ningbo, Zhejiang) and Hangzhou to manage overseas trade, inspecting ships entering and leaving port and collecting customs duties. Song treated foreign merchants favorably, setting up “foreign quarters” (fanfang) at Guangzhou, Quanzhou and elsewhere for them to live in, headed by respected men chosen from among the merchants, and foreigners could also buy land, marry and have families in China. More than fifty countries and regions traded with Song, and Chinese ships reached nearby Korea and Japan and as far as Southeast Asia, India, the Arabian Peninsula and the east coast of Africa. Main exports were silk, porcelain, tea and copper coins; imports included spices, medicines, pearls, ivory and rhinoceros horn. Guangzhou and Quanzhou were world-famous trading ports; in late Southern Song Quanzhou gradually overtook Guangzhou, and in the Yuan it was called the “greatest port of the East”. Overseas trade income held an important place in Southern Song revenue, reaching two million strings in a year at most. The Southern Song shipwreck “Nanhai No. 1”, found in 1987 off Yangjiang, Guangdong, yielded great quantities of porcelain, ironware, and gold and silver objects, vividly attesting to the prosperity of the Song maritime Silk Road.

events.title: Genghis Khan Unites the Mongols
events.short: The Mongol leader Temujin united the tribes of the Mongolian steppe and in 1206 was proclaimed “Genghis Khan” on the Onon River, founding the Mongol Empire and ending long strife on the steppe.
events.detail: The Mongols were an ancient people of northern China, originally in the Ergun River basin, who later migrated west into the Mongolian steppe. Skilled at riding and archery, they followed water and grass and lived as nomads. In the 12th century the tribes of the steppe fought constantly over people, pastures, water and livestock, and people longed for unity and an end to war. The unification of the Mongol tribes was achieved by Temujin. Temujin (c. 1162–1227) came from a noble family of the Mongol Kiyat tribe; when he was nine his father Yesugei was poisoned by Tatars, his followers scattered, and he lived in hardship with his mother and brothers, enduring many trials. As an adult, supported by his father's sworn brother Toghrul, chief of the Kereit, he gradually gathered followers and grew in strength. He was good at employing people, fair in reward and punishment, and knew men's worth. He then defeated the Tatars, Taichiud, Kereit, Naiman, Merkit and other tribes and united the Mongol steppe. In 1206 the Mongol nobles held an assembly at the source of the Onon River, chose Temujin as great khan with the title “Genghis Khan”, and founded the Mongol Empire. After founding the state Genghis Khan organized all herders into units of a thousand, a hundred and ten, a military-civil system of thousand-households, and had the Mongolian language written in Uyghur script, creating the Mongol script. Mongol unification ended the long strife on the steppe and boosted the Mongol economy, and the Mongols entered history as a unified people. Genghis Khan then led armies against Western Xia and Jin and died in 1227 during the campaign against Western Xia.

events.title: Mongols Destroy Western Xia
events.short: Genghis Khan attacked Western Xia six times and Jin refused to help; in 1227 the last Xia emperor surrendered and Western Xia fell, while Genghis Khan died near the Liupan Mountains.
events.detail: After uniting Mongolia, Genghis Khan first turned toward Western Xia and Jin. Western Xia lay on the Mongols' road south and controlled the Hexi Corridor; before attacking Jin and the Western Regions the Mongols had to remove the threat from Western Xia. From 1205 Genghis Khan attacked Western Xia six times. In 1209 Mongol troops besieged the Xia capital Zhongxing (present-day Yinchuan, Ningxia) and flooded it with Yellow River water; Western Xia was forced to offer a princess and sue for peace, submit to the Mongols and agree to send troops to help in their wars. Western Xia appealed to Jin for help, but because of old conflicts the Jin emperor refused, saying “when enemies attack each other, it is good fortune for our state”, and Song, Xia and Jin never united against the Mongols. Later Western Xia refused to join the Mongol western campaign and made peace with Jin, angering Genghis Khan. In 1226, returning from the western campaign, Genghis Khan personally led a great army against Western Xia a sixth time, taking Khara-Khoto, Ganzhou, Suzhou, Xiliang and other places, defeating the main Xia force at Jiudu on the Yellow River and besieging Zhongxing. The Xia capital was besieged for half a year, its food ran out, and it suffered earthquake and plague. In summer 1227 Genghis Khan fell gravely ill near the Liupan Mountains and soon died. On his deathbed he left instructions to keep his death secret, to kill the Xia ruler and his officials after their surrender, and to pass through Song territory in allying with Song to destroy Jin. That year the last Xia emperor, Li Xian, came out and surrendered and was killed by the Mongols, and Western Xia fell after about 190 years.

sources.title: Wikipedia (Chinese) - Mongol Conquest of Western Xia

events.title: Mongols Destroy Jin
events.short: After Genghis Khan's death Ogedei allied with Song against Jin. In 1234 the joint armies broke Caizhou, Emperor Aizong hanged himself and Jin fell, leaving Song and the Mongols face to face.
events.detail: In late Jin, politics were corrupt, national strength was weak, and the Mongols attacked constantly. From 1211 Genghis Khan repeatedly campaigned south against Jin, defeating the main Jin army at Yehuling and elsewhere and besieging the Central Capital (present-day Beijing). In 1214 Jin was forced to move its capital to Nanjing (present-day Kaifeng, Henan), and the next year the Mongols took the Central Capital, and Jin lost large areas north of the Yellow River. In 1229 Genghis Khan's third son Ogedei succeeded as great khan and continued the attack on Jin. In 1231 the Mongol army advanced in three columns, one under Tolui passing through Southern Song's Hanzhong region to circle behind Jin. In 1232 Tolui defeated the main Jin army at Sanfengshan in Junzhou, destroying Jin's elite forces. The Mongols then besieged Bianjing, Emperor Aizong of Jin fled and finally reached Caizhou (present-day Runan, Henan). In 1233 Southern Song allied with the Mongols, agreeing to destroy Jin together and to return the Henan lands to Song afterward. Southern Song sent Meng Gong with grain to join the Mongols in besieging Caizhou. In early 1234 the Mongol–Song armies broke Caizhou; Emperor Aizong passed the throne to the last emperor, Wanyan Chenglin, and hanged himself, and Jin fell after 120 years. After Jin's fall Southern Song tried to take back the old Northern Song capitals, sending troops into Kaifeng, Luoyang and elsewhere, but was counterattacked by the Mongols and failed, the “Duanping Entry into Luoyang”. From then on Southern Song and the Mongols faced each other directly and Mongol armies attacked Southern Song.

events.title: Liangzhou Meeting and Tibet's Submission to the Mongols
events.short: In 1247 the Mongol prince Godan met the Sakya leader Sakya Pandita at Liangzhou and agreed terms for Tibet's submission to the Mongols, bringing Tibet under the central government's administration.
events.detail: After the Tibetan Empire collapsed in the mid-9th century, Tibet remained divided for a long time, and local powers allied with the various Buddhist schools to form many regional religious and political authorities. In the early 13th century the Mongols rose rapidly and united the north. In 1239 Prince Godan (a son of Ogedei), stationed at Liangzhou (present-day Wuwei, Gansu), sent the general Doordanata with troops into Tibet to learn about conditions there. In 1244 Godan wrote inviting Sakya Pandita to talks at Liangzhou. Though over sixty, Sakya Pandita made the long journey with his two nephews, Phagpa and Chana Dorje, and arrived in 1246. In 1247 Godan and Sakya Pandita met at Liangzhou and agreed the terms of Tibet's submission to the Mongols: the lay and monastic leaders of Tibet would submit and accept officials sent by the Mongols; the Mongols would protect them, existing officials would stay in post, and the Sakya school would help the Mongols administer Tibet. After the talks, Sakya Pandita wrote an open letter to the Tibetan leaders, the Letter from Sakya Pandita to the People of Tibet, urging them to submit to the Mongols. This is the famous Liangzhou Meeting. Afterwards the Mongol rulers began to register households, set up postal stations and levy taxes in Tibet. The meeting is regarded as marking Tibet's formal incorporation under the Chinese central government, laying the foundation for the Yuan dynasty to set up administrative bodies in Tibet and govern it directly, and is seen as highly significant in the history of China as a unified multi-ethnic state. Today the Baita Temple in Wuwei, Gansu, houses a memorial museum for the Liangzhou Meeting.

events.title: Widespread Use of Gunpowder Weapons (Fire Lance, Hand Cannon)
events.short: Gunpowder, invented in the Tang, came into wide military use in the Song and Yuan; in 1259 the Southern Song made the bamboo-barrel fire lance, and the Yuan later cast metal-barreled hand cannons.
events.detail: Gunpowder was invented by ancient Chinese alchemists while refining elixirs. By the Tang, people knew that saltpeter, sulfur and charcoal mixed in set proportions made gunpowder. In the late Tang it began to be used in warfare, with incendiary weapons such as "flying fire". Gunpowder weapons developed greatly under the Song; the official military treatise Wujing Zongyao (Collection of the Most Important Military Techniques) of the Northern Song recorded three gunpowder formulas, the earliest in the world. In the Song and Yuan periods such weapons were widely used in war. In the wars between the Song and the Jin, the Song army used weapons such as the "thunderclap bomb"; the Jin learned to make and use gunpowder weapons from the Song and produced more powerful "thunder-crash bombs" and "flying fire lances". In 1132 the Southern Song commander Chen Gui, defending De'an, made fire lances from long bamboo poles, the earliest tube-shaped fire weapons. In 1259, in Shouchun Prefecture (present-day Shou County, Anhui), a "fire-erupting lance" was made, with a thick bamboo tube holding gunpowder and "pellets"; when lit it first shot out flame and then fired the pellets, with a noise that carried far. It is regarded as the world's earliest tube-shaped projectile firearm and the ancestor of modern guns and cannons. The Mongols also used firearms extensively in their wars against the Jin and the Song. The Yuan cast tubes of metal in place of bamboo and invented the hand cannon, which was more powerful, longer-ranged and more durable. In the 13th century gunpowder and firearms passed to Europe through the Arabs, with profound effects on European society. Gunpowder is one of the Four Great Inventions of ancient China.

events.title: Kublai Khan Founds the Yuan Dynasty
events.short: Kublai Khan took the throne as Great Khan in 1260, adopted Han Chinese practices and an era name, renamed the state "Great Yuan" in 1271 and made Dadu (now Beijing) his capital the next year.
events.detail: Kublai Khan (1215–1294) was a grandson of Genghis Khan and a son of Tolui. From early on he recruited Han Confucian scholars, gathering around him Liu Bingzhong, Yao Shu, Xu Heng, Hao Jing and others, known as the "Jinlianchuan Secretariat". After Mongke became Great Khan in 1251, he put Kublai in charge of military and civil affairs in the Han lands south of the Gobi; Kublai built the city of Kaiping (later Shangdu) in what is now Zhengxianbai Banner, Inner Mongolia. In 1259 Mongke died while attacking Diaoyu Castle in Hezhou, Sichuan; Kublai, then besieging Ezhou, made peace with the Southern Song on hearing the news and returned north. In 1260 Kublai took the throne at Kaiping and adopted the era name Zhongtong, the first time the Mongols used an era name. His younger brother Ariq Boke was also proclaimed Great Khan in the northern steppe, and after four years of war Ariq Boke surrendered. Kublai accepted the advice of Han Confucian officials to "follow Han ways", "govern with benevolence" and "avoid needless killing", set up an agricultural promotion office and issued the farming manual Nongsang Jiyao. Following the model of Central Plains dynasties, he established the Secretariat, the Bureau of Military Affairs and the Censorate at the center and introduced the provincial system locally. In 1271, on Liu Bingzhong's advice, Kublai took the name "Great Yuan" from the Book of Changes phrase "Great is the primal power", formally founding the Yuan dynasty; he is known as Emperor Shizu of Yuan. The next year he made Dadu (present-day Beijing) the capital, with Kaiping as the upper capital, and the court moved between the two. The Yuan went on to attack the Southern Song and unified the country in 1279.

events.title: Marco Polo Comes to China
events.short: The Italian traveler Marco Polo came to Yuan China with his father and uncle and lived there for 17 years; his dictated Travels of Marco Polo stirred European longing for the East.
events.detail: Marco Polo (1254–1324) was a Venetian from a merchant family. His father Niccolo and uncle Maffeo had earlier visited the Mongols, met Kublai Khan and been entrusted with a letter to the Pope. In 1271 the seventeen-year-old Marco set out from Venice with them along the Silk Road; after more than three years they reached the Yuan summer capital Shangdu in 1275 and were received by Kublai Khan. Clever and eager to learn, Marco quickly picked up Mongolian and other languages, won Kublai's trust and lived in Yuan China for 17 years, undertaking missions to various regions. In 1291 the Polo family was ordered to escort the Yuan princess Kokachin to her marriage in the Ilkhanate; they sailed from Quanzhou and Marco returned to Venice in 1295. Later, captured in a war between Venice and Genoa, he dictated his account of the East in prison, and a fellow prisoner, the writer Rustichello, wrote it down, producing The Travels of Marco Polo. The book describes the prosperity of cities such as Dadu, Hangzhou and Quanzhou, introduces paper money and coal, calls Hangzhou the "City of Heaven" and Quanzhou one of the world's largest ports, reflecting China's wealth and advancement. It circulated widely in Europe and stirred great longing for the Eastern world, and had some influence on the later opening of new sea routes. Some scholars question whether he actually reached China, but most hold that much of what the book records matches Chinese sources and that he did come.

events.title: The Yuan Destroys the Southern Song and Unifies China
events.short: Yuan forces entered Lin'an in 1276 and the Southern Song surrendered; in 1279 the Song fleet was destroyed at Yamen, where Lu Xiufu carried the child emperor into the sea, and the Yuan unified China.
events.detail: After destroying the Jin, the Mongols faced the Southern Song directly, and the Song-Mongol war lasted over forty years. Southern Song soldiers and civilians resisted stubbornly for long periods in Sichuan, Xiangyang, the Huai region and elsewhere. In 1268 Yuan forces besieged the key fortresses of Xiangyang and Fancheng; the defender Lu Wenhuan held out for nearly six years, while the Song chief minister Jia Sidao concealed the military situation and sent no relief. Fancheng fell in 1273 and Lu Wenhuan surrendered Xiangyang to the Yuan, throwing open the gateway of the Southern Song's Yangtze defenses. In 1274 Kublai Khan sent the general Bayan with 200,000 troops down the Han River into the Yangtze and eastward. The Southern Song court was corrupt; Jia Sidao led an army against them and was crushed at Dingjiazhou. In 1276 Yuan troops entered the Song capital Lin'an, and Empress Dowager Xie and the young Emperor Gong of Song came out to surrender, ending the Southern Song court. Loyal ministers including Lu Xiufu, Zhang Shijie and Wen Tianxiang refused to yield and successively enthroned the emperor's brothers Zhao Shi and Zhao Bing in Fuzhou and Guangdong to continue resisting. Wen Tianxiang raised volunteer armies in Jiangxi, Fujian and Guangdong, and was defeated and captured at Wupoling in Haifeng, Guangdong, in 1278. In 1279 the Yuan attacked the last Song stronghold at Yamen in Xinhui, Guangdong; Zhang Shijie led over a thousand warships in a decisive battle, and the Song fleet was annihilated. Lu Xiufu carried the young emperor Zhao Bing on his back into the sea, and many Song soldiers and civilians followed, in what is known as the Battle of Yamen. The last Song forces were finished.

events.title: Guo Shoujing Completes the Shoushi Calendar
events.short: The Yuan scientist Guo Shoujing and others compiled the Shoushi Calendar, which fixed the year at 365.2425 days, the same as today's Gregorian calendar but about 300 years earlier.
events.detail: Guo Shoujing (1231–1316), courtesy name Ruosi, was from Xingtai in Shunde (present-day Xingtai, Hebei), an outstanding Yuan astronomer, mathematician and hydraulic engineer. After the Yuan unified China, the calendar in use grew ever less accurate, and Kublai Khan ordered Wang Xun, Guo Shoujing and others to revise it. Guo held that "the basis of a calendar lies in observation, and for observation nothing comes before instruments", so he first improved or created nearly twenty astronomical instruments. Among them the simplified armillary sphere reduced the armillary sphere to two independent observing devices and was highly accurate, over three hundred years ahead of comparable European instruments; the tall gnomon raised the traditional eight-chi gnomon to forty chi, improving the accuracy of measuring the sun's shadow, and the observatory at Dengfeng, Henan, is the remains of that gnomon site. He also led large-scale astronomical observations, setting up twenty-seven observation points across the country, from the North Sea (the Siberian region of present-day Russia) to the South China Sea, known as the "Four Seas Survey". After several years of work, Guo Shoujing and others completed the new Shoushi Calendar in 1280, promulgated the next year. 2425 days, only 26 seconds off the actual time of the Earth's orbit and identical to the present Gregorian calendar, but about 300 years before the Gregorian calendar was established. The Shoushi Calendar was used in China for over 360 years, one of the longest-used and most accurate calendars of ancient China. Guo also contributed in water management, directing the digging of the Tonghui Canal from Dadu to Tongzhou so that grain barges on the Grand Canal could reach the Jishuitan lake inside Dadu.

events.title: Yuan Drama and Guan Hanqing's The Injustice to Dou E
events.short: Yuan qu comprises sanqu verse and zaju drama; Guan Hanqing, the finest Yuan dramatist, wrote The Injustice to Dou E and is counted among the "Four Great Yuan Dramatists".
events.detail: Under the Yuan, urban economies flourished and townspeople's culture developed, while many literati, blocked from official careers by the long suspension of the civil service examinations, turned to writing for the theater, making Yuan drama unprecedentedly flourishing. Yuan qu comprises sanqu and zaju. Sanqu is a new form of poetry that can be sung without staging; zaju is a composite stage art merging music, song and dance, movement and spoken lines, generally in four acts. Yuan qu is ranked with Tang poetry and Song ci as another peak of Chinese literature. There were about two hundred Yuan zaju writers who produced some six hundred plays, of which over 150 survive. The finest was Guan Hanqing of Dadu, familiar with the life of the lower classes, who wrote over sixty zaju in his life, of which more than ten survive. His masterpiece is the tragedy The Injustice to Dou E, in which the kind young widow Dou E is falsely accused by the rogue Zhang Lüer and, under severe torture by a muddled official, is wrongly executed. Before her execution Dou E makes three vows: her blood will spatter the white silk, snow will fall in midsummer, and drought will last three years; all come true. The work exposes the corruption of Yuan officials and the darkness of society and expresses the people's spirit of resistance to oppression. Guan Hanqing also wrote plays including Rescuing a Courtesan, Single Sword Meeting and Pavilion by the River, and in 1958 the World Peace Council named him a "World Cultural Figure". Other dramatists of comparable fame are Ma Zhiyuan, Zheng Guangzu and Bai Pu, who with him are the "Four Great Yuan Dramatists".

events.title: Wen Tianxiang Is Executed
events.short: The Southern Song chancellor Wen Tianxiang resisted the Yuan; captured, he refused to yield, wrote Crossing Lingding Ocean and Song of Righteousness, and was executed in Dadu in 1283.
events.detail: Wen Tianxiang (1236–1283), courtesy name Lüshan, art name Wenshan, was from Luling in Jizhou (present-day Ji'an, Jiangxi), and took first place in the palace examination at twenty. In 1275, as Yuan forces came down the Yangtze toward Lin'an, the Southern Song court called on all regions to raise troops to defend the dynasty; Wen responded at once, recruiting over ten thousand volunteers to go to its aid. In 1276 the court appointed him Right Chancellor and Commissioner of Military Affairs and sent him to negotiate at the Yuan camp. He spoke boldly and denounced the Yuan side, and was detained by the Yuan commander Bayan. Soon Lin'an fell and Wen was taken north, but he escaped at Zhenjiang and, after many hardships, reached Fujian, where he continued to organize the remaining Song forces and local volunteers against the Yuan. In 1278 he was defeated and captured at Wupoling in Haifeng, Guangdong. The Yuan general Zhang Hongfan forced him to write urging Zhang Shijie, holding Yamen, to surrender; Wen answered with the poem Crossing Lingding Ocean, whose lines "Who since antiquity has not died? Let my loyal heart shine in the annals" became famous for all time. After the last Song forces were destroyed at Yamen in 1279, Wen was taken to Dadu and held for over three years. The Yuan rulers urged him repeatedly to submit; Kublai Khan received him in person and offered high office such as chancellor, and the captive Emperor Gong of Song was even sent to persuade him, but Wen would rather die, saying, "Beyond death, there is nothing more for me to do." In prison he wrote the stirring Song of Righteousness, expressing his resolve to keep his integrity.
