events.title: The Yuan Provincial System
events.short: The Yuan had the Secretariat, Bureau of Military Affairs and Censorate at the center and ten Branch Secretariats locally, the beginning of China's provincial system.
events.detail: After the Yuan was founded, Kublai Khan, helped by Han scholars and following the practice of earlier Central Plains dynasties, gradually established an autocratic, centralized system. At the center, the Secretariat handled national administration, with six ministries (Personnel, Revenue, Rites, War, Justice and Works) under it; the Bureau of Military Affairs directed military affairs and the deployment of armies; the Censorate oversaw supervision; and the Bureau of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs governed Buddhist matters and the military and civil affairs of Tibet. Locally, the Yuan created the provincial system. As the empire was vast, to strengthen control the Yuan called today's Shandong, Shanxi, Hebei and parts of Inner Mongolia the "inner region" (Fuli), ruled directly by the Secretariat; Tibet came under the Bureau of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs; and the rest was divided into ten Branch Secretariats, called "provinces" for short, including Lingbei, Liaoyang, Henan, Shaanxi, Sichuan, Gansu, Yunnan, Jiangzhe, Jiangxi and Huguang. A Branch Secretariat was originally an outpost of the Secretariat but gradually became the permanent highest local administrative body, with officials appointed by the center and charge of local military and civil affairs; its powers were great, but major matters had to be referred to the center. Below the province were circuits, prefectures, subprefectures and counties. Provincial boundaries were often drawn deliberately across natural barriers so that no province could hold out behind natural defenses. The system strengthened central control over the localities, consolidated national unity and promoted the development of frontier regions.

events.title: Yuan Territory and the Formation of the Hui
events.short: The Yuan's territory exceeded that of the Han and Tang, among the largest in Chinese history; peoples migrated and mingled widely, and under the Yuan a new ethnic group, the Hui, gradually took shape.
events.detail: The Yuan was the first nationwide unified dynasty in Chinese history founded mainly by minority-ethnic nobility. Its territory was vast; the History of Yuan (Geography) describes it as reaching "north beyond the Yin Mountains, west to the shifting sands, east to Liaodong, south across the seas", "beyond the Han and Tang at their height". Present-day Xinjiang, Tibet, Yunnan, the vast Northeast, Taiwan and the South China Sea islands were all within its rule. Under the Yuan, with the country unified and communications developed, frontier peoples including the Mongols moved in large numbers into the Central Plains and the Jiangnan region and lived mixed with the Han, while many Han also moved to frontier areas. In this great migration and fusion a new ethnic group, the Hui, took shape. During the Mongol western campaigns of the 13th century, large numbers of Muslims from Central and West Asia were relocated to China and were called "Huihui"; descendants of Arab and Persian merchants who had come to trade and settled in the Tang and Song were also a source of the Hui. The Huihui were scattered across the country ("in the Yuan the Huihui were everywhere"); with Islam as their bond, they long lived among and intermarried with other peoples, absorbed Han culture and gradually adopted Chinese as their common language, forming by the Ming a new ethnic group, the Hui. Under the Yuan the Huihui were active in politics, economy and culture: Sayyid Ajall Shams al-Din governed Yunnan with great success, the astronomer Jamal al-Din compiled the Wannian Calendar, and the architect Yeheidie'er took part in designing the city of Dadu. The ethnic fusion of the Yuan period enriched the Chinese nation and promoted the development of a unified multi-ethnic state.

events.title: Bureau of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs Governs Tibet
events.short: The Yuan set up the Bureau of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs (first the Bureau of General Regulation) to oversee Buddhism and Tibet's affairs, bringing Tibet under central administration.
events.detail: After the Liangzhou Meeting of 1247, Tibet submitted to the Mongols. After the Yuan was founded, it further strengthened its management of Tibet. In 1264 Kublai Khan set up the Bureau of General Regulation to oversee Buddhist affairs nationwide and the military and civil affairs of Tibet, with the State Preceptor Phagpa in charge; in 1288 it was renamed the Bureau of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs, its officials recommended by the Imperial Preceptor and appointed by the emperor, drawing on both monks and laypeople. Phagpa, a nephew of Sakya Pandita, was named State Preceptor by Kublai and later raised to Imperial Preceptor; ordered to devise a script, he created the "Phagpa script" as the Yuan's national script. In Tibet the Yuan set up three pacification commissions with military command, including Uchang and Narisgulsun, under the direct control of the Bureau and responsible for local military and civil affairs. Below them were myriarchies and thousand-household offices, with local monastic and lay leaders appointed as officials and given seals. The central government also repeatedly registered households in Tibet, set up postal stations and a communication line from Dadu to Sakya, levied taxes, stationed troops and sent officials on inspection, exercising full and effective administration. From then on Tibet came formally under the administration of the Chinese central government, becoming an administrative region directly governed by the Yuan court.

events.title: Penghu Inspectorate Established
events.short: The Yuan set up an inspectorate on Penghu, under Jinjiang County, Fujian, covering Penghu and Liuqiu (Taiwan): the first formal central government body in the Taiwan area.
events.detail: The Penghu archipelago lies in the southeastern Taiwan Strait, made up of dozens of large and small islands, and was an important stepping stone between the mainland and Taiwan. As early as the Song, coastal mainland residents went to Penghu to fish and settle, and in the Southern Song Penghu belonged to Jinjiang County, Quanzhou, Fujian, with troops stationed there. After the Yuan unified China, to govern its vast territory effectively, it adapted its approach to local conditions and set up corresponding administrative bodies in the northeast, northwest, southeast and southwest. In the southeast the Yuan established the Penghu Inspectorate, attached to Jinjiang County, Quanzhou Circuit, Fujian Province, responsible for the affairs of Penghu and Liuqiu (today's Taiwan), including patrols, arrest of bandits, civil administration and the collection of salt taxes and other levies. The inspectorate was the first formal administrative body established by the Chinese central government in the Taiwan area in history, and marked the formal inclusion of Taiwan and its attached islands under central government administration. In his Daoyi Zhilue (A Brief Account of the Island Barbarians), the Yuan writer Wang Dayuan recorded that Penghu "has grass but no trees, and the soil is poor and unfit for rice", that the people "boil seawater for salt, brew liquor from sorghum, and catch fish, shrimp, snails and clams to eat", that there were "merchants and traders who delight in the profit", and that the place "belongs to Jinjiang County, Quanzhou, where an inspectorate was set up in the Zhiyuan years". The Yuan also twice sent troops to Liuqiu.

events.title: The Four-Class System
events.short: The Yuan rulers practiced ethnic discrimination, dividing the population into four classes (Mongols, Semu, Han and Southerners) with unequal treatment in politics, law and other matters.
events.detail: To preserve Mongol nobles' rule over the Han and other peoples, the Yuan rulers pursued a policy of ethnic division and discrimination, and society gradually formed four classes: Mongols, Semu, Han and Southerners, known as the "four-class system". The first class was the Mongols, the ruling people of the Yuan, who enjoyed many privileges. The second was the "Semu", mainly the Tanguts (Xixia), Uyghurs, Huihui and people of Central Asian, West Asian, European and other origins, who had submitted early and helped the Mongols rule, and ranked just below the Mongols. The third was the "Han", meaning Han people formerly under the Jin north of the Huai River, plus Khitans, Jurchens, Koreans and others. The fourth was the "Southerners", broadly the Han and other peoples formerly under the Southern Song, who were conquered last by the Yuan and ranked lowest. The four classes were treated unequally in politics, economy and law. Politically, important posts at the center and in the localities, and the supervising office of darughachi in each place, were generally held by Mongols, next by Semu, while Han and Southerners could rarely hold major posts. In the civil service examinations, Mongols and Semu sat separate papers from Han and Southerners, with easier questions but the same number of places. Legally, a Mongol who killed a Han Chinese was only sentenced to military service and made to pay burial money, while a Han who killed a Mongol was put to death; Han and Southerners were also forbidden to keep weapons privately or to assemble and form societies. The system aggravated ethnic and social conflicts and was one of the important reasons the Yuan's rule was unstable and ended in under a hundred years.

events.title: Yuan Post Stations and the Maritime Silk Road at Its Height
events.short: The Yuan built a far-reaching post-station network, with land routes to Europe and sea routes to East Africa; Quanzhou was hailed as the "greatest port of the East".
events.detail: In the Song and Yuan periods, communication with other countries grew greatly. The Yuan's territory was vast, and to strengthen rule and links it built a national road network centered on Dadu and a far-reaching system of post stations. The Yuan post stations were called "zhanchi"; over 1,500 were set up nationwide, each equipped with horses, oxen, donkeys, carts and boats for officials, envoys and the relay of official documents, and the government-issued travel credentials were called "paizi". The Yuan's land routes ran west to Central Asia, West Asia and Europe, and the ancient overland Silk Road was more open than ever; European merchants, missionaries and envoys came to China in an endless stream, and Marco Polo reached the Yuan along this route. By sea, the Yuan inherited and developed the Song's overseas trade, setting up maritime trade offices at ports such as Quanzhou, Guangzhou, Qingyuan (present-day Ningbo), Shanghai and Hangzhou. Quanzhou was one of the world's largest ports, hailed as the "greatest port of the East", with merchant ships from around the world in its harbor and many foreign merchants living in the city. Yuan ships sailed to Southeast Asia, South Asia, the Arabian Peninsula and the east coast of Africa, trading with over a hundred countries and regions. The Yuan navigator Wang Dayuan twice went to sea on merchant ships, visiting many places in Southeast Asia and along the Indian Ocean, and wrote Daoyi Zhilue (A Brief Account of the Island Barbarians), recording the customs and products of over two hundred countries and regions. In 2021 "Quanzhou: Emporium of the World in Song-Yuan China" was inscribed on the World Heritage List.

events.title: Peasant Uprisings at the End of the Yuan
events.short: Amid corruption and ethnic oppression, Liu Futong and others rose in 1351 as the Red Turbans; anti-Yuan forces spread, and Zhu Yuanzhang grew strong and united the south.
events.detail: In the middle and late Yuan, struggles for the throne within the ruling circle were fierce, with eight emperors in over twenty years, politics was highly corrupt and official graft was rife. Together with severe ethnic oppression, intense land annexation and repeated Yellow River floods, famine struck year after year and the people could not survive. In 1351 the Yuan conscripted 150,000 laborers to repair the Yellow River, and the workers were badly mistreated by officials. The White Lotus leaders Han Shantong and Liu Futong secretly buried a one-eyed stone figure in the riverbed, carved on its back with the words "Do not say the stone man has only one eye; it will stir up the Yellow River and the realm will rebel". When the workers dug it up, unrest spread. Han Shantong and Liu Futong seized the chance to launch an uprising at Yingzhou (present-day Fuyang, Anhui), and the rebel army, wearing red headscarves, was called the "Red Turbans". Peasants everywhere responded, and several anti-Yuan forces appeared in the Jianghuai region, including those of Xu Shouhui, Chen Youliang, Zhang Shicheng and Fang Guozhen. In 1355 Liu Futong set up Han Shantong's son Han Lin'er as emperor with the state name Song, and later sent armies north in three columns, at one point capturing the Yuan upper capital and dealing a heavy blow to Yuan rule. Zhu Yuanzhang was originally a Red Turban commander under Guo Zixing; after Guo's death he took over his troops and in 1356 captured Jiqing (present-day Nanjing), renaming it Yingtian Prefecture. He took the advice of his adviser Zhu Sheng: "Build high walls, store up grain, and be slow to proclaim yourself king."

events.title: Founding of the Ming Dynasty
events.short: In 1368 Zhu Yuanzhang proclaimed the Ming at Yingtian with the era name Hongwu; Ming forces took Dadu that year and the Yuan emperor fled north.
events.detail: Zhu Yuanzhang (1328–1398) was from Zhongli in Haozhou (present-day Fengyang, Anhui), born to a poor peasant family. At seventeen, drought and plague struck his home region and his parents and brother died one after another; he was forced to become a monk at Huangjue Temple and later wandered begging for food. In 1352 he joined the Red Turban army led by Guo Zixing and gradually became a leader of the rebels. Following the strategy of "building high walls, storing up grain and being slow to proclaim himself king", he grew in strength and eliminated rival regimes such as those of Chen Youliang and Zhang Shicheng. In the first month of 1368 Zhu Yuanzhang proclaimed himself emperor at Yingtian (present-day Nanjing, Jiangsu), with the state name Great Ming and the era name Hongwu; he is known as the Ming Taizu or Hongwu Emperor. That year he sent Xu Da and Chang Yuchun north, and Ming forces captured the Yuan capital Dadu; the Yuan emperor Shundi fled to Shangdu, ending Yuan rule in the Central Plains. Ming forces then pacified Sichuan, Yunnan, Liaodong and other regions and essentially unified the country. The Yuan remnants who withdrew to the steppe retained considerable strength, known as the "Northern Yuan", and stood off against the Ming for a long time. After the founding, noting the social devastation caused by the wars of the late Yuan, Taizu adopted a policy of rest and recovery: he encouraged peasants to open wasteland, ruled that reclaimed land belonged to the reclaimer and exempted it from taxes for three years; organized migrations and military farming colonies and built irrigation works; lightened taxes; and surveyed households and land, compiling the Yellow Registers of taxes and labor service and the Fish-scale Registers of land.

events.title: Romance of the Three Kingdoms and Water Margin Take Shape
events.short: In the late Yuan and early Ming, Luo Guanzhong wrote Romance of the Three Kingdoms and Shi Nai'an wrote Water Margin, long novels refined from Song and Yuan storytellers' scripts.
events.detail: In the Ming, literature and the arts combined with townspeople's culture and produced a number of popular long novels in chapter form. The chapter-style novel grew out of the storytellers' scripts of the Song and Yuan, with chapters divided under headings and a continuous plot. The Popular Romance of the Records of the Three Kingdoms, commonly known as Romance of the Three Kingdoms, took shape in the late Yuan and early Ming; its author was Luo Guanzhong (given name Ben), who lived roughly in that period. Based on histories such as Chen Shou's Records of the Three Kingdoms and drawing on folk legends, storytellers' scripts and plays, the novel vividly depicts the struggles among Wei, Shu and Wu over nearly a century, from the Yellow Turban uprising at the end of the Eastern Han to the Western Jin's unification, with vivid characters such as Zhuge Liang, Cao Cao, Guan Yu, Liu Bei and Zhou Yu, and stories such as the Peach Garden Oath, the Three Visits to the Thatched Cottage, borrowing arrows with straw boats and the Battle of Red Cliffs known in every household. Described as "seventy percent fact, thirty percent fiction", it is China's first long historical novel in chapter form. Water Margin is generally attributed to Shi Nai'an, though some think Luo Guanzhong also had a hand in it. Set against the historical Song Jiang uprising of the late Northern Song and built on folk tales, scripts and plays, it tells how 108 heroes led by Song Jiang gathered at Mount Liang and defied the authorities, expressing the theme that "officials force the people to rebel" and creating heroes such as Lin Chong, Wu Song, Lu Zhishen and Li Kui.

events.date: Reigns of Ming Taizu and Chengzu
events.title: Abolition of the Chancellor and Stronger Imperial Power
events.short: Ming Taizu replaced the Branch Secretariats with three provincial commissions and in 1380 abolished the chancellorship, the six ministries answering directly to the emperor.
events.detail: Zhu Yuanzhang held that the Yuan had fallen because of decentralized local power and over-powerful court officials, so while restoring the economy he took a series of political measures. Locally, he abolished the Branch Secretariats and set up three commissions: the Provincial Administration Commission for civil affairs and finance, the Provincial Surveillance Commission for justice and supervision, and the Regional Military Commission for military affairs. Their heads were appointed by the center, were not subordinate to one another and answered directly to the center, preventing regional separatism. At the center, in 1380 Zhu executed the chancellor Hu Weiyong on a charge of "treason" and used the case to abolish the Secretariat and the chancellorship; the emperor directly managed the six ministries of Personnel, Revenue, Rites, War, Justice and Works, whose ministers answered to him alone, and he held all power himself. The chancellorship, which had lasted in China for over a thousand years, was thus abolished and autocracy was strengthened as never before. As state business was heavy and one emperor could hardly handle it, Taizu appointed Grand Secretaries as advisers. Under Chengzu, Hanlin Academy officials were chosen to serve in the Wenyuan Pavilion and take part in state affairs, called the Grand Secretariat, which gradually became the central body assisting the emperor with government, though its Grand Secretaries could only advise and the final decision rested with the emperor. To tighten control over officials, Taizu also created the secret-police organ the "Embroidered Uniform Guard" answering directly to the emperor, and under Chengzu the Eastern Depot, run by eunuchs, was added.

events.title: The Eight-Legged Essay Examinations
events.short: Ming examinations drew on the Four Books and Five Classics, followed Zhu Xi's commentaries and required fixed-format eight-legged essays, which constrained thought.
events.detail: After the Ming was founded, the rulers vigorously promoted reverence for Confucius and Confucianism, made Cheng-Zhu Neo-Confucianism the official orthodoxy and perfected the civil service examinations. Ming examinations had several levels: the prefectural, provincial, metropolitan and palace examinations. Those who passed the prefectural examination were called shengyuan (commonly xiucai), those passing the provincial examination juren, and those passing the metropolitan examination gongshi; after the palace examination presided over by the emperor, successful candidates were called jinshi and divided into three grades, with the top three of the first grade called zhuangyuan, bangyan and tanhua. The Ming strictly required that questions come from the Four Books and Five Classics. Candidates' interpretations had to follow standards such as Zhu Xi of the Southern Song's Collected Commentaries on the Four Books and could not be freely developed, otherwise they were deemed heretical. Answers had to take the fixed form of the "eight-legged essay", each composed of parts called the opening, the receiving, the preliminary exposition, the entry, the beginning leg, the middle leg, the latter leg and the concluding leg; the last four sections each had two balanced, antithetical legs, eight in all, hence the name. Candidates had to "speak on behalf of the sages" and could not state their own views. The system led scholars to devote themselves to the Four Books, the Five Classics and the techniques of eight-legged writing, severely constraining thought and hindering the development of science and culture. The Qing kept the system.

events.title: The Jingnan Campaign
events.short: The Jianwen Emperor's curtailing of the princes led Zhu Di, Prince of Yan, to revolt; after four years he took Nanjing and the throne as the Yongle Emperor, later moving the capital to Beijing.
events.detail: To secure the Zhu family's rule, Ming Taizu Zhu Yuanzhang enfeoffed his sons as princes across the country to guard key places. Those guarding the northern frontier had strong forces, the strongest being Zhu Di, Prince of Yan, stationed at Beiping. In 1398 Taizu died; as the crown prince Zhu Biao had died early, the imperial grandson Zhu Yunwen took the throne with the era name Jianwen, and is known as the Jianwen Emperor. Seeing the princes grow ever stronger, he took the advice of the ministers Qi Tai and Huang Zicheng and ordered the princes' power curtailed, stripping the titles of the princes of Zhou, Qi, Dai, Xiang and Min in turn; the Prince of Xiang was driven to burn himself to death. Feeling threatened, Zhu Di in 1399 rose against the Jianwen Emperor under the slogan of "clearing the emperor's side and quelling the national crisis", the Jingnan Campaign. The Jianwen Emperor lacked battlefield experience, and the court's veteran generals had mostly been killed in the great purges of the early Ming, while the Yan army was battle-hardened and strong. In 1402 Zhu Di avoided the court's main forces, marched south, crossed the Yangtze and entered the capital Nanjing; fire broke out in the palace and the Jianwen Emperor's fate is unknown, one account saying he burned himself to death and another that he became a monk and fled. Zhu Di seized the throne with the era name Yongle and is known as the Yongle Emperor (Ming Chengzu). The great scholar Fang Xiaoru refused to draft the enthronement edict and was executed, and many of his kin and students were implicated. To strengthen northern defense, Zhu Di formally moved the capital to Beijing in 1421, keeping Nanjing as a secondary capital, creating a pattern of "the emperor guarding the gate of the state".

events.title: Shunfeng Xiangsong Earliest Records the Diaoyu Islands
events.short: The navigation manual Shunfeng Xiangsong, first compiled in 1403, is the earliest extant text to record the Diaoyu Islands, indicating Chinese discovery and naming of them.
events.detail: The Diaoyu Islands and their affiliated islets lie to the northeast of Taiwan Island and are regarded in Chinese accounts as affiliated islands of Taiwan. Chinese sources hold that the Chinese were the first to discover, name and use the Diaoyu Islands; fishermen on the southeast coast fished in these waters from early times and used them as navigation markers. The earliest extant text recording names such as Diaoyu and Chiwei Islets is Shunfeng Xiangsong (Fair Winds for Escort), first compiled in 1403 (the first year of Yongle in the Ming). It is a navigation manual of compass bearings that, in recording the route from Fujian to the Ryukyus, mentions places such as "Diaoyu Islet" and "Chikan Islet", showing that China had already discovered and named the Diaoyu Islands by the 14th to 15th centuries. From 1372 the Ming repeatedly sent investiture envoys to the Ryukyus, and their records mention the Diaoyu Islands many times. Chen Kan's Record of the Mission to the Ryukyus of 1534 says that after the ship passed Diaoyu Islet, Huangmao Islet and Chi Islet, "Gumi Mountain was seen, which belongs to the Ryukyus", indicating that islands west of Gumi, including the Diaoyu Islands, did not belong to the Ryukyus. In the early Ming, to defend against Japanese pirates, the Diaoyu Islands were included in the coastal defense area; the Chouhai Tubian of 1562, edited by Zheng Ruozeng under Hu Zongxian, placed Diaoyu Islet and other islands in Fujian's coastal defense zone. The Qing followed the Ming and clearly placed the Diaoyu Islands under Taiwan's local administration, as recorded in works such as Huang Shujing's Taihai Shicha Lu. Many maps from China and abroad also show the Diaoyu Islands as belonging to China.

events.title: Zheng He's Voyages
events.short: From 1405 to 1433 Zheng He led seven voyages to over 30 countries of Asia and Africa, reaching East Africa and the Red Sea, a landmark in the history of navigation.
events.detail: In the early 15th century the Ming economy was prosperous and its power great. The Yongle Emperor sent Zheng He with a fleet to the "Western Seas" (in the early Ming, Southeast Asia west of present-day Brunei and the Indian Ocean region), to "show China's wealth and strength" and develop friendly relations and trade with overseas countries. Zheng He (1371–1433), originally surnamed Ma with the childhood name Sanbao, was a Hui from Yunnan, captured after the Ming conquest of Yunnan and made a eunuch in the palace; he later followed Zhu Di, distinguished himself in the Jingnan Campaign, was granted the surname Zheng and promoted to Grand Director of the Directorate of Palace Attendants, and was known as the "Three-Jewel Eunuch". In 1405 Zheng He set out with over 27,000 men from Liujiagang in Suzhou, putting to sea via Changle in Fujian on the first voyage. Up to 1433 he made seven voyages in all, reaching more than thirty countries and regions of Asia and Africa, as far as the east coast of Africa and the Red Sea. The fleet at its largest had over 200 ships, and according to the History of Ming the biggest treasure ships were 44 zhang long and could hold a thousand people. The ships were loaded with silk, porcelain, tea, lacquerware, gold and silver for gifts and trade, bringing back spices, gems, medicines and rare birds and animals, and Bengal presented a giraffe. The fleet navigated by the compass and by "celestial navigation" using stars, making good use of monsoons and currents. Many countries sent envoys back with the fleet; on the return of the sixth voyage, over 1,200 envoys from sixteen countries and regions came together.

events.title: Early Ming Foreign Relations (Visits by the Kings of Brunei and Sulu)
events.short: The early Ming developed friendly ties with neighbors; the kings of Brunei and Sulu died while visiting China and were buried in Nanjing and Dezhou as they wished.
events.detail: After the Ming was founded, Ming Taizu actively developed friendly relations with neighboring countries and regions and sent envoys abroad, "commissioning envoys to go beyond the borders in all directions, passing through states, with thirty-six countries actually visited". After the Yongle Emperor took the throne, besides sending Zheng He on his voyages he sent envoys to other countries over fifty times, and many overseas countries sent envoys to China, with the kings of several countries visiting in person. In 1408 the King of Brunei (in the north of Borneo, around present-day Brunei), Maharaja Kali, came to Nanjing with his queen, children and over 150 attendants and was grandly received by the Yongle Emperor. Soon after he fell ill and died in Nanjing, leaving a will asking that "my body be entrusted to burial in China". The emperor buried him with royal rites at Shiziganggang outside Nanjing's Andemen gate, bestowed the posthumous title "Gongshun" and had the prince escorted home to succeed him. The Brunei king's tomb is now in Nanjing's Yuhuatai District, with stone figures and animals from the Ming still before it, and was rediscovered in 1958. In 1417 the Eastern, Western and Cave kings of Sulu (in the Sulu Archipelago of the present-day Philippines) came to China with over 340 family and attendants and were warmly entertained by the Yongle Emperor. On the way home the Eastern King, Paduka Pahala, died in Dezhou, Shandong; the emperor buried him there with royal rites, gave the title "Gongding" and left his consort and two princes to keep the tomb.

events.title: Building Beijing and the Forbidden City
events.short: The Yongle Emperor ordered Beijing's palaces built in 1406; they were largely complete in 1420 and the capital moved in 1421. The Forbidden City is the largest surviving palace complex.
events.detail: After taking the throne, the Yongle Emperor Zhu Di decided, to strengthen the northern defenses, to move the capital to Beiping, the base of his rise, renaming it Beijing in 1403. In 1406 he ordered the construction of the Beijing palaces, gathering skilled craftsmen and large numbers of laborers from across the country and cutting precious timber such as nanmu in Sichuan, Huguang, Jiangxi and elsewhere. After over ten years of preparation and building, the palaces and city walls were largely complete in 1420, and the Ming formally moved its capital to Beijing in 1421. Beijing was rebuilt on the basis of the Yuan capital Dadu, symmetrical about a north-south central axis, with the palace city (the Forbidden City) at the center, surrounded by the Imperial City and the Inner City, embodying the traditional planning idea of "ancestral temple on the left, altar of the soil on the right"; in the mid-Ming an outer city was added, giving the city its "convex" shape. The Forbidden City covers about 720,000 square meters with a floor area of about 150,000 square meters, with over seventy palaces and nearly 9,000 rooms, surrounded by walls and a moat. It is divided into the Outer Court and the Inner Court: the Outer Court, centered on the Halls of Supreme Harmony, Central Harmony and Preserving Harmony, was where the emperor held great ceremonies and handled government; the Inner Court, centered on the Palace of Heavenly Purity, the Hall of Union and the Palace of Earthly Tranquility, was the residence of the emperor and his consorts. The palaces, with yellow glazed tiles, red walls and painted beams, are magnificent and show the high level of ancient Chinese architecture. Twenty-four emperors of the Ming and Qing lived and ruled here.

events.title: Building the Ming Great Wall
events.short: To defend against Mongol nobles, the Ming rebuilt the Great Wall 18 times, from the Yalu River to Jiayuguan; it forms the main part of the Wall seen today.
events.detail: After the Ming was founded, Mongol nobles who had withdrawn north of the Gobi kept raiding southward, and later the Jurchens of the northeast also rose. To secure the northern frontier, the Ming over more than two hundred years built the Great Wall 18 times, forming the Ming Great Wall running from the Yalu River in the east to Jiayuguan in Gansu in the west, over ten thousand li long. 8 kilometers. Along it the Ming set up nine military garrisons, including Liaodong, Jizhou, Xuanfu, Datong, Yansui and Gansu, called the "Nine Frontier Garrisons", with heavy troops stationed and military farming carried out. The Ming Great Wall, with walls as its main body, comprises passes, wall platforms, watchtowers and beacon towers, forming a complete defensive system. From the mid-Ming the Wall was largely built of brick and stone and was very strong. In the Longqing reign the famed anti-pirate general Qi Jiguang was transferred to Jizhen as garrison commander and oversaw building the Wall there, creating hollow watchtowers that could house troops and store munitions and greatly strengthening defense. Along the Wall many fortified passes were built, famous ones including Shanhaiguan, Juyongguan, Pingxingguan, Yanmenguan and Jiayuguan. Well-known sections today such as Badaling, Mutianyu and Jinshanling were all built in the Ming. The Wall lay at the border between farming and nomadic regions, and in the late Ming many "horse markets" were opened along it for trade in farm and herding products, so the Wall also became a link between peoples. In 1987 the Great Wall was inscribed on the World Heritage List. It embodies the wisdom and toil of ancient laborers and is regarded as a symbol of the Chinese nation's spirit.

events.title: Portuguese Gain Residence at Macao
events.short: In 1553 Portuguese colonists, claiming they needed to dry their cargo, bribed local officials for the right to stay at Macao, though sovereignty over Macao remained with China.
events.detail: After the opening of new sea routes, the Portuguese were the first Europeans to reach the East. In 1511 Portugal took Malacca and then came to the Chinese coast. Their several incursions on the coasts of Guangdong, Fujian and Zhejiang were driven off by Chinese soldiers and civilians; for example, in 1521 Ming forces defeated the Portuguese at the Battle of Tunmen in Guangdong. In 1553 the Portuguese falsely claimed that their ships had met a storm and their cargo had been soaked, and asked to borrow land to dry it; bribing Guangdong officials and promising 500 taels of silver a year, they were able to land at Macao and gradually established a settlement. In 1573 the 500 taels became "ground rent" paid to the Ming government, and the Portuguese gained the right to reside at Macao by lease. Sovereignty over Macao, however, remained with China. The Ming government appointed a Macao guard official and stationed troops there to administer it fully. Macao gradually became an important international trading port in the Far East and a window for East-West cultural exchange, and many Western missionaries entered inland China through it. The A-Ma Temple in Macao is one of its oldest temples; it is said that when the Portuguese landed nearby and asked the name of the place, the locals answered "Ma Ge", from which the name "Macau" comes. After the Opium War, Portugal took advantage of Qing weakness to stop paying the rent and gradually occupied the Macao peninsula and the islands of Taipa and Coloane, and in 1887 forced the Qing government to sign the Sino-Portuguese Treaty of Peace, Amity and Commerce, in effect occupying Macao.

events.title: Ming Economic Growth (American Crops, Merchant Groups)
events.short: The Ming adopted American crops such as maize and sweet potato, spread cotton weaving, made Jingdezhen a porcelain center and saw merchant groups like the Shanxi and Huizhou merchants arise.
events.detail: Under the Ming, agriculture, handicrafts and commerce continued to grow on earlier foundations. In agriculture, as contact between East and West increased after the opening of new sea routes, crops native to the Americas such as maize, sweet potato, potato, peanut and tobacco reached China one after another. Maize and sweet potato were drought-resistant and high-yielding, suited to hills and mountains, and played an important part in raising grain output and feeding a larger population. In 1593 Chen Zhenlong of Fujian brought sweet potato vines back from Luzon (present-day Philippines), grew them successfully in Fujian, and they spread to other regions. In handicrafts, cotton growing and weaving spread from the south to the north; Songjiang (around present-day Shanghai) was the national cotton-weaving center, said to "clothe the whole realm"; Suzhou was the silk-weaving center, where "loom owners" with looms who hired workers and "loom hands" who sold their labor appeared; Jingdezhen was the national porcelain center, its blue-and-white ware in varied shapes and bright colors selling at home and abroad. In commerce, Beijing and Nanjing were nationwide trading cities, with dozens of other large commercial cities elsewhere; large amounts of silver flowed into China through overseas trade and silver became the main currency. In the late Ming the "Single Whip" reform, collecting taxes and labor service in silver, further promoted the commodity economy. Many wealthy merchants carried large sums in long-distance trade, forming regional merchant groups, the best known being the Shanxi merchants and the Huizhou merchants of Anhui, who dealt in salt, grain, cloth, tea and pawnbroking; it was said that "without Huizhou merchants there is no market town".

events.title: Qi Jiguang Fights the Japanese Pirates
events.short: Qi Jiguang raised the "Qi Family Army" and devised the "Mandarin duck formation", winning nine battles in nine at Taizhou in 1561 and, with Yu Dayou, largely ending the pirate threat.
events.detail: Ancient China called Japan the land of Wo. In the late Yuan and early Ming, some Japanese warriors, rōnin and unscrupulous merchants formed pirate bands that smuggled and raided along the Chinese coast, known as "wokou". In the mid-Ming, Japan was in its Warring States period while the Ming was weakened and its coastal defenses lax; the wokou colluded with Chinese pirates and shady merchants and raided the southeast coast ever more boldly, killing residents and looting goods, causing great damage in coastal regions, known as the "Japanese pirate troubles". Qi Jiguang (1528–1588), from Dengzhou, Shandong, came from a military family, loved military books from childhood and as a young man set the ambition: "Being made a marquis is not what I want, only that the waves of the sea be calm." In 1555 he was transferred to Zhejiang to fight the pirates. Seeing that the existing troops were slack and weak, he recruited peasants and miners at Yiwu and elsewhere in Zhejiang and trained them strictly; this disciplined, hardy army became known as the "Qi Family Army". To suit the pirates' fighting style and the marshy, water-laced terrain of Jiangnan, Qi devised the "Mandarin duck formation", a 12-man unit combining long and short weapons, balancing offense and defense. In 1561 the pirates invaded Taizhou, Zhejiang in force, and Qi led his army to nine victories in nine battles, ending the pirate trouble in eastern Zhejiang. He then led his army into Fujian and Guangdong and with Yu Dayou, Liu Xian and other generals defeated the pirates, and by about 1565 the trouble on the southeast coast was largely ended. Qi Jiguang was later transferred to Jizhen as garrison commander, guarding the northern frontier for sixteen years and overseeing the building of the Great Wall.

events.title: Wu Cheng'en Writes Journey to the West
events.short: In the mid-Ming Wu Cheng'en wrote the mythological novel Journey to the West, based on Xuanzhang's pilgrimage, creating the mythic hero Sun Wukong.
events.detail: Journey to the West is a long mythological novel of the mid-Ming, generally attributed to Wu Cheng'en. Wu Cheng'en (c. 1500–c. 1582), courtesy name Ruzhong, art name Sheyang Shanren, was from Shanyang in Huai'an (present-day Huai'an, Jiangsu). He loved stories of gods and spirits but repeatedly failed the civil service examinations, holding only minor posts such as county assistant magistrate of Changxing, and in old age devoted himself to writing. The novel is based on the historical pilgrimage of the Tang monk Xuanzang to India for scriptures, drawing on tales, storytellers' scripts and plays circulating since the Song and Yuan, such as The Poetic Tale of the Tripitaka's Quest for Scriptures in the Great Tang, which the author reworked. In 100 chapters, the first seven tell of Sun Wukong's birth, his learning from a master and his havoc in Heaven, ending with his imprisonment under the Five Elements Mountain by the Buddha; the rest tell how he protects Xuanzang and, with Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing, goes through eighty-one trials to reach the Western Heaven and obtain the true scriptures. The novel centers on the mythic hero Sun Wukong, bold, highly skilled, clear in his loves and hatreds, quick-witted and brave; he knows seventy-two transformations, can somersault 108,000 li in one leap, dares to defy the authority of Heaven and subdues demons, and is much loved. With bold imagination and an exaggerated style, the author draws a strange and wondrous world and uses the realm of gods and demons to satirize the darkness of real society and express a wish to root out evil. The language is lively and humorous and the story gripping.

events.title: Li Shizhen Writes the Compendium of Materia Medica
events.short: The physician Li Shizhen spent 27 years compiling the Compendium of Materia Medica, recording over 1,800 drugs and 10,000 prescriptions, hailed as the "great medical canon of the East".
events.detail: Li Shizhen (1518–1593), courtesy name Dongbi, art name Binhu, was from Qizhou (present-day Qichun, Hubei) and came from a family of physicians. In youth he failed the provincial examination three times, so he resolved to carry on his father's work and devote himself to medicine. In long medical practice he found many errors and omissions in earlier materia medica texts and felt it necessary to organize and supplement the ancient pharmacological works. From 1552 Li consulted over eight hundred medical works and went into the countryside to investigate, consulting peasants, herb gatherers and hunters, collecting specimens and tasting drugs himself, gathering a great deal of first-hand material. After 27 years of effort and three drafts, he completed the Compendium of Materia Medica in 1578. In 52 volumes and about 1.9 million characters, it records 1,892 drugs, 374 of them newly added, over 11,000 prescriptions and more than 1,100 illustrations of drug forms. Using the method of "organizing the details under main headings", it classifies drugs into 16 divisions and 60 categories, including water, fire, earth, metals and stones, herbs, grains, vegetables, fruits, trees, clothing and utensils, insects, scaled animals, shelled animals, birds, beasts and humans, describing each drug's origin, form, taste and effect, a classification advanced for its time. The work sums up China's pharmacological achievements before the 16th century. It was formally published in Nanjing in 1596, reached Japan and Korea in the early 17th century and was later translated into several languages; Darwin also cited material from it. It is hailed as the "great medical canon of the East". In 2011 the Jinling edition was inscribed on the Memory of the World Register.

events.title: Tang Xianzu's The Peony Pavilion
events.short: The late Ming dramatist Tang Xianzu wrote The Peony Pavilion, whose love story of Du Liniang and Liu Mengmei criticizes feudal propriety; it is a Kunqu classic.
events.detail: Under the Ming, opera developed further and became an important cultural activity for people in town and country. In the Jiajing reign, Wei Liangfu and others refined the Kunshan tune into the smooth, delicate "water-polished style"; Kunqu gradually spread across the country and became the most influential form of drama in the Ming and Qing. Tang Xianzu (1550–1616), courtesy name Yireng, art name Ruoshi, was from Linchuan, Jiangxi, the most celebrated dramatist of the late Ming. He passed the jinshi examination in his thirties but was demoted to Xuwen, Guangdong, for criticizing the government, later became magistrate of Suichang, Zhejiang, and in 1598 resigned and returned home to devote himself to writing plays. His masterpiece is The Peony Pavilion, also called The Soul's Return, which with Zichai Ji, Nanke Ji and Handan Ji forms the "Four Dreams of Linchuan". It tells how Du Liniang, daughter of the governor of Nan'an, falls in love in a dream with the scholar Liu Mengmei after a stroll in the garden and, on waking, dies of lovesickness; Liu later finds her self-portrait, her spirit meets him and she is restored to life, and the two finally marry. The play's idea that "love arises from one knows not where, yet grows ever deeper; the living may die for it, and the dead may live again" forcefully criticizes the feudal norms that bind human nature and celebrates young people's pursuit of freedom in love and individual liberation. Its lyrics are flowing and beautiful and its inner portrayal of characters delicate, and scenes such as "Strolling in the Garden" and "Startled Dream" are still staged today. Tang Xianzu died in the same year, 1616, as the English dramatist Shakespeare, and is called the "Shakespeare of the East".

events.title: Xu Guangqi and Matteo Ricci Translate Elements
events.short: Xu Guangqi and the Italian missionary Matteo Ricci translated the first six books of Euclid's Elements, fixing Chinese terms such as "geometry", "point" and "line".
events.detail: In the mid and late Ming, European Jesuit missionaries came to China to preach and brought Western knowledge of astronomy, mathematics, geography and other sciences. The Italian missionary Matteo Ricci (1552–1610) was a leading figure; he reached Macao in 1582 and the next year went to Zhaoqing, Guangdong, to preach. He learned Chinese, wore Confucian dress, studied the Confucian classics and befriended scholar-officials, and was respected as a "Confucian scholar of the Far West"; in 1601 he was permitted to go to Beijing and presented the Wanli Emperor with items such as a striking clock. His world map, Kunyu Wanguo Quantu, broadened Chinese horizons. Xu Guangqi (1562–1633), courtesy name Zixian, art name Xuanhu, was from Shanghai; he converted to Catholicism in 1603, passed the jinshi examination the next year, eagerly studied Western science and rose to Minister of Rites and Grand Secretary of the Dongge Hall. From 1606 Xu worked with Ricci to translate the Greek mathematician Euclid's Elements, completing and publishing the first six books in 1607. Elements starts from definitions and axioms and proves a series of theorems by rigorous logic; Xu praised it as "seemingly most obscure, yet in truth most clear" and held that it "can make students of theory shed their rashness and refine their minds". "Jihe" (geometry) and terms such as "point", "line", "triangle" and "quadrilateral" were fixed in this translation and are still used today. Xu also translated with Ricci works such as Celiang Fayi (On Surveying). Their cooperation was an important result of Sino-Western cultural exchange in the late Ming and deeply influenced the development of Chinese mathematics.

events.title: Nurhaci Founds the Later Jin
events.short: In 1616 Nurhaci united the Jurchen tribes and founded the Later Jin at Hetu Ala; his Eight Banners system joined military and civil rule.
events.detail: The Jurchens were an ancient people of northeast China, divided in the Ming into three main groups: the Jianzhou, Haixi and Wild Jurchens. Nurhaci (1559–1626), of the Aisin Gioro clan, a Jianzhou Jurchen, had a grandfather and father who held posts in the Ming Jianzhou Left Guard. In 1583 his grandfather and father were killed by mistake when Ming forces attacked Gure, and Nurhaci raised troops with the thirteen sets of armor they left, beginning the work of uniting the Jurchen tribes. After more than thirty years of campaigns he united the Jianzhou Jurchens and largely united the Haixi tribes. In the process Nurhaci created the Eight Banners system, first four banners (yellow, white, red and blue), later adding four bordered banners, eight in all. The system combined production, administration and military functions in "unity of soldier and people": bannermen "were soldiers when they went out and civilians when they came home", greatly raising fighting strength. He also had a Manchu script created from the Mongolian alphabet. In 1616 Nurhaci proclaimed himself khan at Hetu Ala (present-day Xinbin, Liaoning) and established a regime with the state name Great Jin, known as the Later Jin. In 1618 he announced the "Seven Grievances" to Heaven, rose against the Ming and took Fushun. In 1619 the Later Jin won a victory against the odds over the Ming army at Sarhu, after which the Ming went on the defensive in Liaodong. The Later Jin then took Shenyang, Liaoyang and other places, and in 1625 moved its capital to Shenyang. In 1626 Nurhaci attacked Ningyuan, was defeated by the Ming general Yuan Chonghuan and died soon after.

events.title: Ming Political Corruption and Social Unrest
events.short: In the mid and late Ming emperors neglected government, eunuchs seized power and factions fought; the Wanli Emperor skipped court for over twenty years and land annexation worsened.
events.detail: In the mid and late Ming, though the economy clearly grew, politics grew ever more corrupt and most emperors indulged in pleasure and neglected government. The Zhengtong Emperor trusted the eunuch Wang Zhen and in 1449 was captured by the Oirats in the Tumu Incident. The Zhengde Emperor left government to the eunuch Liu Jin and amused himself in the "Leopard Chamber" and traveled widely. The Jiajing Emperor revered Daoism and did not attend court for over twenty years, while the powerful minister Yan Song monopolized power for twenty years and took bribes. The Wanli Emperor reigned 48 years, did not attend court or read memorials for over twenty years and left many official posts unfilled, paralyzing many offices. The Tianqi Emperor loved carpentry, making wooden objects year after year and leaving government to the eunuch Wei Zhongxian. Wei ran the Eastern Depot, purged rivals, and officials everywhere built "living shrines" to him; he was called "Nine Thousand Years". The ruling elite was riven by intrigue and ministers formed cliques, with the Donglin faction and the eunuch faction attacking each other. Meanwhile Zhang Juzheng in the early Wanli reign carried out reforms, tightening official discipline, surveying land and introducing the "Single Whip" tax, which improved finances for a time, but most were abandoned after his death. Court chaos steadily weakened the center's control of society, law and discipline slackened, and officials at all levels took bribes and squeezed the people. The imperial family, nobles, eunuchs, officials and landlords seized land wildly; for example, Zhu Changxun, Prince of Fu, son of the Wanli Emperor, was granted 20,000 qing of land in Henan, and many peasants lost their land and drifted.

events.title: Hong Taiji Renames the State Qing
events.short: After Nurhaci, Hong Taiji renamed his people Manchu in 1635 and in 1636 proclaimed himself emperor at Shenyang with the state name Qing, raiding south of the Wall.
events.detail: After Nurhaci died in 1626, his eighth son Hong Taiji (1592–1643) succeeded as khan and changed the era name to Tiancong the next year. On taking power he strengthened the khan's authority, gradually ending the practice of "jointly deliberating state affairs" with the other beile, and set up six ministries on the Ming model, appointed Han officials, improved Manchu-Han relations and developed agriculture, strengthening the state. He sent troops to Korea and finally forced it to sever its tributary relationship with the Ming, and repeatedly marched on the Mongols south of the Gobi, defeating Ligdan Khan, after which the Mongol tribes there submitted one after another. In 1635 Ligdan's son Ejei surrendered and presented the Yuan jade seal, the "Seal of Imperial Edicts"; the same year Hong Taiji ordered the ethnic name "Jurchen" changed to "Manchu". In 1636 he proclaimed himself emperor at Shenyang, changed the state name to "Qing" and the era name to Chongde, and is known as Emperor Taizong of Qing. Qing forces then repeatedly went around through Mongolia, broke through the Great Wall and penetrated north China, seizing people and goods and seriously damaging the Ming. From 1640 to 1642 the Qing army defeated the Ming at the Battle of Songshan and Jinzhou and captured the Ming governor-general Hong Chengchou, leaving the Ming with only a few cities such as Ningyuan beyond Shanhaiguan. In 1643 Hong Taiji died and his son Fulin succeeded as the Shunzhi Emperor, with his uncle Dorgon and others as regents.

events.title: Song Yingxing Writes Tiangong Kaiwu
events.short: Song Yingxing's Tiangong Kaiwu surveys ancient farming and craft techniques with over 120 illustrations, called the "encyclopedia of crafts of 17th-century China".
events.detail: Song Yingxing (1587–c. 1666), courtesy name Changgeng, was from Fengxin, Jiangxi. He passed the provincial examination in 1615 but failed the metropolitan examination five times. On his journeys to and from the capital for the examinations he observed agriculture and handicraft production in many regions. He later served as an instructor at the Fenyi County school in Jiangxi and in his spare time devoted himself to science and technology, publishing Tiangong Kaiwu in 1637. The title draws on the phrase in the Book of Documents, "Heaven's work, man takes its place", and the Book of Changes, "opening up things and accomplishing tasks", meaning to make use of nature and develop all things. In three parts and eighteen chapters, it covers nearly every branch of farming and handicraft production in China at the time, including grain, cotton and hemp cultivation, silkworm rearing, dyeing, grain processing, salt making, sugar making, pottery, smelting and casting, boat and cart building, forging, oil pressing, papermaking, mining and metallurgy, weapons, brewing and the cutting of pearls and jade. It records many techniques then leading the world, such as smelting zinc with coal, continuous smelting of pig iron and wrought iron, and cross-breeding silkworms for good strains. Song also supplied over 120 illustrations that vividly show production processes and laborers in various trades. In his preface he says that the arrangement of the book, "with the volumes in front and behind, follows the principle of valuing the five grains and despising gold and jade", reflecting an emphasis on agriculture.

events.title: Xu Guangqi's Complete Treatise on Agriculture
events.short: Xu Guangqi's Nongzheng Quanshu (60 volumes) systematically sums up ancient Chinese farming experience and introduces Western irrigation techniques.
events.detail: Xu Guangqi (1562–1633) was an outstanding scientist of the late Ming. Born to a small merchant and farming family in Shanghai, he knew agriculture from childhood and valued practical learning useful to the state and the people. He opened wasteland and trial-grew rice on military farming land at Tianjin; in Shanghai he successfully trial-grew sweet potatoes introduced from Fujian and wrote Ganshu Shu (Treatise on the Sweet Potato) to promote them as a famine crop. He also learned Western hydraulic techniques from the missionary Sabatino de Ursis, and together they translated Taixi Shuifa (Western Methods of Water Management). On the basis of long practice and research, Xu collected agricultural books and documents of past ages and compiled Nongzheng Quanshu. In 60 volumes and about 700,000 characters, it has twelve sections: agricultural fundamentals, land systems, farm work, irrigation, tools, cultivation, sericulture, extended sericulture, planting, animal husbandry, processing and famine relief, covering almost every aspect of ancient farming and life. It not only summarizes the advanced experience and techniques of ancient Chinese agriculture but also presents many of the author's own ideas, such as the cotton-growing experience of "carefully selecting seeds, planting early, deep roots, short stalks, thin planting and heavy manuring", and introduces Western water technology. Irrigation and famine relief are especially stressed; the famine-relief section takes up 18 volumes and records over four hundred plants that could be eaten in lean years. Xu did not finish the final draft in his lifetime; after his death Chen Zilong and others edited and revised it and it was published in 1639.

events.title: The Travel Diaries of Xu Xiake
events.short: Over thirty years Xu Xiake traveled much of China; his diaries became The Travel Diaries of Xu Xiake, with limestone-landform studies among the world's most advanced of the time.
events.detail: Xu Xiake (1587–1641), given name Hongzu, art name Xiake, was from Jiangyin in Nanzhili (present-day Jiangyin, Jiangsu). From childhood he loved books on geography, history and travel and exploration, set the ambition that "a real man should be at the blue sea in the morning and Cangwu in the evening", and was unwilling to take the examination path to office. With his mother's support he began traveling at 22, and over more than thirty years his footprints covered a dozen present-day provinces and regions, much of China. He traveled mainly on foot, often climbing cliffs and entering caves in the face of great danger. In 1636 Xu began his last and longest "ten-thousand-li journey", going through Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Hunan, Guangxi and Guizhou to Yunnan, as far as Tengchong in western Yunnan; in 1640 he was brought home ill and died the next year. He insisted on writing a diary every day recording his observations, leaving over 600,000 characters of travel material, later compiled as The Travel Diaries of Xu Xiake. The book records in detail natural phenomena such as geography, hydrology, geology and plants in each place, along with economy, transport, towns and villages and local customs. He systematically surveyed and described the limestone (karst) landforms of Guangxi, Guizhou and Yunnan and analyzed the origin of caves and peaks, ahead of comparable European studies; he also established that the Jinsha River is the upper course of the Yangtze, correcting the old view that "the Min Mountains are the source of the Yangtze". Xu's descriptions are concrete and vivid, blending scene and feeling, and the Diaries are both a great geographic work and a literary classic.

events.title: Li Zicheng Takes Beijing; the Ming Falls and the Qing Enters the Pass
events.short: In 1644 Li Zicheng founded the Shun and took Beijing, the Chongzhen Emperor hanged himself and the Ming fell; Wu Sangui let the Qing in, and the Qing made Beijing its capital.
events.detail: In the late Ming, political corruption grew worse and the state's finances were in deep crisis; besides regular taxes the court levied the "Liaodong levy", "bandit-suppression levy" and "training levy", together the "Three Levies", which the people could not bear. In northern Shaanxi years of severe drought left famished people everywhere while officials pressed on with collections, and peasants in northern Shaanxi rose in revolt. Li Zicheng (1606–1645), from Mizhi, Shaanxi, of peasant origin, worked as a post-station clerk and then joined the rebels; for his bravery he was called the "Dashing General" and later became a rebel leader, known as the "Dashing King". In 1641 Li took Luoyang and killed Zhu Changxun, Prince of Fu, putting forward the slogan "equalize land, exempt taxes", which won enthusiastic support from the peasantry, and his force grew to a million. In early 1644 Li established a regime at Xi'an with the state name Shun and promptly marched east to Beijing. In April 1644 the rebels entered Beijing and the Chongzhen Emperor hanged himself on Coal Hill (now Jingshan), ending the Ming dynasty after 276 years. The Ming general Wu Sangui, guarding Shanhaiguan, surrendered to the Qing and let the Qing army through the pass. Li fought Wu and the Qing army at Shanhaiguan, was defeated, returned to Beijing, hurriedly proclaimed himself emperor and then withdrew west, and was killed the next year at Jiugong Mountain in Tongshan, Hubei. That year the Qing Shunzhi Emperor moved the capital from Shenyang to Beijing and began his rule over the country. Qing forces then marched south and destroyed the Southern Ming regimes and anti-Qing forces elsewhere, gradually unifying the country.

events.title: Investiture of the Dalai Lama and Panchen Erdeni
events.short: In 1653 the Shunzhi Emperor invested the Fifth Dalai Lama and in 1713 the Kangxi Emperor the Fifth Panchen Lama; later Dalai and Panchen Lamas needed central investiture.
events.detail: The Gelug school of Tibetan Buddhism was founded by Tsongkhapa in the early Ming, and the Dalai Lama and Panchen Lama are its two great lines of reincarnated lamas. After entering the pass, the Qing paid great attention to the administration of Tibet. In 1652 the Fifth Dalai Lama, Ngawang Lobsang Gyatso, came at the invitation of the Shunzhi Emperor to Beijing with three thousand attendants; the emperor received him grandly and had the Xihuang Temple built as his residence. In 1653, as the Fifth Dalai Lama was returning to Tibet, the Shunzhi Emperor sent a gold certificate and gold seal formally investing him as the "Dalai Lama, Vajradhara, Great Good Self-Existent Buddha of the Western Heaven, in charge of Buddhism under Heaven". In the late 17th and early 18th centuries Tibet was unsettled, and Dzungar Mongol forces troubled it. In 1713 the Kangxi Emperor invested the Fifth Panchen Lama, Lobsang Yeshe, as "Panchen Erdeni" and gave him a gold certificate and seal; "erdeni" is Manchu for "treasure". In 1720 Qing troops entered Tibet and drove out the Dzungars, stabilizing the situation. Thereafter investiture by the central government became the established rule for every Dalai Lama and Panchen Erdeni. In 1727 the Qing established Imperial Residents in Tibet to oversee local administration on the center's behalf. In 1793 the Qianlong Emperor promulgated the Twenty-Nine Article Ordinance, requiring that the reincarnations of great lamas such as the Dalai and Panchen Lamas be determined by the "golden urn" lot-drawing system, overseen by the Imperial Resident and reported to the central government for approval. These measures strengthened the central government's administration of Tibet.

events.title: Koxinga Recovers Taiwan
events.short: In 1661 Zheng Chenggong (Koxinga) sailed from Kinmen with 25,000 men; after an eight-month siege the Dutch surrendered in 1662 and Taiwan returned to Chinese rule.
events.detail: Mainland residents began moving to Taiwan to farm in the Song and Yuan. In the late Ming, Yan Siqi, Zheng Zhilong and others recruited coastal Fujian residents to build settlements in Taiwan and open wasteland. In 1624 Dutch colonists, taking advantage of the Ming's decline, occupied southern Taiwan, built Fort Zeelandia and Fort Provintia and ruled it as a colony; in 1652 the anti-Dutch uprising led by Guo Huaiyi broke out. Zheng Chenggong (1624–1662), given name Sen, was from Nan'an, Fujian, born in Hirado, Japan, and son of Zheng Zhilong. After the fall of the Ming he gave up scholarship for soldiering and held out against the Qing on the Fujian coast, and was granted the imperial surname Zhu by the Southern Ming Longwu Emperor. After his failed northern expedition against Nanjing in 1659, he resolved to retake Taiwan as a base against the Qing. In 1661 he set out from Kinmen with 25,000 men and landed at Lu'ermen. His forces sank Dutch warships at sea and on land surrounded the Dutch in their two strongholds, Fort Provintia and Fort Zeelandia; the Dutch at Provintia soon surrendered. Zheng chose a long siege of Fort Zeelandia. In a letter to the Dutch governor he declared: "Taiwan is Chinese land, long occupied by your country; now that I have come to claim it, the land should return to me." In February 1662, after an eight-month siege, the Dutch governor Frederick Coyett was forced to surrender, and Taiwan, occupied by the Dutch for 38 years, returned to Chinese rule. Zheng set up Chengtian Prefecture and the two counties of Tianxing and Wannian on Taiwan, established military farming colonies and invited mainland settlers to open land, promoting the island's development. He died of illness that same year.

events.date: Reigns of Kangxi, Yongzheng and Qianlong
events.title: Literary Inquisitions and Cultural Control
events.short: Under Kangxi, Yongzheng and Qianlong, literary inquisitions built charges from phrases in writings, and the Siku Quanshu project banned and destroyed many books, stifling thought.
events.detail: To preserve autocratic rule, the Qing rulers paid great attention to tightly controlling intellectuals' thought. Under the Kangxi, Yongzheng and Qianlong emperors, rulers often picked out odd phrases from scholars' essays and poems, twisted their meaning and built charges, producing many unjust cases, known as "literary inquisitions". Their scale and number far exceeded earlier ages, with over a hundred in the Qianlong reign alone. In the early Kangxi "Ming History case", the wealthy Zhuang Tinglong of Zhejiang privately compiled a History of the Ming that used Southern Ming era names, and over seventy people involved in writing, printing or selling it were executed, with over two hundred more implicated. In the late Kangxi "Nanshan Collection case", Dai Mingshi was executed because his book used Southern Ming era names. Under Qianlong, the official Hu Zhongzao had a line in a poem, "a heart that discusses the clear and the muddy", and the emperor asked what he meant by putting the character "muddy" before "Qing" (the dynastic name, also meaning "clear"); Hu was beheaded. The Qing rulers also used the compilation of the Siku Quanshu (Complete Library of the Four Treasuries) to inspect books nationwide, listing those thought harmful to Qing rule as banned and confiscating, destroying or altering them; the Qianlong-era book bans lasted nearly twenty years and destroyed over three thousand titles. The inquisitions spread terror and ruined many talented people; intellectuals dared not discuss politics or reveal their thoughts, were careful even with wording, and many scholars turned to textual criticism, so that scholarship became detached from reality.

events.title: The Qing Unifies Taiwan and Sets Up Taiwan Prefecture
events.short: In 1683 Shi Lang took Penghu and Zheng Keshuang surrendered, bringing Taiwan into the Qing realm; Taiwan Prefecture was set up in 1684 and Taiwan became a province in 1885.
events.detail: After Zheng Chenggong's death in 1662, his son Zheng Jing continued to govern Taiwan, renaming Dongdu "Dongning", setting up schools, holding examinations and developing agriculture and trade, and Taiwan's society and economy grew further. But the Zheng regime stood off against the Qing for a long time and at one point sent troops to the mainland coast during the Revolt of the Three Feudatories. After the Kangxi Emperor put down that revolt, he resolved to use force to reunify the country. He appointed Shi Lang, a former Zheng general who had surrendered and knew naval warfare, as Fujian naval commander and planned the advance on Taiwan. In 1683 Shi Lang set out from Tongshan, Fujian (present-day Dongshan Island) with over 20,000 troops and over three hundred warships and crushed the main Zheng force at the Battle of Penghu; Zheng Jing's son Zheng Keshuang and his followers surrendered and Taiwan came into the Qing realm. After the unification, some in the Qing court argued for abandoning Taiwan and moving its people to the mainland; Shi Lang submitted a memorial, Gongchen Taiwan Qi-Liu Shu (Respectful Memorial on Abandoning or Keeping Taiwan), stressing Taiwan's importance and urging that it be held, and the Kangxi Emperor accepted his view. In 1684 the Qing set up Taiwan Prefecture under Fujian Province, with the three counties of Taiwan, Fengshan and Zhuluo, a circuit intendant and a garrison commander and 10,000 troops. The prefecture strengthened the central government's administration of Taiwan and consolidated southeast coastal defense; mainland people moved to Taiwan in large numbers to open land and build irrigation works, and Taiwan's society and economy entered a new period of growth.

events.title: The Sieges of Albazin
events.short: Tsarist Russia occupied Albazin in the Amur basin; in 1685 and 1686 the Kangxi Emperor had Qing troops besiege it, forcing Russia to agree to negotiate the eastern border.
events.detail: In the mid-17th century Tsarist Russia expanded eastward and its forces entered the Heilongjiang (Amur) basin, burning, killing and looting, and built forts at Yaksa (Albazin, in present-day Russia) and Nerchinsk as bases for further aggression, against which the Daur, Evenki and other local peoples rose. In the early years after entering the pass the Qing was busy unifying the country and sent troops several times to drive out the Russians but did not root out their power. The Qing government repeatedly demanded that the Russians withdraw from Chinese territory; they ignored it and even sent reinforcements. After putting down the Revolt of the Three Feudatories, the Kangxi Emperor turned to solving the northeastern frontier problem with full force. He sent people to scout the enemy, built Aigun city on the Heilongjiang, set up the General of Heilongjiang, built post stations and stockpiled grain, making careful war preparations. In 1685 he ordered the commander Pengchun and others to advance by land and water and besiege Albazin; they bombarded the fort and the Russian leader Alexei Tolbuzin was forced to surrender and withdraw with his remnant to Nerchinsk, and the Qing army burned Albazin and withdrew. Soon the Russians returned, reoccupied Albazin and rebuilt the fort. In 1686 Qing troops under Sabsu and others besieged Albazin again; Tolbuzin was killed by a cannonball, the Russians suffered heavy losses and only a few dozen remained in the city. The Russian government was forced to ask for a truce and agreed to settle the eastern Sino-Russian border by negotiation, and the Qing lifted the siege.

events.title: Sino-Russian Treaty of Nerchinsk
events.short: In 1689 China and Russia signed the Treaty of Nerchinsk after equal negotiation, fixing the eastern border and confirming the Heilongjiang and Ussuri basins, including Sakhalin, as Chinese.
events.detail: After the sieges of Albazin, Russia was forced to agree to negotiate the eastern Sino-Russian border. In 1689 a Qing delegation headed by Songgotu, Minister of the Imperial Bodyguard, and a Russian delegation headed by Fyodor Golovin held talks at Nerchinsk. At first the Russians proposed the Heilongjiang as the border, which the Qing side rejected. To win peace on the eastern border, the Qing made concessions, agreeing to hand Russia land around Nerchinsk that had belonged to China. After equal negotiation, the two sides signed the Treaty of Nerchinsk in September 1689. It provided that the border ran from the Gorbitsa River, a tributary of the Heilongjiang, to the Outer Xing'an (Stanovoy) Range and on to the sea, with land south of the range Chinese and north of it Russian; in the west the Argun River was the boundary, with the south bank Chinese and the north Russian; Russia was to destroy the fort at Albazin and withdraw its troops. The treaty also allowed subjects of both countries with passports to cross the border and trade. The Latin text was the official text, and border markers were set up inscribed in five languages: Manchu, Chinese, Russian, Mongolian and Latin. The treaty was the first border treaty between China and Russia and the first equal treaty between China and a foreign country with the meaning of modern international law; it legally confirmed that the vast area of the Heilongjiang and Ussuri basins, including Sakhalin, was Chinese territory, and kept the eastern border stable for over 160 years. In 1858 and 1860 Russia, taking advantage of the Qing's weakness, seized over a million square kilometers of Chinese territory south of the Outer Xing'an Range and east of the Ussuri through the Treaty of Aigun and the Convention of Peking.

events.title: Kangxi Suppresses Galdan's Rebellion
events.short: Galdan of the Dzungars rebelled with Russian backing; the Kangxi Emperor campaigned three times, crushing him at Ulan Butong and Zuunmod, and the northern frontier was secured.
events.detail: The Qing divided the Mongols into three main groups: southern Mongolia, northern (Khalkha) Mongolia and western (Oirat) Mongolia. In the late 17th century the Dzungars among the western Mongols grew strong and their leader Galdan, ambitious and supported and incited by Russia, absorbed the western Mongol tribes and crossed the Tianshan to take the Muslim oasis cities, controlling both sides of the Tianshan. In 1688 Galdan attacked the northern Khalkha Mongols, who were forced south and asked for Qing protection. In 1690, claiming to pursue the Khalkha, Galdan advanced into southern Mongolia as far as Ulan Butong (in present-day Hexigten Banner, Inner Mongolia), only seven hundred li from Beijing. The Kangxi Emperor led the army in person, and the Qing broke Galdan's "camel fortress" of camels with cannon and defeated the rebels, and Galdan fled with his remnants. In 1691 the emperor held an assembly with the Khalkha leaders at Dolon Nor and introduced the league-and-banner system in northern Mongolia, strengthening control over it. In 1696 Galdan invaded again; the Kangxi Emperor campaigned in person in three columns, and the General Who Pacifies the Distant, Fiyanggu, crushed Galdan's army at Zuunmod (south of present-day Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia), where Galdan's wife also fell in battle. In 1697 the emperor went on his third campaign; Galdan, abandoned by his followers and with nowhere to turn, soon died. The three campaigns put down Galdan's rebellion, preserved unity and secured the northern frontier. But Dzungar separatism did not end, and not until the Qianlong reign did the Qing finally pacify the Dzungars and unify the lands north and south of the Tianshan.

events.title: The Height of Kunqu (The Palace of Eternal Life, The Peach Blossom Fan)
events.short: Kunqu reached its height in the early Qing; Hong Sheng's The Palace of Eternal Life and Kong Shangren's The Peach Blossom Fan, "Hong of the South, Kong of the North", are its masterpieces.
events.detail: Kunqu, also called Kun opera, began as the Kunshan tune popular around Kunshan, Suzhou. In the Jiajing reign of the Ming, Wei Liangfu and others refined the Kunshan tune, after which Kunqu gradually became a national form of drama, with works such as Tang Xianzu's The Peony Pavilion. Kunqu gathered the strengths of southern and northern music, with delicate, flowing singing and graceful stage movement, and is called the "ancestor of a hundred operas", with a deep influence on Peking opera and many regional operas. In the early Qing it reached its height and was popular both at court and among the people; the most famous works were Hong Sheng's The Palace of Eternal Life and Kong Shangren's The Peach Blossom Fan, their authors being ranked together as "Hong of the South, Kong of the North". Hong Sheng (1645–1704), from Qiantang, Zhejiang, took over ten years and three drafts to complete The Palace of Eternal Life in 1688; centered on the love story of Emperor Xuanzong of Tang and Yang Guifei, it reflects social and political life around the An Lushan Rebellion, celebrating true love while criticizing the rulers' dissipation that ruined the state. Kong Shangren (1648–1718), from Qufu, Shandong, a 64th-generation descendant of Confucius, completed The Peach Blossom Fan in 1699; through the love story of the Restoration Society scholar Hou Fangyu and the Qinhuai courtesan Li Xiangjun, it reflects the fall of the Southern Ming Hongguang regime, in the author's words, "using the feelings of parting and reunion to express the sense of rise and fall". The two plays caused a sensation and were staged everywhere. After the Qianlong reign, local operas arose, a contest between "Huabu" (local operas) and "Yabu" (Kunqu) took shape, and Kunqu gradually declined.

images.caption: Ancient Kunqu theater in Suzhou

events.title: The Chengde Mountain Resort
events.short: The Qing built the Chengde Mountain Resort and the Eight Outer Temples, where emperors handled state affairs and received envoys and ethnic leaders, reflecting its policy of ethnic unity.
events.detail: The Chengde Mountain Resort, in present-day Chengde, Hebei, also called the Rehe Travel Palace, was where Qing emperors spent the summer and handled state affairs. The Kangxi Emperor set up the Mulan hunting ground north of Chengde, where each autumn he led princes, ministers and Eight Banners troops to hunt and practice martial skills, called the "Mulan autumn hunt". In 1703 he ordered a travel palace built at Chengde; over the Kangxi, Yongzheng and Qianlong reigns, nearly ninety years, it was completed in 1792. The Resort covers about 5.64 million square meters and is the largest surviving classical imperial garden in China, divided into a palace area and a garden area with lakes, plains and mountains, recalling both the water towns of Jiangnan and the grasslands north of the Wall; Kangxi and Qianlong named "seventy-two scenes". Each year the Qing designated Mongol princes in turn to come to the Resort to accompany the emperor in hunting and martial exercises and gave them rewards; Uyghur, Tibetan and other minority leaders also often came to pay their respects. In 1771 the Qianlong Emperor received here Ubashi, leader of the Torghut Mongols who had returned from the Volga; in 1780 the Sixth Panchen Lama came to congratulate him on his birthday; and in 1793 he received the British Macartney mission here. To unite the Mongols, Tibetans and other minorities, the Qing built twelve grand temples outside the Resort, popularly the "Eight Outer Temples", blending Han, Tibetan and Mongol architectural styles; the Putuo Zongcheng Temple was modeled on the Potala Palace in Lhasa and the Temple of Sumeru Happiness and Longevity on Tashilhunpo Monastery in Shigatse. In 1994 the Resort and the surrounding temples were inscribed on the World Heritage List.
