events.title: Establishment of the Imperial Residents in Tibet
events.short: In 1727 the Qing set up Imperial Residents in Tibet; in 1751 the Kashag was created, the Dalai Lama and the Residents jointly managing Tibet's religious and political affairs.
events.detail: After entering the pass the Qing invested the Dalai Lama and Panchen Erdeni. In the early 18th century the Dzungars troubled Tibet, and in 1720 Qing troops entered Tibet, drove them out and stationed troops there. Fierce struggles then broke out among Tibetan nobles, and in 1727 civil strife erupted when Arbuba and others killed the chief minister Khangchenas. To strengthen administration of Tibet, the Yongzheng Emperor that year formally established the Imperial Residents in Tibet, stationing officials permanently at Lhasa to oversee local affairs on behalf of the central government and command the Qing troops there. The next year Qing troops entered Tibet and put down the strife, and the Qing appointed Polhanas, who had distinguished himself in the suppression, to run Tibetan affairs. In 1750 Polhanas's son Gyurme Namgyal plotted rebellion and the Residents Fuqing and Labdon killed him, and both Residents were killed by his followers. In 1751 the Qianlong Emperor promulgated the Thirteen-Article Ordinance, abolishing rule by a prince and setting up the "Kashag" as the Tibetan local government, made up of four kalons, authorizing the Dalai Lama and the Imperial Residents jointly to manage Tibet's religious and political affairs. "Ka" means command and "shag" means room, so Kashag means the place from which orders are issued. In 1793 the Qing promulgated the Twenty-Nine Article Ordinance, further defining the Residents as equal in status to the Dalai Lama and Panchen Erdeni, jointly managing Tibetan affairs and in charge of Tibet's military, foreign and financial matters. From 1727 to 1912 the Qing sent over a hundred Imperial Residents to Tibet.

events.title: The Grand Council Is Established
events.short: The Yongzheng-era Grand Council, set up for northwestern campaigns, became a permanent body whose ministers took down and relayed the emperor's edicts; autocracy reached its peak.
events.detail: In the early Qing the Deliberative Council of Princes and Ministers, made up of Manchu nobles, was retained; all major state and military matters had to be discussed there, and once it decided, even the emperor could hardly change the decision. The Qing also inherited the Ming Grand Secretariat, but its procedures were cumbersome and hard to keep secret. Under Kangxi, to curb the power of Manchu nobles and strengthen autocracy, the Southern Study was set up, with trusted civil officials on duty drafting edicts and handling memorials for the emperor, thus bypassing the Deliberative Council. In the Yongzheng reign, to handle urgent military affairs in the campaigns in the northwest, the court set up a temporary Military Affairs Office, later renamed the Grand Council. It stood inside the Longzong Gate next to the Hall of Mental Cultivation where the emperor lived, so he could summon it at any time. Grand Councilors were chosen by the emperor from trusted Manchu and Han grand secretaries, ministers and vice-ministers, in no fixed number; summoned daily, they knelt to receive the emperor's will, drafted edicts and sent them as instructed directly to local officials, a procedure called "court letters". The Council had no formal office, only a duty room, and its members could make no decision on their own but only carried out the emperor's will, all power remaining with the emperor alone. It later became permanent and took over most of the Grand Secretariat's functions, and the Deliberative Council faded into a nominal body and was formally abolished in 1791. The Grand Council raised administrative efficiency and ensured the emperor's will was carried out quickly, marking the peak of ancient Chinese autocracy.

events.title: Early Qing Agriculture ("When Huguang Has a Harvest, the Realm Has Enough")
events.short: The early Qing promoted land reclamation and merged the poll tax into the land tax; farmland grew, maize and sweet potato spread, and Huguang became the granary of China.
events.detail: The great upheavals at the end of the Ming seriously damaged the economy, and the early Qing rulers recognized that restoring and developing agriculture was "the great plan of the state". The Shunzhi, Kangxi, Yongzheng and Qianlong emperors all valued farming and vigorously promoted land reclamation, exempting newly opened land from taxes for a number of years to encourage drifters to settle; they built irrigation works and managed the Yellow and Huai Rivers; and under Kangxi the "renamed land" policy gave part of the Ming princes' land to those who had been farming it and recognized it as theirs. In 1712 the Kangxi Emperor declared that the population count of 1711 would be the fixed basis for the poll tax, and that thereafter "added population will never add to the tax". Under Yongzheng the "land-and-poll tax merger" was carried out nationwide, spreading the poll tax evenly into the land tax, abolishing the head tax of over two thousand years and easing the burden on landless and land-poor peasants while also loosening the government's control over peasants' persons. These measures soon restored and developed agricultural output, and by the mid-Qianlong reign China's cultivated land exceeded 700 million mu. Maize and sweet potato, native to the Americas, spread widely in the Qing, opening up many mountain areas and greatly raising grain output. Many southern regions grew double-crop rice, some even three crops a year. Huguang (present-day Hubei and Hunan) became an important national granary, and the saying "When Huguang has a harvest, the realm has enough" was widely repeated. Cash crops such as cotton, sugarcane, tobacco, tea and mulberry were also widely grown, and frontier regions such as the northeast and Taiwan were further developed.

events.title: Closed-Door Policy and the Canton System
events.short: Under the Qing closed-door policy, the Qianlong Emperor ruled in 1757 that Western merchants could trade only at Guangzhou, through the licensed “Thirteen Hongs,” under tight restrictions.
events.detail: Qing rulers believed the Celestial Empire was rich in products and had no need for economic exchange with foreign countries. At the same time, Western colonial powers were expanding eastward, and the Qing feared for its sovereignty and worried that contact between coastal people and foreigners would endanger its rule. It therefore adopted a “closed-door” policy that strictly limited foreign trade. Under the Shunzhi Emperor, to cut off support for anti-Qing forces such as Zheng Chenggong, a “sea ban” was issued and coastal residents were forced to move 30 to 50 li inland. After Taiwan was unified in 1683 the ban was lifted, and customs offices were set up in Guangdong, Fujian, Zhejiang and Jiangsu. In 1757 the Qianlong Emperor closed the Fujian, Zhejiang and Jiangsu offices and allowed Western merchants to trade only at Guangzhou, where the government-licensed “Thirteen Hongs” managed all foreign trade. Foreign merchants had to live in the trading factories at Guangzhou and could not come and go freely, had to leave when the trading season ended, and were forbidden to hire Chinese servants, learn Chinese or buy Chinese books. In 1793 Britain sent the Macartney Mission, asking for more open ports and the cession of islands; the Qianlong Emperor refused. For a time the policy served as a defense against Western colonial aggression, but it obstructed economic and cultural exchange, hindered the growth of capitalist sprouts, and kept China blind to changes in the world. China gradually fell behind, which ultimately contributed to its defeats in modern times.

events.title: Pacifying the Khoja Revolt; General of Ili Established
events.short: Under the Qianlong Emperor the Qing crushed the Dzungars and the Khoja brothers’ revolt, unified Xinjiang, and in 1762 set up the General of Ili to govern the region, including Lake Balkhash.
events.detail: In the early Qing, the Dzungars of the northwest long held a separate regime. Taking advantage of Dzungar infighting, the Qianlong Emperor sent troops in 1755 and 1757 and put down the rebellions of Davachi and Amursana, unifying the area north of the Tianshan. The broad region south of the Tianshan was home to Uyghurs and others and was called the “Muslim Region” in Qing times. Its religious leaders, the elder Khoja Burhan al-Din and the younger Khoja Jahan, had been held captive by the Dzungars; the Qing released them and sent the elder Khoja back to administer southern Xinjiang. In 1757 the two brothers rebelled and killed Qing officials, and Khoja Jahan proclaimed himself “Baturu Khan,” intending to set up a separate state south of the Tianshan. Their brutal extortion aroused strong resentment. In 1758 the Qianlong Emperor ordered an attack, declaring that only the two Khojas would be captured and no one else implicated. With the support of Uyghurs and others, Qing forces took Kashgar and Yarkand in 1759 after two years of fighting; the Khojas fled to Badakhshan, where the local ruler captured and killed them. The Qing unified the area north and south of the Tianshan and named it “Xinjiang.” In 1762 it established the General of Ili, who governed the whole region including the area around Lake Balkhash from Huiyuan City in Ili, with military governors and ministers stationed elsewhere. The Qing also promoted military farming and irrigation to develop the frontier. These measures strengthened central control over Xinjiang and consolidated the northwest frontier.

events.title: Flourishing Handicrafts and Commerce in the Early Qing
events.short: In the early Qing, silk, cotton and porcelain industries thrived and larger workshops appeared; commerce boomed, and Shanxi merchants founded draft banks while merchant groups were active nationwide.
events.detail: In the early Qing, as agriculture recovered, handicrafts and commerce also flourished. Silk and cotton weaving, dyeing, mining and smelting, porcelain, sugar and tea industries all grew greatly, with many fine products. Fairly mature workshops had appeared, some on a considerable scale: in Jiangning (present-day Nanjing), the loom owners Li Biandan and Li Dongyang each had five or six hundred looms; Foshan’s ironworking was so developed that it was said “Foshan’s iron goods are found everywhere”; Jingdezhen porcelain continued to prosper, and the famille-rose and enamel wares of the Yongzheng and Qianlong reigns were exquisite; Yunnan’s copper mines were huge, often employing tens of thousands. Commercial cities and market towns multiplied. Beijing, Nanjing, Suzhou, Hangzhou, Yangzhou, Guangzhou and Hankou were bustling centers, and Hankou, Foshan, Jingdezhen and Zhuxianzhen were known as the “Four Famous Towns.” Xu Yang’s Qianlong-era painting Prosperous Suzhou (Gusu Fanhua Tu) depicts the city’s bustle. Merchant groups were very active, the Shanxi and Huizhou merchants being the strongest, along with those of Shaanxi, Guangdong and Fujian. Besides trading in salt, tea, grain and cloth, Shanxi merchants ran money shops and pawnshops and later founded “piaohao” (draft banks) for remittances, deposits and loans; the Rishengchang in Pingyao, Shanxi, set up around 1823, is regarded as China’s first, and for a time Shanxi draft banks “remitted funds across the land.” However, the Qing policy of promoting agriculture and restraining commerce placed many limits on trade and industry, and together with the closed-door policy, capitalist sprouts developed slowly.

events.title: Return of the Torghut Mongols
events.short: In 1771 the Torghuts, who had migrated west to the Volga, could no longer bear Russian oppression and led by Ubashi made a perilous journey back east, where the Qing government resettled them.
events.detail: The Torghuts were a division of the Western Mongols (Oirat Mongols) of China, originally nomadic around Tacheng in Xinjiang. Around the 1630s, after conflicts with the Dzungars, their chief Khoo Orlug led them west to graze along the lower Volga. They kept in touch with the Qing and repeatedly sent envoys with tribute. Tsarist Russia steadily tightened its control and oppression, forcing their young men into its wars with heavy casualties and trying to control them completely in politics and religion. Unable to endure this, the Torghuts resolved to return to their homeland. In January 1771 their young leader Ubashi led about 170,000 people in burning their tents and setting out east. On the way they were pursued and blocked by Russian troops and Cossack cavalry and suffered cold, plague and hunger, with great losses of people and livestock. After more than half a year and a journey of over ten thousand li, only about 70,000 reached Ili. The Qing government resettled them well, providing livestock, grain, tea, clothing and felt tents as relief and assigning them pastures with abundant water and grass. The Qianlong Emperor received Ubashi at the Chengde Mountain Resort and made him Khan Zhuolitu, and in the Putuo Zongcheng Temple he erected two steles recounting the event. The Torghuts’ return is regarded as a glorious chapter in the consolidation and development of a multi-ethnic state; their descendants still live in places such as Hejing in Xinjiang.

events.title: Compiling the Kangxi Dictionary and the Siku Quanshu
events.short: From the Kangxi to Qianlong reigns, the Kangxi Dictionary with over 40,000 characters, the 10,000-volume Gujin Tushu Jicheng and the Siku Quanshu, China’s largest ancient collection, were compiled.
events.detail: In the early Qing, the rulers placed great importance on collecting classics and compiling books. From the Kangxi to Qianlong reigns, many large works were produced, wide in scope and surpassing earlier dynasties in scale. Under Kangxi, Zhang Yushu, Chen Tingjing and others compiled the Kangxi Dictionary, completed in 1716; it contains over 47,000 characters under 214 radicals and greatly influenced later dictionaries. The Gujin Tushu Jicheng (Complete Collection of Illustrations and Writings from the Earliest to Current Times), compiled by Chen Menglei under Kangxi and revised by Jiang Tingxi under Yongzheng, has 10,000 juan and about 160 million characters, in 6 sections and 32 divisions covering astronomy, geography, human relations, natural history, philosophy and economics; it is the largest surviving Chinese leishu (encyclopedic compendium). In 1773 the Qianlong Emperor ordered a Siku Quanshu office set up, with Ji Yun and others as chief compilers, who led over 300 scholars for about ten years to complete the first Siku Quanshu (Complete Library of the Four Treasuries) in 1782. Arranged in the four divisions of classics, history, philosophy and literature, it includes over 3,400 titles in more than 79,000 juan, about 800 million characters, and preserved a vast body of ancient literature. Seven sets were copied and kept at Wenyuan Pavilion in the Forbidden City, Wenyuan at the Yuanmingyuan, Wensu in Shenyang, Wenjin in Chengde, Wenhui in Yangzhou, Wenzong in Zhenjiang and Wenlan in Hangzhou; the sets at the Yuanmingyuan, Yangzhou and Zhenjiang were destroyed in war. During the compilation, however, the Qing banned, destroyed and altered books deemed harmful to its rule on a large scale, severely damaging many precious works.

events.title: Anhui Troupes in Beijing and the Birth of Peking Opera
events.short: In 1790 the Sanqing and other Anhui troupes came to Beijing for the Qianlong Emperor’s birthday; absorbing Hanju, Kunqu and other forms, they gradually formed Peking Opera in the Daoguang era.
events.detail: In the Qianlong era Beijing became a gathering place for opera troupes, with all kinds of regional opera performed there. In 1790, for the Qianlong Emperor’s eightieth birthday, the Sanqing Troupe led by Gao Langting came from Yangzhou to perform; the Anhui troupes’ easy-to-follow singing and beautiful melodies were warmly received. The Sixi, Hechun and Chuntai troupes followed, and together they were called the “Four Great Anhui Troupes.” Built mainly on the erhuang tune, they broadly absorbed strengths from Kunqu, Qinqiang, Jingqiang and other forms. In the Daoguang era, Hubei performers of Hanju came to Beijing and performed with the Anhui troupes; the erhuang tune merged with the xipi tune of Hanju into a new genre centered on “pihuang” singing, which took on features of Beijing speech and gradually became Peking Opera. Its accompaniment centers on the jinghu; roles are divided into sheng, dan, jing and chou; performance stresses singing, speech, acting and acrobatics; and the face paint, costumes and movements follow fixed conventions, with strong suggestiveness and symbolism. After its formation Peking Opera spread across the country, producing famous performers such as Cheng Changgeng and Tan Xinpei, and it flourished at court in the Tongzhi and Guangxu reigns. In the Republican period Mei Lanfang, Cheng Yanqiu, Shang Xiaoyun and Xun Huisheng were hailed as the “Four Great Dan,” and Mei Lanfang toured Japan, the United States and the Soviet Union, introducing the art to the world. Drawing on many sources, Peking Opera gathers the essence of Chinese theatre and is regarded as a “national treasure.” In 2010 it was inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

events.title: Population Reaches 300 Million
events.short: In the early Qing, social stability and economic growth made the population surge; by the end of the Qianlong reign it reached 300 million, about a third of the world’s total.
events.detail: At the height of the Ming dynasty China’s population exceeded 100 million. Economic decline and years of war from the late Ming sharply reduced it. In the early Qing, the rulers took measures to restore the economy; society was stable, and the population rose greatly. By the Kangxi reign it had reached about 150 million. By the end of the Qianlong reign it was 300 million, roughly a third of the world’s population, and in the Daoguang era it passed 400 million. There were many causes. Long-term stability and economic growth provided the conditions; high-yield crops such as maize, sweet potatoes and potatoes spread, greatly raising grain output and feeding more people; and after the policies of “increasing population without ever raising taxes” and “merging the poll tax into the land tax,” the poll tax was no longer levied per head, people no longer had to hide their numbers, and official figures came closer to reality. The growth supplied ample labor and promoted the development of frontier and mountain areas, as many inland farmers moved to the Northeast, Inner Mongolia, Taiwan and the southwestern mountains. But population grew far faster than farmland, so land per person kept shrinking and the problem of “many people, little land” became acute; with serious land concentration, many peasants lost their land and became drifters, and social tensions mounted. The late Qianlong scholar Hong Liangji pointed out in his essay Zhiping Pian that population was growing far faster than fields and houses, which would bring serious social problems. The population problem became one root of the Qing’s mid-to-late social crisis.

events.title: Cao Xueqin’s Dream of the Red Chamber
events.short: Cao Xueqin’s novel Dream of the Red Chamber (first titled Story of the Stone) centers on the tragic love of Jia Baoyu and Lin Daiyu and is regarded as the peak of classical Chinese fiction.
events.detail: Fiction in the Qing achieved unprecedented success, and the most accomplished and influential work was Cao Xueqin’s Dream of the Red Chamber (Honglou Meng). Cao Xueqin (c. 1715–c. 1763), personal name Zhan, came from a “century-old distinguished family” in which four people over three generations served as Textile Commissioner of Jiangning. In the early Yongzheng reign the family was ruined when its property was confiscated on charges including financial shortfalls. In his later years Cao moved to the western suburbs of Beijing and lived in poverty, “the whole household eating gruel, wine often bought on credit.” With firm perseverance he devoted himself to the novel, “reading and revising for ten years and altering it five times.” It was first called Story of the Stone, and he essentially finished the first eighty chapters in his lifetime. After his death, the last forty chapters are generally believed to have been written by Gao E; in 1791 Cheng Weiyuan printed it in movable type under the title Dream of the Red Chamber, in 120 chapters. Set against the rise and fall of the four great families of Jia, Shi, Wang and Xue, with the tragic love of Jia Baoyu and Lin Daiyu as its main thread, the novel portrays a noble household’s decline, exposes the rot and darkness of feudal society, and expresses dissatisfaction with feudal ethics and the examination system. It creates hundreds of vivid characters, including Jia Baoyu, Lin Daiyu, Xue Baochai and Wang Xifeng, with a grand, tight structure and beautiful language, and weaves in poetry, architecture, gardens, food, clothing and medicine. It has been called “an encyclopedia of Chinese feudal society,” gave rise to the field of “Redology,” and has been translated into many languages.

events.title: Imperially Approved Regulations for Tibet and the Golden Urn
events.short: In 1793 the Qing issued 29 articles setting the Amban on par with the Dalai and Panchen Lamas and requiring “Golden Urn” lot-drawing for the reincarnations of major lamas.
events.detail: In the late 18th century the Gurkhas (of present-day Nepal) invaded Tibet twice, and in 1791 they reached Shigatse and plundered Tashilhunpo Monastery. The Qianlong Emperor sent Fukang’an to lead Qing troops into Tibet; in 1792 they defeated the Gurkhas and advanced close to their capital, whereupon the Gurkhas sued for peace. Afterward, to reorganize Tibet’s administration, the emperor had Fukang’an and others consult with the Dalai Lama and the Panchen Erdeni, and in 1793 the 29-article Imperially Approved Regulations for Tibet were issued. They provided that the Amban stationed in Tibet would oversee Tibetan affairs and, in political standing, be equal to the Dalai Lama and Panchen Erdeni, handling affairs jointly with them; that military, foreign, financial and judicial matters would be managed by the Amban; that Tibet would have a regular army of 3,000 men; that Tibet would mint silver coins stamped “Qianlong Baozang”; and that the reincarnations of the Dalai Lama, Panchen Erdeni and other major lamas must be determined by “Golden Urn” lot-drawing. The Qing made two golden urns, one kept in the Jokhang Temple in Lhasa for the reincarnations of the Dalai Lama, Panchen and other major lamas, the other in the Yonghe Temple in Beijing for those of Mongol regions. The names of candidate children were written on ivory slips and placed in the urn, with the Amban presiding, and the result was reported to the central government for approval. The regulations established in law the central government’s system of administering Tibet, and the Golden Urn system is still used; the 11th Panchen Erdeni was identified in 1995 through the Golden Urn and approved by the State Council.

events.title: He Shen’s Fall and the Mid-Qing Crisis
events.short: Official corruption spread in the late Qianlong reign; in 1799 the Jiaqing Emperor had the powerful minister He Shen put to death and his property seized, and the Qing began to decline.
events.detail: Under the Qing’s autocratic monarchy, officials used every connection to win promotion or protect themselves, bribing superiors and forming cliques. In the late Qianlong reign the emperor, fond of grandeur and extravagant, also favored the powerful minister He Shen, and corruption grew worse. He Shen (1750–1799), a Manchu of the Plain Red Banner, began as a guard and won the emperor’s trust through his shrewdness and flattery; he rose to Grand Secretary and head of the Grand Council, also overseeing the Boards of Revenue and Civil Office, and his son married the emperor’s favorite daughter, the tenth princess. For over twenty years He Shen monopolized power, formed cliques, sold offices, took bribes and amassed vast wealth. In 1799, when the retired Emperor Qianlong died, the Jiaqing Emperor promptly announced twenty major charges against He Shen, ordered him to die and confiscated his property. The amount seized was reportedly enormous, and a saying spread: “When He Shen fell, the Jiaqing Emperor feasted.” Corruption was widespread; officials deceived the court above and extorted the people below. It reached the army, where the Eight Banners and Green Standard troops, long without war, grew lax and much weaker. Meanwhile, rapid population growth and land concentration sharpened social tensions. In 1796 the White Lotus Rebellion broke out in Sichuan and Hubei; it lasted nine years and cost the Qing about 200 million taels of silver to suppress. In 1813 Eight Trigrams rebels even briefly entered the Forbidden City. By the Jiaqing and Daoguang years the Qing had passed from prosperity to decline, while Western countries were undergoing the Industrial Revolution and the gap with China kept widening.

events.title: Lin Zexu Destroys Opium at Humen
events.short: In 1839 Imperial Commissioner Lin Zexu seized over two million jin of opium from British and American traffickers in Guangdong and destroyed it publicly on the Humen beach over 23 days.
events.detail: Since the late 18th century, Britain had smuggled large amounts of opium into China to reverse its trade deficit, and by the late 1830s some 30,000 to 40,000 chests entered China each year. The smuggling drained silver from China, making silver dear and copper cash cheap, which burdened the people and strained state finances; more and more people smoked opium, severely damaging their health. In 1838 Huang Juezi memorialized in favor of a strict ban, and Lin Zexu, Governor-General of Huguang, also submitted a memorial warning that if opium were not banned, in a few decades China would have “almost no soldiers to resist the enemy and no silver to pay them.” The Daoguang Emperor appointed Lin Imperial Commissioner to suppress opium in Guangdong. Lin Zexu (1785–1850) was from Houguan (present-day Fuzhou), Fujian. Arriving in Guangzhou in March 1839, he and the Governor-General of Liangguang, Deng Tingzhen, ordered foreign traffickers to hand over their opium by a deadline, declaring, “As long as opium is not eradicated, this commissioner will not return.” The British Superintendent of Trade, Charles Elliot, at first obstructed him; Lin ordered the foreign factories blockaded and eventually forced the traffickers to surrender over 20,000 chests, more than 2.3 million jin. On 3 June 1839 Lin had the opium publicly destroyed on the Humen beach, adding salt brine and lime to seawater pits to break it down; destruction was completed only on 25 June. It dealt a heavy blow to foreign opium dealers and showed the Chinese people’s resolve to resist foreign aggression. It was a great victory in China’s anti-drug struggle, and Lin Zexu was honored as a national hero.

events.title: The Sanyuanli Resistance against the British
events.short: In 1841 British troops plundered the Sanyuanli area near Guangzhou; local villagers rose up and surrounded them at Niulangang, a large-scale spontaneous anti-aggression struggle in modern China.
events.detail: During the Opium War, in May 1841 British forces attacked Guangzhou. Qing commander Yishan and others were defeated and sued for peace, concluding the Convention of Canton and handing over a “ransom of the city” of six million silver dollars. The British were stationed around the Sifang Fort north of the city and often raided nearby villages such as Sanyuanli, looting property, insulting women and digging up graves, which aroused fierce local anger. Led by vegetable farmer Wei Shaoguang and others, the people of Sanyuanli made the Sanyuan Ancient Temple their base and the three-star banner there their signal flag, uniting people from 103 neighboring villages in the “Pingying Tuan” (Anti-British Corps). On the morning of 30 May, thousands of villagers armed with swords, spears and hoes surrounded Sifang Fort. The British sent troops in pursuit, and as planned the villagers fought and retreated, luring them into Niulangang, where seven or eight thousand hidden villagers rushed out and surrounded them. Heavy rain then soaked the British powder, so their muskets were useless; they had to fix bayonets and form squares in the muddy paddy fields, where they were cut down by swords and spears. The next day tens of thousands of villagers kept Sifang Fort surrounded, and the British called for help. Guangzhou Prefect Yu Baochun was ordered to intervene and persuaded the crowds to disperse, and only then could the British withdraw to their ships. The struggle was the first large-scale spontaneous armed anti-aggression struggle of the Chinese people in modern times, showing their fearless patriotic spirit, while exposing the weakness and compromise of Qing officials. A monument and the Sanyuan Ancient Temple Memorial Hall now stand in Sanyuanli, Guangzhou.

events.title: The Opium War and the Treaty of Nanjing
events.short: Britain launched the Opium War in 1840; the Qing was defeated and in 1842 forced to sign the Treaty of Nanjing, the first unequal treaty of modern times, marking the start of modern Chinese history.
events.detail: When news of Lin Zexu’s destruction of opium reached London, the British government decided to wage war on China. In June 1840 a British expeditionary force reached the Guangdong coast and the Opium War began. Finding Guangdong well defended, the British moved north, took Dinghai in Zhejiang and reached the mouth of the Baihe River near Tianjin, threatening the Qing court. The panicking Daoguang Emperor dismissed Lin Zexu for “mismanagement” and sent Qishan to negotiate in Guangdong. During the talks, in January 1841 the British seized the Shajiao and Dajiao forts at Humen and occupied Hong Kong Island. The emperor was forced to declare war; in February the British took the Humen forts, and naval commander Guan Tianpei fought to the death. The war then widened: Dinghai fell again, with three brigade generals including Ge Yunfei killed; Zhenhai fell, and Governor-General Yuqian drowned himself. In 1842 the British entered the Yangtze, took the Wusong forts, where Chen Huacheng was killed, and then Zhenjiang. In August British warships reached Nanjing, and the Qing sued for peace and signed the Treaty of Nanjing. It ceded Hong Kong Island to Britain; required an indemnity of 21 million silver dollars; opened Guangzhou, Xiamen, Fuzhou, Ningbo and Shanghai as treaty ports; and required China to agree tariffs on British goods with Britain. The first unequal treaty in modern Chinese history, it gravely damaged China’s territorial sovereignty and tariff autonomy and began China’s slide into a semi-colonial, semi-feudal society. The Opium War marks the start of modern Chinese history, when the Chinese people began their struggle against foreign aggression and for national independence.

events.title: Wei Yuan’s Illustrated Treatise on the Maritime Countries
events.short: After the Opium War, Wei Yuan built on Lin Zexu’s translations to compile the Illustrated Treatise on the Maritime Countries, urging China to “learn the barbarians’ skills to control them.”
events.detail: China’s defeat in the Opium War shook some officials and thinkers, who began to study world affairs and foreign history and geography in search of ways to resist. During his anti-opium and anti-British work in Guangdong, Lin Zexu took care to “gather information on the foreigners,” had foreign books and periodicals translated, and compiled the Gazetteer of the Four Continents, earning him the name of the first person in modern China to “open his eyes to the world.” Wei Yuan (1794–1857), from Shaoyang, Hunan, was a friend of Lin Zexu. In 1841, when Lin was dismissed and exiled to Ili, he met Wei at Zhenjiang and gave him the Gazetteer and other materials. Wei gathered much more material and in 1842 completed the Illustrated Treatise on the Maritime Countries (Haiguo Tuzhi) in 50 juan, later expanded to 100. It describes the history, geography, politics, economy, religion and science and technology of countries around the world, with many maps and drawings of ships and cannon. In its preface he wrote that the book was compiled “to use barbarians against barbarians, to deal with barbarians through barbarians, and to learn the barbarians’ superior skills in order to control them.” He held that the West’s “superior skills” lay mainly in warships, firearms and methods of raising and training troops, and urged learning advanced Western military technology and setting up shipyards and arsenals. This idea broke with the traditional notion of China as the “Celestial Empire,” began modern China’s learning from the West, and influenced the later Self-Strengthening Movement and reform thought. The book drew little attention at home, but was reprinted many times in Japan, where it had some influence on the Meiji Restoration.

events.title: Treaties of the Bogue, Wanghia and Whampoa
events.short: In 1843 Britain forced the Qing to sign the Treaty of the Bogue, and in 1844 the US and France extracted the Treaties of Wanghia and Whampoa, widening foreign powers’ privileges.
events.detail: After the Treaty of Nanjing, Western powers sought further privileges. In 1843 Britain forced the Qing to sign the General Regulations of Trade and the Treaty of the Bogue (Humen) as supplements to the Treaty of Nanjing, gaining consular jurisdiction, unilateral most-favored-nation treatment, and the right to lease land and build houses in the treaty ports. Consular jurisdiction meant that foreigners who committed crimes in China or were defendants in civil suits were not subject to Chinese law but tried by their own consuls under their own law, seriously undermining China’s judicial sovereignty. Unilateral most-favored-nation treatment meant that any privilege China granted another country was automatically extended to Britain, while Britain owed China no equivalent. Seeing Britain’s gains, the US and France seized their chance. In 1844 the US sent Caleb Cushing, who threatened force and compelled the Qing to sign the Treaty of Wanghia at Wanghia village in Macao; the same year France sent Théodore de Lagrené, who forced the Qing to sign the Treaty of Whampoa aboard a French warship at Whampoa, Guangzhou. Besides all the privileges Britain had won, apart from territory and indemnity, the two added more: the US gained the right to build churches and hospitals in the treaty ports, and China could change tariffs only with the “agreement” of US consuls; France gained the right to build churches in the treaty ports and later forced the Qing to lift its ban on Catholicism. These unequal treaties further damaged China’s sovereignty, let foreign powers penetrate deeper, and deepened China’s semi-colonization.

events.title: The Jintian Uprising and Founding of the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom
events.short: On 11 January 1851 Hong Xiuquan, founder of the God Worshippers’ Society, launched an uprising at Jintian village in Guiping, Guangxi, and proclaimed the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom.
events.detail: After the Opium War the Qing government squeezed the people harder to pay indemnities and military costs, and imported foreign goods hit the natural economy and ruined many craftsmen. Social tensions sharpened and peasant resistance broke out repeatedly. Hong Xiuquan (1814–1864), from Huaxian, Guangdong, a peasant’s son, failed the civil service examinations several times. Influenced by the Christian missionary pamphlet Good Words to Admonish the Age, in 1843 he founded the “God Worshippers’ Society,” preaching equality for all. He and fellow villager Feng Yunshan went to Guangxi to preach; Feng won followers among poor peasants and charcoal burners in the Zijing Mountains of Guiping, and Yang Xiuqing, Xiao Chaogui, Shi Dakai, Wei Changhui and others joined. Hong also wrote works such as Original Exhortation to Awaken the World, setting out the idea that “all men under heaven are brothers and all women are sisters.” In 1850 he called followers to assemble at Jintian village, gathering about 20,000. On 11 January 1851 he launched the uprising there, proclaiming the “Taiping Heavenly Kingdom”; the rebel army was called the “Taiping Army.” In March he took the title Heavenly King. In September the Taiping army captured Yong’an (present-day Mengshan, Guangxi), and in December it enfeoffed kings there: Yang Xiuqing as East King, Xiao Chaogui as West King, Feng Yunshan as South King, Wei Changhui as North King and Shi Dakai as Assistant King, establishing a rudimentary government. The Jintian Uprising opened the Taiping movement, the largest peasant war in Chinese history, which lasted fourteen years and spread to eighteen provinces.

events.title: Taiping Capital at Tianjing and the Land System
events.short: In 1853 the Taipings took Nanjing and made it their capital, Tianjing, then issued the Land System of the Heavenly Dynasty, an ideal of shared land and food that was never put into practice.
events.detail: In spring 1852 the Taiping army broke out of Yong’an and marched north, besieging Guilin and Changsha. South King Feng Yunshan and West King Xiao Chaogui both died on the march. In January 1853 it took Wuchang, capital of Hubei, and grew to 500,000 men. It then left Wuchang and advanced east along the Yangtze by land and water, taking Jiujiang, Anqing, Wuhu and other places, and in March 1853 captured Nanjing, renamed it Tianjing (Heavenly Capital) and made it the capital, formally establishing a peasant regime facing the Qing. There it issued the Land System of the Heavenly Dynasty, which divided land into nine grades by yield and distributed it equally by population and age regardless of sex, with those over sixteen receiving a full share and those fifteen and under half. Every twenty-five families formed a unit with a public treasury and a worship hall, and each household kept only the grain it needed and handed the rest to the treasury. It set out an ideal society in which “land is farmed together, food is eaten together, clothes are worn together, money is spent together, everything is evenly shared, and no one lacks food or warmth.” The system reflected the peasants’ strong wish to abolish feudal land ownership and gain land, and served as a programmatic document of anti-feudal struggle, but its strong absolute egalitarianism was divorced from reality and could not be carried out. In practice the Taiping in its territory kept the policy of “paying grain and taxes as before.” It also sent northern and western expeditions: the northern force pushed deep alone, came close to Tianjin and ultimately failed, while the western force won great victories and took much of the middle Yangtze.

events.title: The Second Opium War and the Treaties of Tianjin
events.short: Using the Arrow incident and a French priest’s killing as pretexts, Britain and France began the Second Opium War in 1856, took the Dagu forts in 1858 and forced the Treaties of Tianjin on the Qing.
events.detail: After the Opium War the Western powers, not satisfied with their gains, sought to open the Chinese market further and widen their privileges. In 1854 Britain, France and the US demanded “treaty revision,” which the Qing refused. In October 1856 Britain used the “Arrow incident” as a pretext to attack Guangzhou. The Arrow was a Chinese-owned ship that had once been registered in Hong Kong but whose license had expired; Guangdong naval forces boarded it to arrest pirates, and the British consul Harry Parkes falsely claimed Chinese soldiers had pulled down the British flag. France used as its pretext the execution in Xilin County, Guangxi, of the French priest Auguste Chapdelaine for illegal preaching, and joined Britain; the Second Opium War began. At the end of 1857 the Anglo-French force took Guangzhou and captured Governor-General Ye Mingchen. In 1858 it went north, took the Dagu forts at Tianjin and threatened Beijing. The Qing sent Grand Secretary Guiliang and others to sign separate Treaties of Tianjin with Britain, France, Russia and the US. They provided for foreign ministers to reside in Beijing; ten more treaty ports including Niuzhuang, Dengzhou, Tainan, Tamsui, Hankou, Jiujiang, Nanjing and Zhenjiang; free navigation on the Yangtze for foreign merchant ships and warships; the right of foreigners to travel, trade and preach inland; and indemnities of four million taels of silver to Britain and two million to France. Trade regulations signed in Shanghai that year also legalized the opium trade. The Treaties of Tianjin cost China further sovereignty and carried foreign influence from the coast into the interior.

events.title: The Tianjing Incident
events.short: In 1856 the Taiping leaders turned on each other: Wei Changhui killed Yang Xiuqing, who sought the title “Ten Thousand Years,” and was then executed; Shi Dakai left in 1857 and the Taipings declined.
events.detail: After making Tianjing its capital the Taiping won great military successes, and in the first half of 1856 it destroyed the Qing’s Jiangbei and Jiangnan Camps, reaching its military peak. But its leaders gradually lost touch with the masses, indulged in pleasure and corruption, and fought over power. East King Yang Xiuqing held military and political power, grew arrogant over his achievements, and often claimed that “the Heavenly Father had descended” to suppress Hong Xiuquan and the other kings, sharpening conflicts. In August 1856 Yang used the Heavenly Father’s name to force Hong to name him “Ten Thousand Years.” Hong outwardly agreed but secretly ordered North King Wei Changhui and Assistant King Shi Dakai, who were away commanding troops, to return and kill Yang. In September Wei rushed back to Tianjing overnight, killed Yang and his family, and slaughtered over twenty thousand of the East King’s men and innocent civilians. When Shi Dakai returned and rebuked Wei for the killings, Wei tried to harm him too; Shi escaped over the city wall by night, and his family was killed. Shi raised troops at Anqing to set things right, Wei then attacked the Heavenly King’s palace, and in November Hong ordered Wei executed. Shi was summoned back to run the government, but Hong distrusted him. In 1857 Shi angrily left Tianjing with many elite troops and fought independently across Jiangxi, Zhejiang, Hunan, Guangxi, Guizhou, Yunnan and elsewhere; in 1863 he was surrounded by Qing forces at Zidadi by the Dadu River in Sichuan, captured and killed. The incident split the Taiping leadership, cost many outstanding commanders and elite troops, and let the Qing counterattack. It was the turning point of the Taiping’s decline, and exposed the limits of the peasant class.

events.title: Tsarist Russia Seizes China’s Northern Territory
events.short: From 1858 to 1881, tsarist Russia seized over 1.5 million square kilometers of Chinese territory in the Northeast and Northwest through unequal treaties such as the Treaties of Aigun and Beijing.
events.detail: In the mid-19th century tsarist Russia took advantage of the Qing’s domestic and foreign troubles to seize Chinese land. During the Second Opium War, in 1858, Muravyov, Governor-General of Eastern Siberia, threatened force and compelled Heilongjiang General Yishan to sign the Treaty of Aigun, seizing over 600,000 square kilometers north of the Heilong River and south of the Outer Xing’an Range, and placing about 400,000 square kilometers east of the Ussuri River under “joint administration.” In 1860 Russia, claiming credit for “mediation,” obtained through the Sino-Russian Treaty of Beijing the territory east of the Ussuri, including Sakhalin, about 400,000 square kilometers; China thereby lost its Sea of Japan outlet in the Northeast, and Russia founded Vladivostok there. The treaty also set the course of the western Sino-Russian border, laying the groundwork for further seizures in the Northwest. In 1864 Russia obtained, through the Protocol on the Northwestern Boundary, over 440,000 square kilometers east and south of Lake Balkhash. In 1871 it used unrest in Xinjiang to occupy the Ili region. After Xinjiang was recovered, the Qing sent Chonghou to Russia to negotiate; he signed the Treaty of Livadia without authorization, betraying China’s interests, and it met strong opposition at court and in the country. In 1881 Zeng Jize, after hard negotiations, concluded the revised Treaty of Ili, regaining the nine cities of Ili and the Tekes River valley, though areas west of the Khorgos River and elsewhere were still ceded. From the 1850s to the 1880s Russia took over 1.5 million square kilometers of Chinese territory.

events.title: Hong Rengan and A New Treatise on Aids to Administration
events.short: In 1859 the Shield King Hong Rengan wrote A New Treatise on Aids to Administration, urging China to learn from the West and build modern industry, its first plan for capitalist development.
events.detail: After the Tianjing Incident the Taiping was in difficulty. To turn things around, Hong Xiuquan promoted young commanders such as Chen Yucheng and Li Xiucheng, and relied on his kinsman Hong Rengan, who came to Tianjing from Hong Kong. Hong Rengan (1822–1864), from Huaxian, Guangdong, joined the God Worshippers’ Society early; after the Jintian Uprising he drifted to Hong Kong, where he had close ties with Western missionaries and learned much about Western politics, economy and society. He reached Tianjing in 1859, was made Shield King and put in charge of government. That year he wrote A New Treatise on Aids to Administration (Zizheng Xinpian), proposing reforms modeled on the West. Politically, he favored stronger centralization, “forbidding the evil of factions,” setting up newspaper offices so that “high and low communicate,” and “governing the country by law.” Economically, he urged developing modern mining, industry and transport, founding banks, building railways and steamships, opening mines, encouraging private investment and invention, and protecting patents. Socially, he urged founding schools, hospitals and welfare, and abolishing foot-binding, infanticide and opium smoking. In foreign affairs he favored equal relations and free trade, but no foreign interference in China’s internal affairs. Hong Xiuquan approved and ordered it issued. It was modern China’s first fairly systematic plan to develop capitalism, but because the Taiping was at war and lacked the social basis for such a plan, it was never carried out. After Tianjing fell in 1864 Hong Rengan was captured and died bravely in Nanchang, Jiangxi.

events.title: The Burning of the Yuanmingyuan and the Convention of Beijing
events.short: In 1860 Anglo-French forces entered Beijing and looted and burned the Yuanmingyuan; the Qing was forced to sign the Convention of Beijing, ceding the Kowloon district to Britain.
events.detail: After the Treaties of Tianjin Britain and France were still unsatisfied. In 1859 their envoys, citing the exchange of ratifications in Beijing, forced their way into the Dagu estuary with a fleet and were driven back by Qing troops at the Dagu forts. In 1860 the two countries formed a joint force again, took Dagu, entered Tianjin and pressed on Beijing. The Xianfeng Emperor made his brother Prince Gong Yixin the peace negotiator to stay in Beijing and fled to the Chengde Mountain Resort. In October the Anglo-French force entered Beijing and broke into the imperial garden Yuanmingyuan in the northwest suburbs. Begun in the Kangxi reign and built up over more than 150 years from the Yuanmingyuan, Changchunyuan and Qichunyuan, it held great treasures and was called the “garden of gardens.” The invaders looted it extensively. To cover up the crime, the British plenipotentiary Lord Elgin ordered it burned; the fire burned for days and the unrivaled imperial garden became ruins. The French writer Victor Hugo condemned it: “One day two bandits entered the Summer Palace; one plundered, the other burned.” That year Yixin was forced to sign the Convention of Beijing with Britain and France, confirming the Treaties of Tianjin, opening Tianjin as a port, ceding the Kowloon district to Britain and raising the indemnity to eight million taels each for Britain and France. Russia, claiming credit for “mediation,” forced the Qing to sign the Sino-Russian Treaty of Beijing, seizing about 400,000 square kilometers east of the Ussuri. The Second Opium War cost China much more sovereignty and deepened its semi-colonization. The remains of the Western-style buildings in the Yuanmingyuan ruins today bear witness to the powers’ crimes.

events.title: Establishing the Zongli Yamen
events.short: In 1861 the Qing set up the Zongli Yamen under Prince Gong Yixin to handle foreign affairs, trade and customs, the first dedicated foreign affairs body of modern China.
events.detail: Before the Second Opium War the Qing had no body dedicated to foreign affairs, which were handled by the Board of Rites, the Court of Colonial Affairs, the Governor-General of Liangguang and others. After the war foreign ministers were allowed to reside in Beijing, and the traditional system could no longer cope. In January 1861 Prince Gong Yixin, with Grand Secretary Guiliang and Vice Minister of Revenue Wenxiang, jointly petitioned to set up a special body. With the Xianfeng Emperor’s approval, the Qing established in Beijing the Office for the General Management of the Affairs of All Foreign Countries, called the “Zongli Yamen” or “Zongshu,” headed by Yixin, Guiliang and Wenxiang. It first handled foreign negotiations, but its powers grew to cover trade, customs, sending envoys abroad, new-style schools, railways, mines and arms purchases, making it a powerful central organ and the leading body of the Self-Strengthening Movement. It had British, French, Russian, American and coastal defense sections, and ran the Tongwen Guan language school to train interpreters. The Qing also set up Superintendents of Trade at Tianjin and Shanghai, later held concurrently by the Governors-General of Zhili and of Liangjiang as the Northern and Southern Superintendents of Trade. Its founding marked the start of a shift in Qing diplomacy from the traditional tribute system to a modern diplomatic system and the beginning of the modernization of Chinese diplomacy, though it often yielded to the powers. In 1901, under the Boxer Protocol, it became the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, ranked first among the ministries.

events.title: The Self-Strengthening Movement
events.short: From the 1860s to the 1890s, reformers seeking “self-strengthening” and wealth brought in Western technology, built modern arsenals and civilian enterprises, and founded a new navy.
events.detail: After the Second Opium War, more open-minded officials in the Qing ruling circle argued for using advanced Western technology to strengthen the army and enrich the country; they were called the “Foreign Affairs faction.” Prince Gong Yixin led them at the center, and Zeng Guofan, Li Hongzhang, Zuo Zongtang and Zhang Zhidong in the provinces; their guiding principle was later summarized as “Chinese learning as the essence, Western learning for practical use.” From the 1860s, under the slogan of “self-strengthening,” they founded modern military industry, such as Zeng Guofan’s Anqing Arsenal, Li Hongzhang’s Jiangnan Arsenal and Jinling Machine Works, and Zuo Zongtang’s Fuzhou Shipyard, making guns, ammunition and steamships. From the 1870s, under the slogan of “seeking wealth,” they founded civilian enterprises such as the China Merchants Steam Navigation Company, Kaiping Mines, Shanghai Machine Weaving Mill, Hanyang Iron Works and Hubei Textile Mill. They also set up new schools such as the Tongwen Guan, the Fuzhou Naval Academy and the Tianjin Naval Academy and sent students abroad; from 1872 the Qing sent 120 young boys to the US, among them Zhan Tianyou. In the 1880s they also built the Beiyang, Nanyang and Fujian fleets. The movement brought in advanced Western production technology, objectively stimulated the birth and growth of Chinese national capitalism, and began China’s modernization. But it left the feudal system untouched, its enterprises were corruptly run and dependent on foreigners, and the destruction of the Beiyang Fleet in the 1894 Sino-Japanese War marked its failure.

events.title: Founding of the Tongwen Guan
events.short: In 1862 the Qing opened the Tongwen Guan (School of Combined Learning) in Beijing to train interpreters, later adding astronomy and mathematics; it was China’s first state-run modern school.
events.detail: After the Second Opium War the Qing’s dealings with foreigners grew, and because of “language barriers and difficult writing,” it urgently needed foreign-language experts. When Prince Gong Yixin asked to set up the Zongli Yamen, he also proposed a school to teach foreign languages. In 1862 the Tongwen Guan opened in Beijing, at first with only an English section, later adding French, Russian, German and Japanese. It first admitted Banner youths under fourteen, later also Manchu and Han juren and officials of the fifth rank and below from regular backgrounds. In 1866 Yixin proposed adding an astronomy and mathematics department; Grand Secretary Woren and other conservatives fiercely opposed it, holding that “the way to build a state lies in propriety and righteousness, not in scheming,” but it was still set up. The curriculum then widened to chemistry, physics, international law, medicine, astronomy, geography, foreign history and geography and political economy. Foreigners taught there, with the American missionary William Martin long serving as head instructor. The course lasted eight years (with a five-year option), and top students could receive official posts. The school also had a press that translated and published Western books such as the Chemistry Guide and Political Economy, and trained diplomats and translators; many graduates became envoys and diplomatic officials. The Tongwen Guan was China’s first state-run modern school and pioneered modern education in China. In 1902 it was merged into the Imperial University of Peking.

events.title: The Fall of Tianjing and the Defeat of the Taiping
events.short: After 1860 the Taiping briefly built bases in Jiangsu and Zhejiang but were crushed by combined Chinese and foreign forces; in 1864 the Hunan Army took Tianjing and the Taiping movement failed.
events.detail: After the Tianjing Incident, through the efforts of Hong Rengan, Chen Yucheng, Li Xiucheng and others, the Taiping briefly won victories such as the second destruction of the Jiangnan Camp and set up bases in southern Jiangsu and Zhejiang, but could not turn the tide. The main force against it was the Hunan Army raised by Zeng Guofan. Zeng (1811–1872), from Xiangxiang, Hunan, in 1853 recruited peasants at home into the Hunan Army on the basis of local militia and fought the Taiping repeatedly. Li Hongzhang later raised the Huai Army on its model and Zuo Zongtang led the Chu Army, together suppressing the Taiping. After the Second Opium War, foreign aggressors and the Qing colluded; the American Frederick Townsend Ward led a “Foreign Arms Corps” (later the “Ever-Victorious Army”) to help attack the Taiping. In 1861 the Hunan Army took Anqing, gateway to Tianjing. In 1862 Heroic King Chen Yucheng was betrayed, captured and killed. From 1863 the Hunan Army besieged Tianjing, while the Huai Army and Ever-Victorious Army took Suzhou and other cities and Zuo’s Chu Army took Hangzhou. With Tianjing besieged, Li Xiucheng proposed “giving up the city and going elsewhere,” but Hong Xiuquan refused. Hong died of illness in June 1864. In July the Hunan Army blew up the city wall with explosives laid in tunnels and entered Tianjing, which fell. Li Xiucheng was captured after breaking out and was killed. Taiping remnants allied with the Nian army fought on until 1868. The movement lasted fourteen years and dealt heavy blows to Qing rule and foreign aggressors. Its failure showed that in a semi-colonial, semi-feudal society a peasant war alone could not accomplish the historic tasks of anti-imperialism and anti-feudalism.

events.title: Founding of Shen Bao
events.short: Founded in Shanghai in 1872 by British merchant Ernest Major and later run by Chinese owners until 1949, Shen Bao was one of modern China’s longest-running and most influential newspapers.
events.detail: After the Opium War, foreigners founded many newspapers and periodicals in Hong Kong, Shanghai and elsewhere, at first mainly for foreign readers in China, though Chinese-language papers soon appeared. On 30 April 1872 the British merchant Ernest Major and partners founded Shen Bao in Shanghai, originally called Shenjiang Xinbao (“Shen” is another name for Shanghai). It hired Chinese literati as chief writers and carried news, commentary, market prices, advertisements and literary works, suiting Chinese readers’ habits at a low price, and quickly found a market. It sent reporters out early and reported social news such as the “Yang Naiwu and Xiao Baicai” case at length, drawing wide attention. In 1882 it first used the telegraph to transmit news, greatly improving timeliness. In 1909 it was bought by the Chinese comprador Xi Zipei, and in 1912 Shi Liangcai and others took it over, after which it grew into one of the country’s most influential papers. In the 1930s its supplement Free Talk published many articles by writers such as Lu Xun and Mao Dun. After the Mukden Incident it actively promoted resistance to Japan and criticized the Nationalist government’s policy of “internal pacification before external resistance.” In 1934 Shi Liangcai was assassinated by Nationalist agents. After Shanghai’s liberation in May 1949 Shen Bao ceased publication, having published over 25,000 issues. It recorded 77 years of modern Chinese history and has been called an “encyclopedia” for studying modern China. The appearance of modern newspapers accelerated the spread of information and helped change social attitudes and advance ideas.

events.title: Zuo Zongtang Recovers Xinjiang
events.short: After Yakub Beg seized Xinjiang, Zuo Zongtang took charge of its military affairs in 1875, recovered all of Xinjiang except Ili by 1878, and Xinjiang became a province in 1884.
events.detail: In the 1860s uprisings against the Qing broke out across Xinjiang. In 1865 Yakub Beg, an officer of the Central Asian Khanate of Kokand, invaded, took southern Xinjiang and parts of the north and set up a reactionary regime. In 1871 Russia sent troops to occupy the Ili region on the pretext of “recovering it on China’s behalf.” Meanwhile Japan invaded Taiwan and the southeast coast was under threat, and a debate arose in the Qing court between “coastal defense” and “frontier defense”: Li Hongzhang urged giving up Xinjiang to concentrate on the coast, while Zuo Zongtang, Governor-General of Shaanxi and Gansu, insisted on recovering it, arguing that “to value Xinjiang is to protect Mongolia, and to protect Mongolia is to defend the capital.” The Qing adopted Zuo’s view and in 1875 appointed him Imperial Commissioner overseeing military affairs in Xinjiang. Zuo set the strategy of “north first, then south” and “advance slowly, fight swiftly.” In 1876 Qing forces first recovered northern Xinjiang, and in 1877 they took Dabancheng, Turpan and other gateways to the south; Yakub Beg, with nowhere to turn, died at Korla. By early 1878 the Qing had recovered all of Xinjiang except Ili. To win back Ili, in 1880 the nearly seventy-year-old Zuo went to Hami with a coffin carried behind him, to show his resolve to fight Russia. The Qing sent Zeng Jize to negotiate with Russia, and in 1881 the Treaty of Ili was signed, recovering the Ili region though some territory was still lost. In 1884 Xinjiang formally became a province, with Liu Jintang as first governor and the capital at Dihua (present-day Urumqi). Zuo’s recovery preserved national unity and territorial integrity, and the willows his troops planted along the way are called “Zuo’s willows.”

events.title: Building the Beiyang Fleet and Taiwan Province
events.short: In the 1880s the Qing built a new-style navy, with the Beiyang Fleet formally established in 1888; Taiwan became a province in 1885, with Liu Mingchuan as its first governor.
events.detail: From the 1870s China’s southeast coast was seriously threatened by the powers. In 1874 Japan sent troops against Taiwan, and in 1884, in the Sino-French War, the French fleet nearly wiped out the Fujian Fleet at the Battle of Mawei, exposing the weakness of China’s coastal defense. At the urging of Li Hongzhang, Governor-General of Zhili and Superintendent of Trade for the Northern Ports, and others, the Qing began large-scale modern coastal defense building. In 1885 it set up the Admiralty Office under Prince Chun Yixuan, with Li Hongzhang assisting. It ordered many warships from Britain and Germany, among them the ironclads Dingyuan and Zhenyuan built in Germany, then among the largest in Asia, and built naval bases and forts at Lüshun and Weihaiwei. In 1888 the Beiyang Fleet was formally established with Ding Ruchang as admiral and more than twenty ships, called “first in Asia.” By the 1880s the Fujian, Guangdong, Nanyang and Beiyang fleets were roughly in place, the Beiyang being the largest. But the Qing then diverted naval funds to build the Summer Palace, and after 1888 the fleet bought no new ships and gradually fell behind Japan’s navy. Taiwan was a shield for the southeast coast. In the Sino-French War the French attacked Keelung and Tamsui and were driven back by troops and civilians under Liu Mingchuan. Recognizing Taiwan’s importance, in 1885 the Qing made it a province with Liu Mingchuan as first governor. He reorganized its defenses, built railways, strung telegraph lines and founded new schools and a postal service, making Taiwan one of China’s more advanced provinces.

events.title: Portugal Gradually Takes Over Macao
events.short: After the Opium War Portugal gradually took control of Macao, and in 1887 forced the Qing into a treaty granting Portugal “perpetual occupation and government” of Macao.
events.detail: Since the Portuguese were allowed to live in Macao in 1553, sovereignty over Macao had always belonged to China; the Portuguese paid ground rent to the Chinese government each year, and China kept officials there to govern and collect taxes. After the Opium War Portugal sought to take over administration, turning from residents into rulers. In 1844 the Portuguese government ignored China’s sovereignty and announced an “overseas province” made up of Macao, Timor and other places, and in 1845 unilaterally declared Macao a free port. In 1846 Governor João Maria Ferreira do Amaral took office, imposed colonial rule, forced Macao’s Chinese residents to pay taxes, from 1849 stopped paying ground rent to China and expelled Chinese officials, arousing strong local anger. In August 1849 Amaral was assassinated by local youths including Shen Zhiliang. Portugal then occupied Wangxia and other villages in northern Macao, and the islands of Taipa and Coloane. In 1887, using China’s need for cooperation in collecting opium duties, Portugal forced the Qing to sign the Sino-Portuguese Treaty of Friendship and Commerce, which stated that “Portugal shall perpetually occupy and govern Macao and its dependencies, as with any other Portuguese possession,” and that Portugal could not cede Macao to a third country without China’s consent, with the boundaries to be surveyed later. Portugal thus gained “perpetual occupation and government” of Macao, but its boundaries were never formally set. Portugal ruled Macao as a colony for over a hundred years. On 20 December 1999 China resumed sovereignty over Macao and the Macao Special Administrative Region was established.

events.title: British and Russian Designs on Tibet; Two British Invasions
events.short: In the late 19th century Britain and Russia vied for Tibet; Britain invaded in 1888 and 1903, and Tibetan troops and people fought bravely at Lungthur and Gyantse.
events.detail: Tibet lies on China’s southwestern frontier and is strategically important. In the late 19th century both Britain and Russia coveted it. Between 1870 and 1909 tsarist Russia sent a dozen or more so-called “expeditions” into Tibet to gather intelligence. Britain, based in India, tried to make Tibet its sphere of influence and block Russia’s southward advance. In 1888 Britain used the pretext that Tibet had set up a post at Lungthur “across the border” to start its first invasion. Tibetan troops and people resisted at Lungthur and elsewhere but were defeated by inferior weapons. In 1890 the Qing Amban Shengtai signed the Sino-British Convention relating to Sikkim and Tibet, recognizing a British protectorate over Sikkim and fixing the Sikkim-Tibet boundary; in 1893 the Regulations regarding Trade, Communication and Pasturage opened Yadong as a trade mart. At the end of 1903 Britain sent Francis Younghusband to invade again. In 1904 Tibetan troops and people resisted stubbornly at Quxixiangu, Gyantse and elsewhere; the defense of Gyantse Dzong lasted over three months, and when ammunition and food ran out the defenders refused to surrender, many leaping off the cliffs to their deaths. British troops entered Lhasa and the 13th Dalai Lama was forced to flee. Britain forced the Tibetan authorities to sign the Treaty of Lhasa, but the Qing refused to recognize it. In 1906 China and Britain signed the Convention between Great Britain and China Respecting Tibet, in which Britain promised not to annex Tibetan territory or interfere in Tibetan government. In 1907 Britain and Russia agreed to recognize China’s “suzerainty” over Tibet. The Tibetan people’s anti-aggression struggle defended national sovereignty, and the Gyantse Dzong site is now an important patriotic education base.

events.title: Sun Yat-sen Founds the Revive China Society
events.short: In November 1894 Sun Yat-sen founded the Revive China Society in Honolulu, pledging to “expel the Tartars, restore China, and establish a united government”; it was China’s first revolutionary group.
events.detail: Sun Yat-sen (1866–1925), personal name Wen, courtesy name Yixian, was from Xiangshan (present-day Zhongshan), Guangdong. While living in Japan doing revolutionary work he used the alias “Nakayama Shō” (Zhongshan Qiao), and so people later called him Sun Zhongshan. As a boy he loved stories of the Taiping and praised Hong Xiuquan as “the first anti-Qing hero.” At twelve he went to Honolulu to join his elder brother Sun Mei, received a Western education, and later studied medicine in Hong Kong and practiced after graduating. Seeing Qing corruption and foreign aggression, he gradually resolved to save the nation, “using the school as a place to spread ideas and medicine as a way into the world.” In 1894 Sun submitted a petition to Li Hongzhang, Governor-General of Zhili, proposing reforms so that “people can make the best of their talents, land of its benefits, things of their uses, and goods flow freely,” but it was ignored; he gave up on reform and resolved to overthrow the Qing by revolution. In November 1894, in Honolulu, he rallied overseas Chinese and founded the Revive China Society (Xingzhonghui), China’s first bourgeois revolutionary group, with the oath to “expel the Tartars, restore China, and establish a united government.” In 1895 the society’s headquarters opened in Hong Kong and planned the Guangzhou uprising, which failed when the plot leaked; Lu Haodong and others were captured and killed, and Sun was wanted by the Qing and went into exile. In 1896 he was detained by the Qing legation in London and rescued; this “London kidnapping” made him a world-famous revolutionary. The society’s founding marks the beginning of China’s bourgeois democratic revolution, and in 1905 it joined others to form the Tongmenghui.

events.title: The First Sino-Japanese War
events.short: Japan provoked the First Sino-Japanese War in 1894; the Beiyang Fleet was mauled in the Battle of the Yellow Sea, where Deng Shichang died, and destroyed when Weihaiwei fell in 1895.
events.detail: After the Meiji Restoration Japan rapidly embarked on foreign expansion, adopting a “continental policy” centered on invading Korea and China. In 1894 the Donghak uprising broke out in Korea; at the Korean king’s request the Qing sent troops to help suppress it, and Japan seized the chance to send large forces. After the uprising ended Japan refused to withdraw and kept adding troops, deliberately provoking war. In July 1894 the Japanese fleet attacked a Chinese troopship off Pungdo, Korea, starting the war. In September Japanese forces attacked Pyongyang, where Qing general Zuo Baogui was killed and commander Ye Zhichao fled, and Japan took all of Korea. The same month the Beiyang Fleet fought the Japanese Combined Fleet in the Yellow Sea; Deng Shichang, captain of the Zhiyuan, led his men bravely, and with ammunition nearly gone and the ship badly damaged, he ordered full speed at the Japanese ship Yoshino, but the Zhiyuan sank, and Deng and most of the crew died heroically. Li Hongzhang, to preserve his strength, ordered the fleet into Weihaiwei and forbade it to sail out. In October Japanese forces invaded Northeast China in two columns, and in November took Lüshun, carrying out the “Lüshun Massacre” of over 20,000 Chinese residents. In early 1895 the Japanese attacked Weihaiwei by land and sea; the Beiyang Fleet was besieged, Admiral Ding Ruchang refused to surrender and killed himself, and the fleet was wiped out. The defeat proclaimed the failure of the Self-Strengthening Movement, and the Qing sued for peace and signed the humiliating Treaty of Shimonoseki. The war brought an unprecedented national crisis and awakened the Chinese people’s national consciousness.

events.title: The Treaty of Shimonoseki
events.short: In 1895 the Qing was forced into the Treaty of Shimonoseki, ceding Liaodong, Taiwan and Penghu, paying 200 million taels of silver and letting Japan open factories at treaty ports.
events.detail: In the war the Qing army kept losing ground, and the Qing was forced to sue for peace. In spring 1895 it sent Li Hongzhang as plenipotentiary to Shimonoseki, Japan, to negotiate with Prime Minister Ito Hirobumi and Foreign Minister Mutsu Munemitsu. During the talks Li was shot and wounded by a Japanese ruffian. On 17 April 1895 the Treaty of Shimonoseki was signed. It provided that China recognize Korea’s “independence,” in effect making it a Japanese dependency; cede the Liaodong Peninsula, all of Taiwan with its affiliated islands, and the Penghu Islands to Japan; pay Japan an indemnity of 200 million taels of silver; open Shashi, Chongqing, Suzhou and Hangzhou as trading ports; and allow Japan to open factories at China’s treaty ports, with their goods shipped inland free of internal taxes. It was the most serious unequal treaty since the Treaty of Nanjing and greatly deepened China’s semi-colonization: ceding Taiwan and other places severely damaged territorial sovereignty; the huge indemnity, about three years of Qing revenue, forced heavy foreign borrowing and gave the powers control of China’s finances; treaty ports reached the middle and upper Yangtze; and allowing Japanese factories met the powers’ need to export capital and seriously hindered the development of Chinese national capitalism. After it was signed, Russia, Germany and France intervened for their own interests and forced Japan to give up the Liaodong Peninsula, while Japan extorted 30 million taels of silver from China as a “redemption fee,” known as the Triple Intervention. The treaty greatly deepened the national crisis, and the powers launched a frenzy of carving up China.

events.title: The Petition of the Examination Candidates (Gongche Shangshu)
events.short: When the Treaty of Shimonoseki became known in 1895, Kang Youwei led examination candidates in Beijing to petition the emperor to reject it and reform, launching the reform movement.
events.detail: The defeat in the Sino-Japanese War made progressive Chinese realize that importing foreign goods alone could not save the nation, and institutional change came onto the agenda. Kang Youwei (1858–1927), from Nanhai, Guangdong, had traveled early to Hong Kong and Shanghai and read many books introducing the West, concluding that the West’s strength lay in its political system. In 1888 he first petitioned the Guangxu Emperor for reform, but it did not reach him. He taught at his Wanmu Caotang school in Guangzhou, training students such as Liang Qichao, and wrote works including Forged Classics of the Xin Period and Confucius as a Reformer. In spring 1895 news of the Treaty of Shimonoseki reached Beijing and aroused public fury. Provincial juren were then gathered for the metropolitan examination, and Kang and his student Liang Qichao rallied over 1,300 of them to petition the Guangxu Emperor, setting out the grave consequences of ceding land and paying indemnities and proposing to “reject the peace, move the capital, train troops and reform.” Because in the Han dynasty candidates were sent to the capital in official carriages (“gongche”), the term later meant juren going to the capital for examinations, hence “the Gongche Petition.” It never reached the emperor, but its contents spread widely and had great influence. It opened the Reform Movement and marked the entry of the bourgeois reformers onto the political stage. Kang then passed the jinshi examination, kept petitioning, and with Liang Qichao and others founded the Society for National Strengthening in Beijing and Shanghai and ran newspapers such as Zhongwai Jiwen and Shiwu Bao to promote reform.

images.caption: Portrait of Kang Youwei
Important newspapers around the country during the Reform Movement

events.title: Taiwan’s Armed Resistance against Japan
events.short: After the Qing ceded Taiwan in 1895, troops and civilians under Liu Yongfu, Xu Xiang and others resisted Japan for nearly five months in over a hundred battles, dealing the invaders heavy blows.
events.detail: When news of the Treaty of Shimonoseki reached Taiwan, its people were filled with grief and swore never to be subjects of a conquered country. Taiwan gentry such as Qiu Fengjia petitioned in blood, declaring that “our native land will live or die with righteousness.” In May 1895 Japan landed the Imperial Guard Division and other forces in northern Taiwan and began to seize it by force. Short of pay and arms and with no outside help, Taiwan’s troops and civilians resisted stubbornly. After taking Keelung the Japanese occupied Taipei. The people formed volunteer forces and fought fierce battles with the Japanese at Hsinchu, Miaoli, Changhua and elsewhere. Volunteer leaders Xu Xiang, Wu Tangxing, Jiang Shaozu and others fought bravely and repeatedly hurt the Japanese. In August, when the Japanese attacked Changhua, Wu Tangxing and others died heroically in the Battle of Baguashan. Liu Yongfu’s Black Flag Army then held Tainan, fighting alongside the volunteers. In October Xu Xiang was gravely wounded and, dying, cried out, “A man who dies for his country has no regret!” With supplies exhausted and no relief, Liu Yongfu crossed to the mainland in late October and Tainan fell. From May to October, Taiwan’s troops and civilians fought over a hundred battles with the Japanese, inflicting thousands of casualties, and the Japanese division commander Prince Kitashirakawa Yoshihisa died of illness in Taiwan. The resistance did not end there: during fifty years of Japanese colonial rule, Taiwanese kept resisting, as in the 1915 Xilaian Incident and the 1930 Wushe Incident. Their struggle showed the unyielding patriotic spirit of the Chinese nation. After victory in the War of Resistance in 1945, Taiwan returned to China.
