events.title: Zhang Jian Founds Dasheng Cotton Mill and “Saving the Nation through Industry”
events.short: After the war the top-ranked scholar Zhang Jian gave up office to found the Dasheng Cotton Mill in Nantong, along with other firms and schools, a leader of “saving the nation through industry.”
events.detail: In the 1860s and 1870s Chinese national capitalism appeared but grew slowly. After the Sino-Japanese War foreign capital opened factories and mines in China, and some patriots put forward “saving the nation through industry,” giving national industry an initial boost. Zhang Jian (1853–1926), courtesy name Jizhi, from Nantong, Jiangsu, became the top scholar (zhuangyuan) in the 1894 examinations and was appointed a Hanlin compiler. The defeat and the Treaty of Shimonoseki shocked him; holding that “industry and education support each other,” he resolutely gave up an official career and returned home to start enterprises. In 1895, at the request of Zhang Zhidong, Governor-General of Liangjiang, he began planning a cotton mill in Nantong, and the Dasheng Cotton Mill opened in 1899; “Dasheng” comes from the Book of Changes line “the great virtue of heaven and earth is to give life.” Using Nantong’s cotton, the mill produced good yarn with wide sales. Zhang then founded a land reclamation company, oil mill, flour mill, steamship company and more, forming the Dasheng group, one of the largest national capitalist groups of the time. He also supported education and public welfare, founding Tongzhou Normal School (China’s first independent normal school), the Nantong Museum (the first museum founded by Chinese), a library, a hospital and a home for the aged, making Nantong a nationally known model city. After the 1911 Revolution he served as Minister of Agriculture and Commerce of the Beiyang government. His work led many Chinese to “save the nation through industry” and boosted national capitalism; Mao Zedong said that in discussing light industry one must not forget Zhang Jian.

images.caption: The Dasheng Cotton Mill founded by Zhang Jian in Nantong, Jiangsu

events.title: Founding of the Commercial Press
events.short: In 1897 Xia Ruifang, Bao Xianchang and others founded the Commercial Press in Shanghai, publishing many textbooks, dictionaries and scholarly works and becoming modern China’s largest publisher.
events.detail: In 1897 Xia Ruifang, Bao Xian’en, Bao Xianchang, Gao Fengchi and others raised funds to found the Commercial Press in Shanghai; it began as a small print shop, hence the name “Commercial.” In 1902 the noted scholar Zhang Yuanji joined and ran its editorial office, aiming to “promote education” and turning the press from printing into a cultural institution centered on publishing. From 1904 it issued series of modern primary and middle school textbooks such as the Newest Textbooks, widely used across the country. It also published Western scholarly classics and literature translated by Yan Fu and Lin Shu, compiled China’s first large comprehensive dictionary Ciyuan (1915), launched periodicals including Eastern Miscellany, Short Story Monthly and Education Magazine, and published large series of ancient texts such as Sibu Congkan. By the early 1930s it had become one of Asia’s largest publishers. In the January 28 Incident of 1932 its main plant and the Oriental Library were bombed by Japanese forces, and over 400,000 volumes burned. The Press recovered quickly in hardship under the slogan “sacrifice for the nation’s crisis, strive for culture.” It was the first and largest cultural publisher founded by Chinese in modern times and promoted culture and education. Zhonghua Book Company, Kaiming Bookstore and Life Bookstore also made important contributions to modern publishing. In 1954 the Commercial Press moved to Beijing, and its Xinhua Dictionary and Contemporary Chinese Dictionary became household names.

images.caption: Textbooks published by the Commercial Press

events.title: The Scramble for Concessions and the Open Door Policy
events.short: After the Sino-Japanese War the powers seized leased territories and spheres of influence in a scramble to carve up China; in 1899 the US called for an “Open Door” of equal access.
events.detail: After the Treaty of Shimonoseki, Russia, France and Germany intervened to return Liaodong, and Japan extorted a 30-million-tael “redemption fee” from China. Seizing this chance, the powers launched a scramble in China for rights and interests, leased territories and “spheres of influence.” In 1897 Germany, using the killing of two missionaries at Juye, Shandong, as a pretext, seized Jiaozhou Bay by force, and the next year forced the Qing to lease it and made Shandong its sphere of influence. Russia then seized Lüshun and Dalian, made the area north of the Great Wall its sphere, and gained the right to build the Chinese Eastern Railway and its branches. Britain leased Weihaiwei and northern Kowloon (later the “New Territories”) and made the Yangtze valley its sphere. France leased Guangzhouwan and made Yunnan, Guangdong and Guangxi its sphere, and Japan claimed Fujian. China faced a grave crisis of partition, and someone drew the Map of the Current Situation. The US, busy with the Spanish-American War, could not join the partition. In 1899 US Secretary of State John Hay proposed the “Open Door” policy to Britain, Germany, Russia, Japan, Italy and France, recognizing the powers’ spheres of influence and existing interests while requiring that each open its sphere to the US on equal terms of trade, that is, “equal sharing of benefits.” The powers accepted it, but in essence it was a US policy of widening its own aggressive interests in China. The scramble provoked strong resistance among the Chinese people and spurred the reformers to speed up their drive for strength through reform.

images.caption: Map of the Current Situation

events.title: Yan Fu Translates Evolution and Ethics
events.short: In 1898 Yan Fu published his translation Tianyan Lun (Evolution and Ethics), spreading the ideas of “survival of the fittest” and urging the nation to save itself, influencing a generation of Chinese.
events.detail: Yan Fu (1854–1921), courtesy name Jidao, was from Houguan (present-day Fuzhou), Fujian. He studied navigation at the Fuzhou Naval Academy, and in 1877 was sent to study naval science in Britain. After returning in 1879 he long taught at the Beiyang Naval Academy in Tianjin and later became its head. During the Sino-Japanese War he published essays in Tianjin’s Zhi Bao such as On the Urgency of World Change, On Strength and Refuting Han Yu, advocating “strengthening the people’s power, opening their minds and renewing their morals” and supporting reform. In 1897 he founded the newspaper Guowen Bao in Tianjin to spread reform ideas. Based on Thomas Huxley’s Evolution and Ethics, he wrote Tianyan Lun in classical Chinese, as a free translation with his own commentary, and it was published in 1898. The book spread Darwin’s theory of evolution and the idea of “survival of the fittest,” applied it to human society, and warned that unless China reformed and strengthened itself it would perish, giving theoretical grounds for reform. It caused a strong reaction; phrases such as “struggle for existence” and “natural selection” became household sayings, and many young people took names like “Jingcun” or “Zhi” from them; Hu Shi’s name came from this. Yan Fu also translated Adam Smith’s The Wealth of Nations, Montesquieu’s The Spirit of the Laws and Mill’s On Liberty, introducing Western political, economic and philosophical thought systematically. In translating he proposed the standards of “fidelity, clarity and elegance,” which deeply influenced Chinese translation.

images.caption: Portrait of Yan Fu

events.title: The Hundred Days’ Reform
events.short: In 1898 the Guangxu Emperor decreed a program of reform; after 103 days Empress Dowager Cixi staged a coup in September, the Six Gentlemen were executed, and the reform ended.
events.detail: In winter 1897 Germany seized Jiaozhou Bay. Kang Youwei again petitioned the Guangxu Emperor to reform and save the nation. In spring 1898 Kang and others founded the Society to Protect the Nation in Beijing. Prompted by the reformers, the emperor said he was “unwilling to be a ruler who loses his country” and resolved to reform. On 11 June 1898 he issued the “Edict Defining the National Policy,” announcing reform. Over the next 103 days he issued a series of reform edicts: politically, cutting redundant posts and allowing officials and commoners to submit memorials; economically, setting up bureaus for agriculture, industry and commerce and for railways and mining, building railways and opening mines; militarily, cutting old-style forces and training troops by Western methods; and in culture and education, abolishing the eight-legged essay in favor of policy essays, founding new schools and the Imperial University of Peking. The emperor also appointed Tan Sitong, Yang Rui, Lin Xu and Liu Guangdi as Grand Council secretaries to take part in the reforms. The measures harmed the interests of the conservatives led by Empress Dowager Cixi, who strongly opposed them. On 21 September Cixi staged a coup, confined the emperor and ordered the arrest of the reformers; Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao fled to Japan. Tan Sitong refused to flee, saying “every country’s reform has been won with blood… if so, let it begin with me.” On 28 September Tan Sitong, Kang Guangren, Lin Xu, Yang Shenxiu, Yang Rui and Liu Guangdi were executed at Caishikou in Beijing, known as the “Six Gentlemen of 1898.” The reform was a bourgeois reformist movement that enlightened society, but its failure showed that in semi-colonial, semi-feudal China a top-down path of reform could not succeed.

images.caption: Weng Tonghe had supported the Society for National Strengthening founded by Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao, but soon after the reform began Cixi had the emperor dismiss him from his posts and send him back to his native place
Painting of Tan Sitong’s martyrdom

events.title: Founding of the Imperial University of Peking
events.short: Founded during the 1898 reform, the Imperial University of Peking was modern China’s first national university and its top education authority, and the forerunner of Peking University.
events.detail: After the Sino-Japanese War the reformers actively urged the founding of new schools to train new talent. In 1896 Li Duanfen, Vice Minister of Justice, formally proposed a university in the capital. During the Hundred Days’ Reform the Guangxu Emperor’s edict stated that “the Imperial University of Peking should lead the provinces and be set up first.” In July he approved the Regulations of the Imperial University drafted by Liang Qichao, appointed Sun Jia’nai, Minister of Personnel, as head, and the American missionary William Martin as chief Western instructor. With the aim of “training talent widely and studying current affairs,” it planned ten departments, including astronomy, geography, moral philosophy, politics, literature, military science, agriculture, engineering, commerce and medicine. It was both the nation’s highest school and its highest educational administration. In December it formally opened in the former mansion of Princess Hejia near Mashen Temple, east of Jingshan in Beijing. After the reform failed almost all new policies were abolished, but the university survived. In 1900 the Eight-Power Allied Forces occupied Beijing, damaged it and forced it to close. In 1902 the Qing appointed Zhang Baixi to restore it. In 1905, with the founding of the Ministry of Education, the university no longer oversaw national education. In 1912 it was renamed Peking University, with Yan Fu as first president. After Cai Yuanpei became president in 1917, he promoted “freedom of thought and inclusiveness,” making it the center of the New Culture Movement. The founding of the Imperial University marks the beginning of modern higher education in China.

events.title: The Boxer Movement
events.short: The Boxers rose in Shandong and Zhili with the slogan “support the Qing, destroy the foreigners,” entered Beijing and Tianjin in 1900 to fight the powers, and were crushed by combined forces.
events.detail: The Boxers grew out of folk secret societies and martial arts groups such as the Yihe Quan (Righteous and Harmonious Fists) in Shandong and Zhili. In the late 19th century, as the powers carved up China and foreign missionaries grew bolder, some missionaries seized land and meddled in lawsuits while some converts bullied others using their backing, and conflicts between people and church sharpened. These groups gradually became mass organizations against foreign aggression, known collectively as the “Yihetuan” (Boxers). They organized people by setting up altars and practicing boxing, claimed to be “immune to swords and bullets,” and raised the slogan “support the Qing, destroy the foreigners.” At the end of 1899 Yuan Shikai became governor of Shandong and brutally suppressed them, and their center shifted to Zhili. In spring and summer 1900 they grew rapidly and large numbers entered Tianjin and Beijing and besieged the foreign legation quarter. The Qing court was divided, and Empress Dowager Cixi finally decided to use the Boxers against the powers, “declaring war” on them on 21 June. After the Eight-Power Allied Forces invaded, the Boxers and patriotic Qing troops fought them bravely at Tianjin, Beijing and elsewhere, and at Langfang they stopped the Seymour column and forced it back to Tianjin. But after the allies took Beijing the Qing ordered the Boxers “ruthlessly suppressed,” and the movement was crushed by combined Chinese and foreign reactionary forces. It was an anti-imperialist patriotic movement that dealt a heavy blow to imperialist aggression, foiled the powers’ plans to partition China and showed the great strength of the Chinese people. But owing to the limits of the peasant class it had a tinge of indiscriminate xenophobia and superstition, and its slogan made it easy for the Qing court to exploit.

images.author: Government of the People's Republic of China

events.title: The Eight-Power Allied Invasion
events.short: In 1900 eight powers (Britain, the US, Russia, Japan, France, Germany, Italy, Austria) took Tianjin and Beijing; Cixi fled with the emperor to Xi’an while the allies looted the capital.
events.detail: The rapid growth of the Boxer movement drew the close attention of the powers. At the end of May 1900 Britain, Russia and others sent over three hundred troops into Beijing’s legation quarter. In June a force of over two thousand from eight countries, Britain, the US, Russia, Japan, France, Germany, Italy and Austria, led by British Vice Admiral Seymour, advanced on Beijing from Tianjin, was stopped at Langfang and elsewhere by the Boxers and Qing troops, and was forced back to Tianjin. The allies then took the Dagu forts, and the Qing declared war on them on 21 June. In July they took Tianjin, where Qing general Nie Shicheng died heroically at Baliqiao. In early August about 20,000 allied troops advanced from Tianjin on Beijing and entered it on 14 August; the next day Empress Dowager Cixi hurriedly fled to Xi’an with the Guangxu Emperor. The allies killed, burned and looted in Beijing; vast treasures and relics were plundered from the Forbidden City, the Summer Palace and elsewhere, rare texts such as the Yongle Encyclopedia were largely destroyed or carried off, and many innocent residents were killed. They divided Beijing into occupation zones under military rule. Meanwhile Russia sent over 100,000 troops to occupy Northeast China, committing the Blagoveshchensk massacre and the “Sixty-Four Villages East of the River” massacre and killing many Chinese residents. The allies also sent “punitive” columns that occupied many places in Zhili, Shanxi and elsewhere. On the run, the Qing ordered the Boxers “ruthlessly suppressed” and named Li Hongzhang plenipotentiary to negotiate with the powers. The invasion brought deep suffering to the Chinese people and ended with the Boxer Protocol.

events.title: The Boxer Protocol
events.short: In 1901 the Qing was forced to sign the Boxer Protocol with eleven countries, paying 450 million taels of silver and fixing a legation quarter, and China became fully semi-colonial and semi-feudal.
events.detail: After the Eight-Power force took Beijing, the Qing sent Li Hongzhang and Prince Qing Yikuang as plenipotentiaries to negotiate. On 7 September 1901 the Qing was forced to sign the humiliating Boxer Protocol with eleven countries: Britain, the US, Russia, Japan, France, Germany, Italy, Austria, Belgium, the Netherlands and Spain. Its main terms were: the Qing would pay an indemnity of 450 million taels of silver over 39 years, about 980 million with interest, secured on customs and salt taxes, known as the “Boxer Indemnity”; Beijing’s Dongjiaominxiang was designated a legation quarter in which Chinese could not live and which the powers could garrison; the Qing guaranteed to forbid anti-foreign activity on pain of death and to dismiss officials who suppressed it poorly; and it would raze the Dagu forts and let the powers station troops at twelve places along the railway from Beijing to Shanhaiguan. It was the largest indemnity and most severe loss of sovereignty of any unequal treaty in modern China. The indemnity amounted to a tael of silver per Chinese person and made the people’s burden heavier; the legation quarter became a “state within a state” in the capital; razing the Dagu forts and allowing foreign troops left Beijing open; and the ban on anti-foreign activity showed that the Qing had become a tool of the powers, a “foreigners’ court.” The Protocol marks China’s complete fall into a semi-colonial, semi-feudal society. Later the US and other countries returned part of the indemnity to China for education and study abroad; Tsinghua School (today’s Tsinghua University) was founded with part of the US refund.

events.title: Spread of Revolutionary Ideas (The Revolutionary Army, Turn Your Head Around)
events.short: In the early 1900s Zou Rong’s The Revolutionary Army, Chen Tianhua’s Turn Your Head Around and Zhang Binglin’s polemics against Kang Youwei spread calls to overthrow the Qing.
events.detail: After the Boxer Protocol the Qing had become a “foreigners’ court,” the national crisis was unprecedentedly grave, and revolutionary feeling rose at home. Meanwhile growing numbers of Chinese students in Japan founded periodicals and wrote books promoting democratic revolution. In 1903 Zhang Binglin published his Refutation of Kang Youwei on Revolution, rebutting Kang’s royalist views, mocking the Guangxu Emperor as an ignorant “little clown,” and arguing the need for revolution. That year the 18-year-old Zou Rong wrote The Revolutionary Army with a preface by Zhang. It passionately praised revolution, called for overthrowing Qing autocracy and founding a “Republic of China,” and sold over a million copies. Chen Tianhua wrote Turn Your Head Around and Warning Bell in plain language and storytelling form, exposing the danger of partition, pointing out that the Qing had become a “foreigners’ court” and calling on people to rise in revolution; they spread widely. That year the Shanghai newspaper Subao, which had published an article introducing The Revolutionary Army and Zhang’s writings, was shut down when the Qing colluded with the Shanghai concession authorities; Zhang and Zou were jailed in the “Subao case,” and Zou died in prison in 1905. In 1905 Chen Tianhua drowned himself in Tokyo to protest the Japanese ban on Chinese students and awaken his countrymen. Revolutionary groups were founded around the country, such as the China Revival Society founded by Huang Xing and others in Changsha and the Restoration Society founded by Cai Yuanpei and Zhang Binglin in Shanghai. The wide spread of bourgeois revolutionary ideas prepared the ground for the 1911 Revolution, and revolution became the tide of the times.

events.title: The Tongmenghui and the Three Principles of the People
events.short: In 1905 Sun Yat-sen merged the Revive China Society and other groups in Tokyo into the Tongmenghui, China’s first national revolutionary party, built on his Three Principles of the People.
events.detail: In the early 20th century revolutionary groups sprang up in many places, but they were scattered and fought separately, and the revolution urgently needed a unified organization. On 20 August 1905 Sun Yat-sen united the Revive China Society, China Revival Society, Restoration Society and others and founded the Tongmenghui (Chinese Revolutionary Alliance) in Tokyo, Japan. Sun was elected premier, Huang Xing became head of the executive department, and branches were set up at home and abroad. Its political program was to “expel the Tartars, restore China, establish a republic and equalize land rights,” and it founded the Min Bao. In November Sun’s foreword to the Min Bao summarized the program as three principles, nationalism, democracy and people’s livelihood, the “Three Principles of the People.” Nationalism meant “expelling the Tartars and restoring China,” overthrowing Qing rule by revolution; democracy meant “establishing a republic,” overthrowing feudal monarchy and founding a bourgeois democratic republic; people’s livelihood meant “equalizing land rights,” fixing land prices. The Three Principles were a fairly complete bourgeois democratic program and became the guiding ideology of the 1911 Revolution, though they did not clearly oppose imperialism or propose a thorough anti-feudal land program. After its founding the Tongmenghui used the Min Bao to wage a great debate with royalists led by Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao over whether to overthrow the Qing by revolution, and launched many armed uprisings. It was China’s first national bourgeois revolutionary party, and its founding marked a new stage of the bourgeois democratic revolution.

events.title: Abolition of the Imperial Examinations
events.short: The late-Qing “New Policies” reformed education; in 1905 the Qing announced the end of the examinations from the next year, abolishing the 1,300-year-old system as new-style schools grew rapidly.
events.detail: The imperial examination system began in the Sui dynasty, but by the Ming and Qing the eight-legged essay examinations seriously confined thinking. In the Self-Strengthening period reformers founded new schools such as the Tongwen Guan and Fuzhou Naval Academy. After the Sino-Japanese War the Qing founded the Beiyang Western Learning Hall (later Peiyang University) in Tianjin and Nanyang Public School in Shanghai. During the Hundred Days’ Reform it announced the abolition of the eight-legged essay and founded the Imperial University. In 1901, to preserve its rule, the Qing announced the “New Policies”: in education it abolished the eight-legged essay for policy essays, ordered new schools set up everywhere and encouraged study abroad. In 1902 and 1904 it issued the Imperially Approved School Regulations (Renyin system) and the Regulations Approved by Memorial (Guimao system), the latter being China’s first modern school system formally applied nationwide. Because the examinations remained, scholars still pursued them and new schools were hampered. In 1905 Yuan Shikai, Zhang Zhidong and others jointly petitioned to end them at once. In September the Qing announced that examinations would end from 1906, and the system that had lasted 1,300 years was abolished. At the end of that year it set up the Ministry of Education to oversee education nationwide. New schools then grew rapidly: by 1909 there were over 50,000 with over 1.6 million students, and a wave of study abroad appeared. The abolition was a major change in Chinese educational history, shook the feudal education system and promoted modern education and the rise of a new intellectual class.

events.title: China’s First Film, Dingjun Mountain
events.short: In 1905 the Fengtai Photography Studio in Beijing filmed scenes from the Peking Opera Dingjun Mountain starring Tan Xinpei, the first film made by Chinese, marking the birth of Chinese cinema.
events.detail: In 1895 the Lumière brothers first screened films publicly in Paris, marking the birth of cinema. Films soon reached China, and in 1896 “Western shadow plays” were shown at the Youyicun in Shanghai’s Xu Garden. Early films had images but no sound and were called silent films. In 1905 Ren Qingtai, owner of the Fengtai Photography Studio in Beijing, decided to make a Chinese film. He invited the Peking Opera star Tan Xinpei and filmed scenes from Tan’s Dingjun Mountain, including “Asking for Orders,” “Wielding the Sword” and “Fighting.” Drawn from Romance of the Three Kingdoms, it tells how the old Shu Han general Huang Zhong defeated the Cao Cao army at Dingjun Mountain and killed Xiahou Yuan. It was shown at the Daguanlou theater by Beijing’s Qianmen to crowds. As the first film made by Chinese, it makes 1905 the birth year of Chinese cinema, and the Fengtai studio and Daguanlou are called the “cradle of Chinese film.” In 1913 Zheng Zhengqiu and Zhang Shichuan made China’s first short feature, The Difficult Couple, in Shanghai. In 1931 China’s first sound film, Singing Girl Red Peony, was completed by the Mingxing Film Company. In the 1930s Shanghai became China’s film center, with fine works such as Song of the Fishermen and Street Angel, and the theme song of the film Children of Troubled Times, March of the Volunteers, later became the national anthem of the People’s Republic of China. Film enriched cultural life and became an important tool for spreading new ideas.

images.caption: Still from Dingjun Mountain

events.title: The Ping-Liu-Li Uprising and the Uprisings of Xu Xilin and Qiu Jin
events.short: In 1906 Tongmenghui members launched the Ping-Liu-Li Uprising; in 1907 Xu Xilin of the Restoration Society assassinated Governor Enming in Anqing and Qiu Jin was captured and executed in Shaoxing.
events.detail: After the Tongmenghui was founded, revolutionaries launched many armed uprisings. In winter 1906 Tongmenghui members Liu Daoyi, Cai Shaonan and others, at Pingxiang, Liuyang and Liling on the Jiangxi-Hunan border, rallied secret societies and Anyuan coal miners in an uprising of over 30,000 people; after more than a month of fighting it failed and Liu Daoyi and others were killed in Changsha. It was the first large-scale armed uprising led by the Tongmenghui. The Restoration Society also planned uprisings. In 1907 its members Xu Xilin and Qiu Jin prepared to rise together in Anhui and Zhejiang. Xu Xilin (1873–1907), from Shaoxing, Zhejiang, entered the Qing bureaucracy by purchasing an office. On 6 July 1907, at the graduation ceremony of the police academy, he assassinated Anhui governor Enming and led students in an uprising; after four hours of fighting it failed, and Xu was captured and cruelly killed. Qiu Jin (1875–1907), from Shaoxing, styled herself “Woman Knight of Jianhu,” studied in Japan, joined the Restoration Society and the Tongmenghui, then founded the China Women’s Journal in Shanghai and headed the Datong School in Shaoxing. After Xu’s failure Qing troops surrounded the school; Qiu refused to leave and was captured, writing only the seven characters “autumn wind and rain make one sad to death” under interrogation, and was executed bravely at Xuantingkou in Shaoxing on 15 July. The Tongmenghui also launched uprisings at Huanggang, Zhennanguan, Hekou and elsewhere in Guangdong, Guangxi and Yunnan. Though all failed, the revolutionaries’ tireless spirit inspired the people, struck heavy blows at Qing rule and laid the basis for the 1911 Revolution.

events.title: Zhan Tianyou Builds the Beijing–Zhangjiakou Railway
events.short: In 1905 the Qing decided to build the Beijing–Zhangjiakou Railway itself with Zhan Tianyou as chief engineer; using methods such as the zigzag line, it opened two years ahead of schedule in 1909.
events.detail: The Beijing–Zhangjiakou Railway runs about 200 kilometers from Fengtai in Beijing to Zhangjiakou in Hebei and is a main route linking North and Northwest China. Britain and Russia competed for the right to build it. In 1905 the Qing decided to build it itself and named Zhan Tianyou chief engineer. Some foreigners sneered that “the engineer who can build this line in China has not yet been born.” Zhan Tianyou (1861–1919), from Nanhai, Guangdong, went to the US in 1872 as one of the first Chinese Educational Mission boys, graduated in civil engineering from Yale, and long worked on railway building after returning. The line had to cross the steep mountains around Juyongguan and Badaling, making the work very hard. Zhan personally led the survey. For the Juyongguan tunnel he had workers dig from both ends toward the middle; for the longest, the Badaling tunnel, he used the “shaft method,” sinking a shaft in the middle and digging toward both ends to speed the work. To get trains up the steep slope from Nankou to Badaling he designed a zigzag line with one locomotive pulling and one pushing, easing the gradient, and he also introduced automatic couplers for safety. Under Zhan’s direction the railway overcame shortages of funds and technical difficulties and opened in 1909, two years ahead of schedule. It was the first trunk railway designed and built by Chinese themselves, showed the wisdom and strength of the Chinese people, and made Zhan Tianyou known as the “Father of China’s Railways.” In 2019 the Beijing–Zhangjiakou high-speed railway opened, echoing the original line of a century earlier.

images.caption: Trains on the zigzag track west of Qinglongqiao Station

events.title: Huanghuagang Uprising
events.short: In April 1911 Huang Xing led revolutionaries in an uprising at Guangzhou, storming the Viceroy's office before being overwhelmed; 72 martyrs' remains were later buried together at Huanghuagang.
events.detail: After a series of uprisings launched since the founding of the Tongmenghui failed, revolutionaries decided to concentrate their strength on one large-scale uprising in Guangzhou. In 1910, Sun Yat-sen, Huang Xing, Zhao Sheng and others met in Penang to plan it. Afterwards Sun went to Europe and the Americas to raise funds from overseas Chinese, while Huang Xing set up a planning office in Hong Kong as the command center. Word leaked out and the Qing government tightened its guard. On 27 April 1911, before preparations were complete, Huang Xing led more than a hundred members of a suicide squad in an attack on the office of the Viceroy of Guangdong and Guangxi, and Viceroy Zhang Mingqi fled. The rebels were outnumbered in fierce fighting and suffered heavy losses; the uprising failed. Huang Xing lost two fingers of his right hand and made his way back to Hong Kong wounded. Before the uprising Lin Juemin wrote his farewell letter “To My Wife” (Yu Qi Shu), expressing his resolve to sacrifice his personal happiness “to seek lasting happiness for all people”; he was captured and died bravely at the age of 24. Afterwards the revolutionary Pan Dawei took the risk of collecting the remains of 72 martyrs and burying them together at Honghuagang outside Guangzhou, renaming it “Huanghuagang”. The uprising is therefore called the Huanghuagang Uprising, and the dead the “72 Martyrs of Huanghuagang” (later research found more than eighty named victims). Sun Yat-sen said of the uprising that it “could shake heaven and earth and move the spirits, and deserves to share a lifespan with the Wuchang Uprising”. Although it failed, it greatly stirred revolutionary enthusiasm and hastened a nationwide revolutionary upsurge; the Wuchang Uprising broke out six months later.

images.caption: Tomb of the 72 Martyrs of Huanghuagang
Huang Xing's final letter

events.title: Wuchang Uprising and the Xinhai Revolution
events.short: On 10 October 1911 revolutionaries in the Hubei New Army launched the Wuchang Uprising; provinces declared independence one after another and Qing rule swiftly collapsed.
events.detail: In May 1911 the Qing government formed a “Royal Cabinet” dominated by imperial clansmen and announced the “nationalization of railways”, taking over the Sichuan–Hankou and Guangzhou–Hankou lines that had been built with private funds. This provoked railway protection movements in Hunan, Hubei, Guangdong and Sichuan; in Sichuan the movement was fiercest and grew into an armed uprising. Meanwhile, the Hubei revolutionary groups Literary Society and Progressive Association, encouraged by the Tongmenghui, had recruited many members in the New Army and were planning an uprising. On 9 October, Sun Wu, a leader of the Progressive Association, accidentally set off a bomb while making explosives in the Russian concession at Hankou; the plan was exposed and the government made mass arrests from its lists of revolutionaries. In this desperate situation, on the night of 10 October, revolutionaries of the New Army's Eighth Engineer Battalion, led by Xiong Bingkun, were the first to act and fired the first shot of the Wuchang Uprising. After a night of fighting the rebels held Wuchang, and Hanyang and Hankou were soon recovered. They established the Hubei Military Government and chose Li Yuanhong, a New Army brigade commander, as military governor. Hunan, Shaanxi and other provinces followed, and within a little over a month more than ten provinces declared independence from the Qing, whose rule swiftly collapsed. Because 1911 was the xinhai year of the traditional calendar, the revolution is called the Xinhai Revolution. It overthrew the monarchy that had ruled China for over two thousand years, established the Republic of China and planted the idea of democratic republicanism in people's minds; it was a great bourgeois democratic revolution in modern Chinese history.

images.caption: Hubei Military Government

events.title: Founding of the Republic of China
events.short: On 1 January 1912 Sun Yat-sen took office in Nanjing as provisional president, proclaiming the Republic of China, the first bourgeois republic in Chinese history.
events.detail: After the Wuchang Uprising succeeded, provinces declared independence one after another, and the revolution needed a unified central government. In December 1911 Sun Yat-sen returned to Shanghai from abroad. On 29 December, delegates of seventeen provinces met in Nanjing and elected Sun provisional president. On 1 January 1912 Sun was sworn in at Nanjing, proclaiming the founding of the Republic of China, with Nanjing as its capital, the Gregorian calendar adopted, and 1912 as Year 1 of the Republic. In his inaugural declaration he stated that the lands of the Han, Manchu, Mongol, Hui and Tibetan peoples were united as one country, and those peoples as one: the “Five Races Under One Union”. The Nanjing Provisional Government headed by Sun was then formed, with a Provisional Senate as its legislature. It issued a series of decrees to sweep away the old and bring in the new. Politically, it guaranteed democratic rights, abolished titles such as “Your Excellency” and “Master”, and banned the trade in people. Economically, it encouraged industry and protected private property. In social customs, it ordered queues cut and banned foot-binding, gambling and opium smoking. In education, it abolished the study of the classics and promoted modern schooling. These measures favored capitalist development and changed social attitudes. The founding of the Republic established the first bourgeois republic in Chinese history and planted the idea of democratic republicanism in people's minds. But the Nanjing Provisional Government lasted only briefly: facing pressure from imperialist powers and financial difficulties, Sun was forced to compromise with Yuan Shikai, and just three months later the provisional government moved to Beijing.

events.title: Qing Abdication and Yuan Shikai Seizes Power
events.short: On 12 February 1912 the child emperor Puyi abdicated and the Qing fell; Sun Yat-sen resigned, the Senate elected Yuan Shikai provisional president, and in April the government moved to Beijing.
events.detail: After the Wuchang Uprising broke out, the Qing government recalled the dismissed Yuan Shikai as Prime Minister of the Cabinet, giving him control of military and political power. Yuan sent the Beiyang Army to attack Wuhan, taking Hankou and Hanyang, while negotiating peace with the revolutionaries with the backing of the foreign powers. After the Nanjing Provisional Government was founded, it faced pressure from the imperialist powers and financial trouble, and constitutional monarchists and old officials within the revolutionary camp also urged compromise with Yuan. Sun Yat-sen was forced to say that if the emperor abdicated and Yuan declared support for the republic, he would resign and recommend Yuan as provisional president. Yuan then pressed the court and had Beiyang generals such as Duan Qirui jointly telegraph a demand for abdication. On 12 February 1912, Empress Dowager Longyu issued the abdication edict in the name of the Xuantong Emperor, Puyi; the Qing dynasty came to an end, and with it the monarchy of over two thousand years. The next day Sun resigned to the Senate, attaching conditions in an attempt to restrain Yuan: the provisional government must stay in Nanjing, the new president must take office in Nanjing, and he must abide by the Provisional Constitution. On 15 February the Senate elected Yuan provisional president. Citing unrest in the north, Yuan refused to go south. On 10 March he was sworn in at Beijing. In April Sun formally stepped down and the provisional government moved to Beijing. China then entered the era of Beiyang warlord rule. Yuan's seizure of the fruits of the revolution showed that the Xinhai Revolution had not completed its anti-imperialist and anti-feudal tasks, and China's semi-colonial, semi-feudal character was unchanged.

events.title: Provisional Constitution of the Republic of China
events.short: In March 1912 Sun Yat-sen promulgated the Provisional Constitution, vesting sovereignty in the people and setting up separation of powers and a responsible cabinet.
events.detail: After Sun Yat-sen resigned as provisional president, the Nanjing Provisional Senate hurried to draw up a constitutional charter to consolidate the revolution's gains and guard against dictatorship by Yuan Shikai. On 11 March 1912 Sun, in the name of provisional president, promulgated the Provisional Constitution of the Republic of China drawn up by the Senate. It provided that sovereignty belonged to all citizens; that citizens were equal regardless of race, class or religion; that they enjoyed freedom of person, residence, property, speech, publication, assembly, association, correspondence and belief; and that the territory of the Republic comprised the twenty-two provinces, Inner and Outer Mongolia, Tibet and Qinghai. For the form of government it adopted the bourgeois principle of separation of powers: the Senate exercised legislative power, the provisional president and cabinet ministers executive power, and the courts judicial power. To limit Yuan's power, it changed the originally planned presidential system into a responsible cabinet system, requiring a minister's countersignature for the president's laws and orders to take effect, and giving the Senate power to impeach the president. As fundamental law it affirmed bourgeois democratic republicanism and rejected feudal monarchical autocracy, and so had anti-feudal, progressive significance. But it had clear limitations: it set no anti-imperialist task and did not address the land question. Later, to establish a dictatorship, Yuan abolished it in 1914 and issued the Constitutional Compact of the Republic of China, while Sun launched the “Constitutional Protection Movement” to defend it.

events.title: Song Jiaoren's Assassination and Second Revolution
events.short: In 1913 the Kuomintang won the elections and Song Jiaoren was assassinated in Shanghai; Sun Yat-sen's “Second Revolution” against Yuan Shikai failed within two months.
events.detail: After becoming provisional president, Yuan Shikai repeatedly undermined the responsible cabinet system. Song Jiaoren, a Tongmenghui member, hoped to limit Yuan's power through parliamentary elections and a party cabinet. In August 1912 he built on the Tongmenghui and merged several other parties to form the Kuomintang. In the first parliamentary elections, from late 1912 to early 1913, the Kuomintang won a majority of seats in both houses and became the largest party, and Song prepared to form a responsible cabinet as leader of the majority party. On 20 March 1913, as Song was about to board a train north at Shanghai railway station, he was shot by an assassin and died, aged only 30. Investigation showed that the masterminds were linked to Yuan Shikai's government. Sun Yat-sen saw Yuan's reactionary face and called for armed action against him. In April, without parliamentary approval, Yuan took a loan of 25 million pounds from a five-nation banking consortium of Britain, France, Germany, Russia and Japan, the “Reorganization Loan”. He then dismissed Li Liejun, military governor of Jiangxi, Hu Hanmin of Guangdong and Bai Wenwei of Anhui. In July Li Liejun declared independence at Hukou in Jiangxi and raised troops against Yuan; Huang Xing responded in Nanjing, and Anhui, Guangdong, Hunan and other provinces followed. This is known as the “Second Revolution”. But because of divisions and lack of cohesion within the Kuomintang, Yuan crushed it in under two months, and Sun, Huang Xing and others were forced into exile in Japan. Its failure showed that a bourgeois republic would not work in China. In 1914 Sun formed the Chinese Revolutionary Party in Japan to continue the struggle against Yuan.

images.caption: Song Jiaoren after his assassination

events.title: The “Brief Spring” of National Industry
events.short: Early Republican policies encouraged industry, and during World War I the powers eased pressure on China; national industry grew in a “brief spring”, with entrepreneurs such as the Rong brothers.
events.detail: The Xinhai Revolution overthrew the Qing and cleared away some obstacles to the growth of national capitalism. The provisional government and the Beijing government issued a series of decrees encouraging industry, industrial associations sprang up, and people rushed to invest in factories, setting off an industrial boom. During World War I the European powers, busy with the war, temporarily eased their economic aggression against China, and imports of European goods fell sharply, while the war greatly increased international demand for grain, cotton yarn and other goods. Mass patriotic anti-imperialist campaigns at home, such as boycotting Japanese goods and promoting domestic products, also helped national industry. Under these conditions, China's national industry grew rapidly, textiles and flour milling fastest of all, in what was called a “brief spring”. The brothers Rong Zongjing and Rong Desheng of Wuxi expanded rapidly in this period; the Maoxin and Fuxin flour mills and the Shenxin textile mills they founded kept growing, and they were called the “Flour Kings” and “Cotton Yarn Kings”. Others such as Zhang Jian's Dasheng Cotton Mill, the Jian brothers' Nanyang Brothers Tobacco Company and Fan Xudong's Jiuda Refined Salt Company also grew considerably. But this growth was concentrated in light industry; heavy industry was weak, and capital, technology and equipment depended heavily on foreign countries. After the war ended, the powers returned and stepped up their economic aggression, and national industry fell into difficulty again. Its growth strengthened the national bourgeoisie and the working class, creating social conditions for the New Culture Movement and the May Fourth Movement.

images.caption: Fuxin Flour Company, founded by the Rong brothers

events.title: Yuan Shikai's Dictatorship and Twenty-One Demands
events.short: Yuan Shikai dissolved parliament and abolished the Provisional Constitution; to win Japanese backing for a monarchy he accepted most of Japan's “Twenty-One Demands” in 1915.
events.detail: After crushing the Second Revolution, Yuan Shikai forced parliament to elect him full president. In early 1914 he dissolved parliament. Soon after, he abolished the Provisional Constitution and issued the Constitutional Compact of the Republic of China, replacing the responsible cabinet system with a presidential system in which the president's powers were almost unlimited. At the end of the year the Presidential Election Law was revised so that the president served a ten-year term, could be re-elected and could nominate his successor, making him president for life. After World War I broke out in 1914, Japan used a declaration of war on Germany as a pretext to send troops into Shandong, occupying Qingdao and the Jiaozhou–Jinan Railway and seizing Germany's rights in Shandong. In January 1915 the Japanese minister Hioki Eki secretly presented Yuan with the “Twenty-One Demands”, aimed at subjugating China. They included: recognition of Japan's succession to all of Germany's rights in Shandong; recognition of Japan's special interests in South Manchuria and eastern Inner Mongolia, with the leases of Lushun, Dalian and the South Manchuria Railway extended to 99 years; joint Sino-Japanese operation of the Hanyeping Company; and a ban on leasing or ceding any coastal harbors or islands to other powers. On 7 May Japan issued an ultimatum, and on 9 May Yuan's government accepted most of the demands, except Group Five, which was left “for later negotiation”. When the news came out, the whole nation was outraged and an anti-Japanese patriotic movement swept the country; 7 and 9 May were designated “National Humiliation Days”. The Twenty-One Demands exposed Japan's ambition to monopolize China, and also fully exposed Yuan Shikai's betrayal of the nation.

images.caption: Beiyang government ceremony of worship to Heaven in Beijing, late 1914

events.title: New Culture Movement
events.short: In 1915 Chen Duxiu founded Youth Magazine (later New Youth) in Shanghai, raising the banners of “democracy” and “science” and opening the New Culture Movement.
events.detail: After the Xinhai Revolution the Republic soon fell into political chaos, and a fashion for revering Confucius and restoring the old ways spread. After painful reflection, some progressive intellectuals concluded that political reform alone could not save China; the thinking of the people had to be remade. In September 1915 Chen Duxiu founded Youth Magazine in Shanghai, renamed New Youth the next year, opening the New Culture Movement. In 1917 Chen was appointed Dean of Letters at Peking University, the New Youth editorial office moved to Beijing, and the university became the movement's center. Its basic slogans were democracy and science. Democracy, “Mr. De” (Democracy), meant opposing feudal autocracy and demanding democratic politics; science, “Mr. Sai” (Science), meant opposing superstition and blind obedience. They attacked the “ancient sages” represented by Confucius and criticized feudal ethics. In the literary revolution, Hu Shi published “A Preliminary Discussion of Literary Reform”, advocating vernacular Chinese in place of classical Chinese; Chen Duxiu published “On Literary Revolution”, calling for the overthrow of the old literature and building of a new one; and in 1918 Lu Xun published “Diary of a Madman”, the first vernacular short story in modern Chinese literature, exposing the “man-eating” nature of feudal ethics. The New Culture Movement was an unprecedented movement of intellectual emancipation. It dealt a heavy blow to the feudal orthodox thought that had ruled China for over two thousand years and created conditions for the spread of Marxism in China, though some of its participants tended to wholly affirm or wholly reject Eastern or Western culture.

events.title: National Protection War Against Yuan Shikai
events.short: Yuan Shikai restored monarchy in late 1915; the National Protection War began in Yunnan, provinces joined, and Yuan abandoned the monarchy in March 1916 and died in June.
events.detail: To realize his dream of becoming emperor, Yuan Shikai had confidants organize the “Peace Planning Society” (Chou'an Hui). In December 1915 he announced his acceptance of the throne, renamed the Republic of China the “Chinese Empire” and ordered that the next year be called Year 1 of “Hongxian”, preparing to ascend the throne. His restoration caused uproar. Sun Yat-sen issued a declaration against him, calling on patriots to rise together and defend the republic. Liang Qichao published “Strange Is the So-called Question of the National Polity” attacking the monarchy. Liang's student Cai E secretly left Beijing and returned to Yunnan by way of Japan. On 25 December 1915 Cai E, Yunnan military governor Tang Jiyao, Li Liejun and others declared Yunnan's independence, formed the National Protection Army and sent troops against Yuan, beginning the National Protection War. Cai led the main force into Sichuan and, though outnumbered, defeated the Beiyang army in fighting around Luzhou and Naxi. Guizhou, Guangxi, Guangdong, Zhejiang and other provinces declared independence in turn, and the Beiyang clique itself split, with Feng Guozhang, Duan Qirui and others cool toward the monarchy. Opposed by the whole nation and abandoned by his own followers, Yuan was forced on 22 March 1916 to cancel the monarchy and restore the title “Republic of China”, having played emperor for only 83 days. He still tried to remain president, but the National Protection Army and many sectors firmly opposed this. On 6 June 1916 Yuan died, in anger and isolation. The war defended the democratic republic, crushed Yuan's plot, and showed that the idea of democratic republicanism had taken root. In 1917 Zhang Xun restored Puyi, but it failed within twelve days.

events.title: Beiyang Warlord Fragmentation
events.short: After Yuan Shikai's death the Beiyang warlords split into Anhui, Zhili and Fengtian cliques, each holding a region with foreign backing and fighting over Beijing; years of war brought great suffering.
events.detail: After Yuan Shikai died in 1916, the Beiyang warlords lost their single leader and split into several cliques. The Anhui clique, headed by Duan Qirui (so called because Duan was from Anhui), controlled the Beijing government and relied on Japanese support. The Zhili clique, headed by Feng Guozhang, Cao Kun and Wu Peifu (so called because Feng was from Zhili), controlled Jiangsu, Jiangxi, Hubei and Zhili and relied on British and American support. The Fengtian clique, headed by Zhang Zuolin, controlled the three northeastern provinces and relied on Japan. In the south there were also regional warlords such as the Yunnan and Guangxi cliques. Each warlord kept his army as his own power base and held his region, and under foreign manipulation they fought each other for the central government and for territory. From 1917 Duan Qirui, in office, took large Japanese loans in the name of joining the war, the “Nishihara Loans”, to build up his own power. The Zhili–Anhui War broke out in 1920; the Anhui clique lost, and the Zhili and Fengtian cliques jointly controlled the Beijing government. Zhili–Fengtian wars broke out again in 1922 and 1924, and power in Beijing changed hands among the cliques several times, with presidents and cabinets replaced frequently. Under warlord rule politics was dark; to expand their armies the warlords levied heavy taxes, issued paper money recklessly and pressed men into service, and together with constant war this seriously damaged the economy and left the people in extreme hardship. The resulting anger also pushed progressive Chinese to seek a new path to national salvation. The Northern Expedition of the National Revolutionary Army, begun in 1926, dealt the warlords a heavy blow, and their rule ended in 1928.

events.title: Cai Yuanpei at Peking University
events.short: In 1917 Cai Yuanpei became president of Peking University, advocating “freedom of thought and tolerance of all views” and hiring Chen Duxiu, Hu Shi and Li Dazhao.
events.detail: Cai Yuanpei (1868–1940), a native of Shaoxing, Zhejiang, was a late-Qing jinshi and Hanlin Academy compiler who later joined the revolution, helping found the Restoration Society and joining the Tongmenghui. After the Republic was founded he served as Minister of Education in the Nanjing Provisional Government, advocating “five kinds of education in parallel”: military citizen, utilitarian, civic moral, world-view and aesthetic education. In January 1917 he became president of Peking University. He worked to create an academic atmosphere of “freedom of thought and tolerance of all views” and recruited talent without regard to background: he hired a large group of scholars with new ideas, including Chen Duxiu, Li Dazhao, Hu Shi, Lu Xun and Qian Xuantong, while also keeping learned scholars of the old school such as Gu Hongming and Liu Shipei. He appointed Chen Duxiu Dean of Letters, and the New Youth editorial office moved to Beijing with him. Cai also reformed the school's administration, introducing “professors governing the university” and a university council; he replaced the year system with an elective-course system; and in 1920 the university began admitting women, the first coeducation in a Chinese public university. Peking University thus became the center of the New Culture Movement. In 1917 Hu Shi published “A Preliminary Discussion of Literary Reform” in New Youth, setting out “eight don'ts” and advocating vernacular in place of classical Chinese, and Chen Duxiu followed with “On Literary Revolution”, launching the literary revolution. After Lu Xun published the vernacular story “Diary of a Madman” in 1918, New Youth switched entirely to vernacular and vernacular literature rose quickly.

events.title: Constitutional Protection Movement
events.short: In 1917 Sun Yat-sen formed a military government in Guangzhou to defend the Provisional Constitution and parliament; sidelined by southwestern warlords, the movement failed in 1918.
events.detail: After Yuan Shikai died in 1916, Li Yuanhong succeeded as president and Duan Qirui became premier, holding real power in the Beijing government. In 1917, over whether to declare war on Germany in World War I, President Li and Premier Duan fell into the “Presidential Office versus State Council dispute”. After Li dismissed Duan, he summoned Zhang Xun to Beijing to mediate; Zhang instead used the chance to enter Beijing with his “pigtail army”, dissolved parliament and restored Puyi, but soon failed. After Duan regained control of the Beijing government, he refused to restore the Provisional Constitution and parliament. In July 1917 he led part of the navy south to Guangzhou and called members of parliament to an “Extraordinary Parliament”. In September the Extraordinary Parliament set up the Military Government of the Republic of China in Guangzhou and elected Sun Grand Marshal; troops were sent north and the movement began. But the southwestern warlords joined only to preserve and expand their own territories. In May 1918 the Guangxi clique and the Political Study Clique manipulated the Extraordinary Parliament into reorganizing the military government, replacing the grand marshal system with a collective directorate and sidelining Sun. Sun resigned as grand marshal in anger and left Guangzhou for Shanghai, saying in his resignation telegram: “The greatest scourge of our country is the contest for supremacy among military men; north and south are birds of a feather.” The movement failed. Its failure marked the end of the old democratic revolution led by the bourgeois democrats represented by Sun, who realized that relying on one warlord faction to defeat another would not work and began to seek a new revolutionary path.

events.title: Li Dazhao and the Spread of Marxism
events.short: After the October Revolution Li Dazhao published “The Victory of the Common People”, “The Victory of Bolshevism” and “My Marxist View”, becoming a pioneer of Marxism in China.
events.detail: Before the May Fourth Movement very few people in China knew of Marxism. The victory of the Russian October Socialist Revolution in 1917 showed a new direction to progressive Chinese searching for a way to save the nation: “the guns of the October Revolution brought us Marxism-Leninism”. Li Dazhao (1889–1927), courtesy name Shouchang, from Laoting, Hebei, studied in Japan in his youth and from 1918 was head of the Peking University library, later also a professor. He was the first in China to accept and spread Marxism. In 1918 he published “A Comparison of the French and Russian Revolutions”, “The Victory of the Common People”, “The Victory of Bolshevism” and other articles, warmly praising the October Revolution and declaring: “Look at the world of the future; it will surely be a world of the red flag.” In 1919 Li edited New Youth's special issue on Marxism and published “My Marxist View”, marking the start of a fairly systematic spread of Marxism in China. After the May Fourth Movement more and more progressive intellectuals began to study and promote Marxism, and Chen Duxiu also turned to it. In 1920 Chen Wangdao's complete Chinese translation of The Communist Manifesto was published in Shanghai. Marxists also debated opponents of Marxism, as in the “problems versus isms” controversy, widening Marxism's influence. In 1920 Li established an early communist group in Beijing, making an important contribution to founding the Communist Party of China. In April 1927 Li was arrested by the Fengtian warlord Zhang Zuolin and died heroically in Beijing, aged 38.

events.title: May Fourth Movement
events.short: In 1919 the Paris Peace Conference rejected China's just demands; on 4 May Beijing students marched shouting “Secure sovereignty abroad, punish traitors at home”, and China refused to sign.
events.detail: After World War I the victorious powers, including Britain, the United States, France and Japan, held a “peace conference” in Paris from January to June 1919. China, as one of the victors, sent delegates, who put forward just demands: abolition of the powers' privileges in China, cancellation of the “Twenty-One Demands”, and the return of Germany's rights in Shandong that Japan had seized during the war. They were refused, and the conference decided to transfer Germany's rights in Shandong to Japan. On 4 May 1919, more than three thousand students from over a dozen Beijing schools gathered before Tiananmen, shouting slogans such as “Secure sovereignty abroad, punish traitors at home” and marching in demonstration, demanding punishment of the pro-Japanese officials Cao Rulin, Zhang Zongxiang and Lu Zongyu. Angry students burned Cao Rulin's residence, Zhao Jialou, and beat Zhang Zongxiang. From 5 June, Shanghai workers staged large-scale strikes in support, the movement's center shifted from Beijing to Shanghai, and the working class stepped onto the political stage. The “three strikes” (of students, merchants and workers) then spread to more than twenty provinces and over a hundred cities. Under pressure from the people, the Beiyang government was forced to release arrested students and dismiss the three pro-Japanese officials. On 28 June the Chinese delegates refused to sign the treaty, a first victory for the movement. The May Fourth Movement was a thoroughgoing anti-imperialist and anti-feudal patriotic movement and the beginning of China's new-democratic revolution. The May Fourth spirit that took shape in it, of “patriotism, progress, democracy and science”, has had lasting influence, and 4 May was later designated Chinese Youth Day.

events.title: Early Communist Groups Established
events.short: In 1920, with Comintern help, Chen Duxiu founded the first early communist group in Shanghai; groups followed in Beijing, Wuhan, Changsha and elsewhere, including overseas.
events.detail: After the May Fourth Movement, Marxism spread widely in China and gradually merged with the Chinese labor movement, and conditions for founding a Communist Party matured. In spring 1920 the Comintern sent Voitinsky and others to China. In August 1920, with Comintern help, Chen Duxiu and others founded China's first early communist group in Shanghai, with members including Li Hanjun, Li Da, Chen Wangdao and Yu Xiusong, and Chen Duxiu as secretary. The Shanghai group coordinated and promoted party-building elsewhere. In October Li Dazhao and others founded an early communist group in Beijing. Groups were then established by Dong Biwu, Chen Tanqiu and others in Wuhan, Mao Zedong, He Shuheng and others in Changsha, Wang Jinmei, Deng Enming and others in Jinan, and Tan Pingshan and others in Guangzhou; groups also formed among Chinese students and overseas Chinese in Japan and France. Once founded, the groups studied and propagated Marxism in an organized way: they published periodicals such as the monthly The Communist and Marxist works such as the complete Chinese translation of The Communist Manifesto; went into factories to organize workers, ran night schools and helped set up trade unions; and founded the Socialist Youth League, training a body of revolutionary cadres. These activities promoted the merging of Marxism with the Chinese labor movement and prepared the ground ideologically and organizationally for the formal founding of the Communist Party of China. In July 1921 delegates from the groups held the First National Congress in Shanghai, proclaiming the Party's formal founding.

events.title: Lu Xun and The True Story of Ah Q
events.short: Lu Xun, the founder of modern Chinese literature, published the first modern vernacular story “Diary of a Madman” in 1918 and later The True Story of Ah Q, exposing flaws in the national character.
events.detail: Lu Xun (1881–1936), original name Zhou Shuren, was from Shaoxing, Zhejiang. In 1902 he went to Japan to study medicine, but later concluded that curing the nation's spirit mattered more than curing bodies, so he gave up medicine for literature, hoping to change the national spirit through writing. In 1918 he published “Diary of a Madman” in New Youth, for the first time under the pen name Lu Xun. It was the first vernacular short story in modern Chinese literature, and through the “madman” exposed the “man-eating” nature of feudal ethics. In 1921 he published the novella The True Story of Ah Q, creating Ah Q, a peasant who suffers every oppression yet consoles himself with “spiritual victory”. It deeply exposed weaknesses of the national spirit and reflected the Xinhai Revolution's failure to truly mobilize the peasantry. Lu Xun's stories were collected in Call to Arms (Nahan), Wandering (Panghuang) and other volumes; he also wrote the prose collection Morning Blossoms Plucked at Dusk and the prose-poem collection Wild Grass. In his later years he wrote mainly essays, using a sharp pen to criticize social ills and fight reactionary forces, and was hailed as the “soul of the nation”. In 1930 he helped found the League of Left-Wing Writers. Mao Zedong praised him as the “chief commander of China's cultural revolution”, whose “bones were the hardest”. Modern Chinese literature flourished as never before: Guo Moruo's poetry collection The Goddesses set a new style, and Mao Dun's Midnight, Ba Jin's Family, Lao She's Rickshaw Boy and Cao Yu's play Thunderstorm are all representative works of the period. They reflected the changes of the era and the people's suffering, advanced intellectual emancipation and laid the foundations of modern Chinese literature.

events.title: Founding of the Communist Party of China
events.short: The Party's First Congress opened in Shanghai on 23 July 1921, with its last session held on a boat on South Lake in Jiaxing, Zhejiang, proclaiming the founding of the Communist Party of China.
events.detail: After the May Fourth Movement, Marxism spread widely in China, early communist groups were set up in many places, and conditions were ripe to found a unified national Communist Party. On 23 July 1921 the First National Congress of the Communist Party of China opened at 106 Wangzhi Road (now 76 Xingye Road) in the Shanghai French Concession. Thirteen delegates attended, representing more than 50 Party members nationwide: Mao Zedong, Dong Biwu, Chen Tanqiu, He Shuheng, Wang Jinmei, Deng Enming, Li Da, Li Hanjun, Zhang Guotao, Liu Renjing, Chen Gongbo, Zhou Fohai and Bao Huiseng. The Comintern representatives Maring and Nikolsky also attended. Chen Duxiu and Li Dazhao did not attend for various reasons. On the evening of 30 July the meeting place was searched by French Concession police and the congress was interrupted; its last session moved to a pleasure boat on South Lake in Jiaxing, Zhejiang. The congress adopted the Party's first program, named it the “Communist Party of China”, and set its goals as overthrowing bourgeois rule, establishing a dictatorship of the proletariat, abolishing class distinctions and realizing communism, with organizing and leading the labor movement as its central task. It elected the Central Bureau, with Chen Duxiu as secretary. The founding of the Party was an epoch-making event in Chinese history: the Chinese revolution now had a strong leading core and a completely new look. 1 July was later designated the Party's founding anniversary. The site of the First Congress in Shanghai and the Red Boat on South Lake in Jiaxing are important revolutionary memorials.

sources.title: Wikipedia (Chinese) - First National Congress of the Communist Party of China

events.title: Early Peasant Movement in Zhejiang and Guangdong
events.short: After its founding the Party began leading peasant movements, from the Yanqian Peasant Association in Zhejiang (1921) to Peng Pai's peasant associations in Haifeng, Guangdong (1922).
events.detail: China was a large agrarian country in which peasants were the great majority of the population. After the Communist Party was founded, while concentrating on the labor movement it also began organizing peasant associations and leading peasant movements. In September 1921, through the efforts of Communists such as Shen Dingyi, the Yanqian Peasant Association was founded in Yanqian Village, Xiaoshan, Zhejiang, the first new-style peasant organization under Communist leadership. It led a rent-reduction struggle that peasants in more than 80 nearby villages joined, but was soon suppressed. In 1922 the Communist Peng Pai began a peasant movement in his home county of Haifeng, Guangdong. Peng Pai (1896–1929), from a landlord family, studied in Japan in his youth and on returning publicly burned the land deeds he had inherited and went to live in the countryside. In July 1922 he founded the first secret peasant association in Haifeng, which grew into the Haifeng County General Peasant Association with over 100,000 members, leading struggles for rent reduction and against exorbitant taxes. After the First Kuomintang–Communist Cooperation began in 1924, a Peasant Movement Training Institute was opened in Guangzhou, headed in turn by Peng Pai, Mao Zedong and others, training many peasant-movement cadres. During the Northern Expedition peasant movements flourished in Hunan, Hubei, Jiangxi and elsewhere. The early peasant movement led the Party to see peasants as the main force of the Chinese revolution and built experience for the later land revolution. Mao Zedong called Peng Pai the “King of the Peasant Movement”; in 1927 he led the Hai-Lufeng Uprising, which set up China's first county-level soviet government, and he was killed in Shanghai in 1929.

events.title: Second Party Congress and Democratic Program
events.short: The Party's Second Congress met in Shanghai in July 1922 and for the first time put forward a clear anti-imperialist, anti-feudal democratic revolution program.
events.detail: After its founding the Party began exploring a revolutionary path suited to China's conditions. In early 1922 the Comintern held the First Congress of the Toilers of the Far East, which stated that the present task in Eastern countries was a national democratic revolution against imperialism and feudalism, and the Chinese Communist Party sent delegates. From 16 to 23 July 1922 the Party held its Second National Congress in Shanghai, attended by 12 delegates representing 195 Party members nationwide. The congress analyzed the nature of Chinese society, stating that China was a semi-colonial, semi-feudal country and that the revolution was a bourgeois democratic one. It reaffirmed the Party's ultimate goal of realizing communism as its maximum program, and drew up a minimum program for the democratic revolution stage: end internal strife, overthrow the warlords and establish peace at home; overthrow oppression by international imperialism and achieve the complete independence of the Chinese nation; and unify China as a true democratic republic. This was the first time the Party clearly put forward an anti-imperialist, anti-feudal democratic revolution program, pointing the way for the revolutionary struggles of China's peoples. The congress also raised the idea of a democratic united front, calling for the union of all revolutionary parties and bourgeois democrats in the country. It adopted the first Constitution of the Communist Party of China and decided to join the Comintern. Chen Duxiu was elected chairman of the Central Executive Committee. The Second Congress was an important achievement of the Party in its infancy.

events.title: Beijing–Hankou Railway Strike, February 7 Massacre
events.short: In February 1923 Beijing–Hankou Railway workers struck for a general union; Wu Peifu suppressed them by force in the “February 7 Massacre”, in which Lin Xiangqian and Shi Yang died heroically.
events.detail: After its founding the Party set up the China Labor Union Secretariat to lead the national labor movement in a concentrated way. Under Party organization and encouragement, a first upsurge of the labor movement swept the country from early 1922 to spring 1923; the Hong Kong seamen's strike and the Anyuan railway and mine workers' strike, led by Li Lisan, Liu Shaoqi and others, both won. On 1 February 1923 the Beijing–Hankou Railway General Union held its founding meeting in Zhengzhou, but was obstructed by force by the Zhili warlord Wu Peifu; the union was forced to move to Jiang'an in Hankou and decided on a general strike along the whole line under the slogan “Fight for freedom, fight for human rights”. On 4 February over thirty thousand railway workers went on strike. With the support of the imperialist powers, on 7 February Wu sent troops and police to crush the strikers bloodily at Changxindian, Zhengzhou, Jiang'an and elsewhere, killing 52, wounding over 300 and arresting over 40, in the “February 7 Massacre” that shocked China and the world. Lin Xiangqian, a Communist and chairman of the General Union's Jiang'an branch, was arrested; when his captors demanded that he order a return to work he refused and died heroically. Shi Yang, a Communist and lawyer who defended the workers, was also killed. After the massacre, the national labor movement entered a low tide. The Beijing–Hankou strike was the peak of the first upsurge of the labor movement. It showed the strength of the Chinese working class, and also led the Party to realize that the working class must unite all forces that could be united and build a broad revolutionary united front.

images.caption: February 7 Memorial Tower, Zhengzhou, Henan

events.title: Kuomintang First Congress and First United Front
events.short: In January 1924 the Kuomintang First Congress effectively set the policies of allying with Russia and the Communists and aiding workers and peasants, forming the First United Front.
events.detail: After the February 7 Massacre the Communist Party realized that defeating a powerful enemy required a broad revolutionary united front. Sun Yat-sen, after repeated setbacks, had also concluded that relying on warlords for revolution would not work; he resolved to seek a new path and received help from Soviet Russia and the Communists. In June 1923 the Party held its Third National Congress in Guangzhou and formally decided to cooperate with the Kuomintang led by Sun in a revolutionary united front, with Communists joining the Kuomintang as individuals while keeping the Party's political, ideological and organizational independence. In January 1924 the Kuomintang's First National Congress met in Guangzhou, attended by Communists including Li Dazhao, Mao Zedong and Lin Boqu. The manifesto it adopted gave the Three Principles of the People a new interpretation: nationalism stressed opposing imperialism and the equality of all peoples in China; democracy stressed that democratic rights belonged to ordinary people generally; and the people's livelihood rested on the principles of “equalizing land rights” and “regulating capital”. This New Three Principles of the People became the political basis of Kuomintang–Communist cooperation. The congress effectively established the three policies of “allying with Russia, allying with the Communists, and supporting workers and peasants”, and elected central leading bodies that included Communists. Thereafter, with Guangzhou as the center, the revolution advanced quickly and the labor and peasant movements revived, laying the foundation for the Northern Expedition. In March 1925 Sun died of illness in Beijing, leaving the testament: “The revolution has not yet succeeded; comrades must still strive.”

images.caption: Sun Yat-sen and others leaving the venue of the Kuomintang First Congress
images.author: Kuomintang

events.title: Founding of the Whampoa Military Academy
events.short: In May 1924, with Soviet and Communist help, Sun Yat-sen opened an army officers' academy at Whampoa, Guangzhou, with Chiang Kai-shek as president and Zhou Enlai heading political training.
events.detail: Sun Yat-sen had led the revolution for many years but, lacking his own revolutionary army, often relied on warlords and repeatedly failed. To build a true revolutionary army, in May 1924, with help from the Soviet Union and the Communist Party, Sun founded the Kuomintang Army Officers' Academy on Changzhou Island at Whampoa (Huangpu), Guangzhou, also called the “Whampoa Military Academy”. Sun served as its director-general, Chiang Kai-shek as president and Liao Zhongkai as Party representative; the Soviet Union sent military advisers to help with training and supplied arms and funds. Many Communists worked at the academy: Zhou Enlai became head of the political department in autumn 1924, and Yun Daiying, Xiao Chunu, Nie Rongzhen and Ye Jianying also served there. Its aim was “to create a revolutionary army to save China from destruction”, and the couplet beside its gate read: “Those seeking rank and wealth go elsewhere; those who fear death need not enter here.” It stressed military and political education equally. Many students were Communists and Communist Youth League members, such as Xu Xiangqian, Chen Geng, Zuo Quan and Lin Biao. The cadets formed the backbone of the National Revolutionary Army, helping put down the Guangzhou Merchants' Corps rebellion in 1924 and fighting two Eastern Expeditions against Chen Jiongming in 1925, winning repeated victories and unifying the Guangdong revolutionary base. In July 1925 the Guangzhou National Government was founded and its forces were then reorganized as the National Revolutionary Army. The academy trained many military and political figures for both parties and had far-reaching influence in modern Chinese history. Its old site in Guangzhou is now a memorial museum.
