events.title: Northern Expedition
events.short: In July 1926 the National Revolutionary Army marched north from Guangdong, defeated Wu Peifu and Sun Chuanfang and took Wuhan, Nanjing and Shanghai, extending revolutionary power to the Yangtze basin.
events.detail: In July 1925 the Guangzhou National Government was founded and then unified the Guangdong revolutionary base. At that time Beiyang warlords led by Wu Peifu, Sun Chuanfang and Zhang Zuolin each held their own regions. To overthrow Beiyang rule and unify the country, the National Government decided on a Northern Expedition. In July 1926 the National Revolutionary Army, 100,000 strong, swore an oath in Guangzhou to march north, with Chiang Kai-shek as commander-in-chief. The expedition concentrated its forces to defeat enemies one by one, attacking Wu Peifu first. The Independent Regiment led by Ye Ting, with Communists as its backbone, was the vanguard and fought bravely at the Battles of Dingsi Bridge and Heshengqiao, defeating Wu's main force; the Fourth Army, to which the regiment belonged, was hailed as the “Ironsides”. It then advanced into Jiangxi and, after fierce fighting, destroyed Sun Chuanfang's main force. In March 1927 Shanghai workers, led by Zhou Enlai and others, staged their Third Armed Uprising and took Shanghai in coordination with the Northern Expedition, and the army then took Nanjing. In a little over half a year it advanced from the Pearl River basin to the Yangtze basin, dealing the warlords' rule a heavy blow. Its victories owed much to Kuomintang–Communist cooperation and strong support from workers and peasants, whose movements rose quickly everywhere. At the end of 1926 the National Government moved to Wuhan. In early 1927 the people of Wuhan and Jiujiang recovered the British concessions, the first time in modern China that a concession was recovered by mass struggle. The Northern Expedition was an anti-imperialist, anti-feudal revolutionary war led jointly by the two parties, but contradictions within the revolutionary ranks grew sharper.

images.caption: Portrait of Ye Ting
Map of the Northern Expedition

events.title: April 12 Coup and Failure of the Great Revolution
events.short: On 12 April 1927 Chiang Kai-shek launched a coup in Shanghai, massacring Communists and revolutionary masses; on 15 July Wang Jingwei split with the Communists and the Great Revolution failed.
events.detail: During the Northern Expedition, revolutionary movements of workers and peasants rose quickly, touching the basic interests of the imperialist powers, big landlords and the big bourgeoisie. Chiang Kai-shek and other Kuomintang right-wingers, backed by the imperialist powers and Jiangsu–Zhejiang financiers, decided to betray the revolution. On 12 April 1927 Chiang launched a counter-revolutionary coup in Shanghai, seizing the arms of the workers' pickets, staging the Baoshan Road massacre and arresting and killing Communists and revolutionary masses on a large scale. Within three days more than three hundred people were killed, over five hundred arrested and over five thousand went missing; Communists including Wang Shouhua, Chen Yannian and Zhao Shiyan were killed one after another. On 18 April Chiang set up a rival National Government in Nanjing. On 28 April Li Dazhao was killed in Beijing by the Fengtian warlord Zhang Zuolin. Meanwhile the Party's General Secretary Chen Duxiu committed the error of Right opportunism, making only concessions to the Kuomintang. On 15 July the Wuhan National Government led by Wang Jingwei held a meeting to “split from the Communists”, formally broke with the Communist Party and then massacred Communists and revolutionary masses. The National Revolution (Great Revolution) jointly led by the two parties thus failed. By one count, from April 1927 to the first half of 1928, over 310,000 Communists and revolutionary masses were killed. Objectively the failure was due to the strength of the counter-revolutionary forces; subjectively, the Central Committee under Chen Duxiu made a Right opportunist error and gave up leadership of the proletariat, especially of the armed forces.

images.caption: Reactionary Kuomintang cliques massacring revolutionaries

events.title: Nanchang Uprising
events.short: On 1 August 1927 Zhou Enlai, He Long, Ye Ting, Zhu De, Liu Bocheng and others led the Nanchang Uprising, firing the first shot in armed resistance to the Kuomintang reactionaries.
events.detail: After the Great Revolution failed, the Kuomintang reactionaries' policy of bloody massacre provoked fierce resistance from the Communist Party and the revolutionary masses. Learning from the defeat the importance of independently holding armed forces, the Party decided to launch armed uprisings. In July 1927 the Central Committee decided to stage an uprising in Nanchang and set up a Front Committee headed by Zhou Enlai to lead it. The participants were mainly units that the Party controlled or influenced, including the National Revolutionary Army's 20th Army, the 24th Division of the 11th Army and the Nanchang Officers' Training Corps led by Zhu De, over 20,000 men in all. In the early hours of 1 August, led by Zhou Enlai, He Long, Ye Ting, Zhu De, Liu Bocheng and others, the rebels attacked the Kuomintang troops garrisoning Nanchang; after more than four hours of fighting they wiped out over three thousand defenders and took the city. Under the Central Committee's original plan, the rebel army then left Nanchang and marched south toward Guangdong. In the Chaozhou–Shantou area of Guangdong it was besieged by Kuomintang troops and its main force was defeated; the remnants, led by Zhu De and Chen Yi, later went up Jinggangshan and joined the forces led by Mao Zedong. The Nanchang Uprising fired the first shot of armed resistance to the Kuomintang reactionaries, marking the start of the Party's independent leadership of armed struggle and of building a people's army. In 1933 the Provisional Central Government of the Chinese Soviet Republic designated 1 August as the founding anniversary of the Chinese Workers' and Peasants' Red Army; it later became Army Day of the People's Liberation Army.

images.caption: Former headquarters of the Nanchang Uprising
The Nanchang Uprising (painting)

events.title: August 7 Conference and Jinggangshan Base
events.short: The August 7 Conference of 1927 set a policy of land revolution and armed resistance; after the Autumn Harvest Uprising Mao Zedong led his troops into Jinggangshan and built the first rural base.
events.detail: After the Great Revolution failed, the Communist Party faced a grave test of survival. On 7 August 1927 the Central Committee held an emergency meeting in Hankou, the “August 7 Conference”. It corrected Chen Duxiu's Right opportunist errors, removed him from leadership, set the general policy of land revolution and armed resistance to the Kuomintang reactionaries, and decided to launch Autumn Harvest Uprisings in Hunan, Hubei, Guangdong and Jiangxi. At the meeting Mao Zedong put forward the famous thesis that “political power grows out of the barrel of a gun”. Afterwards Mao returned to Hunan as the Central Committee's special envoy to lead the Autumn Harvest Uprising on the Hunan–Jiangxi border. It broke out on 9 September, the troops raising the banner of the “Workers' and Peasants' Revolutionary Army”. After setbacks on the way to attack Changsha, Mao decisively changed the plan and led the troops toward the countryside, where enemy control was weak. At the end of September the force reached Sanwan Village in Yongxin, Jiangxi, and was reorganized in the “Sanwan Reorganization”, which established the principles of “building Party branches at company level” and “the Party commands the gun”. In October Mao led the troops to Maoping in Ninggang, in the Jinggangshan area, where they waged guerrilla war, mobilized the masses to attack local despots and divide the land, and set up workers' and peasants' political power, creating China's first rural revolutionary base, the Jinggangshan base. Its creation opened a new path for the Chinese revolution: encircling the cities from the countryside and seizing power by armed force.

images.caption: Portrait of Mao Zedong

events.title: Jinggangshan Meeting and Armed Separatist Regime
events.short: In April 1928 Zhu De and Chen Yi's troops joined Mao Zedong's at Jinggangshan to form the Fourth Red Army, and Mao summed up the idea of an “armed separatist regime of workers and peasants”.
events.detail: After the Nanchang Uprising failed, Zhu De and Chen Yi led the remnants through the border areas of Fujian, Guangdong, Jiangxi and Hunan, and in January 1928 launched the Southern Hunan Uprising, setting up soviet governments in several counties. In April 1928 their forces joined Mao Zedong's Workers' and Peasants' Revolutionary Army at Longshi in Ninggang on Jinggangshan, the “Meeting at Jinggangshan”. The two forces merged into the Fourth Army of the Chinese Workers' and Peasants' Revolutionary Army, soon renamed the Fourth Army of the Chinese Workers' and Peasants' Red Army, with Zhu De as commander and Mao Zedong as Party representative, over 10,000 men in all. The Fourth Red Army repeatedly broke Kuomintang “suppression” and “joint suppression” campaigns, and the base kept growing. In the struggle the Red Army summed up the sixteen-character guerrilla formula: “When the enemy advances, we retreat; when the enemy halts, we harass; when the enemy tires, we attack; when the enemy retreats, we pursue”, and drew up the “Three Main Rules of Discipline and Six Points for Attention” (later developed into the “Three Main Rules of Discipline and Eight Points for Attention”). Mao summed up the base's experience in “Why Is It That Red Political Power Can Exist in China?” and “The Struggle in the Jinggang Mountains”, advancing the idea of an “armed separatist regime of workers and peasants”. In January 1929 Mao and Zhu led the main force of the Fourth Red Army into southern Jiangxi and western Fujian, opening up the Central Revolutionary Base. The Jinggangshan struggle gave rise to the Jinggangshan spirit: “firm conviction and arduous struggle, seeking truth from facts and blazing new paths, relying on the masses and daring to win”.

events.title: Northeast Flag Replacement and Nominal Unification
events.short: In 1928 the Northern Expedition entered Beijing, Zhang Zuolin was killed by a Japanese bomb, and in December Zhang Xueliang's “Northeast Flag Replacement” nominally unified China under Nanjing.
events.detail: In April 1927 Chiang Kai-shek founded the National Government in Nanjing. While “splitting from and purging the Communists” and suppressing worker and peasant movements, it continued the Northern Expedition. In April 1928 Chiang allied with regional power-holders such as Feng Yuxiang, Yan Xishan and Li Zongren, and attacked the Fengtian warlord Zhang Zuolin with four army groups. In June the expedition reached the Beijing–Tianjin area, and Zhang was forced out of Beijing and back to the Northeast. As Zhang retreated by train beyond the Great Wall, Japan's Kwantung Army blew up his train at Huanggutun near Shenyang; he was gravely wounded and soon died, in the “Huanggutun Incident”. His son Zhang Xueliang succeeded as Commander-in-Chief of Northeast Security. Despite Japanese obstruction and threats, on 29 December 1928 he telegraphed that the Northeast would “abide by the Three Principles of the People, obey the National Government, and change flags”, the “Northeast Flag Replacement”. It marked the end of Beiyang warlord rule and the nominal unification of China under the Nanjing government, and also frustrated Japan's plot to split off the Northeast. But conflicts among the Kuomintang's new warlords remained sharp, and each faction kept its own army. From 1929 to 1930 Chiang fought several wars with regional leaders such as Feng Yuxiang, Yan Xishan and Li Zongren, the largest being the Central Plains War of 1930, which Chiang won. The Nanjing government imposed one-party rule at home, suppressing Communists and revolutionary masses, while also carrying out some economic construction, such as the 1935 currency reform that unified the currency.

events.title: Gutian Conference
events.short: The Fourth Red Army's Ninth Party Congress met at Gutian, Fujian, in December 1929, establishing the principles of building the Party ideologically and the army politically.
events.detail: In January 1929 Mao Zedong and Zhu De led the main force of the Fourth Red Army out of Jinggangshan toward southern Jiangxi and western Fujian, opening a new base. Because the Red Army consisted mainly of peasants and soldiers from old armies, mistaken ideas existed in the Party and army: a purely military viewpoint, ultra-democracy, disregard of organization, absolute egalitarianism, roving-rebel thinking and remnants of warlordism. In September 1929 the Central Committee sent the Fourth Army's Front Committee a letter of instruction (the “September Letter”). On 28–29 December 1929 the Ninth Party Congress of the Fourth Red Army met at Gutian Village, Shanghang County, Fujian, known as the “Gutian Conference”. Chen Yi presided and Mao Zedong gave the political report; the congress adopted the Gutian Conference Resolution drafted by Mao, whose first part is the famous “On Correcting Mistaken Ideas in the Party”. The resolution analyzed the manifestations, sources and remedies of non-proletarian ideas in the Party and army, stressed building the Party with proletarian ideology, and established the principles of building the Party ideologically and the army politically. It set out the nature, purpose and tasks of the Red Army, stating that it was an armed body carrying out the political tasks of the revolution and must obey the Communist Party absolutely, and made clear the principle of the Party's absolute leadership over the army. The congress elected a new Front Committee, with Mao Zedong as secretary. The Gutian Conference was an important milestone in the history of Party and Red Army building, and its resolution became a programmatic document for both. The meeting site at Gutian, Shanghang, Fujian, is a nationally protected historic site.

events.title: Mukden Incident
events.short: On 18 September 1931 Japanese troops staged the Liutiaohu Incident and attacked Shenyang; with no resistance ordered, all three northeastern provinces fell in under six months.
events.detail: In 1927 Japan held the “Eastern Conference”, which set a policy of separating Manchuria and Mongolia from China. On the night of 18 September 1931 Japan's Kwantung Army blew up a section of the South Manchuria Railway near Liutiaohu on the northern outskirts of Shenyang, falsely blaming Chinese troops, and used this as a pretext for a surprise attack on the Northeast Army's Beidaying barracks and for shelling Shenyang. Because Chiang Kai-shek held to the policy of “first internal pacification, then resistance to foreign aggression”, the Northeast Army was ordered not to resist and its main force withdrew inside the Great Wall; Japanese troops took Shenyang the next day. They then swiftly occupied Jilin and Heilongjiang, and by February 1932 all three northeastern provinces had fallen, leaving over thirty million compatriots under occupation. The incident was the start of Japan's war of aggression against China, and of China's partial resistance. Northeastern soldiers and civilians rose up: Ma Zhanshan's troops fought the Japanese at the Heilongjiang (Nenjiang) Bridge; patriotic officers, soldiers and civilians formed anti-Japanese forces such as the Northeast Volunteer Armies, and the Communist Party later organized the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army, in which heroes such as Yang Jingyu, Zhao Yiman and Zhao Shangzhi carried on a long, hard struggle. A national movement to resist Japan and save the nation arose, with student strikes and petitions, workers' strikes and merchants' boycotts of Japanese goods. The League of Nations sent the Lytton Commission; its report recognized the Northeast as Chinese territory but also proposed “international joint administration”.

events.title: Chinese Soviet Republic Provisional Government
events.short: In November 1931 the First National Soviet Congress met at Ruijin and set up the Provisional Central Government of the Chinese Soviet Republic, with Mao Zedong as chairman.
events.detail: In 1930–1931 soldiers and civilians of the Central Revolutionary Base, under Mao Zedong and Zhu De, defeated three large Kuomintang “encirclement and suppression” campaigns in a row, and the base grew and consolidated. Meanwhile other bases, including the Hubei–Henan–Anhui, Hunan–Hubei–Western Hunan, Fujian–Zhejiang–Jiangxi and Hunan–Jiangxi bases, also developed. To build a unified national Red regime, the First National Congress of Chinese Soviets met at Yeping, Ruijin, Jiangxi, on 7 November 1931. It announced the founding of the Provisional Central Government of the Chinese Soviet Republic, with Ruijin as its capital, and elected Mao Zedong chairman of the Central Executive Committee and of the Council of People's Commissars, Xiang Ying and Zhang Guotao vice-chairmen, and Zhu De chairman of the Central Revolutionary Military Commission. The congress adopted the Constitutional Outline of the Chinese Soviet Republic, which defined it as a state of the democratic dictatorship of workers and peasants. The provisional government set up ministries and commissions, founded a state bank, issued currency and carried out economic, cultural and educational work. This was the Communist Party's first attempt at governing in part of the country, and it gave valuable experience for later building people's government. Under its leadership land revolution was carried out in the Soviet areas, peasants received land and their enthusiasm for production rose greatly, and officials were honest and public-spirited: “Good Soviet cadres bring their own food to work.” In 1934, after the failure of the Fifth Encirclement Campaign, the Central Red Army was forced to begin the Long March and the government left Ruijin.

events.title: January 28 Incident and Founding of Manchukuo
events.short: On 28 January 1932 Japanese troops attacked Shanghai and the 19th Route Army resisted, the “January 28 Incident”; in March Japan set up the puppet state of Manchukuo under Puyi.
events.detail: After the Mukden Incident, Japan stirred up trouble in Shanghai to divert international attention from its occupation of the Northeast. On the night of 28 January 1932 Japanese troops attacked Zhabei in Shanghai, the January 28 Incident. The Kuomintang's 19th Route Army stationed in Shanghai, under commander-in-chief Jiang Guangnai and army commander Cai Tingkai, rose to resist, and Zhang Zhizhong's Fifth Army later came to reinforce. Chinese troops fought stubbornly, and the Japanese were forced to send reinforcements several times and replace their commander three times. Because the National Government held to a policy of compromise, and because Japanese troops landed at Liuhe and threatened to outflank them, the Chinese forces were forced to withdraw. In May the government signed the Shanghai Ceasefire Agreement with Japan. The Shanghai resistance dealt a heavy blow to Japanese arrogance and inspired the nation's anti-Japanese enthusiasm. Meanwhile Japan hastened to set up a puppet regime in the Northeast. In March 1932 it installed Puyi, the last Qing emperor, in Changchun as head of the puppet state of Manchukuo, with Changchun as its “New Capital”; Puyi was “Chief Executive”, becoming “Emperor” in 1934. All real power in Manchukuo was in the hands of the Kwantung Army, and it was an instrument of Japanese rule; the people of the Northeast suffered long colonial rule and cruel enslavement. Japan also sent large numbers of “development group” settlers to the Northeast and set up Unit 731 in Harbin to conduct biological warfare research and human experiments, committing monstrous crimes. The League of Nations Assembly passed a resolution not recognizing Manchukuo, and Japan then announced its withdrawal from the League.

events.title: Start of the Long March and Xiang River Battle
events.short: After the failure of the Fifth Encirclement Campaign the Central Red Army began the Long March in October 1934; at the Battle of the Xiang River it suffered heavy losses, falling to just over 30,000.
events.detail: The growth of the Red Army and its bases alarmed the Kuomintang. From October 1930 it launched four large-scale military “encirclement and suppression” campaigns against the Central Revolutionary Base, all defeated by the Red Army. In September 1933 Chiang Kai-shek assembled a million troops for a fifth campaign against all the revolutionary bases, sending 500,000 against the Central Base and using “blockhouse” tactics. By then the Party's Provisional Central Committee, headed by Bo Gu, had moved from Shanghai into the Central Base, and Otto Braun (Li De), the Comintern military adviser, held command of the Red Army. They followed a “Left” adventurist military line, fighting a war of attrition against a well-equipped enemy, and the Red Army suffered severe losses; the fifth campaign was lost. In October 1934 the Central Committee and the main force of the Central Red Army, over 86,000 men, were forced to leave the Central Base from Ruijin, Yudu and other places on a strategic transfer, the Long March. Because the “Left” leaders also committed errors of flight in the transfer, after breaking through three Kuomintang blockade lines the army fought a bloody battle with the enemy at the Xiang River around Quanzhou and Xing'an, Guangxi, from late November to early December 1934. It was the most harrowing battle of the Long March: the Red Army crossed the Xiang in the end, but at a terrible price. The Central Red Army fell from over 80,000 at the start to a little over 30,000, and the 34th Division was almost wiped out; its commander Chen Shuxiang, wounded and captured, died by tearing out his own intestines. The heavy losses at the Xiang River brought the commanders' and soldiers' dissatisfaction with the “Left” leadership to a peak.

events.title: Zunyi Conference
events.short: In January 1935 the Central Committee met at Zunyi and established Mao Zedong's leadership of the Party and Red Army, a turning point of life-and-death importance in Party history.
events.detail: After the Battle of the Xiang River, Bo Gu, Otto Braun and others still insisted on joining the Second and Sixth Army Groups in western Hunan, though the enemy had massed heavy forces on the way. At this critical moment Mao Zedong proposed changing the original plan and marching into Guizhou, where Kuomintang control was weak. In December 1934 the Central Committee held meetings at Tongdao, Hunan, and Liping, Guizhou, and accepted his proposal. In January 1935 the Red Army forced a crossing of the Wu River and took Zunyi. From 15 to 17 January 1935 the Central Committee held an enlarged Politburo meeting at Zunyi, the “Zunyi Conference”. It dealt with the decisive military and organizational questions of the time, criticized the military errors of Bo Gu and Otto Braun, affirmed Mao's correct military views, elected Mao to the Politburo Standing Committee and removed Bo and Braun from supreme military command. Afterwards Zhang Wentian replaced Bo as the Party's top responsible person, and soon a new three-man military command group of Mao Zedong, Zhou Enlai and Wang Jiaxiang was formed. At an extremely critical juncture the conference saved the Party, the Red Army and the Chinese revolution, and in effect established Mao's leadership of the Party Central Committee and the Red Army. It was the first time the Party independently applied the basic principles of Marxism to resolve its own line, policies and tactics, marking its passage from infancy to maturity and a turning point of life-and-death importance in Party history. After Zunyi the Red Army, under Mao and others, moved toward victory. The conference site in Zunyi, Guizhou, is a nationally protected historic site.

images.caption: Site of the Zunyi Conference

events.title: Four Crossings of the Chishui and Luding Bridge
events.short: After Zunyi, Mao Zedong directed the Red Army across the Chishui four times, the Jinsha and Dadu rivers and Luding Bridge, and over snow mountains and grasslands, shaking off its pursuers.
events.detail: After the Zunyi Conference the Red Army was reorganized and its fighting power rose. From late January to late March 1935 Mao Zedong directed the Central Red Army around the Sichuan–Guizhou–Yunnan border, feinting east and striking west, crossing the Chishui four times, threatening Guiyang and Kunming, drawing in and destroying enemy troops on the move and upsetting the Kuomintang's pursuit plans. In early May the Red Army skillfully crossed the Jinsha River (upper Yangtze), escaping encirclement by hundreds of thousands of enemy troops. In late May it reached Anshunchang on the Dadu River, where seventeen heroes crossed in a small boat and forced the river. With too few boats for the main force, the Red Army marched hard along the west bank, covering 120 kilometers in a day and a night to reach Luding Bridge. The bridge was formed of thirteen iron chains, its planks removed by the enemy, and twenty-two assault troops climbed along the chains under fire to the far bank and took the bridge. In June the Red Army crossed the perpetually snow-covered Jiajin Mountain and joined the Fourth Front Army at Mougong. Zhang Guotao then opposed the Central Committee's northward course, and the Central Committee led the First and Third Army Groups north. In August the Red Army entered the vast grasslands, where many soldiers gave their lives; it came out through extraordinary endurance and in September broke through the natural barrier of Lazikou. On the Long March the Red Army crossed eighteen mountain ranges, five of them perpetually snow-capped, and twenty-four rivers, achieving a miracle in human history. Mao wrote the poem “The Long March”: “The Red Army fears not the trials of the distant march; to them the thousand mountains and rivers are nothing.”

events.title: North China Incident and December 9th Movement
events.short: In 1935 Japan staged the North China Incident, promoting “autonomy” of five northern provinces; on 9 December Beiping students marched to resist Japan, raising a new national upsurge.
events.detail: After occupying the Northeast, Japan reached out for North China. In January 1933 Japanese troops took Shanhaiguan, then Rehe, and attacked the passes of the Great Wall. Chinese troops resisted and fought the Japanese along the Great Wall at Xifengkou, Gubeikou and elsewhere. In May the National Government signed the Tanggu Truce with Japan, in effect acquiescing in Japan's occupation of the Northeast and Rehe. In 1935 Japan stepped up its aggression in North China, extracting most of the sovereignty in Hebei and Chahar through the He–Umezu and Qin–Doihara agreements and promoting “autonomy of the five northern provinces” in an attempt to split North China off as a second “Northeast”, the “North China Incident”. In November Japan installed the collaborator Yin Rugeng to set up the “East Hebei Anti-Communist Autonomous Council” in Tongxian. The Chinese nation faced an unprecedented crisis of survival: “The whole of North China has no room left for a quiet desk.” On 9 December 1935, under the leadership of the Party's Beiping temporary work committee, several thousand students from Beiping universities and middle schools marched in demonstration, shouting “Down with Japanese imperialism” and “Stop the civil war and unite against foreign aggression”. The December 9th Movement drew responses across the country, raising a new national upsurge of resistance to Japan. In the same year the Party issued the August 1st Declaration calling for an end to civil war and united resistance; in December the Central Committee held the Wayaobao Conference, setting the policy of building an anti-Japanese national united front. The movement advanced the awakening of the Chinese nation and marked a new stage in the anti-Japanese national salvation movement.

events.title: Nie Er Composes “March of the Volunteers”
events.short: In 1935 “March of the Volunteers”, words by Tian Han and music by Nie Er, was sung across China as a film theme song, and later became the national anthem of the People's Republic.
events.detail: After the Mukden Incident the Chinese nation faced a grave crisis; encouraged by the Communist Party, revolutionary art and literature flourished, and left-wing artists produced many works on resisting Japan and saving the nation. Nie Er (1912–1935), original name Nie Shouxin, was born in Kunming, Yunnan, loved music from childhood, went to Shanghai in 1930, joined left-wing musical activities and in 1933 joined the Communist Party. He composed over thirty songs including “Graduation Song” and “Song of the Newspaper Boy”. In 1934 the playwright Tian Han wrote the lyrics for the theme song of the film Children of Troubled Times, and was soon arrested by the Kuomintang authorities. In early 1935 Nie volunteered to set the song to music. The film was released in May 1935, and its theme song “March of the Volunteers”, with its opening “Arise! You who refuse to be slaves! With our flesh and blood, let us build our new Great Wall”, expressed in a stirring, majestic melody the Chinese nation's unyielding spirit of resistance. It spread quickly across the country and became a bugle call of the resistance movement. In July 1935 Nie drowned while swimming off the coast at Fujisawa, Japan, aged only 23. During the War of Resistance the song was sung widely at home and abroad, inspiring the Chinese people's heroic resistance. In September 1949 the first plenary session of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference decided that, until a national anthem was formally adopted, “March of the Volunteers” would serve as the anthem; in 1982 the National People's Congress formally confirmed it, in 2004 it was written into the Constitution, and in 2017 the NPC Standing Committee passed the National Anthem Law. Nie Er's tomb is at Xishan, Kunming, Yunnan.

events.title: Three Red Army Forces Unite; Long March Ends
events.short: In October 1935 the Central Red Army reached Wuqi in northern Shaanxi; in October 1936 the three main Red Army forces met in Gansu, ending the Long March.
events.detail: In September 1935, after the main force of the Central Red Army broke through Lazikou, the leadership learned from newspapers at Hadapu, Gansu, that there were Red Army forces and a base in northern Shaanxi, and the Central Committee decided to go there. The troops were reorganized as the Shaanxi–Gansu Detachment of the Chinese Workers' and Peasants' Red Army, with Peng Dehuai as commander and Mao Zedong as political commissar. On 19 October 1935 the Central Committee led the Central Red Army to Wuqi in the Shaanxi–Gansu revolutionary base and joined the northern Shaanxi Red Army, ending the Central Red Army's Long March of a year and 25,000 li (about 12,500 km). The Central Red Army had left with over 80,000 men and reached northern Shaanxi with only a little over 7,000. In November the Red Army won the Battle of Zhiluozhen, laying a foundation for the Party to place the national revolution's base in the northwest. Meanwhile Zhang Guotao led the Fourth Front Army south into Sichuan and Xikang, was badly defeated, and was forced to abolish his rival “Central Committee”; in July 1936 he marched north together with the Second Front Army formed from the Second and Sixth Army Groups. In October 1936 the Second and Fourth Front Armies joined the First Front Army at Huining and Jiangtaipu (now in Xiji, Ningxia), Gansu, marking the end of the Long March. The Long March was a great miracle in human history: with firm ideals and tenacious will the Red Army overcame countless hardships, preserved and tempered the revolutionary core, moved the revolution's base to the northwest and laid the foundation for the War of Resistance and the revolution's victory. Mao Zedong said: “The Long March is a manifesto, a propaganda force, a seeding machine.”

events.title: Xi'an Incident
events.short: On 12 December 1936 Zhang Xueliang and Yang Hucheng detained Chiang Kai-shek in Xi'an to press him to resist Japan; settled peacefully, it turned China from civil war to resistance.
events.detail: After the North China Incident the national crisis deepened, and calls across the country to end civil war and unite against Japan grew louder. Inspired by the Communist Party's policy of an anti-Japanese national united front, Zhang Xueliang, commander of the Northeast Army, and Yang Hucheng, commander of the Northwest Army, who had been sent to “suppress” the Red Army in the northwest, made a truce with the Red Army and repeatedly urged Chiang Kai-shek to ally with the Communists against Japan. Chiang, however, held to “first internal pacification, then resistance to foreign aggression” and obstinately refused. On 12 December 1936, after repeated remonstrances failed, Zhang and Yang staged a “military remonstrance”, detaining Chiang at the Huaqing Pool in Lintong and telegraphing the nation eight anti-Japanese demands, including reorganizing the Nanjing government, ending all civil war and immediately freeing arrested patriotic leaders: the “Xi'an Incident”. Putting national interests first, the Communist Party favored a peaceful settlement and sent Zhou Enlai and others to Xi'an to negotiate. Through the efforts of all sides Chiang accepted conditions including “halting the suppression of the Communists and uniting with the Red Army to resist Japan”, and the incident was settled peacefully. On 25 December Zhang accompanied Chiang from Xi'an; on returning to Nanjing he was detained and placed under long house arrest, and Yang Hucheng was later also imprisoned and was killed in 1949. The peaceful settlement became a pivot of the situation: the ten years of civil war largely ended, domestic peace was achieved at first, and the two parties began their Second Cooperation.

events.title: Marco Polo Bridge Incident
events.short: On 7 July 1937 Japanese troops, claiming a soldier had gone missing, attacked Wanping and the Marco Polo Bridge; Chinese defenders resisted, and the incident began China's all-out War of Resistance.
events.detail: On the evening of 7 July 1937 Japanese troops stationed at Fengtai, southwest of Beiping, held military exercises near the Marco Polo Bridge and, claiming that a soldier had “gone missing”, demanded to enter Wanping town to search, which Chinese troops sternly refused. The well-prepared Japanese then attacked Wanping and the bridge, and the Chinese defenders, the regiment of Ji Xingwen of the 37th Division of the 29th Army, resisted. This was the incident that shocked China and the world, known as the July 7th Incident or Marco Polo Bridge Incident. It marked the start of Japan's long-planned full-scale war of aggression against China and of the whole nation's resistance. The day after, the Communist Party telegraphed: “Peiping and Tianjin are in peril! North China is in peril! The Chinese nation is in peril! Only resistance by the whole nation is our way out!” On 17 July Chiang Kai-shek said at Lushan that “if war once begins, there will be no distinction between north and south, old and young; everyone will have the responsibility of defending the land and resisting, and must resolve to sacrifice everything”. In late July Japanese troops launched a general attack on Beiping and Tianjin, and Deputy Army Commander Tong Linge and Division Commander Zhao Dengyu died heroically at Nanyuan. By the end of July Beiping and Tianjin had fallen. In September the Kuomintang's Central News Agency published the Communist Party's declaration on Kuomintang–Communist cooperation, and Chiang made a statement in effect recognizing the Communist Party's legal status, marking the formal formation of the anti-Japanese national united front based on cooperation of the two parties. The nationwide resistance began.

events.title: Battle of Shanghai
events.short: On 13 August 1937 Japanese forces attacked Shanghai and Chinese troops fought back for three months, defeating Japan's boast of conquering China in three months; Shanghai fell in November.
events.detail: After the Marco Polo Bridge Incident, Japan, seeking to force the National Government to submit, spread the fighting to China's economic center, Shanghai. On 9 August 1937 a Japanese officer who forced his way with troops into the cordon around Shanghai's Hongqiao Airport was shot dead by Chinese guards, and Japan used this as a pretext to send large reinforcements to Shanghai. On 13 August Japanese forces attacked and the Battle of Shanghai began. Chinese troops resisted, committing over 700,000 men in all, while Japan raised its force to over 200,000. The Chinese air force also fought bravely, shooting down Japanese aircraft in the air battle over Jianqiao on 14 August, a day later designated “Air Force Day”. With backward equipment, Chinese troops fought the Japanese to the death with flesh and blood. At the end of October they were ordered to withdraw, and Xie Jinyuan led over four hundred officers and men (known as the “Eight Hundred Heroes”) in holding the Sihang Warehouse on the north bank of Suzhou Creek to cover the main force's retreat, fighting alone for four days and nights; the girl scout Yang Huimin risked her life to bring them a national flag, raising the morale of soldiers and civilians nationwide. In early November Japanese troops landed at Jinshanwei on Hangzhou Bay and threatened the Chinese rear, and the Chinese were forced to withdraw along the whole front; Shanghai fell on 12 November. The three-month battle was one of the largest and most brutal of the war. It shattered Japan's arrogant plan to “conquer China in three months”, bought time to relocate factories, schools and offices from Shanghai and the coast to the interior, and showed the Chinese nation's united determination to resist to the end.

Sketch map of the Battle of Shanghai

events.title: Second United Front Established
events.short: After the Marco Polo Bridge Incident the Red Army was reorganized as the Eighth Route Army and New Fourth Army, and in September 1937 the Anti-Japanese National United Front was formally established.
events.detail: After the Xi'an Incident was settled peacefully the two parties began talks on cooperating against Japan. After the Marco Polo Bridge Incident, with the nation in a crisis of survival, each issued statements protesting Japanese aggression and stating its resistance stand, and the pace of cooperation quickened. On 15 July the Communist Central Committee handed the Kuomintang its Declaration on Kuomintang–Communist Cooperation, setting out three basic demands, to launch resistance by the whole nation, achieve democratic politics and improve the people's livelihood, and declaring that it would strive for the thorough realization of the Three Principles of the People, abandon the policy of armed uprisings to overthrow the Kuomintang regime and of confiscating landlords' land, abolish the Soviet government and reorganize the Red Army. In August the main Red Army force in northern Shaanxi was reorganized as the National Revolutionary Army's Eighth Route Army (later renamed the Eighteenth Army Group), with Zhu De as commander-in-chief and Peng Dehuai as deputy, and went to the North China front. In October the Red Army guerrilla forces in eight southern provinces were reorganized as the National Revolutionary Army's New Fourth Army, with Ye Ting as commander and Xiang Ying as deputy. On 22 September the Kuomintang's Central News Agency published the Declaration; on 23 September Chiang Kai-shek made a statement in effect recognizing the Communist Party's legal status. The Front brought the nation together in resistance, produced coordination between the frontal and behind-the-lines battlefields against the Japanese, and laid the political foundation for victory in the War of Resistance.

images.caption: Chiang Kai-shek
images.author: Office of the President of the Republic of China (portrait provided by Academia Historica)

events.title: Battle of Pingxingguan
events.short: In September 1937 the Eighth Route Army's 115th Division ambushed Japanese troops at Pingxingguan, Shanxi, killing over a thousand; the first major Chinese victory since all-out resistance began.
events.detail: After being reorganized as the Eighth Route Army, the Red Army went quickly to the North China front, fighting alongside Kuomintang forces on the frontal battlefield while also penetrating behind enemy lines to wage guerrilla war widely. In September 1937 the elite Itagaki Division (Fifth Division) of the Japanese army advanced into Shanxi, seeking to break through the Inner Great Wall line and take Taiyuan. The National Government's Second War Zone organized the Pingxingguan campaign, and the Eighth Route Army was ordered to cooperate. The 115th Division, under division commander Lin Biao and deputy commander Nie Rongzhen, laid an ambush on the steep ground on both sides of the road northeast of Pingxingguan. In the early morning of 25 September, the rear units and supply convoy of the Fifth Division's 21st Brigade entered the ambush zone and the Eighth Route Army suddenly attacked. It was the first major Chinese victory since the nationwide resistance began; it broke the myth that the Japanese army was invincible, lifted the spirits of soldiers and civilians and raised the prestige of the Communist Party and the Eighth Route Army. Afterwards the 120th Division ambushed Japanese troops at Yanmenguan and the 129th Division raided Yangmingbao airfield at night, burning over twenty Japanese aircraft and effectively supporting the Battle of Xinkou on the frontal front. In the Battle of Xinkou, Ninth Army commander Hao Mengling and other generals died heroically, a successful example of two-party cooperation against Japan. In November Taiyuan fell, regular warfare in North China, mainly by Kuomintang troops, essentially ended, and guerrilla warfare, led chiefly by the Communist Eighth Route Army, became primary.

images.caption: Eighth Route Army ambushing Japanese troops at Pingxingguan

events.title: Mao Yisheng Completes the Qiantang River Bridge
events.short: In 1937 Mao Yisheng completed the Qiantang River Bridge, the first modern double-deck road-and-rail bridge designed and built by Chinese; it was later blown up to hinder the Japanese advance.
events.detail: In the 1930s China urgently needed a bridge over the Qiantang River to link the Zhejiang–Jiangxi and Shanghai–Hangzhou railways. Nearly all large bridges in China had then been designed and built by foreigners, and the Qiantang's swift current, deep quicksand and tidal bore made bridge-building extremely hard; a popular saying held that “building a bridge over the Qiantang cannot be done”. The noted bridge engineer Mao Yisheng was appointed director of the bridge project office, in charge of design and construction. Mao Yisheng (1896–1989), from Zhenjiang, Jiangsu, earned a doctorate in engineering in the United States. During construction he drove piles with the “water-jet method”, using high-pressure water to wash away sand so that wooden piles sank to the riverbed; built piers on the riverbed with the “caisson method”; and erected steel girders by the “floating method”, using the rise and fall of the tide, overcoming many difficulties. In September 1937 the Qiantang River Bridge opened to traffic. It was the first modern double-deck road-and-rail bridge designed and built by Chinese, 1,453 meters long, with the road above and the railway below. In December 1937, as Japanese troops closed in on Hangzhou, Mao was ordered to blow up the bridge, only 89 days after it opened, to stop the Japanese advance south; in grief he wrote: “If we are sure to win the war, this bridge will surely be rebuilt.” After the war he oversaw its repair, and it reopened in full in 1953. The bridge is a milestone in Chinese bridge-building and showed the wisdom and strength of Chinese engineers. Mao later also took part in building the Wuhan Yangtze River Bridge and is hailed as the “father of modern Chinese bridges”.

events.title: Nanjing Massacre
events.short: After Japanese troops took Nanjing in December 1937, over six weeks they killed more than 300,000 Chinese civilians and disarmed soldiers in appalling atrocities.
events.detail: After the Battle of Shanghai, Japanese troops advanced on Nanjing in three columns. They took the city on 13 December 1937; the National Government had already announced the move of the capital to Chongqing, designated the wartime capital. After the occupation the Japanese army carried out a bloody massacre in and around the city lasting six weeks, killing Chinese civilians and disarmed soldiers by mass shooting, live burial, hacking and burning; the dead numbered over 300,000. Japanese troops also raped women on a massive scale, looted property and burned buildings. Japanese newspapers even openly reported a “killing contest” between two army second lieutenants. During the massacre more than a dozen foreigners who stayed in Nanjing, including the German John Rabe and the American Minnie Vautrin, organized the International Committee for the Nanjing Safety Zone, set up the Safety Zone and protected over 200,000 Chinese refugees. The American missionary John Magee filmed the Japanese atrocities, leaving valuable historical evidence. The Nanjing Massacre was one of the gravest crimes committed by Japan in its war of aggression against China and an appalling atrocity in the history of human civilization. After the war, the International Military Tribunal for the Far East and the Nanjing War Crimes Tribunal tried the main persons responsible, sentencing war criminals including Matsui Iwane and Tani Hisao to death. In 1985 the Memorial Hall of the Victims in Nanjing Massacre by Japanese Invaders opened. In 2014 the NPC Standing Committee designated 13 December each year as the National Memorial Day for Victims of the Nanjing Massacre. In 2015 the Nanjing Massacre Archives were inscribed in UNESCO's Memory of the World Register.

images.caption: Japanese troops burying Nanjing civilians alive
Newspaper report of the Japanese “killing contest”
images.author: Shinju Sato (佐藤振壽)

events.title: Battle of Taierzhuang
events.short: In March–April 1938 Li Zongren directed Chinese forces in fierce fighting at Taierzhuang, Shandong, killing over ten thousand Japanese troops, the largest victory on the front since the war began.
events.detail: After taking Nanjing, Japan sought to open the Tianjin–Pukou Railway and link its northern and southern battlefields by pincer attack on Xuzhou from north and south. In March 1938 the Seya Detachment of the Japanese 10th Division advanced south along the Tianjin–Pukou line while part of the Fifth Division moved west along the Jiaozhou–Jinan line, intending to meet at Taierzhuang and then attack Xuzhou. Taierzhuang, on the north bank of the Grand Canal in southern Shandong, was the gateway to Xuzhou and of great strategic importance. Li Zongren, commander of the Fifth War Zone, directed Chinese forces to meet the Japanese there. Earlier, Chinese troops had blocked part of the Fifth Division at Linyi, and at Tengxian Wang Mingzhang, commander of the Sichuan Army's 122nd Division, held the county seat to the death and died heroically, buying time for the victory. In late March the Japanese attacked Taierzhuang fiercely, and Sun Lianzhong's Second Army Group defended it in fierce street fighting, the two sides contesting every house in the town in extremely brutal combat. Division commander Chi Fengcheng led stubborn resistance and organized suicide squads for night raids. While the defenders held on, Tang Enbo's army corps struck from outside and cut off the Japanese retreat; in early April the Chinese counterattacked along the whole front, the Japanese suffered heavy losses and the remnants broke out and fled. Chinese forces killed over ten thousand Japanese troops, winning the biggest victory on the frontal front since the nationwide resistance began, blunting Japanese arrogance and raising the nation's confidence. Afterwards Japan massed large forces to surround Xuzhou, and the Chinese withdrew, losing the city in May.

images.caption: Li Zongren at Taierzhuang
Chinese troops fighting the Japanese at Taierzhuang

events.title: Mao Zedong Publishes On Protracted War
events.short: In May 1938 Mao Zedong published On Protracted War, refuting “defeatism” and “quick victory” theories and arguing that the war would be protracted and victory would belong to China.
events.detail: After the all-out resistance began, the Communist Party fully mobilized and relied on the masses and held to the line of total resistance. As Shanghai, Nanjing and other major cities fell one after another, a “theory of national subjugation” holding that China was bound to perish spread in the Kuomintang; after the victory at Taierzhuang, others promoted a “theory of quick victory”, holding that China could soon defeat Japan. To refute these mistaken views, in May–June 1938 Mao Zedong gave a long lecture at the Yan'an Anti-Japanese War Research Society, On Protracted War. Mao analyzed the basic features of both sides: Japan was a strong imperialist country, but its war was retrogressive and barbarous, its manpower and finances were insufficient, and it had little support; China was a weak semi-colonial, semi-feudal country, but lived in an age of progress, was large and rich in resources with many people and troops, and fought a just war that won much support. The War of Resistance would therefore be protracted, and final victory would belong to China. Mao predicted that it would pass through three stages, strategic defensive, strategic stalemate and strategic counter-offensive, the stalemate being the key stage in which China would turn from weak to strong and Japan from strong to weak. He also stated that “the richest source of the power to wage war lies in the masses of the people”, so a line of total resistance had to be followed, mobilizing the masses fully for a people's war. On Protracted War scientifically foresaw the course of the war, systematically set out the general strategy of protracted resistance, and was a programmatic document guiding the Chinese people to victory.

events.title: Huayuankou Dike Breach
events.short: In June 1938, to halt the Japanese advance, the National Government breached the Yellow River dike at Huayuankou, slowing the Japanese but causing a vast disaster in the flooded zone.
events.detail: After Xuzhou fell in May 1938, Japanese troops advanced west along the Longhai Railway, took Kaifeng and approached Zhengzhou, intending to go south along the Beijing–Hankou Railway to attack Wuhan. To stop their advance west and south, Chiang Kai-shek ordered Kuomintang troops in Henan to breach the Yellow River dikes, using water in place of troops. In June 1938 Kuomintang troops first failed to breach the dike at Zhaokou in Zhongmu, then breached the south-bank dike at Huayuankou north of Zhengzhou. The Yellow River poured out and flooded southeast, flowing through the Jialu, Ying and other rivers into the Huai River and inundating large areas in 44 counties and cities of Henan, Anhui and Jiangsu. The flood temporarily checked the Japanese advance, forced them to abandon the plan of going south along the Beijing–Hankou line against Wuhan and to move west along the Yangtze instead, buying time for the Battle of Wuhan; but it brought deep suffering to the people. 9 million (figures vary). The Yellow River then flowed south by a new course for nine years, creating a large “Yellow River flooded zone” in eastern Henan, northern Anhui and northern Jiangsu, where land turned to sand and floods, droughts and locusts were frequent. The National Government afterwards claimed the breach was caused by Japanese bombing. After the war, with United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration aid, work to close the breach began in 1946; the dike was closed in March 1947 and the river returned to its old course. The Huayuankou breach is a painful page of using water as a weapon in the war and remains disputed.

events.title: Battle of Wuhan and the Stalemate Stage
events.short: In 1938 about a million Chinese troops defended Wuhan for over four months, wearing down large Japanese forces; after Guangzhou and Wuhan fell, the war entered a stalemate stage.
events.detail: After Nanjing fell, the National Government moved its capital to Chongqing, but the military, political and economic center was in fact Wuhan, which became the center of national resistance. From June 1938 Japan massed about 400,000 troops in turn and advanced on Wuhan along both banks of the Yangtze and the northern foot of the Dabie Mountains. To defend Wuhan, China committed about a million troops, who fought the Japanese across a wide area of Anhui, Henan, Jiangxi and Hubei. In the Battle of Wanjialing in Jiangxi, Xue Yue directed Chinese forces in surrounding and badly mauling the Japanese 106th Division, a major victory. During the battle the National Government moved many factories, schools and supplies to the southwest rear area. In late October Japan took Guangzhou, and the three towns of Wuhan fell by the end of the month. The Battle of Wuhan lasted four and a half months and was one of the largest and longest of the war; Chinese troops, at heavy cost, wore down much of Japan's manpower, and Japan's strategy of quick decisive victory completely failed. After Guangzhou and Wuhan fell, Japan's lines were overstretched and its forces insufficient for large strategic offensives, and the war entered a strategic stalemate stage. Japan shifted toward political inducement of the National Government as its main policy, with military pressure secondary, and used most of its forces against the anti-Japanese bases behind its lines, so the behind-the-lines battlefield gradually became the main one. After Wuhan the government's political and military center moved to Chongqing, which suffered long “indiscriminate bombing” by Japan, but its people kept on resisting, showing an unyielding national spirit.

images.caption: Chinese troops fighting the Japanese at the Battle of Wanjialing, Jiangxi
images.author: 唐古樵

events.title: Bethune and Kotnis Aid China
events.short: The Canadian doctor Norman Bethune and the Indian doctor Dwarkanath Kotnis came to China to treat wounded resisters and both died at their posts, embodying a great spirit of internationalism.
events.detail: China's War of Resistance won the deep sympathy and warm support of people worldwide, and many foreign friends traveled great distances to help the Chinese people. Norman Bethune (1890–1939) was a Canadian Communist and a noted thoracic surgeon. In early 1938, sent by the Communist Parties of Canada and the United States, he led a medical team to China and, on reaching Yan'an, was received by Mao Zedong. He then went to the Shanxi–Chahar–Hebei Border Region as medical adviser to the military region, treating wounded and sick Eighth Route Army soldiers at the front. In October 1939 he cut a finger while operating on a wounded soldier, the wound became infected and turned to septicemia, and he died on 12 November in Tang County, Hebei. Mao wrote the essay “In Memory of Norman Bethune”, praising his spirit of “utter devotion to others without any thought of self”. In 1938 the Indian National Congress sent a medical mission to China; one of its members, Dr. Dwarkanath Kotnis (1910–1942), worked in Yan'an and the Shanxi–Chahar–Hebei Border Region, once working for seventy-two hours straight in a battle to treat the wounded, later became the first director of the Bethune International Peace Hospital and joined the Communist Party of China. In December 1942 Kotnis died of overwork in Tang County, Hebei, aged only 32. Mao wrote the elegiac couplet: “The army has lost a helping hand, the nation has lost a friend.” Other foreign friends, including the American journalists Edgar Snow and Agnes Smedley and the New Zealander Rewi Alley, also supported China's resistance in various ways. Bethune and Kotnis are buried at the North China Military Region Martyrs' Cemetery in Shijiazhuang, Hebei.

events.title: Xian Xinghai Composes the Yellow River Cantata
events.short: Written by Xian Xinghai in Yan'an in 1939 to lyrics by Guang Weiran, the Yellow River Cantata uses the river as a symbol of the Chinese nation and its unyielding resistance to Japan.
events.detail: Xian Xinghai (1905–1945) had ancestral roots in Panyu, Guangdong, and was born in Macao. He loved music from childhood. In 1929 he went to Paris on a work-study program to study composition and later entered the Paris Conservatoire. After returning to China in 1935 he threw himself into the anti-Japanese national salvation movement and wrote many songs for the cause, including Song of the National Salvation Army and On the Taihang Mountains. In 1938 he came to Yan'an, where he served as head of the music department of the Lu Xun Academy of Arts, and the next year he joined the Chinese Communist Party. In early 1939 the poet Guang Weiran crossed the Yellow River with an anti-Japanese theater troupe and wrote the long poem Yellow River Chant. Deeply moved on hearing it, Xian Xinghai, though ill, set it to music in six days in a cave dwelling in Yan'an. The Yellow River Cantata premiered on 13 April 1939 in the main hall of the Shaanbei Public School in Yan'an to a powerful response, and Mao Zedong applauded warmly after watching it. The cantata has eight movements, including Song of the Yellow River Boatmen, Ode to the Yellow River and Defend the Yellow River. It portrays the majesty of the river and the suffering and resistance of the people on its banks, celebrates the long history and great spirit of the Chinese nation, and issues the call to arms "Defend our homeland! Defend the Yellow River! Defend North China! Defend all of China!" It spread quickly across the country and became an enduring work that lifted the people's fighting spirit during the War of Resistance. In 1940 Xian Xinghai went to the Soviet Union to compose music for a documentary, but was stranded there when the Soviet-German war broke out. He died of illness in Moscow in October 1945 at only 40. Mao Zedong wrote an inscription of mourning: "In mourning for Comrade Xian Xinghai, the people's musician."

events.title: Anti-Japanese Base Areas Behind Enemy Lines
events.short: The Eighth Route Army and New Fourth Army carried out guerrilla warfare behind enemy lines and set up many base areas such as Shanxi-Chahar-Hebei; by 1940 the rear became the main arena of resistance.
events.detail: After the full-scale War of Resistance began, the anti-Japanese forces led by the Chinese Communist Party, including the Eighth Route Army and the New Fourth Army, pushed into the enemy's rear and waged guerrilla war. In November 1937 part of the Eighth Route Army's 115th Division, led by Nie Rongzhen, established the Shanxi-Chahar-Hebei base area centered on Mount Wutai, the first anti-Japanese base area the Party created behind enemy lines. The Eighth Route Army then created the Shanxi-Suiyuan, Shanxi-Hebei-Shandong-Henan and Shandong base areas, while the New Fourth Army built the southern Jiangsu, central Anhui and northern Jiangsu base areas in central China. By 1940 more than ten base areas had been set up in North, Central and South China, and the Eighth Route Army and New Fourth Army had grown to nearly 500,000 men. The base areas practiced the "three-thirds system" of government, in which Communists, left-wing progressives and moderates each held one third of the seats, uniting people of all strata against Japan. Soldiers and civilians developed tunnel warfare, mine warfare and other guerrilla tactics to strike at Japanese and puppet forces. In 1941–1942 the Japanese army launched fierce "mopping-up" campaigns against the base areas, applying the "three alls policy" of burning all, killing all and looting all, and the bases faced severe hardship. To overcome it, the base areas launched a production campaign, and the Eighth Route Army's 359th Brigade under Wang Zhen moved into Nanniwan and turned the desolate land into "a southern Jiangnan of northern Shaanxi." The battlefield behind enemy lines tied down and fought most of the Japanese forces in China and nearly all the puppet troops, and gradually became the main battlefield of the war. By the time of victory, the liberated areas covered nearly one million square kilometers and had a population of nearly 100 million.

images.caption: Map of the anti-Japanese base areas behind enemy lines (1937–1940)
Tunnel Warfare (painting)

events.title: Wang Jingwei's Puppet National Government
events.short: Kuomintang deputy leader Wang Jingwei defected to Japan in late 1938, and in March 1940 set up a Japanese-sponsored puppet National Government in Nanjing that served Japan's invasion.
events.detail: After the fall of Guangzhou and Wuhan, Japan, with its front overextended, short of troops and strained at home, changed its strategy toward China, tempting the National Government with political overtures and fostering collaborator regimes. In November 1938 Japanese Prime Minister Konoe Fumimaro issued a statement proposing the "construction of a new order in East Asia" to lure the National Government into abandoning resistance. Within the Kuomintang, a pro-Japanese faction formed around deputy leader Wang Jingwei. In December 1938 Wang secretly left Chongqing, fled through Kunming to Hanoi in Vietnam, and soon issued the "Yan telegram," openly endorsing the Konoe statement and advocating "peace talks" with Japan, a public act of defection and betrayal. The Kuomintang promptly expelled Wang from the party and stripped him of all posts. In 1939 Wang reached Shanghai and secretly signed with Japan the Outline for Adjusting New Japan-China Relations, which sold off national sovereignty. On 30 March 1940, under Japanese sponsorship, Wang set up a puppet "National Government" in Nanjing, with himself as "acting chairman" and "president of the Executive Yuan." It later signed the Japan-China Basic Treaty with Japan, recognizing the puppet state of Manchukuo and agreeing to Japanese troops being stationed in China. The Wang regime obeyed Japan completely, cooperated with the Japanese army in "rural pacification" campaigns against the base areas, suppressed anti-Japanese forces and helped Japan plunder China's resources. Wang Jingwei died of illness in Nagoya, Japan, in November 1944. After Japan surrendered in 1945 the regime collapsed; leading collaborators such as Chen Gongbo, Chu Minyi and Liang Hongzhi were sentenced to death, and Zhou Fohai's death sentence was commuted to life imprisonment.

events.title: Hundred Regiments Offensive
events.short: From August 1940 to January 1941 Peng Dehuai led 105 Eighth Route Army regiments against Japanese lines of communication in North China, inflicting over 40,000 casualties.
events.detail: After the War of Resistance entered its stalemate phase, the Japanese army sought to destroy the base areas by adopting a "cage policy" in North China, using railways as pillars, roads as chains and blockhouses as locks to blockade and gradually encroach on them. To break the cage policy and raise the nation's confidence in resistance, from August 1940 to January 1941 Peng Dehuai, deputy commander of the Eighth Route Army, directed a large-scale offensive in North China, centered on sabotaging the Zhengtai Railway and attacking Japanese-held communications lines and strongpoints across the region. Because 105 regiments and over 200,000 men took part, it became known as the "Hundred Regiments Offensive." During the campaign the Eighth Route Army fought more than 1,800 engagements, killed, wounded or captured over 40,000 Japanese and puppet troops, destroyed more than 400 kilometers of railway and over 1,500 kilometers of highway, took nearly 3,000 strongpoints, and captured large quantities of weapons and supplies. In battles such as those at Niangziguan and Guanjianao, Eighth Route Army soldiers fought heroically and suffered heavy losses. During the fighting, soldiers rescued two Japanese girls from the battlefield, and Nie Rongzhen sent them back to a Japanese post, an act long remembered. The offensive was the largest and longest campaign the Eighth Route Army fought in North China during the war. It dealt a heavy blow to the cage policy, lifted the nation's confidence, raised the standing of the Communist Party and the Eighth Route Army, effectively supported operations on the main front, and exposed as a lie the Kuomintang hardliners' slander that the Eighth Route Army "roamed but did not fight."

images.caption: Peng Dehuai at the front
images.author: 徐肖冰

events.title: National Resistance: Zhang Zizhong and Zuo Quan Fall
events.short: In the War of Resistance, all ethnic groups, parties and classes fought together, and commanders such as Zhang Zizhong of the 33rd Army Group and Zuo Quan of the Eighth Route Army died heroically.
events.detail: Under the banner of the anti-Japanese national united front, people of all ethnic groups, parties, political factions and strata, along with overseas Chinese, set aside differences, united against the aggressor and fought together. In May 1940, in the Battle of Zaoyang-Yichang, Zhang Zizhong, commander of the 33rd Army Group, personally led his troops across the Xiang River (Han River), but was surrounded by Japanese forces at Nanguadian in Yicheng, Hubei. Hit by several bullets, he kept commanding until he died a martyr's death at 49. Zhang was one of the highest-ranking Allied generals killed in World War II, and Mao Zedong wrote the elegiac inscription "Loyal to the end, serving the country." In May 1942 the Japanese army launched a major "mopping-up" of the Taihang Mountains, where the Eighth Route Army headquarters was based. Zuo Quan, deputy chief of staff of the Eighth Route Army, was struck by a shell at Shiziling in Liaoxian, Shanxi, while commanding troops covering the headquarters' breakout, and was killed at only 37; he was the highest-ranking Eighth Route Army officer to die in the war. In his memory Liao County was renamed Zuoquan County. Elsewhere, Yang Jingyu of the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army kept Japanese forces at bay in the ice and snow until he died fighting when out of ammunition and food; when the Japanese cut open his stomach they found only dried grass, bark and cotton wadding. Zhao Yiman endured brutal torture after her capture and never yielded. The Five Heroes of Langya Mountain of the Eighth Route Army led the enemy onto a dead end to cover the retreat of civilians and the main force, then leapt off a cliff. Ethnic minorities also took an active part in the war; the Hui Detachment led by Ma Benzhai was hailed as the "ever-victorious Hui Detachment." The unity of the whole nation in resistance was the fundamental reason for victory.

images.caption: Portrait of Zhang Zizhong
The Hui Detachment, an anti-Japanese force active on the Central Hebei Plain

events.title: Southern Anhui Incident
events.short: In January 1941 Kuomintang hardliners ambushed and destroyed the New Fourth Army headquarters and its southern Anhui units at Maolin; Ye Ting was detained and Xiang Ying killed.
events.detail: After the War of Resistance entered its stalemate phase, the Kuomintang's policy focus shifted from resisting Japan abroad to opposing the Communists at home, and its hardliners repeatedly stirred up anti-Communist "frictions." In October 1940, He Yingqin, chief of the General Staff of the National Government's Military Affairs Commission, and Bai Chongxi, its deputy chief, issued the "Hao telegram," ordering the Eighth Route Army and New Fourth Army south of the Yellow River to withdraw northward. For the sake of the overall anti-Japanese cause, the Communist Party agreed to move the New Fourth Army in southern Anhui north of the Yangtze River. On 4 January 1941 the New Fourth Army headquarters and its southern Anhui units, over 9,000 men, set out northward as ordered. On 6 January, as they reached Maolin in Jing County, Anhui, they were ambushed by 80,000 Kuomintang troops in seven divisions. The New Fourth Army fought for seven days and nights, but, hopelessly outnumbered and out of ammunition and food, all but about 2,000 who broke out were killed or captured. Commander Ye Ting was detained while negotiating with the Kuomintang, and deputy commander Xiang Ying was killed during the breakout. On 17 January Chiang Kai-shek falsely branded the New Fourth Army a "mutinous army" and announced the abolition of its designation. This was the Southern Anhui Incident, which shocked China and the world during the second anti-Communist upsurge. Zhou Enlai wrote in the Xinhua Daily: "The most unjust wrong of all time, a single leaf in Jiangnan; kin turning weapons on kin, why such haste to destroy each other?" On 20 January the Central Military Commission of the Chinese Communist Party ordered the reconstruction of the New Fourth Army headquarters, appointing Chen Yi acting commander and Liu Shaoqi political commissar. Holding to the principles of being justified, advantageous and restrained, the Party both beat back the anti-Communist upsurge and preserved the anti-Japanese national united front. In 1946, soon after his release, Ye Ting died in a plane crash on the way to Yan'an.

images.caption: Zhou Enlai's inscription
images.author: Central Military Commission of the Communist Party of China

events.title: Third Battle of Changsha
events.short: In late 1941 and early 1942 Xue Yue used the "Heaven Furnace" tactic to repel the Japanese at Changsha, the first major Allied victory after the outbreak of the Pacific War.
events.detail: After the War of Resistance reached its strategic stalemate, the Japanese army launched two battles of Changsha, in September 1939 and September 1941, trying to take the city, and failed both times. In December 1941 Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, the Pacific War broke out, and China formally declared war on Japan. To support its attack on Hong Kong and to pin down Chinese forces that might go south to aid the British, the Japanese 11th Army massed over 100,000 troops for a third attack on Changsha. Xue Yue, commander of the 9th War Area, directed the Chinese forces in the "Heaven Furnace" tactic: set up deep defensive positions in the expected battle zone, resist step by step to lure the enemy in, and once the Japanese reached the city, counterattack from all sides so as to melt them like a furnace. Chinese troops blocked the advance layer by layer along the Xinqiang and Miluo Rivers. In early January 1942 the Japanese reached the outskirts of Changsha, where Li Yutang, commander of the 10th Army, directed the garrison in a stubborn defense from fortifications and fierce fighting with the Japanese. Chinese forces outside then closed in from all sides, the Japanese were caught front and rear and forced to retreat, and the Chinese pursued with heavy Japanese casualties. It was the first great Allied victory since the outbreak of the Pacific War; at the time British and American forces were suffering repeated defeats in the Pacific, and Hong Kong, Manila and Singapore had fallen one after another. The victory at Changsha lifted Allied morale and drew high praise from international opinion; The Times of London commented: "Amid the dark clouds over the Far East, only the sky above Changsha shines with brilliance." In 1944 the Japanese attacked Changsha a fourth time in the Battle of Henan-Hunan-Guangxi, and the city fell.

images.caption: Changsha soldiers and civilians celebrate victory in the Third Battle of Changsha

events.title: Chinese Expeditionary Force in Burma
events.short: In 1942 the Chinese Expeditionary Force entered Burma and rescued British troops at Yenangyaung; it later fought in northern Burma and western Yunnan, reopening the road to India in 1945.
events.detail: After the outbreak of the Pacific War, the Japanese army attacked British Burma, intending to cut the Burma Road, China's most important international supply line. To defend it and support the British, China formed the Chinese Expeditionary Force in early 1942, and 100,000 men under Du Yuming and others entered Burma, the first time Chinese troops fought abroad. Dai Anlan, commander of the 200th Division, fought the Japanese for twelve days at Toungoo against forces several times his own and inflicted heavy losses. In April the British 1st Division was surrounded by the Japanese at Yenangyaung, and the 113th Regiment of the Expeditionary Force's 38th Division, under division commander Sun Liren, went to its rescue, drove off the Japanese, and saved more than 7,000 British soldiers along with hundreds of foreign missionaries and journalists. However, the British were reluctant to fight, the Chinese and British lacked coordination, and the Japanese outflanked them, so the Expeditionary Force suffered a setback and was forced to retreat. Dai Anlan was gravely wounded while leading a breakout and died soon after. Part of the force withdrew to India, and part crossed the Hukawng wilderness (Yeren Mountains) back into China. The troops in India were trained with American help and formed the Chinese Army in India. In October 1943 the Chinese Army in India launched an offensive in northern Burma, and in May 1944 the Expeditionary Force began a counteroffensive in western Yunnan, retaking Tengchong, Longling and other places. In January 1945 the two forces met at Mangyou, reopening the Sino-Indian road (Stilwell Road). The campaign was a model of military cooperation between China and its allies, committing over 400,000 troops and suffering nearly 200,000 casualties, and made a major contribution to victory in the world anti-fascist war. The National Martyrs' Cemetery in Tengchong, Yunnan, holds the remains of fallen Expeditionary Force soldiers.

events.title: Yan'an Forum on Literature and Art
events.short: At the Yan'an Forum on Literature and Art in May 1942, Mao Zedong declared that art should serve the people, above all workers, peasants and soldiers, and art in the liberated areas flourished.
events.detail: During the War of Resistance, large numbers of progressive writers and artists came to Yan'an and other base areas from Kuomintang-ruled and occupied regions, boosting literature and art in the liberated areas. But the field also had problems, and some writers and artists were distant from the workers, peasants and soldiers. In 1942, in connection with the Yan'an Rectification Movement, the Party Central Committee held the Yan'an Forum on Literature and Art. From 2 to 23 May Mao Zedong gave an introduction and a conclusion at the forum, published as Talks at the Yan'an Forum on Literature and Art. The talks held that literature and art must serve the people, first of all workers, peasants and soldiers, a fundamental question of principle, and that writers and artists must go deep among them. After the talks, artists in the liberated areas went to villages, factories and army units and produced many fine works about the people's life and struggles. The new opera The White-Haired Girl, written by He Jingzhi and Ding Yi, expressed through Xi'er's tragic fate the theme that "the old society turned men into ghosts, the new society turns ghosts into men." Zhao Shuli's novels Little Erhei's Marriage and Rhymes of Li Youcai, Ding Ling's The Sun Shines over the Sanggan River, and Li Ji's long poem Wang Gui and Li Xiangxiang are representative works of the period. A new yangge movement also flourished, and yangge operas such as Brother and Sister Reclaim the Wasteland were loved by the public. The talks set the Communist Party's policy on literature and art, spurred the flourishing of art in the liberated areas, and had a profound influence on modern Chinese literature and art.
